May the writer and the reader be strong and steadfast in the very ark which is the house which the author prepared for himself. I now begin to explain the Torah portion, Shemot; which opens the second Book of the Torah.

Now these are. Our book opens with a vav because the end of Genesis relates that Yosef saw the children of the third generation (Bereshit 50:23). Scripture notes that Yosef’s brothers were few in number when they descended to Mitzrayim but that they were fruitful and multiplied there (Shemot 1:7).The word elleh (these) and el (these) are employed equally with the masculine and the feminine. We thus find, For all these abominations (ha-to’evot ha-el) (Vayikra 18:27) and then afterward, any of these abominations (ha-to’evot ha-elleh) (Vayikra 18:29). We similarly read, unto these men (la-anashim ha-el) (Bereshit 19:8); These four (arba’at elleh) were born to the giant (Shmuel II 21:22); and what can I do this day for these (la-elleh) my daughters (Bereshit 31:43). The same is the case with the word laz (that one). We thus find, that Shunamite (ha-shunammit ha-laz) (Melachim II 4:25) and this young man (ha-na’ar ha-laz) (Zecharyah 2:8). The fact that the word elleh is penultimately accented indicates that its heh is superfluous. It is like the heh of laylah (night) and the heh of nachlah (brook) in the Brook of (nachlah) Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 34:5).

[The names of.] Shem (name) is masculine. Its plural form is shemot (names), for the tav is used for both the masculine and the feminine. Compare, mekomot (places) and avot (fathers). The mem is similarly used as a masculine and feminine plural. Compare, nashim (women) and pilagshim (concubines). We also find some nouns employing both the tav and the mem in the plural forms. Compare, nefashim (souls) (Yechezkel 13:20) and nefashot (souls) (Yechezkel 13:18). We similarly find, levavot (hearts) (Divrei Hayamim II 28:9) and levavim (hearts). Compare, al livvehen (upon their hearts) (Nachum 2:8).[Into Mitzrayim.] The heh of mitzrayemah (into Mitzrayim) is in place of the word el (to). Compare, dotayenah (to Dotan) in nelekh dotayenah (let us go down to Dotan) (Bereshit 37:16); and yerushalayemah (to Yerushalayim) in and brought me in the vision of God to Yerushalayim (Yechezkel 8:3).
With Yaakov. Et ya’akov means with Yaakov. Compare, In that day Hashem made a covenant with (et) Avram (Bereshit 15:18).

Every man came with his household. Beto (his household) refers to those who came out of his loins. The term bayit (house, household) in Scripture never refers to a wife. Every man came with his household (beto) is proof of this, for the wives of the tribes are not included in the seventy who descended into Mitzrayim. Do not permit the verse and (the high priest shall) have made atonement for himself, and for his household (beto) (Vayikra 16:18) to cause you any difficulty. For according to the plain meaning of the text, beto (his household) refers to his father’s house. Beto (his household) must be so interpreted because the high priest made three confessions on the Day of Atonement. The priest’s helpmate, who is his wife, is included in the term for himself. She is included with him because a husband and a wife make a “man.”

Reuven. When a word beginning with a letter that is vocalized with a mobile sheva (sheva na), e.g., the zayin of Zevulun, has a bet, vav, kaf, or lamed prefixed to it, the prefix ideally should also be vocalized with a mobile sheva. However, due to the impossibility of sounding two mobile sheva’im in succession these prefixes are vocalized with a chirik rather than with a sheva. Hence if the word zevulun has a bet prefixed to it we say bi-zevulun (in Zevulun), If zevulun has a kaf or lamed prefixed to it we say ki-zevulun (like Zevulun) or li-zevulun (to Zevulun). However, if the word has a vav prefixed to it then it is vocalized with a shuruk rather than a chirik. We sound the vav as if it had an alef preceding it and pronounce the word u-zevulun (and Zevulun) for the word is sounded as if it were written alef vav plus zevulun. However, if we deal with a word whose first letter is a yod, an example being the name yehudah, then the yod is silent, for the yod is one of the quiescent letters. Compare, biyhudah (against Yehudah) in Let us go up against Yehudah (Yeshayahu 7:6) and kiyhudah (like Yehudah) and liyhudah (of Yehudah) in Of Yehudah, Nachshon (Bamidbar 1:7). In the latter case the yod is silent and is not perceived or felt when the word is enunciated. The same is also the case when a vav is prefixed to the word yehudah. The word is pronounced viyhudah.The tribes are here listed in order of their births.

Yissachar. Because the two sins in yissachar (Yissachar) are written in succession only one is sounded. Compare, the word machtzetzrim (did blow) (Divrei Hayamim I 15:24), which is pronounced machtzerim. We do not find a similar case with regard to the sin in Scripture. It is customary for the Hebrews to pronounce a vav prefixed to the labials which are related to the vav, namely, the bet, mem, peh with an alef added to it, and to vocalize the vav with a shuruk. Compare, u-faru (and they shall be fruitful) in and they shall be fruitful and multiply (Yirmiyahu 23:3); and u-male’u (shall be full) in and the houses of the Mitzrim shall he full of swarms of flies (Shemot 8:17). The word u-vinyamin (and Binyamin) is similar. Binyamin is listed before the children of the handmaidens because he was a son of one of Yaakov’s wives.

Dan. Names are connected to each other in Scripture in six different ways. All of these styles are correct. One way of listing names is, Eilam, and Ashur, and Arpachshad (Bereshit 10:22). A second manner is, with carbuncles, purple, and richly woven work, and fine linen (Yechezkel 27:16). A third way is, carnelian, topaz, and smaragd (Shemot 28:17). A fourth way is, Dan and Naftali, Gad and Asher. The fifth is, Myrrh, and aloes, and cassia (Tehillim 45:9). The sixth way is, Adam, Shet, Enosh (Divrei Hayamim I 1:1).

Were. The word yehi (let it be) should have been vocalized like the word yirev (the multitude) in and the multitude of the burdens against him (Divrei Hayamim II 24:27). However, since the heh is a guttural, the word yehi is vocalized with a segol beneath the first yod and the word is read yehi. Furthermore, the final yod of yehi should have been pronounced with a sounded sheva nach (a quiescent sheva) as is the case with the word yirev. The word should thus have been pronounced yihey. However, because of the difficulty involved in the enunciation of the word in the aforementioned manner, the yod was silenced and we vocalized the heh with a chirik. Hence the word is pronounced yehi (sheva beneath the yod) as in, Behold, would it might be (yehi) according to thy word (Bereshit 30:34), or yehi (segol beneath the yod), as in For He spoke, and it was (va-yehi) (Tehillim 33:9). The accent is placed on the last syllable of yehi and a sheva is placed beneath its yod because the word is used often in conversation, as in So be (yehi khen) Hashem (Shemot 10:10). Therefore only this root and the root of va-yechi in And Yaakov lived (Bereshit 47: 28) are found to have an imperfect yod prefix vocalized with a sheva when conjugated in the kal. The reason for this is that two letters of the two roots va-yechi and va-yehi consist of the quiescent letters yod, heh, the root of one being heh, yod, heh and that of the other chet, yod, heh. Now since the yod and the heh are quiescent letters and are at times not pronounced at the end of a word, the yod prefix is vocalized with a sheva. We do not find any such other case in the kal.

That came out of the loins of Yaakov. Loins allude to the male organ which is located near the loins. It is similar to and Shaul went to cover his feet (Shmuel I 24:4).The offspring of Yaakov who descended to Mitzrayim really numbered sixty-nine, not including Yaakov who should be counted first. The Pentateuch therefore first states et ya’akov (with Yaakov), the meaning of which is as we have noted earlier. In the first listing of Yaakov’s descendants in the Torah portion va-yiggash (then Yehudah came near unto him) (Bereshit 44:18), Scripture states, And these are the names of the children of Yisrael who came unto Mitzrayim, Yaakov and his sons (Bereshit 46:8). Thus with Yaakov, all the souls of his sons and his daughters (descended from Yaakov and Leah) were thirty and three (Bereshit 46:15). The verse Thy fathers went down into Mitzrayim with threescore and ten souls (Devarim 10:22) is proof that Yaakov is counted among the seventy, for Yaakov had a soul. Similarly, Yosef and his two sons who were in Mitzrayim are also included in the seventy.

And Yosef died and all that generation. A father and his son comprise two generations. Proof of this is the fact that after Iyov’s fortune was changed for the better, he lived a hundred and forty years and saw four generations (Iyov 42:16). Furthermore, our sages tell us that there were ten generations from Adam to Noach and ten generations from Noach to Avraham (Abot 5:2, 3). Now the years of each of the aforementioned generations were different one from the other.
The meaning of And Yosef died is that he died in his greatness. Similarly, his brothers also did not see the evil days which followed.
[And all that generation.] This refers to the Mitzrim. For Scripture goes on to note, Now there arose a new king over Mitzrayim, who knew not Yosef (v. 8).
And the children of Yisrael were fruitful. They produced children as a tree produces fruit.

And increased abundantly. Va-yishretzu (and increased abundantly) is similar to the word yishretzu (swarm) in Let the waters swarm (yishretzu) (Bereshit 1:20). However, in the first instance the verb is independent. It is like the verbs went, sat, stood, and lay. In the second instance the verb is dependent upon something else. It is like the verbs ate, kept, and hired. We thus say, he ate the bread, he kept the thing, and he hired the donkey. The latter are called transitive verbs. Now yishretzu (swarm) in yishretzu ha-mayim (Let the waters swarm) is a transitive verb, while va-yishretzu (and increased abundantly) is an intransitive verb. Thus the root shin, resh, zadi is sometimes transitive and sometimes intransitive. It is like the root of the word shav which is at times intransitive as in and (Elokim) will return (ve-shav) and gather (Devarim 30:3) and at times transitive, as in that then Hashem thy Elokim will turn (ve-shav) thy captivity (Ibid.). It is possible that the word va-yishretzu alludes to the fact that the Yisraeli wives gave birth to twins and even more. I myself have seen the quadruplets that a women gave birth to. Physicians tell us that a woman can have as many as seven fetuses in her womb at one time.
And multiplied. They did not die in proportion to that of a large nation.
And waxed exceedingly mighty. They had strong bones.

[Exceedingly.] The phrase bi-me’od me’od (exceedingly) indicates that there could not possibly have been any more of them. The bet of bi-me’od me’od is like the bet of ba-rishonah (first) in and they took their first journey (Bamidbar 10:13), for we also encounter the term with out the bet in they shall set forth first (rishonah) (Bamidbar 2:9).

And the land was filled with them. The land of Goshen, also known as the land of Raamses. Raamses is sounded with a quiescent sheva beneath the ayin, for the first sheva in Raamses, the sheva beneath the ayin which is connected to the resh, is called a sheva nach. The second sheva, the one beneath the mem, is called a sheva na (mobile sheva) because the lips seem to begin to first move when it is uttered.

Now there arose a new king. This is to be taken literally without any embellishments. Scripture reads, and there arose (va-yakam) because the new king was not of the royal seed. It is like that my son hath stirred up (hekim) my servant to lie in wait against me (Shmuel I 22:8).
And he said unto his people. The Mitzrim.

Behold the people. The word am (people) is not in the construct with bene yisrael (the children of Yisrael). The term bene yisrael explains am and provides additional information concerning its meaning. It is like the words That I Am in the phrase I Am That I Am (Shemot 3:14) and the words Avraham and Yitzchak in the verse The God before whom my fathers Avraham and Yitzchak did walk (Bereshit 48:15).

For us. When the word mi-mennu (for us) is in the plural the books of the Babylonians adhere to the grammatical rule and always omit the dagesh in the nun in order to differentiate between mi-mennu in the plural and mi-mennu in Out of him (mi-mennu) shall come forth the cornerstone (Zecharyah 10:4). In the latter, nu is a third person singular suffix and has a dagesh placed in the nun in accordance with the grammatical rule. However, all the books coming out of the Land of Yisrael have a dagesh in the nun of mi-mennu both in the singular and in the plural because the nun of mi-menni (from me) in the singular has a dagesh despite the rule. For the nuns of ani (I) and necheni (hath led me) in Hashem hath led me (Bereshit 24:27) do not receive a dagesh.Now the word min (from) is doubled, the nun of mi-menni receives a dagesh to make up for the missing nun of the second min, and the word is read as if written mi-menni. The nun of the first min is represented by the dagesh in the second mem of mi-menni and the nun of the suffix ni serves as if it were in the place of the one speaking. Similarly, the nun of mi-munnu in the plural, spelled mem mem nun nun vav (Bereshit 23:6), receives a dagesh and is read as if written mi-mennu. The reason that the nun of mi-mennu (of him) in the singular receives a dagesh is to compensate for the swallowed heh, for it is only in a few instances when the verb yishmor (he will keep) is combined with a third person suffix that we say yishmero (he will keep him). The same is true of the word yikre’o (he shall be called) in whereby he shall be called (Yirmiyahu 23:6) and the word yirdefo (shall pursue him) in The enemy shall purse him (Hoshea 8:3). The usual form of the third person suffix is yishmerehu (preserve him) (Tehillim 41:8). Thus yishmero (he will keep him) is a shortened form. It is similar to hinnehu in and, behold, he (ve-hinnehu) was at his work (Yirmiyahu 18:3), in which hinnehu is a compound of hinneh (behold) and hu (he); and to ve-hinneh nitzav (and, lo he stood) (Bamidbar 23:6). At other times an additional nun is added, as in yeshacharuneni (they will seek me earnestly) and yimtza’uneni (they will find me) in They will seek me earnestly, but they shall not find me (Mishlei 1:28). Similarly, the word tevarakhani (may bless me) in that thy soul may bless me (Bereshit 27:19) is pronounced tevarekhanni because of the dagesh in the nun. We also find an extra nun in the word yekhabbdaneni (honoreth Me) in whoso offereth the sacrifice of thanksgiving honoreth Me (Tehillim 50:23) and in the words yesovavenhu (He compassed him about), yevonanehu (He cared for him), and yitzrenhu (He kept him) (Devarim 32:10). At other times the third person heh suffix is swallowed by the nun, as in yishmerennu (kept it in) in and its owner hath not kept it in (Shemot 21:29).

Come (havah). The word havah (give) in Give me my wife (Bereshit 29:21) is in the masculine and as such is properly used there. It is similar to the word lekhah (come) in come, I pray thee with us. In the feminine we say havi, as in Bring (havi) the mantle that is upon thee (Rut 3:15), and lekhi (go), as in Go and get thee in (Melachim I 1:23). Now because these words are used often the masculine form is employed both as a plural and as a feminine singular. Scripture thus reads, Come (havah), let us go down (Bereshit 11:7); Come (havah) I Pray thee, let me come in unto thee (Bereshit 38:16). It is like Come (lekhah), let us make our father drink wine (Bereshit 19:32).
Let us deal wisely. Let us search for a wise way to prevent them from multiplying.

With them. The word lo (with them) is to be rendered, because of them. It is similar to the word li (of me) in say of me (Bereshit 20:13).Note that all perfect and imperfect verbs imply a verbal noun. In other words, even though a noun derived from a verb is missing in the text it is implied in the verb. For example, ve-hinneh berakhta varekh (and, behold, thou hast blessed them altogether) (Bamidbar 23:11) and And when He hath blessed, I cannot call it back (Bamidbar 23:20), the meaning of which is: And when he hath blessed a blessing, I cannot call it back. The same is true of But in the multitude of counsellors they are established (Mishlei 15:22). The complete version of the latter is: But in the multitude of counsellors, counsel is established. Similarly, when there befalleth us any war (v. 10) is to be interpreted as, when there befalleth us any accidents of war. Rabbi Merinus says that and get them out of the land means, and we will get us out of the land. He believes that Paroh said and get them out of the land so that Satan would not ensnare him in the utterances of his mouth. However, I see no need for this interpretation.

Taskmasters. Missim (taskmasters) is a plural. Its singular form is mas. This word is similar in form to pittim (pieces of bread) (Vayikra 2:7) and pat (piece of bread) (Bereshit 18:5). The word comes from a stem whose second and third root letters are identical.
[To afflict them.] To cause the semen of the men to dry up.

Store-cities. Miskenot means store-cities. Ha-sokhen (this steward) in unto this steward (Is. 22:15) and sokhenet (companion) in and be a companion for the king (Melachim I 1:2) are similar. For the meaning of the latter verse is, let her be in charge of the king’s treasury so that no one will know that she lies in thy bosom.
Ra'amses. Has a pattach beneath the ayin and does not refer to the place where Yisrael dwelt.
But the more they afflicted them. Even though they were afflicted. THE MORE THEY MULTIPLIED. As they did in the days when they were not afflicted.

And the more they spread abroad. They were fruitful and increased above and beyond the norm. Yifrotz (they spread abroad) is like poretz (breaketh) in And whoso breaketh through a fence (Kohelet 10:8).

To serve. Paroh devised many evils with which to afflict Bnei Yisrael. First he ordered them to do his work. When he saw that this did not diminish their greatly increasing numbers he gave permission to the Mitzrim and their princes to work them harder than slaves are normally worked. The latter is, as Onkelos explains, the meaning of the term be-farekh (with rigor). It is totally wrong to employ the form perukhim (broken) in liturgical poetry. When Paroh saw that the above measures did not stop Bnei Yisrael from increasing, he called the midwives (v. 13), the ones who were in charge of all the other midwives, and commanded them to kill all the males that were born.

And they made their lives bitter. It is known that the tav, in a majority of instances, is the sign of the feminine plural and the mem of the masculine plural. Compare, mo’adot (seasons) (Divrei Hayamim II 8:13) and mo’adim (seasons) (Bereshit 1:14). According to the Spanish scholars verbal forms are kept and do not drop any of their root letters. However, this is not the case with nouns. Nouns are only employed as found in Scripture, for the singular of mo’adot (seasons) is mo’ed, not mo’adah as the person who thinks he is so brilliant believes. The latter would maintain that the plural of makom (place) is mekomim and the singular of mekomot (places) is mekomah. Perhaps he will open his eyes and see that the plural of bekhor (first-born) is bekhorim, as in To Him that smote Mitzrayim in their first-born (bekhorehem) (Tehillim 136:10). However, we also encounter the form bekhorot (firstlings) in and the firstlings of thy herd (Devarim 14:23). Now, shall the singular of bekhorot be bekhorah? The same is the case with levenim (bricks). Its singular is levenah, not leven.

[In mortar and in brick.] To build houses and fences. They also had to plow, harvest, prune, and pick olives. This is the meaning of and in all manner of service in the field. Scripture then alludes to all the other types of work which Yisrael did to fulfill the needs of the Mitzrim by the general term in all their service.

Wherein they made them serve. The word avedu (they made them serve) is to be read as if written twice. Our verse is to be read as if it were written: wherein they made them serve, they made them serve with rigor. When a verb from the root ayin, bet, dalet is not followed by a bet it refers to work performed by a slave. This is the meaning of avadatikha (I have served thee) (Bereshit 30:26). However, when the verb is followed by a bet it has one of the following two meanings. It means for the sake of, as in va-ya’avod yisrael be-ishah (and Yisrael served for a wife) (Hoshea 12:13). Its other meaning is illustrated by thou shalt not make him to serve (lo ta’avod bo) with rigor, which is like which hath not been wrought with (lo ubbad bah) (Devarim 21:3). Which may neither be plowed (lo ye’aved bo) (Devarim 21:4) is similar, for we find, And the land that was desolate shall be tilled (Yechezkel 36:34). In a like manner Scripture reads, As with the lender, so with the borrower (nosheh vo) (Is. 24:2).

And the king of Mitzrayim spoke to the Hebrew midwives. These midwives were in charge of all the other midwives. For there can be no doubt that there were more than five hundred midwives. These two midwives were in charge of all the other midwives and saw to it that they gave a tax to the king from the money they collected for their services. I have seen such a practice in many places. The opinion that the two midwives were mother and daughter was handed down by tradition, for it is correct.

When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women. Whoever comes from the family of ever (Ever) is called a Hebrew. One is called a Hebrew because of his faith. Hence the children of Ever (Ever) in the father of all the children of Ever (Bereshit 10:21) refers to those who came from the side (ever) of the river. The side of the river refers to one of the banks of the river.

[The birthstool.] Ben Kuraish says that the alef of ovnayim (birthstool) is superfluous because ovnayim comes from the same root as banim (sons). The meaning of ovnayim is birthstool. Ovnayim is similar to afsayim (ankles) in waters that were to the ankles (Yechezkel 47:3). In reality, however, ovnayim is similar to ba-ovnayim (at the wheel) and the alef is a root letter.
Then ye shall kill him. In secret so that it will not become known, because he was committing an act of violence.

[Then she shall live.] The word va-chayah (then she shall live) is irregular and presents a very difficult grammatical problem. The rules of grammar require va-chayetah because the heh of the root changes to a tav, as it does in the construct in the case of the word chayat (beast of) in and to every beast of the earth (Bereshit 1:30). The reason for the change is that the heh and the tav are similar in appearance when written. The only difference between them is the extension of the dot that is within the heh. For the letter tav is first a heh. It is only when the dot is extended that it becomes a tav. However, the tav and the heh are pronounced completely differently. They also have different names. This proves that our form of the letters is the original Hebrew script. Generally speaking, the root of the word chai (lived) and the root of the word chayyim (life) are in doubt, for the grammarians have concluded that the root of the word chai (lived) in And Arpachshad lived (Bereshit 11:12) is chet, yod, yod. The word tam (spent) in how that our money is all spent (Bereshit 47:18) is similar, for it comes from the root tav, mem, mem. The grammarians also agree that the plural of the root chet, yod, yod is chayyim (life). However, in my opinion we are dealing with an irregular root. If this is not so let someone show me a case where this root is conjugated in the imperfect according to the paradigm of chet, gimel, gimel, namely, achog (I will celebrate), tachog (you will celebrate), yachog (he will celebrate), la-chog (to celebrate). If the root of chai were chet, yod, yod, it should be conjugated achoy, yachoy, la-choy in the imperfect or like sov (go about) or sobu (walk about) in Walk about Tziyon (Tehillim 48:13) and sobbi (go about) in Go about the city (Is. 23:16). This is proof that the word chai comes from a root ending in a heh. The fact that we do not find the root of chai conjugated in any of the above-mentioned forms is proof that it belongs to those verbs whose stems end in a heh, for we say echeyeh (I will live), nichyeh (we will live), eheyeh (I will be), tiheyeh (you will be), yiheyeh (he will be), all of which come from the root heh, yod, heh. Now if this is the case it comes from the root chet, yod, heh and is like the word haya (was). The fact that we find the word chai (lived) employed as a third person perfect in arpachshad chai (Arpachshad lived) (Bereshit 11:12) does not disturb us. We are not bothered by the aforementioned even though it appears that chai comes from a double root. What forced me to come to this conclusion is the fact that I saw that there is no root in Hebrew that ends in a vav. The word shalev (at ease) (Iyov 16:12) does not disprove my contention. Its vav is in place of a heh, since the letters alef, heh, vav, yod interchange. Proof that what I say is correct is the word shalu (secure) in Wherefore are all they secure that deal treacherously (Iyov 12:1). For the root of shalu is shin, lamed, heh.I will now explain to you why a vav is never employed as a third letter of a root. The latter is so because the vav serves as a third person singular suffix, as in the words avdo va-amato (his man-servant nor his maid-servant) (Shemot 20:14). The vav also serves as the sign of the plural, as in peru u-revu (be fruitful and multiply) (Bereshit 1:22). There are also superfluous vavs, as in beno be’or (the son of Beor) (Bamidbar 24:3). Now if the vav was also used as the final letter of a root it would be confused with one of the three types of vavs that we have just mentioned, namely, the vav indicating a third person singular suffix, the vav indicating a plural, and the superfluous vav; we could not then ascertain the meaning of the word. The same is also true of the yod. The yod cannot serve as the final letter of a stem because it is used as a first person singular suffix, as in the word yadi (my hand) (Bereshit 42:37). It is also employed as a first person plural suffix, as in the word yadai (my hands) (Devarim 9:15). It is also the sign of the plural construct, as in yede (the hands of) in The hands of women full of compassion (Eichah 4:10). It is used as the sign of the feminine imperative, as in de’i and re’i (know and consider) (Shmuel I 25:17). It is used to indicate relationship, as in ha-ivri o ha-ivriyah (a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman) (Devarim 15:22). The yod is also used superfluously in verbs, as in ha-magbihi (that is enthroned) (Tehillim 113:5) and in le-hoshivi (that He may set him) (Tehillim 113:8). It is used superfluously with nouns, as in beni atono (his ass’s colt) (Bereshit 49:11) and also with particles, as in zulati (save) (Devarim 1:36) and minni ephrayim (out of Efraim) (Shoftim 5:14). For these reasons the yod is not employed as a final root letter lest it be confused with one of the above-noted yods. Therefore I maintain that the word va-chayah (then shall she live) is irregular and is a variant of va-chayetah. It belongs, as I have already explained, in the family of verbs ending in a heh.
But the midwives feared God. The alef in va-tirena (feared) is not sounded lest the verb be thought to come from the root resh, alef, heh.
But saved. Even more than at first, they now worked with all of their strength to save the children. Otherwise what need was there for Scripture to be so verbose?

And the king of Mitzrayim called for the midwives, and said unto them. You deserve to die because you have not obeyed my command. There is no difference in the form of the word va-tomarnah (said) in which the vav is vocalized with a pattach when it is in the third person perfect, like the word va-tokhalnah (did eat) in And the ill-favoured, and lean-fleshed kine did eat (Bereshit 41:4), and when it is used as a second person perfect. The meaning of our verse is: Why have ye done this thing and preserved the man-children alive?

And the midwives said unto Paroh. We have not violated your command because the Hebrew women are not like the Mitzri women; they have greater vitality. The yod of the word chayot (lively) in For they are lively does not have a dagesh. This is correct Hebrew usage. Compare, davot (ill), ravot (satiated), and alot (giving suck) in the flocks and herds giving suck are a care to me (Bereshit 33:13). However, the yod in the word chayyim does receive a dagesh because chayyim is an adjective. Compare, ve-nitpesem chayyim (we shall take them alive) (Melachim II 7:12) in which the yod in chayyim (alive) is like the yod of ha-ivriyyim (the Hebrews) in the Elokim of the Hebrews (Shemot 3:18). The word chayyim (life) also receives a dagesh when it is a noun, as in etz chayyim (a tree of life) (Mishlei 3:18). Similarly, the tzadi of tzitzim (flowers) in and open flowers (Melachim II 6:18) receives a dagesh.

And are delivered. Ve-yaladu (and are delivered) is a feminine perfect. The third person perfect has the same form in the masculine and the feminine. Compare, tavu (did spin) (Shemot 35:25) and tzave’u (did service) (Shemot 38:8).

And Hashem dealt well. When a root begins with a yod, the yod does not always drop out when the verb is conjugated, The word va-yetev (dealt well) is an example. At other times a vav is substituted for the yod, as in va-yoshev (He maketh to dwell) in And there He maketh the hungry to dwell (Tehillim 107:36). The root of va-yoshev is yod, shin, bet, as the root of va-yetev is yod, tet, bet.And Hashem dealt well is explained by what follows next, i.e., He (Hashem) made them houses. The meaning of He made them houses is similar to that Hashem make thee a house (Shmuel II 7:11).

And it came to pass, because the midwives feared Hashem. Because the midwives did not fear the king of Mitzrayim but feared Hashem, Hashem dealt well with them. Note that the verb yare’u (feared) is neither transitive nor intransitive, because its meaning is, to be afraid of someone. Hence the correct way of saying “feared Hashem” would be yare’u me’et Adonai. Ovadyah used a short form when he said, yare et Adonai (fear Hashem) (Melachim I 18:12). It is for this reason that the word nora (revered) does not come in the nifal form as the words nolad (was born) (Divrei Hayamim I 2:3), nishbar (broken) (Tehillim 51:19), and ve-nidkeh (and contrite) (Ibid.) do. The intelligent will understand why.

And Paroh charged. All who occupy the throne of Mitzrayim are called Paroh in the Mitzri language. Scripture does not relate the name of this Paroh as it does in the case of Pharaoh-neco (Yirmiyahu 46:2) who was so called in the tongue of his people. The same is the case with Paroh Chofra (Yirmiyahu 44:30).
That is born. Ha-yillod (that is born) is an adjective. It is like gibbor (warrior) and shikkor (drunk).
And there went. Because of their great number Bnei Yisrael lived in many cities. All of the latter were called the land of Raamses. Perhaps this woman was in another city.

A daughter of Levi. Son of Yisrael. She was the sister of his father. The person who says that wheat sown in another field will succeed, while wheat planted in the same field will not, does not speak the truth. The main reason that close relatives are forbidden to have sexual relations with each other is to sanctify Yisrael.

And the woman conceived. There is no doubt that Aharon was older than Moshe. Our sages similarly received a tradition that Puah and Miriam are one and the same person. It is also written, And his sister stood afar off (v. 4).Now we know that the four hundred-year period which ended in Yisrael’s redemption started with the day that Yitzchak was born, for Yitzchak alone is considered to be Avraham’s seed. Now Yitzchak was sixty years old when he begot Yaakov, and Yaakov was eighty-five years old when he begot Reuven, and one hundred and thirty years old when he descended into Mitzrayim. If we add the sixty years of Yitzchak to the one hundred and thirty of Yaakov we come up with a hundred and ninety years. We are thus left with two hundred and ten years. We then subtract the seventy years that Yosef lived afterwards and we are left with one hundred and forty years. Now Levi was forty-three years old when he came down to Mitzrayim and he outlived Yosef by twenty-two years. Thus one hundred and eighteen years are left. For the verse states, So Yosef died, being a hundred and ten years old (Bereshit 50:26). Now when did the new king reign? For how many years did Bnei Yisrael build the store-cities? Behold close to the birth of Moshe it was decreed that all male children be put to death. Ben Zuta says whoever relates a story will not out of respect mention the most honored first. Therefore when Scripture states, and she (Yocheved) bore unto Amram Aharon and Moshe, and Miriam their sister (Bamidbar 26:59), it indicates that Miriam was the youngest. Now the “blind one” (Ben Zuta) forgot Shem, Cham, and Yefet, concerning whom it is written, and Noach begot Shem, Cham and Yefet (Bereshit 5:32). Now Yefet was the eldest of the three. Furthermore, Scripture states, There they buried Avraham and Sarah his wife (Bereshit 49:31) even though Sarah was buried in the cave of Machpelah thirty-eight years before Avraham was interred there. Note that the nun is often dropped or is swallowed by a dagesh when it is the first root letter of a verb, as in the case of the nun of gesh in gesh holah (stand back) (Bereshit 19:9) and va-yiggash (came near) in Then Yehudah came near unto him (Bereshit 44:18). The nun is also dropped when it serves as the middle letter of a root, as in the case of af (anger) in And anger also went up against Yisrael (Tehillim 78:21). Observe, the middle nun is swallowed. Therefore the peh of appo (his wrath) in that his wrath was kindled (Bereshit 39:19) and the peh of appekah (thine anger) in Thine anger is turned away (Is. 12:1) receive a dagesh. The same is true of the nun of the root nun, tav, nun in the word titti (that I give) (Bereshit 29:19), for titti is like tinti because its final tav is not a root letter. It is rather like the tavs of shivti (my downsitting) (Tehillim 139:2), lekhti (when I went) (Melachim I 2:8), and lidti (I delivered) (Melachim I 3:18). It is also so at the end of the word, as in tet (to put) in to put the dread of thee (Devarim 2:25) and in titti (that I give) in that I give her to thee (Bereshit 29:19). The same is true of nouns. The word for daughter (bat) should have been banah since the feminine of ben (son) is banah. However, in this case it would have been confused with the verb banah (hath built), as in that hath built (banah) a new house (Devarim 20:5). A tav was therefore substituted for the heh. It is similar to givirah (lady) and geveret (lady) as well as to atarah (crown) and ateret (crown) in which we find both the construct and the absolute forms used in the absolute. Compare, ateret (crown of) in A crown of glory (Mishlei 4:7). It should be noted that the nun was also dropped for the sake of easing the pronunciation of the word. Hence the word is enunciated bat (daughter). The word bitto (his daughter) in Rachel his daughter (Bereshit 29:6) is similar to the word amitto (his truth) which is the word emet (truth) with the third person pronominal suffix. Compare, chasdo va-amitto (His mercy and His truth) (Bereshit 24:27). Thus the tav is the sign of the feminine and the nun is swallowed up. The plural of truth is emunot, and not amitot or amitiyot. Similarly, the plural of daughters is banot, not batot or battim.

And the woman conceived. Scripture does not mention the birth of Miriam and Aharon because there was nothing special about their birth. When the word tov (good) is used with reference to a mature man it probably refers to the soul, as in “good with Hashem and good with man.” Or it may refer to the eye, as in a bountiful (tov) eye (Mishlei 22:9). It may also refer to the body or its form, as in “of good form, and good to look upon.” However, because we find it used with regard to a child, viz., that he was a goodly (tov) child, we can only explain it as referring to the child’s form, that he was better than all who are born.

Three months. Some say that Moshe was born in the seventh month following his conception. However, this interpretation like so many others is Midrashic, for the Mitzrim had no way of determining when the woman conceived. In my opinion Scripture relates the months that she was able to hide the child since it is impossible for anyone to predict when a women will give birth. It is also far-fetched to say that Moshe was born in the seventh month following conception because those so born are undersized. Those born in the eleventh month are healthier and live longer, as most children are born close to the ninth month. One who knows the time of conception is able to ascertain the time of birth, and one who knows the time of birth can ascertain the time of conception. This was established by the ancients. I myself have tried it five times. For the degree and place of the moon and its constellation at the moment of conception is also the degree of the constellation that flowers at the moment of begetting The degree which flowers at the moment of impregnation will also be the degree at which the moon will be found at the time of birth. Now the time set aside for carrying a child is two hundred and fifty nine and a third days. The median time for pregnancy is two hundred and seventy-three days. The maximum time for being with child is two hundred and eighty-seven days. Those learned in astrology will admit this. The birth of the tribes does not refute this, because the order of their listing is no proof that they were born prematurely. We find many such instances in the Torah. It is therefore possible that Rachel gave her handmaid to Yaakov when Shimon was born, that Yissachar was born before Asher, and that Dinah was Zevulun’s twin. Hence the phrase and afterwards in and afterwards she bore a daughter (Bereshit 30:21) is similar to And after that came forth his brother (Bereshit 25:26). For and she conceived is not mentioned for each one. Also, And it came to pass, when the seasons were come about (Shmuel I 1:20) refers to three seasons.

[Hide him.] The tzadi of hatzefino (hide him), like the kof in the word yikkrekh (happen to thee) in there shall no punishment happen to thee (Shmuel I 28:10), receives a dagesh so that these words may be clearly pronounced. The peh in hatzefino should have received a dagesh. However, it does not because the tzadi is vocalized with a mobile sheva. Hatzefino is a hifil infinitive. There is no reason to speculate as to why Yocheved did not hide him for a longer period of time. Perhaps the Mitzri neighbors heard his voice, for the Hebrews were not the only inhabitants of the land of Raamses. For it is written, but every women shall ask of her neighbor (Shemot 3:22).
[An ark of bulrushes.] The words tevat gome (an ark of bulrushes) are penultimately accented because the cantillical note is placed on the first syllable of the word gome (bulrushes).

And daubed it. The heh of va-tachmerah (and daubed it) is silent. It is like the heh of the word lah (it) in and called it (lah) Novach, after his own name (Bamidbar 32:42). The word va-tachmerah (and daubed it) is derived from the word ba-chemar (with slime). Chemar (slime) is a red sticky clay which is found in the Land of Yisrael. The word chemar (slime) in full of slime pits (Bereshit 14:10) is similar. This substance is called al chamara in Arabic. Yocheved did this for she said, “Let me not look upon the death of the child.” Perhaps the sister of Moshe prophesied that she do this. Hashem’s thoughts are very deep. Who can know His secrets? By Him alone are actions weighed. Perhaps Hashem arranged things so that Moshe would grow up in a royal house and his spirit would thereby be exalted through learning and practice. He would thus not possess a base spirit habituated to being in the house of slaves. Do you not see that Moshe killed a Mitzri because the latter committed an act of violence and that he saved the daughters of Midyan from the shepherds because they were acting violently in trying to water their flocks with the water which the women had drawn? One more thing: had Moshe grown up among his brothers and had they known him from his youth they would not have feared him because they would have considered him as one of themselves.
In the flags (BA-SUF). Compare, The reeds and flags (va-suf) shall wither (Is. 19:6). Suf refers to a plant that grows in the Yeor.

And his sister stood afar off. The word va-tetatzav (stood) is irregular because a missing silent letter has been substituted for a yod between the two tavs.Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that a tav is suffixed to the words laredet (to descend) and la-geshet (to approach) because the first root letter of these words is missing. That is also the case with the word la-da’at (to know). This word is vocalized with a pattach because the ayin is a guttural. Now in the word le-de’ah (to know) the tav was changed to a heh, as in the case of the word tenah (rehearsed) in Whose majesty is rehearsed above the heavens (Tehillim 8:2).
And the daughter of Paroh came down. From her palace.

To bathe in the river. As was the custom of Mitzri women. Scripture notes that her maidens walked by the riverside — the meaning of yad (side, place) here is the same as that of yad (place) in Thou shalt have a place (Devarim 23:13) — because it goes on to say that she sent her handmaid (Amatah), who was one of the maidens, to fetch the ark. For a princess would not go among the flags, and the ark was placed far from the shore so that no one passing by would touch it. Furthermore, from a grammatical point of view the word amah (handmaid) cannot mean an arm, because its mem does not have a dagesh while the mem of ammah (cubit) in A cubit shall be the length thereof (Bereshit 30:2) does. Additionally, ammah (cubit) in A cubit shall be the length thereof refers to a measure and not to an arm.

And she opened it, and saw it. After stating, and saw it, Scripture goes on to elucidate further. Our verse is thus similar to And the house of David shall be as a godlike being, As the angel of Hashem before them (Zecharyah 12:8).

And behold a boy that wept. Moshe’s limbs were as large as if he were a fully developed boy. Paroh’s daughter noticed that Moshe was circumcised. She took pity on him because of his beauty. This is the meaning of that he was a goodly child.

Then said…that she may nurse. The first yod in roots whose first letter is a yod occasionally change, as evidenced in the word todi’a (you shall inform) which comes from the root yod, dalet, ayin and is spelled with a vav. In other cases a silent missing letter which is at times written and at times omitted is substituted for the yod and placed between the prefix and the middle root letter. This is the case with the word ve-tenek (that she may nurse) in that she may nurse the child for thee.
And Paroh’s daughter said to her: go. Lekhi (go) is like shevi (sit). These words are the imperative forms of va-yelekh (and he went) and va-yeshev (and he dwelt).

Take. Helikhi (take) is like heniki (nurse) because the roots yod, lamed, kaf and heh, lamed, kaf are two roots with one meaning. For the heh is not one of the implied vowel letters. Therefore the other heh is also like it. Furthermore, the alef and likewise the yod and the vav are found in the middle of a word at times written and at times silent, that is, pronounced but unwritten, but the heh is always visible when in the middle of a word. The words be-latehem (with their secret arts) (Shemot 7:22) and be-lahatehem (with their secret arts) (Shemot 7:11) are not, as I will explain, one and the same word.

And Paroh’s daughter said. Saadiah Gaon says that helikhi (take) is a composite of two words. However, the Gaon spoke incorrectly. It is, as I have noted, one word following the paradigm of ve-henikehu (and nurse it) in and nurse it for me. The word is in the hifil. The Gaon also said that helikhi is a composite of the words he and lakh, the meaning of he being the same as he (behold) in Behold (heh), I will also bring thy way upon thy head (Yechezkel 16:43). However, we do not find the form lekhi used in Scripture when a female is being addressed. The form employed by Scripture is lakh. Helikhi (take) is thus one word.

And nursed it. Va-tenikehu comes from a root wherein the middle radical is dropped and the other two remain. Observe, we have in our verse two roots with one meaning. It is the same case with the word hetivi (make good) in make good melody (Is. 23:16) which is an imperative following the paradigm of helikhi (take) and the word hetivu (they have well) in they have well said all that they have spoken (Devarim 15:25), which is like hevi’u (they brought) in And they brought yet unto him (Shemot 36:3), which is a word that drops its middle root letter.

And he became her son. This is similar to And these are the sons of Michal, and to Zerubavel the son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2; Chaggai 1:1). Zerubavel was the son of Pedayah the brother of Shealtiel (Divrei Hayamim II 3:17-19). He is called the son of Shealtiel because Shealtiel raised him.

[Moshe.] Moshe (Moshe) is a Hebrew form of a Mitzri name. Moshe was called Monyos in Mitzri. The name is so written in a book on agriculture which was translated from Mitzri into Arabic. This is also recorded in the books of the Greek scholars. Perhaps the daughter of Paroh learned our language, or she asked some one for its Hebrew version. Do not be perplexed as to why moshe was not called mashuy, as nouns do not keep their forms as verbs do.

That he went out unto his brethren. The Mitzrim, for he was in the king’s palace. One of his brethren means one of his family, as in for we are brethren (Bereshit 13:6). Our clause is to be so understood because Scripture has already noted that the man was a Hebrew.
Striving. Nitzim (striving) is a nifal adjective. The complete form is nintzim (striving). Compare, nirim (seen).
To him that did wrong. To him that acted violently.
Sayest thou to kill me. Sayest thou in thy heart.
Surely. Akhen (surely) means if so.

Heard. The land of Midyan was subservient to Paroh; hence Moshe had to herd sheep and not live among people and be recognized. It was at the time that his youngest son was born that Hashem told Moshe that Paroh and his servants from whom he had fled were dead. Upon hearing this Moshe said, and (Hashem) delivered me from the sword of Paroh (Shemot 18:4), as Moshe feared Paroh as long as Paroh lived. After noting and (Moshe) dwelt in the land of Midyan, Scripture goes back and explains why Moshe dwelt in Midyan. Moshe first sat down before the specified well. It is like And Yaakov went out from Beer Sheva and went to Charan (Bereshit 28:10). After stating the aforementioned the Pentateuch backsteps and states, And he lighted upon the place, etc. (Bereshit 28:11).

Now the priest of Midyan. The reference is to Yitro and not Reuel. The term kohen (priest) in Scripture refers to one who ministers either to Hashem or before an idol. That they may minister unto Me in the priest’s office (Shemot 28:41) and the priests of Hashem (Is. 61:6) are proof of this. Yitro, as I will explain, was a priest of Hashem.

And the shepherds came. The mem of va-yegareshum (and drove them away) has the same meaning as a nun. If va-yegareshum was spelled with a nun, the nun might be confused with a superfluous nun. Similarly, the word tzonam (their flock) is spelled with a mem so as not to combine two nuns.

And when they came to Reuel their father. Reuel was their grandfather, while Yitro, who was also known as Chovav, was the father-in-law of Moshe. This is evidenced in these verses: even from the children of Chovav the father-in-law of Moshe (Shoftim 4:11); And Moshe said unto Chovav, the son of Reuel the Midyani (Bamidbar 10:29).
And they said. They embellished what Moshe had actually done. Or the water which they had drawn was insufficient for their flocks.

And he said unto his daughters. A grandfather is often called a father. Examples of the aforementioned are: O Elokim of my father Avraham (Bereshit 32:9) and Nevuchadnetzar thy father (Daniel 5:18). Similarly, a grandson is called a son. Examples of the latter are: The daughters are my daughters, and the children are my children (Bereshit 31:43) and And thou his son, O Belshatzar (Daniel 5:22).
And he said. Behold, Scripture is being brief. It does not mention that they called Moshe, for we may logically infer that they did so.
Call him. Kiren (call) is irregular, as it does not follow its normal paradigm.
And Moshe was content. Perhaps Yitro the son of Reuel was then absent and is therefore not mentioned by Scripture.

And she bore a son, and he called his name Gershom; for he said. He refers to Moshe. Tzipporah is the Kushi woman of whom Scripture later speaks. Do not believe what is written in the book called The History of Moshe. I will give you a general rule: We should not rely on any book not written by prophets or by the sages who transcribed traditions passed on to them. We definitely should not rely on these books when they contradict reason. The same applies to The Book of Zeruhbabel, The Book of Eldad Ha-dani, and similar compositions.

That the king of Mitzrayim died. Moshe was now able to return to Mitzrayim. Bnei Yisrael repented. Yechezkel notes that Bnei Yisrael worshipped the idols of Mitzrayim. It was because of this that Hashem afflicted them. As a punishment for not serving Hashem they served cruel masters.
And God heard…[and God remembered.] The meaning of and God remembered is that the time for their redemption had come.
And God saw. The violence which the Mitzrim openly practiced.
And God took cognizance. Of what was done in secret.

The mountain of Elokim, unto Chorev. This is the manner in which Moshe recorded it. The place is called Chorev because of its great heat and lack of rainfall. As Moshe noted, it is located three days’ journey from Mitzrayim. There is no moisture there and the dryness is overpowering because the Yeor is far away.

Appeared. Some interpret be-labbat esh to mean: in a flame of fire. However, it appears to me that its meaning is, in the heart of the fire, for we indeed find, How weak is thy heart (libbatekh) (Yechezkel 16:30). However, Rabbi Adonim says that if this were so, then be-labbat would have been vocalized with a chirik beneath the lamed like the word ginnat (garden of) in I went down into the garden of nuts (Canticles 6:11). Now, Rabbi Adonim seems to have forgotten the word gannah (garden) in And as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth (Is. 61:11).

The bush. Saadiah Gaon says that seneh (bush) is a type of thorn bush. He further explains that the word seneh in And the good will of Him that dwelt (shokhni) in the bush (seneh) (Devarim 33:16) means heaven; that is, it refers to Hashem the glorious. Rabbi Yehoshua, on the other hand, says that the verse refers to the glory that dwelt in the bush. However, Rabbi Yehoshua spoke incorrectly, for how can Hashem be called “Him that dwelleth in the bush” when he dwelt there for but a moment. Furthermore, why is the word shokhni (dwelt) in the po’el form? The word oseh (makes) in Who makes (oseh) heaven and earth (Tehillim 121:2) is different, as Hashem is constantly making and causing heaven and earth to exist in the same manner as speech issues from the mouth of man. Additionally, after mentioning all the precious things (Devarim 33:13-16), Scripture concludes with the good will of Hashem. Moreover, what reason is there to mention this angel? Furthermore, Scripture should have read, ba-seneh (in the bush) and thereby would have referred to the well-known bush. In my opinion seneh (bush) refers to only one thing, namely, a type of dry thorn bush. This is the case in Arabic. Mount Sinai is so named because this type of bush grew there. Similarly, its interpretation is: and the good will that he who lives in the place of the bush (seneh) seeks; that is, a person living in such a place entreats and prays that Hashem do his will and wet the land that he lives in. He prays that Hashem change it from a dry place, a place where the seneh grows, to an amply watered place so that it becomes like a wet and well-watered garden. Scripture states that an angel of Hashem appeared out of the midst of the bush. The word seneh has the definite article the (heh) prefixed to it because these are Moshe’s very own words in writing the Torah. The word bo’er (burned) is a transitive verb. The phrase a burning fire is similar to a devouring fire (Devarim 4:24). As the fire that burneth (tivar) the forest (Tehillim 83:15) is proof of this. Now the fire that burned in the bush devoured all that was around it. Our verse is similar to They have set Thy sanctuary on fire (Tehillim 74:7). While the mountain did burn with fire (Devarim 5:20) is also similar.

[Was not consumed.] The word ukkal (consumed) is an adjective. It is similar to the pa’ul. The words lukkach (taken), which is vocalized with a kamatz in if thou see me when I am taken (Melachim II 2:10), yullad (shall be born) in unto the child that shall be born (Jud. 13:8), yukashim (snared) in even so are the sons of man snared (Kohelet 9:12) are similar. Now since these verbs are transitive, the word mu’edet (unsteady) in and an unsteady leg (Mishlei 25:19) cannot be classified among these words as these words are transitive. Mu’edet is similar to mo’edet, a po’elet, with the exception that a shuruk has been substituted for a cholam.

And Moshe said: I WILL TURN ASIDE (ASURAH) NOW. When a verb from the root samekh, vav, resh is followed by a mem it means: to distance from, as in suru mi-menni (turn aside from me) (Tehillim 6:9) in which the speaker says, distance yourself from me. However, if the word el (to) which is vocalized with a segol follows it, then it has the opposite meaning, as in suru elai (turn in) (Jud. 4:18), the meaning of which is, turn from your place and come to me. Moshe wanted to turn aside from where he was and to then draw near to the bush.

And see this great sight. This is the first sign recorded in the Torah that Hashem did via his prophet Moshe. Scripture thus says, and this shall be the token (sign) unto thee that I have sent thee (v. 12). Yefet says that the interpretation of the sign is as follows: the enemy is compared to fire and Yisrael to a bush. Hence the bush was not burnt.

And when Hashem saw. These words were also written later by Moshe. The angel was called by Elokim’s revered name in the sense of, for My name is in him (Shemot 23:21). I will explain this when I comment on the latter verse. We find the same with the angel that appeared to Gidon. There it is written, And Hashem said unto him (Jud. 6:23). Or its meaning is that Hashem saw that Moshe turned aside to see the great sight and He commanded an angel to call Moshe. Hence the use of the term elohim (Elokim) in our verse. The name Elokim is not a proper name but is, as I will explain, an adjective. It pertains to all holy beings that are incorporeal and are not forces in a body, as it is written, except the angels, whose dwelling is not with flesh (Daniel 2:11), that is, with a body. Thus elohim refers to the above-noted angel.

And he said: draw not nigh hither. Its meaning is, stand in your place and draw not nigh to the bush where the fire is. Is there yet a man come hither? (Shmuel I 10:22) is similar. A nun is missing in the word shal (put off), as it is in the word ga (touch), for the word shal comes from the same root as ve-nashal (and shall cast out) in and shall cast out many nations (Devarim 7:1).

Moreover he said: I am Hashem of thy father. After stating, I am the Elokim of thy father, He explains that the reference is to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. He starts with Avraham because Avraham was the first to call upon the name of Hashem and he built an altar to Hashem, for his father and his brother worshipped idols. These three are mentioned while those closest to Moshe, namely, Levi, Kehat, and Amram, are not noted because the former were prophets. Furthermore, they were fathers of all of Yisrael. Levi was not, whereas Moshe stood for all of Yisrael. When Elokim told Moshe, I am the Elokim of thy father, He was, as it were, speaking to all of Yisrael because Moshe represented Yisrael.

And Moshe hid his face. This is similar to for I have seen Elokim face, to face, and my life is preserved (Bereshit 32:31). The sensory perception of the eye is like the gate of heaven, for it can see in one moment images that are both far and near. However, this is not the case with the senses of the ears, nose, palate, and hand. Moshe hid his face because he was greatly afraid.
And the Lord said. The messenger speaks the same language as the one who sent him.
[I have surely seen.] Its meaning is: I have seen that which people do not see, namely, the violence that is done to them secretly.
And have heard their cry. I have heard their cry which is heard by all and I know the pain which they bear in their hearts.

And I am come down. Scripture says this because the heavens are more glorious than the earth. Hashem’s glory fills everything. It is only because the decrees come down from heaven that Scripture employs the term And I am come down. Furthermore, the angel was a higher form and Moshe was not able to go up to heaven. Hence Scripture reads, and I am come down to save my people.

And to bring them up. This is in contrast to and I am come down. As I dwell in a high place so will I cause them to dwell in the most elevated place that is upon the earth. The aforementioned are the words of the angel. It is likewise written, He made him ride on the high places of the earth (Devarim 32:13). Behold, Bnei Yisrael went out of a land where they were afflicted to a good land. Scripture does not mention the Girgashi because they were the smallest of the seven. Now, it is fitting to raise the following question: Since six nations were descended from Kenaan, why does Scripture mention the Kenaani? The answer is: The term Kenaani is an ethnic name and includes all the nations living in Kenaan. Hence the entire land was called the land of Kenaan. The Perizi is to be identified with Tzidon. The rest of the sons of Kenaan mentioned in Scripture were few in number and are included in the term Kenaani.
And now, behold. Its meaning is: And now, behold, the cry of the children of Yisrael who have repented is come unto Me.

[Moreover I have seen the oppression.] Its meaning is: Moreover I have seen the oppression with which they in their pride oppress them. Yitro similarly said, for that they dealt proudly against them (Shemot 18:11).
Come now therefore. As My messenger to Paroh.

And Moshe said…who am I. There is no difference between the words ani (I) and anokhi (I). The latter are similar to immi (with me) and immadi (with me). We have found that it is the way of the Hebrew tongue to derive the word ani (I) and the words attah (you in the singular) and attem (you in the plural), whose nuns have been swallowed, from the root of an (whither) in Whither went ye (Shmuel I 10:14), as the place indicates the speaker. It is possible that the word anokhi is derived from the root of anakh (plumbline) (Amos 7:7) in a manner similar to the derivation of the word nechushtekh (thy bottom) (Yechezkel 16:36).Because the Lord told Moshe, come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Paroh (v. 10), Moshe responded, I am a shepherd and Paroh is a great king. Because God told Moshe, that thou mayest bring forth My people the children of Yisrael out of Mitzrayim (v. 10), Moshe answered the Lord, Who am I that I am able to bring forth a great nation such as the children of Yisrael out of Mitzrayim.

And he said: certainly I will be with thee. Now go to Paroh and bring out the children of Yisrael and behold, I have given you a token that I have sent you. The reason they are being brought out of Mitzrayim is that they should serve Me on this mountain where I have shown you this great wonder. It is thus written, (I am Hashem)…that brought you out of the land of Mitzrayim, to be your Elokim (Vayikra 22:23). Moshe similarly said to Paroh, We will go three days’ journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice to Hashem our Elokim (Shemot 8:23) because the latter is the walking distance between eastern Mitzrayim and Mount Sinai. However, when Yisrael left Mitzrayim they did not go there via the land of the Plishtim. Furthermore, Yisrael, as I will explain, dwelt in one place for many days. It is precisely this that Moshe spoke of when he wrote, and (Moshe) builded an altar under the mount…and…offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings (Shemot 24:4, 5). He then made a covenant with Yisrael that they be a people unto Hashem and that Hashem be their Elokim.

And Moshe said. Moshe now asked which of Elokim’s names he should relate to Yisrael, for with the name of El Shaddai (Elokim Almighty) he could not perform signs. The latter are only performed with Elokim’s great and glorious name. Rabbi Yehoshua says that Bnei Yisrael had a tradition from their forefathers that Yisrael’s savior would reveal a new name of Elokim to them, a name that they had never heard. Now when Rabbi Yehoshua heard that Scripture states, I am Hashem that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees (Bereshit 15:7), he explained it by saying that these are the words of Moshe. However, Rabbi Yehoshua is mistaken. In the Torah portion Bereshit at the beginning of the Pentateuch we find that Scripture does not employ the Tetragrammaton but uses the name Elokim (Elokim) until the verse which concludes with the words in creating had made (Bereshit 2:3). After the latter verse Scripture refers to Elokim by the name Adonai Elokim (Hashem Elokim). After the birth of Kayin, Scripture employs the term Adonai (Hashem) for the Deity only by itself. We never find Moshe using the name Elokim for Elokim. Moshe always refers to Him by His great and glorious name. He uses the term Elokim only in one place. He does this because Paroh said, Entreat Hashem, and let there be enough of Elokim’s (Elokim) thunderings (Shemot 9:28). Upon hearing this, Moshe responded, I know that ye will not fear Hashem (Adonai Elokim) (Shemot 9:30). However, there is no other similar case in Scripture.

And Elokim said…I am. Its meaning is, That I Am. Compare, And the house of David shall be as Elokim, As the angel of Hashem before them (Zecharyah 12:8). Angel of Hashem, which follows Elokim, explains the term Elokim.

And Hashem said moreover…Hashem. Another name meaning the same as the first one. However, one name (EHYH) is in the first person and this name (YHVH) is in the third person. It comes from the same root as yah (Hashem). These three names are proper names. I will now go on to explain the meaning of the proper name of Hashem, the meaning of its letters, part of the secret of Hashem’s glorious name, and why it is not read as written.

The words of Avraham the author: Behold, I now begin to elaborate because I need a firm foundation. Note that a proper name serves as a token and as a sign of the one being referred to by those who enunciate it and those who hear it. A proper name is distinguished from an adjective in four ways. The first is that an adjective is derived from an imperative, such as chakham (be wise) in My son, be wise (Mishlei 27:11), or a perfect, as in My son, if your heart gets wisdom (chakham) (Mishlei 23:15), or an imperfect, as in That thou mayest be wise (techkam) in thy latter end (Mishlei 19:20). However, this is not the case with a proper noun such as Avraham, as no perfect or imperfect form can be derived from it. Now even though there are proper nouns that are derived from verbs, such as the name yitzchak (Yitzchak), we do not say yitzchakti (I was Isaaced) or itzchak (I will be Isaaced). A proper name is not used as an adjective. The second difference is that an adjective comes in the plural. For example, chakham (wise) becomes chakhamim (wise). However, we do not have a plural form for the proper name avraham (Avraham). Thus we do not say avrahamim (Abrahams). Neither is there a plural for the proper name yisra’el (Yisrael). Thus if there are two people named Yisrael in a place we do not say yisra’elim (Israels). We would only use the term yisra’elim if we wanted to relate each of them to the people of Yisrael, as the term Yisrael is the name of a group. The third difference is that a definite article is not prefixed to a proper noun as it is to an adjective. From the word chakham (wise) we get he-chakham (the wise man) (Kohelet 2:14). However, it is incorrect to say ha-avraham (the Avraham) or ha-yitzchak (the Yitzchak). The word ha-kohelet (Kohelet 12:8) cannot be used as an argument against the aforementioned because the term kohelet is not a proper name but an adjective describing the wisdom which was accumulated. Similarly, the word va-ha-adam (Bereshit 2:8) is an adjective. It has a secret meaning to it, as it is the name of a genus. The name ha-menasheh (Devarim 3:13) has a definite article before it because it refers to genealogy. The fourth difference is that a proper noun has no construct form whereas an adjective does. For example, we find, chakham lev (wise of heart) (Iyov 9:4). However, it would be incorrect to say yitzchak ha-dor (Yitzchak of the generation), because a proper name stands by itself. The same is the case with the name Eheyeh (I am) and also with the glorious name of Elokim, the Tetragrammaton, because both of these names are proper names. Now, we do find, Adonai tzeva’ot (Hashem of hosts) (Is. 1:9), and as a result many were forced to conclude that tzeva’ot is a proper name or that Hashem is outstanding among His host. However, this is incorrect, because Scripture reads, Elohe ha-tzeva’ot (the Elokim of Hosts) (Amos 3:13). Tzeva’ot is never encountered by itself. It is always connected either to the word Elokim (Elokim) or to Elokim’s glorious name, Adonai (Elokim). Do not be bothered by the phrase Adonai Elokim tzeva’ot (O Hashem Elokim of hosts) (Tehillim 59:6), as its meaning is similar to ve-ha-nevu’ah oded ha-navi (even the prophecy of Oded the prophet) (Divrei Hayamim II 15:8).

Now Hashem’s personal name is sometimes used in an adjectival sense because Elokim alone exists forever and the existence of all things is contingent upon Him. Elokim’s proper name is used here in the same way that the name moshe (Moshe) is used in Then He remembered the days of old, when He drew (moshe) His people (Is. 63:11). The meaning of Adonai when used as an adjective is: the maintainer of existence. Hence in the phrase Adonai Elokim the holy angels are connected to Elokim. Similarly, in the phrase Adonai tzeva’ot (Hashem of hosts) tzeva’ot refers to the hosts of heaven. Pay no attention to Saadiah Gaon who says that Elokim is called Adonai tzeva’ot because of Yisrael. Saadiah offers proof from and I will…bring forth My hosts (tzivotai), My people the children of Yisrael, out of the land of Mitzrayim (Shemot 7:4). However, look at I saw Hashem sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him (Melachim I 22:19). Now the name Elokim is an adjective, because it comes in both the plural and the singular. Compare, Is not Elokim (Elo’a) in the height of heaven (Iyov 22:12). Furthermore, the word Elokim comes in the construct. Compare, Elokim Elohe yisra’el (Elokim, the Elokim of Yisrael) (Tehillim 72:12). The word El (Elokim) means mighty. The same is true of the term Shaddai (Almighty). Compare, Like the noise of great waters, like a mighty voice (Yechezkel 1:24); and, and thy treasure shall be mighty (shaddai) (Iyov 22:25).

Note that the number one is the secret and the foundation of all numbers, and that two is the first of the even numbers and three the first of the odd numbers. Now from one point of view there are only nine numbers. However, from another perspective there are ten numbers. If the numbers one to nine are written in a circle and the last number is multiplied by each of the other numbers, we find that the ones are on the left and the tens, which look like ones, are on the right. Now when we come to the number five which is in the middle, we find the reverse; i.e., the tens become ones and the ones become tens. However, looked upon from another perspective, there are ten numbers without any additions, for one cannot begin to count one without ten. The number ten is thus like the number one. It is a general term for all the ones, i.e., the numbers from one through ten. The number ten includes them because they are the first numbers. It is also similar to the ones because it is the first of the numbers, in the same way that the ones are, because when we reach the number twenty we have two tens paralleling the number two. Similarly, thirty is like three and all the tens till ninety are like the nine ones. When the number one hundred is reached we once again come upon a number which is similar to one. When we reach nine hundred we once again have nine numbers similar to the nine ones. This is so until we reach the number one thousand which consists of ten hundreds. Also, the number one thousand is similar to the number one, and likewise the following numbers correspond to the other nine numbers until nine thousand. When we reach ten thousand the sum is concluded because we now have one myriad. The same applies until we reach ten myriads. The beginning of all the numbers is similar to the number one. Hence mathematicians say that all of the numbers are either fractions of ten or multiples of ten, or the result of adding ten to the ones, or a combination of these two. Now the ten numbers are the same as the fingers on the hand, five corresponding to five. Similarly, there are nine spheres which are in a constant glorious state. The tenth sphere, which is holy, is so called because its power is manifest throughout the throne of glory. It is the most powerful sphere and circles all the bodies. There are two middle digits when we count from one to ten, namely, the numbers five and six. Now the numbers alef (1), heh (5), vav (6), and yod (10) are the most glorious numerals. Any squared number that ends in one will always have the number one in its root. The same is true with its counterpart. Similarly, the number five will be found in the square of five and the number six will be found in the square of six. These four numbers always maintain their identity when squared; therein lies their superiority over all other numbers that are squared. Additionally, every number is potentially present in the number one. Similarly, the number one is found in all the actual numbers. Furthermore, the number one accomplishes on one side what the other numbers accomplish in two sides. Now behold the power of the number one. If you add its square to the square of its double you get five, a number whose cube equals its squares, for if you add its square to the square of its double it will equal its cube. In all the numbers preceding five the relationship of the cube to the sum of the two squared numbers will be the same as the relationship of that number to five. The reverse is the case with the numbers above five. The number six is equal to its parts. There is no other number in the order of the integers that equals its parts aside from this number. When the square of one is added to the square of the first of the odd numbers we get ten. Now if we bisect a circle with a line that is ten units long and a line is drawn across the circle a third of the way up, a triangle two of whose sides are equal may be drawn. The number representing the area of this triangle will equal the circumference of the circle. Similarly the rectangle formed in the circle. Now up to ten the value of the triangle to the circumference will be the same as the diameter is to ten. The reverse will be the case in the numbers above ten.

Now these four letters are very precious. They add up to twenty-two, the number of the letters in the Hebrew alphabet. Do not count the doubled letters twice, as they are the original letters with their horizontal bases straightened to form a line. The reason they have one name even though they are written differently is that they have one sound. The master of Hebrew grammar perceived that the letters have five sources. He classified half of the letters as root letters only, and half as root, prefix, or suffix letters. Now the second group of letters is more important than the first group. It is proper that a letter that is said often be one that is easy to pronounce. It is also fitting that the alef, heh, vav, and yod be easy to pronounce and have important meanings. These four letters are found in the vowels and are implied letters. These letters serve at times as consonants, at times as silent letters, and at times as paragogic letters. At times they drop out. At other times they are swallowed by a dagesh. Finally, at other times they interchange with each other.

Now there are four gutturals. They start with the ayin, which is followed by the chet. Do not consider all the letters that make up the name of a guttural in your definition of a guttural, as the additional letters are not made by the throat. It is best to refer to them as sounded with a pattach. Now the ayin and chet are very hard to sound. A person who is not accustomed to pronouncing them in his youth will not be able to sound them properly. Thus the gentiles cannot sound them. Hence only the alef and heh were chosen from among the gutturals to serve as ministering letters. Ministering letters were also chosen from among the palatals, i.e., gimel, yod, kaf, kof, as the palate is next to the throat. The yod and kaf were chosen from the palatals to serve as ministering letters because they are the easiest palatals to pronounce. The gimel and kof are therefore only used as root letters.

The letters dalet, tet, lamed, nun, and tav are linguals. Two letters, the dalet and the tet, were chosen from the linguals to serve only as root letters. The others serve both as root letters and as ministering letters. The letters zayin, samekh, shin, resh, and tzadi are dentals. They are all hard to pronounce. The shin is the easiest of the dentals to sound. Hence it was chosen as a ministering letter while the others were left to serve only as root letters. Therefore three letters were chosen from among the labials, namely, the bet, vav, mem, and peh, to serve as ministering letters. The peh was left to serve only as a root letter.

It is only right that the alphabet begin with a guttural, because the throat is the first organ in the framework of the human body to produce a sound. It does so from bottom to top. The alef comes before the heh because it is the easiest guttural to pronounce. Hence the alef heads all the other letters of the alphabet and is equivalent to the number one. It is fitting that the heh be the fifth number equivalent to the glorious number five. These two letters are the easiest to enunciate. Now since the first letter of the alphabet is a guttural the second letter in the alphabet was chosen from among the five labials, which are produced by the last of the body’s five organs of speech. Hence the bet follows the alef, the vav also follows the heh, and the peh the ayin. Now it was necessary to put in two letters between the bet and the heh. A palatal, the gimel, was chosen as the third letter and a lingual, the dalet, as the fourth letter. Hence a dental, namely, the zayin, follows the vav. The Hebrew grammarian now had to use the fourth of the implied letters for the tenth letter, which is equivalent to the number ten. He had already used the gutturals alef and heh whose great importance has previously been explained as the first and the fifth letters. He had similarly used the vav, which happens to be a very important and easily sounded labial. Now there are no root letters more easily pronounceable than the palatals. He chose from the palatals the yod and the kaf to serve as ministering letters. The more easily pronounceable of the two is the yod.

Four letters are fit to be implied letters. The alef is silent in all vowels because it is equivalent to the number one. We find the alef with the cholam in the word rosh (head); with the kamatz in roshim (heads); with the chirik in the word rishon (first); with the tzere in reshit (beginning of); with the shuruk in pura (boughs) in Shall lop the boughs (Is. 10:33); with the pattach in chattat (purification) in For purification and for sprinkling (Zecharyah 13:1); and with the segol in pele (wonders) in doing wonders (Shemot 16:11). It serves as a first person imperfect prefix in the masculine and in the feminine because it is the first letter of the alphabet. Since the alef is never sounded when it comes at the end of a word, it does not serve as the sign of the feminine. However, it occasionally takes the place of the heh, as in marah (bitter) in call me Marah (Rut 1:20) and in gaveha (was exalted) in its stature was exalted (Yechezkel 31:5). The alef is also found employed as a superfluous letter at the end of a word, as in ve-attikeiha (and the galleries thereof) (Yechezkel 41:15) and he-halekhu (that went) in that went with him (Yehoshua 10:24). It is also found as a sounded superfluous letter at the beginning of a word, as in etmol (yesterday) (Shmuel II 5:2) and ve-ezro’i (and my arm) (Iyov 31:22). It is similarly used in the middle of a word, as in ve-he’eznihu (shall become foul) in And the rivers shall become foul (Is. 19:6). The alef is also found unsounded at the end of a word, as in the word chet (sin) (Devarim 23:22). At times the silent alef is dropped, as in the word kes (throne) in the throne of the Lord (Shemot 17:14). At times it interchanges with a heh or a yod, as in ha-amon (the multitude) (Yirmiyahu 52:15), which is a variation of he-hamon (Shmuel II 18:29); or tityammeru (shall ye revel) (Is. 61:6), which is a variation of yitammeru (Tehillim 94:4). It is also found sounded with a vav, as in tomeru (say ye) in And say ye to Amasa (Shmuel II 19:14).

Now these three letters are fit to serve as prefixes and suffixes. The letter yod, which is similar to the number one (the alef), serves as a first person suffix both in the masculine and in the feminine. In the verbal forms we find shamarti (I have kept) (Tehillim 17:4) and amarti (I have said) (Shemot 23:13); among the nouns we find shemi (my name) (Shemot 23:21). The yod is also employed as a third person masculine imperfect prefix, as the number ten is like the number one. In the feminine it is oppositely positioned and serves as a suffix, as in de’i (know), re’i (see) (Shmuel I 28:17), and tizkeri (thou mayest remember) in that thou mayest remember (Yechezkel 16:63). This yod also shows relationship because as a numeral it is similar to the number one.
