The yod is a sign of the plural construct connected to the third person, as in yede (hands of) in The hands of women full of compassion (Eichah 4:10) and yadai (my hands) in even My hands have stretched out the heavens (Is. 45:12) because the number ten includes all numbers in it. The yod is encountered as a silent letter when it follows a chirik, as in ragli (my foot) (Tehillim 26:10); a tzere, as in ragle (the feet of) in He will keep the feet of his holy ones (Shmuel I 2:9); or a kamatz, as in yadav (his hands) and raglav (his feet). The yod is found in place of a heh (it is also found in place of a vav), as in hoyah (is) (Shemot 9:3), which is a variation of the word hovah (wouldest be) in and thou wouldest be their king (Nechemyah 6:6). The yod takes the place of a heh in the word yechesayun (take refuge) (Tehillim 36:8), which comes from the root chet, samekh, heh. It takes the place of an alef in yisharti (to be right) in all precepts…all things to be right (Tehillim 119:128). The yod is found as a superfluous letter in the words yitzhar (oil) (Bamidbar 18:12), ha-yoshevi (that art enthroned) (Tehillim 123:1), and rabbati (great) (Eichah 1:1). The heh is also used to indicate the presence of a thing, for this is its meaning in he lakehem zera (Lo, here is seed for you) (Bereshit 47:23). The heh is also sometimes used to introduce a question, as in ha-bemachanim (whether in camps) (Bamidbar 13:19), and ha-niheyeh (whether there hath been) (Devarim 4:32); or as the sign of the definite article, as in ha-eved ha-ivri (the Hebrew servant) (Bereshit 39:17) and ha-anashim (the men) (Bereshit 19:5). The heh suffixed to a verb indicates a third person feminine perfect. It is similarly used with nouns. The masculine form, on the other hand, was left without a sign. Compare the word amar and the word amerah in saith Kohelet (Kohelet 7:27). The heh is also used as a sign of the feminine when the imperfect is combined with the pronoun, as in eshmerenah (I will watch her), yishmerennah (he will watch her), nishmerennah (we will watch her), tishmerennah (you will watch her), yishmeruha (they will watch her), shemarnuha (we watched her), and shimruha (watch her). The heh serves as the sign of the feminine noun, compare, na’arah be-tulah (a damsel that is a virgin) (Devarim 22:28). The heh is appended to the hifil and also to the hitpa’el conjugations. The heh is also at times dropped, as in the word mazzeh (what is that) in What is that in thy hand (Shemot 4:2). It is similar to the yod of etzarekha (I formed thee) in Before I formed thee (Yirmiyahu 1:4), and it is like the alef of va-abbedkha (and I have destroyed thee) in and I have destroyed thee, O covering cherub (Yechezkel 28:16). It is also superfluously appended to the end of a verb, as in eshme’ah (I will hear), or a noun as in laylah (night). It is silent when following the kamatz, tzere, segol, cholam, or shuruk. Compare the words asah (made) and boneh (doth build) in Hashem doth build up Yerushalayim (Tehillim 147:2); boneh (build) in And the house which I build (Divrei Hayamim II 2:4); pera’oh (let them loose) in for Aharon had let them loose (Shemot 32:25), also shelomoh (Shlomo) and yikrechu (they shall not make baldness) (Vayikra 21:5).

The vav is used as a connective and is in such instances placed in front of the word because the vav sound is made by connecting the lips. The vav is used as a connective in the phrases avraham ve-yitzchak (Avraham and Yitzchak) (Bereshit 48:16) and in mi fa’al ve-asah (who hath wrought and done it) (Is. 41:4). The vav is also employed as a masculine and feminine plural perfect suffix. It is also used as a masculine imperfect suffix. It is similarly employed at times as a feminine imperfect suffix, as in im timtze’u (if ye find) (Cant. 5:8) and im ta’iru (that ye awaken not (Cant., 7:2). The vav is found as a silent letter when employed with the shuruk and cholam vowels. It is used as a masculine pronominal suffix with words in the perfect, as in shemaro (he watched him); with a noun, as in yado (his hand), and with a verb in the imperfect, as in yirdefo (will pursue him). It is vocalized with a shuruk following a heh, or a nun with a dagesh, as in yishmerehu (preserve him) (Tehillim 41:3) or yishmerennu be’alav (its owner hath…kept it in) (Shemot 21:36), because the heh is used as a feminine suffix. The vav is also used as a sign of the plural in verbs in the perfect and imperfect.

I have shown that these four letters are implied letters. Therefore the proper names that are constructed from these four glorious letters are glorious names. Now the first of these divine names is only found here. It is not encountered elsewhere in Scripture. We know that when Moshe spoke to Paroh he enunciated Elokim’s name as written. He did not employ any substitute. Moshe acted thus because he was holy. However, the ancients were forced to use a substitute name when referring to Elokim. The meaning of and this is My memorial is the same as this is My name, as our text employs two words with one meaning. Our reading of the divine name as Elokim whenever it is connected to Adonai, the meaning of which is, He is Hashem, is proof of the above. This word comes in the plural out of deference to Elokim in the same way that Elokim does. Hence if someone addresses Hashem in the same way that he addresses a person and says Adoni (my Hashem), as in adoni sha’al (My lord asked) (Bereshit 44:19), he errs.

I will now explain the meaning. Know that there are three worlds. One of them, the lower world, consists of objects that are on various levels of importance. However, they can be classified in three groups. The first is the metals, which number seven and correspond to the seven stars. At a higher level come the plants, which have many levels of value. Above them come living things, which have many levels of importance. Man alone is on the highest level in this lower world. Change befalls him in his body. Also his soul changes with his thoughts. Similarly, change befalls his occupation and his affairs. The wise men have compared the genera which is the group that endures although the individuals which make it up perish. The wise men have compared the intransient species to the shadow of a tree upon the ever-running water.

The next world is the middle world. It too contains objects that are on various levels of importance. The five ministering stars are very important, as they are self-sufficient and do not die or diminish. Neither do their movements change, enlarge, or shrink. They do not ascend or descend. Howbeit, they do change greatly according to the arrangement. At times a given star is seen in the line of the zodiac; at other times it is seen at a greater or nearer distance to the left, or at a greater or nearer distance to the right. Sometimes it ascends in its epicycle, at other times in its large sphere, for the center of the latter is far from the center of the earth. Sometimes its sphere ascends or descends. At other times it runs. Sometimes it tarries. At other times it stands in its place. Sometimes it goes backwards. All of this is vis-à-vis the earth. Sometimes it is seen. At other times it is hidden. Sometimes it is in the east, at other times in the west. Its relation to its companion, and also to the hosts of heaven above and to the moon below, is indeterminately forever changing because it is sometimes in conjunction with one of the seven fixed stars. Now there are one hundred and twenty conjunctions in each one of the three hundred and sixty degrees. It is due to these irregular movements that different things happen to man’s body and certainly to his fortune in this lower world. However, these stars themselves do not change. The moon is therefore on a lower level than they, because whatever happens to the stars happens to the moon, and even more. They have two spheres, neither of which has the earth as its center. Furthermore, the moon’s movement in its epicycle is opposite that of the great sphere. Additionally, the moon by herself has no light. Her light comes from the sun. This can be seen from the fact that when the moon is in conjunction with the sun in the head or tail of the dragon during the day, the sun cannot be seen, and if it faces the sun in one of the above-noted places at night the moon is invisible.

Now the stars that make up the sphere of the constellations are a level above the “ministers.” They are fixed in one sphere and they do not move as the ministers do. Their distances and relationship to each other do not change. They have one motion; it neither increases nor decreases. Their relationship to the earth is always the same. They appear different according to the place on earth where they are seen and the movement of the sun. The highest world is the world of the holy angels who are incorporeal and, unlike the souls of men, do not inhabit bodies. Their importance is far and above the understanding of their insignificant counterparts. This entire world is glorious and unchanging. There is no change in its arrangement. This world is not self-sufficient but its existence is dependent upon Elokim the glorious. Man’s soul is of this same kind. It receives power from above in accordance to the arrangement of the ministers, that is, the arrangement of each “minister” vis-à-vis the great hosts at the time of a person’s birth. If the soul grows wise it will share the secrets of the angels and will be able to receive great power from an upper power that received it from the light of the angels. The person will then cleave to Elokim the glorious. This is precisely what Yaakov meant when he vowed, then shall Hashem be my Elokim (Bereshit 28:21). Yaakov vowed that he would dedicate his entire life to cleave unto Elokim to the fullest of his might. Yaakov therefore said, Put away the strange gods that are among you (Bereshit 35:2). Yaakov did not utter these words till this point, for it was only now that he was going to serve Elokim according to his vow. So too, Yitro, who said, Now I know that Hashem is greater than all gods. (Shemot 18:11). Yitro was a very wise man. Proof of the latter is, And they asked each other of their welfare (Shemot 18:7). Additionally, Scripture states, and bowed down (Ibid.), which implies that Yitro did not stand in awe of Moshe.

When Adam realized that he would die he sired a son so that the human kind would be preserved. He received the power to preserve the human genus. Hence Chavah exclaimed, I have gotten a man with the help of Hashem (Bereshit 4:1). Each one of the sons of the prophets used to isolate himself in the hope of being inspired from on high according to his ability. Now it is via this name that new signs and wonders come into this world. When this name was told to Paroh he asked for signs and wonders. Therefore this name is not found in the book of Kohelet, as this book speaks of things concerning which nothing can be added nor anything taken away (Kohelet 3:4). It deals with those things concerning which there is nothing new under the sun (Kohelet 1:9). It deals with those things which are based on the wisdom that comes from on high.
Go, and gather. Scripture reads, the Elokim of Avraham because Elokim made a covenant with Avraham to give him the land of Kenaan.
[I have surely remembered you.] The meaning of pakod (remembered) is that the time of their visitation had come.

And I have said. I have previously said to your fathers that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Mitzrayim, the reference being to and afterward shall they come out with great substance (Bereshit 15:14), and to and I will also surely bring thee up again (Bereshit 46:4). Or its meaning is, I have now decreed that this shall come to pass, as in Thou shalt also decree a thing (Iyov 22:28).

And they shall hearken. When the word shama (heard) is followed by a lamed or bet its meaning is not to hear a voice but rather to hear the message which a voice carries. The yod in the word ha-ivriyyim (the Hebrews) has a dagesh for euphonic purposes. It is there to emphasize the yod genitive. The yod in ha-ivrim (the Hebrews) that follows the resh with a chirik beneath it is, in accordance with Hebrew grammar, the sign of the plural.

Hath met with us. Nikrah (hath met) means the same whether spelled with a heh or an alef. Compare, nikro nikreti (as I happened by chance) (Shmuel II 1:6). I will now explain the meaning of nikrah. Its meaning is, lest he fall upon us (Shemot 5:3).
And I know that the king of Mitzrayim will not give you. Leave. Or the meaning of yitten (give you) is, let, as in Therefore suffered I thee not (netatikha) to touch her (Bereshit 20:6).
[Except by a mighty hand.] Neither will he let you go because of his mighty hand. However, Saadiah explains it to mean: neither will he let you go if he is struck once with a mighty hand.
And I will put forth my hand. Against his hand.

And I will give. The Mitzrim’s appeasing of Bnei Yisrael by imploring them to ask for jewels and raiments (which is the meaning of va-yashilum) was also a great wonder. This is the opposite of the behavior of the world’s inhabitants.
[Empty.] The mem of rekam (empty) is superfluous. The word rekam is used in the plural as in our verse. It is also used as a feminine in Go not empty (Rut 3:17). The word chinnam is similar.

But every women shall ask. Now elsewhere it is written with regard to both males and females, and let them ask (Shemot 11:2). Scripture mentions females here because women are more in the habit of asking their neighbors for jewelry of gold and silver to put on the necks of their sons and daughters. They are likewise in the habit of asking for ear rings, nose rings, bracelets, crescents, and anklets. This is the contemporary custom in Moslem countries. However, the inhabitants of the land of the uncircumcised do not act in this manner. Scripture similarly speaks of a sorceress, as women are more involved in witchcraft than men.

And of her that sojourneth in her house. For Bnei Yisrael owned land. Some complain and say that our ancestors were thieves. Can’t these murmurers see that this was a command from on high? There is no sense in asking why? Hashem created everything. He gives riches to whom He desires to give it, and when He wishes to, He takes the very same riches away. There is no evil in this, as everything is His.

And ye shall spoil. Ve-nitzaltem (and ye shall despoil) is like ve-dibbartem (and speak ye) (Bamidbar 20:8), for it is possible that its form is that of the nifal conjugation. Compare, ve-niggaftem (and ye shall be smitten) (Vayikra 26:17).

And Moshe answered. Hashem indicated to Moshe that the elders would believe in him. However, He did not mention this explicitly. And they shall hearken to thy voice (Shemot 3:18) relates only to behavior and not to inner belief.

And the Lord said. This sign was not given to Moshe so that he would believe, because He had already given him the sign of the bush. God performed this sign for Moshe so that Moshe would imitate it before the children of Yisrael. It is therefore written, that they may believe (v. 5), which means, thus shall you do before them. God gave Moshe a sign via an object that was always with him, the staff, Moshe’s walking stick, as is the custom with elders. Moshe would not appear as a shepherd before Paroh.

And he said. Those versed in the sciences ask, how is this possible? They were forced to conclude that it was to remove the dryness. However, all their words are empty wind, as we are dealing with a wondrous event, one that did not occur according to the laws of nature.

Yefet says that this wonder was a hint, as Paroh was at first soft like a staff and then turned into a serpent. It is written, Paroh King of Mitzrayim, The great serpent (Yechezkel 29:3). At the end he ended up the way he started; he was like one that never existed.

And Hashem said. The first sign was performed upon the staff that was found in Moshe’s hand. The second one was executed on Moshe’s very hand. Yefet says that his hand became leprous because he suspected that Bnei Yisrael would not believe him. However, if this were the case, this should have been the first sign. Rabbi Yehoshua says that this was a hint about Yisrael, who at first were free and then Hashem plagued them with Mitzri bondage, and that Hashem would eventually heal them and that they would be free once again.

And the Lord said. Saadiah Gaon says that chek (bosom) refers to the sleeve of the arm. Similarly u-ve-cheko yissa (and carrieth them in his bosom) (Is. 40:11) and sa’ehu ve-chekekha (carry them in thy bosom) (Bamidbar 11:12). Others say that it refers to a garment that lies close to the chest.

And it shall come to pass. We know that Hashem knew whether they would believe or not. Scripture, however, speaks with regard to Moshe, viz., if there will be some Bnei Yisrael who will not believe the first sign, then they will believe the latter sign (ha’ot ha-acharon). Scripture speaks of the voice of the sign. Now a sign has no voice. The Torah, however, speaks in the language of man, as it does in Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Mishlei 18:21). Scripture speaks of the latter sign even though there were three signs, because Hashem now showed only two signs to Moshe, as He was yet to perform the third sign.

And it shall come to pass. If there shall still be a few Bnei Yisrael that will not believe the last sign, then you will show them the third sign and they shall believe. Indeed, it is written, and (Moshe) did the signs in the sight of the people (v. 30). This third sign, namely, and the water…shall become blood upon the dry land was part of the first of the ten plagues which were destined to come.

And Moshe said. All the commentaries agree that bi (oh) is to be taken as a supplicatory expression. However, Rabbi Yehudah Ha-Levi says that bi is an abridgement. It is short for bi ani adoni he-avon (Upon me, my lord, upon me be the iniquity) (Shmuel I 25:24), that is, punish me as you wish but relieve me of this task and do not send me. Similarly bi adoni yedabber na avdekha davar (oh my lord, let thy servant, I pray thee, speak a word in my lord’s ears) (Bereshit 44:18). Its meaning is, do to me as you wish but allow me to speak.

A man of words. A person who knows how to speak elegantly, that is, a person who does not halt or stutter or have difficulty in enunciating certain letters. It is the custom of the Hebrews when they went to compare two or three things to add the word gam (also) to the first object, as in Rule over us, also you, also your son and also your son’s son (Jud. 8:22).

[Heretofore.] The explanation of the word shilshom (third day) is as follows. The word temol (yesterday) refers to the day before the one in which the person is speaking. Shilshom thus refers to the third day from which the person is speaking. The mem in shilshom is the mem of the plural as it refers to today and yesterday, even though its shin is not vocalized with a kamatz as the rules of grammar require. On the other hand, it is possible that the mem is appended at the end of the word as it is to the beginning of the word. Compare, the word mishlosh (three) in And it came to pass about three months after (Bereshit 38:24).

Nor since thou hast spoken. Me-az dabberkha (since thou hast spoken) is to be rendered, from the time that thou hast spoken. Me-az (since) in For since I came to Paroh to speak in Thy name (Shemot 5:23) is similar, as the slowness of his speech was not removed but remained as it was. The one who says that Moshe forgot Mitzri is incorrect, because Moshe mentioned two things, viz., slowness of speech and slowness of tongue. Furthermore, we can learn from Hashem’s answer, Who hath made man’s mouth? or who maketh a man dumb? that Moshe was not referring to the Mitzri language. The upshot of this is that Moshe was born with slowness of speech; i.e., he could not pronounce the labials or all of the linguals. However, he was able to pronounce some of them with difficulty. This is the meaning of, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak; i.e., Hashem told Moshe that He would teach him to speak with words that do not contain letters that he had difficulty enunciating.

And the Lord said. We find dumb corresponding to the making of the mouth, blind corresponding to seeing, while the word deaf stands by itself; it has no counterpart. However, in reality the word pike’ach (seeing) corresponds both to blind and to deaf, as it is written, pako’ach oznayim (opening the ears) (Is. 42:20); li-feko’ach enayim ivrot (to open the blind eyes) (Is. 42:7).
Behold, God did not now promise Moshe that He would remove the slowness of his tongue. He only promised to teach him what to speak.

And he said. I have already explained that the word na (I pray) always means now in Scripture. See, Speak now (na) in the ears of the people (Shemot 11:2); Hear now (na), O Yehoshua the high priest (Zecharyah 3:8); Let this man, now (na) be put to death (Yirmiyahu 38:4); Woe now (na) unto us! for we have sinned (Eichah 5:16).

Whom thou wilt send. The word asher (whom) has been omitted. Our verse is to be read as if written be-yad asher tishlach. Im levavam shalem (whose heart is whole) (Divrei Hayamim II 16:9) is similar. Its meaning is, send this message by the hand of Aharon my brother who is a man of words, for he is not of slow speech and he is in the habit of prophesying to Yisrael. Indeed, it is written in the book of Yechezkel that Hashem sent a prophet to Yisrael before he sent our master Moshe. Scripture also states, And Hashem said to Aharon: Go into the wilderness to meet Moshe (Shemot 4:27). Furthermore, since Aharon was older than Moshe, he might be angry if Moshe was appointed Hashem’s messenger to Paroh. It is for this reason that Hashem told Moshe, and when he (Aharon) seeth thee, he will be glad in his heart (Shemot 4:14). Now Moshe did not refuse to go.

What happened was that Moshe first replied, I am not a man of words (v. 10), and it is difficult for one who is slow of speech to speak before the king. Moshe thought that Hashem would miraculously remove his slowness of speech. However, when Hashem answered him, and (I) will teach thee what thou shalt speak (v. 12), Moshe knew that his slowness of speech would not be removed. Moshe thus wondered why Hashem did not send Aharon to Paroh. It is for this reason that he said, send, I pray Thee, by the hand of him whom Thou wilt send. All of this can be clearly derived from Hashem’s answer, Is not Aharon thy brother… (v. 14).

And the anger of Hashem was kindled. Heaven forbid that this be the meaning of the verse, that Hashem…sought to kill him (v. 24), as he should have killed him now when he refused to go, not when he went, as others have interpreted. Why kill him when he went? Our case cannot be compared to that of Bilam. Similarly, the incident with Yaakov is different. Should someone argue, where do we find a case where Elokim’s anger did not cause harm, we will show him, And the anger of Hashem was kindled against them (Bamidbar 12:9), yet no harm befell Aharon. Scripture refers to Aharon as the Levi, for this is the way the Levi prophet was known in Yisrael since there were others who bore this name. Now Aharon’s appointment as spokesman did not entail Moshe’s demotion. On the contrary, Moshe’s status was thereby elevated. Aharon was merely an instrument, similar to the mouth which brings forth the words of the invisible soul which, like the angels, cannot be seen because they are incorporeal. Moshe’s station was thus similar to the station of an angel. This is the meaning of And thou shalt be to him in Elokim’s (Elokim’s)stead (v. 16). Now Elokim in Scripture does not refer to anything but Elokim the glorious or His holy angels or the holy ones below who execute Elokim’s justice in the world. Whenever Scripture refers to an idol by the term elohim it does so in keeping with the beliefs of its worshippers. It is similar to unto the prophet Chananyah (Yirmiyahu 28:5).

And…this rod. Scripture refers to the signs because the rod changed into a serpent before all of Yisrael and into a serpent before Paroh. The rod was also used to strike the Yeor, to bring up frogs, to produce gnats, to bring down hail, to bring locusts, and to cause darkness.

And Moshe went…jether. Yeter and Yitro are one and the same. Similarly, Geshem (Nechemyah 6:2) and Gashmu (Nechemyah 6:6) are one and the same, as are Salmah (Rut 4:20) and Salmon (Rut 4:21). Moshe told Yitro that he was going to see his brethren. He did not reveal the secret to him.

And Hashem said. The Torah is not in chronological order. The meaning of and Hashem said is, and Hashem had said. Similarly, And out of the ground made Hashem to grow (Bereshit 2:9) and many other such instances. Now when Moshe was handing over Yitro’s sheep to Yitro, Elokim assured him that he could go to Mitzrayim without trepidation because Paroh and his servants who knew about the incident of the Mitzri were dead. This is the meaning of that the king of Mitzrayim died (Shemot 2:23); as long as Paroh lived it was improper for Moshe to be a messenger to him.

And Moshe took. We do not know whether Gershom was born at the time that Moshe was a young man, when he fled to Midyan, or during his old age. Do not rely on The History of Moshe, as everything written in it is nonsense. Moshe’s second son, namely, Eliezer, was born now, at the time that Moshe started to prophesy. Moshe planned to bring his wife and sons to Mitzrayim so that they could leave Mitzrayim together with all of Yisrael. However, this was not a good idea; he was going to bring Bnei Yisrael out of Mitzrayim and they would see that he came with his wife and children to live there. Do not be surprised that a prophet should incorrectly assess practical events, for indeed we find that David asked Natan the prophet whether is was proper for him to build a temple to Hashem. Natan then answered him, All that is in thy heart do, for Hashem is with thee. However, in a prophetic vision of the night, Natan was told to inform David that he should not build the temple. The elders were forced to translate upon an ass as upon the man carrier, because it is demeaning that the wife of the prophet and her two sons should ride on one ass. Yefet says that ass is used as a collective noun, as in And I have an ox and an ass (Bereshit 32:6). However, Yefet is incorrect. This is not the place to use collective nouns. The term thus must be taken literally. Now the asses in Mitzrayim are dearer and more precious than the mules. There is nothing to wonder about if his son Gershom rode behind his mother. Perhaps he was small and Eliezer was in her bosom for he was not yet circumcised.

[And he returned to the land of Mitzrayim.] Its meaning is that only Moshe himself returned. When Hashem met Moshe (v. 24) Eliezer was circumcised (v. 25). When Eliezer was healed, Tzipporah and her children returned to her father. Moshe left them and went on to Mitzrayim.

Scripture refers to the staff as the rod of Elokim because of the sign that was performed with it. The rod of Elokim is the same as the rod of Moshe and the rod of Aharon. It was in his hand when he did the signs. Now that the rod of Elokim is mentioned Scripture backtracks and relates that Hashem told Moshe all the wonders that he was destined to do in Mitzrayim. He mentioned to Moshe the sign that would bring Yisrael out of Mitzrayim, namely, the plague of the first-born.

[And it came to pass on the way at the lodging-place.] This should have been connected to And Moshe took his wife and his sons (v. 20). There are many such cases in the Pentateuch, an example being, he shall make restitution (Shemot 22:2). The latter is connected to he shall pay five oxen for an ox (Shemot 21:37).

And Hashem said. This was told to Moshe in Midyan. Hashem informed Moshe that He would harden Paroh’s heart and that Paroh would not let them go despite all of the wonders, including the last one, that He would show them.

And thou shalt say. The meaning of Yisrael is My son, My first-born is: the ancestors of this nation were the first to serve Me. I therefore take pity on this nation as a father pities a son who serves him. You took him for a perpetual slave. I will therefore kill your first-born son.

And I have said unto thee. Behold, I have told you time and time again to let My son go, that he may serve Me by offering sacrifices to Me, and thou hast refused to let him go. I will therefore punish thee. The ignorant say that these words are directed at Moshe. The latter is sheer madness. Furthermore, Eliezer was not Moshe’s first-born.

And it came to pass on the way. They had a tradition that a child should not be circumcised on the eighth day if he was sick, or while traveling when it was not possible for his guardian to tarry and circumcise him. Now because Moshe could not tarry in carrying out Hashem’s mission he concluded that he should not circumcise his son, because the child would be in danger if he were taken along. Hashem therefore sent an angel to tell Moshe to put his decision aside and to circumcise the lad. The child would then remain with his mother until healed and Moshe would continue on by himself.

[That Hashem met him.] Its meaning is that Elokim sent an illness upon Moshe because it did not occur to him. This then is the meaning of and sought to slay him: Elokim sought to slay Moshe if he would not circumcise his son. Now because Moshe was seized with trembling he could not circumcise his son. Tzipporah circumcised him, for Moshe revealed this secret to her. Do not be surprised that it is written, That Hashem met him; the reference is to an angel of Hashem. And Hashem went before them (Shemot 13:21) is similar, and there it is written, And the angel of Elokim…removed (Shemot 14:19). However, Rabbi Shmuel ben Hofni says: Perish the thought that Elokim would seek to slay Moshe who was on Elokim’s mission to redeem His people. It was rather Eliezer whom Hashem sought to slay, and it is to Eliezer that the third person pronominal suffixes of va-yifgeshehu (met him) and hamito (slay him) refer. Scripture then goes on to explain that the reference is to Eliezer. Scripture therefore states, and cut off the foreskin of her son. He is not at first mentioned because he did not as yet have a name. And it came to pass, when she travailed, that one put out a hand (Bereshit 38:28) is similar.

Then Tzipporah took a flint. A sharp instrument. Compare, Make thee knives of flint (Yehoshua 5:2) which refers to sharp knives. Yea, thou turnest back the flint (tzur) of his sword (Tehillim 89:44) is similar.

[And cast it at his feet.] In my opinion the reference is to Moshe’s feet. Our verse is like and when He seeth the blood upon the lintel, and upon the side-posts, the Lord…will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to destroy you (Shemot 12:23). Therefore He let him, that is, Moshe, alone; his illness and shivering ceased. However, Rabbi Shmuel says that his feet refers to Eliezer’s feet, and similarly He let him alone. This being the case we can refute him by asking, “If the illness befell Eliezer how could Tzipporah circumcise him, thereby adding pain to his pain?”
[A bridegroom of blood.] It is the custom of women to refer to a child as a bridegroom when he is circumcised.
[Blood.] Its meaning is, surely thou art a man of blood to me, for because of you my husband will die.

So he let him alone. The word damim (blood) in Hebrew is used in two ways. One way is to indicate bloodshed, as in because thou art a man of blood to me (Shmuel II 16:8). The person who says that damim refers to life is giving the word a meaning that it does not have. The second way is as a plural referring to actual blood, as in be-damayikh chayi (in thy blood live) (Yechezkel 16:6). Now when Tzipporah saw that the illness left Moshe she exclaimed, you my son are not a bridegroom of blood, blood referring to death, but you are a bridegroom wallowing in the blood of circumcision. The word mulot (circumcision) is a noun. It is in the plural because of damim (blood).

And the Lord said to Aharon. Aharon did not prophesy; there was no need for him to do so as Moshe was the messenger sent to Paroh. However, prior to this Aharon had been sent as messenger to the male Bnei Yisrael, and Miriam to the females. The prophet therefore says, And I sent before thee Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam (Michah 6:4).
In the mountain of Elokim. The reference is to Mount Chorev.
And Moshe told. God sent Moshe to Yisrael first.
And all the signs wherewith he had charged him. To first perform before Yisrael and then to perform other signs before Paroh.
And Moshe and Aharon went. The elders are the counselors in each generation, as Moshe and Aharon could not possibly speak to six hundred thousand men. It was rather the elders who spoke to them.
And Aharon spoke. For he was Moshe’s mouthpiece. Moshe therefore never spoke to Yisrael except through Aharon. When Aharon died his son Elazar took his place and similarly became Moshe’s mouthpiece.
And the people believed. After they heard that Hashem had remembered his people. The end of the time period that had been told to Avraham had come.
Their affliction. Onyam comes from the same root as inuy (affliction).

Then they bowed. Va-yikkedu (then they bowed) comes from a double root. It is like the word kodkod (skull). Va-yikkedu follows the paradigm of va-yittemu (were ended) in so the days of weeping in the mourning of Moshe were ended (Devarim 34:8) and yiddemu (they are still) in they are as still as stone (Shemot 16:16). If only those who say that these words come from roots that begin with a nun would be as still as stone. In order to explain the paradigm they add roots that are nonexistent in the holy tongue. Can they not see that the word redu (get you down) (Bereshit 42:2) follows the paradigm of benu (build ye) in Build ye (lakhem) houses (Yirmiyahu 29:5) although they are two different roots. The correct thing is to do everything in our power not to multiply roots because of paradigms.
And afterward. After Aharon did the signs the two of them came to Paroh and the two of them spoke. For Hashem had promised them, and I will be with thy mouth, and with his mouth (Shemot 4:15).

And said…thus saith Hashem, the Elokim of Yisrael. Paroh had never before heard this name. Moshe therefore added the Elokim of Yisrael, the meaning of which is, the people of Yisrael and not only the patriarch Yaakov.

That they may hold a feast (VE-YACHOGU) UNTO ME IN THE WILDERNESS. That they may sacrifice unto me. Compare, bind the offering (chag) to the horns of the altar with cords, and chaggim (offerings) in Let the offerings come round (Is. 29:1).
And Paroh said: who is Hashem, that I should hearken unto his voice. He asked, “Who is Hashem that he is Elokim?” We learn this from Moshe’s answer to Paroh, which follows.

And they said. This name refers to the God of the Hebrews. The Hebrews were a group whom the Mitzrim were familiar with. The term Hebrew refers to Avraham, who is called the Hebrew. It likewise refers to Avraham’s son Yitzchak and to Yaakov and his sons, as I will explain when I comment on the verse if thou buy a Hebrew servant (Shemot 21:2).

And they said. The word nikra (hath met) is similar to nikro nikreti (as I happened by chance) in As I happened by chance upon mount Gilboa (Shmuel II 1:6). It means met. He explained to Paroh why they are obligated to offer sacrifices, i.e., lest a pestilence or sword come upon us.

Lest he fall upon us. Upon us includes us Bnei Yisrael, also you, Paroh, and all the Mitzrim. When Paroh saw that swarms of animals came and devoured many Mitzrim, as it is written, He sent among them swarms of animals, which devoured them (Tehillim 78:45), he said, Go ye, sacrifice to your Elokim in the land (Shemot 8:21). However, Moshe answered him, it is not meet so to do in the land (Tehillim 8:22). On the contrary, they would go a distance of three days’ journey into the wilderness (Tehillim 8:23). The latter is the distance between Mitzrayim and Mount Sinai for one who takes a straight path. It was there that Bnei Yisrael offered sacrifices, as it is written, ye shall serve Elokim upon this mountain (Shemot 3:12). It is furthermore written, and Moshe builded an altar under the mount (Shemot 24:4). Also, the altar that Moshe built after Amalek was defeated was erected on Mount Sinai, as it is written, and (Yisrael) encamped in Refidim (Shemot 17:1), and it is there written, Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Chorev (Shemot 17:6). When the locusts came Paroh gave some of Bnei Yisrael permission to go and sacrifice (Shemot 10:11). After the plague of darkness Paroh gave them all permission to go, with the exception that their cattle were to remain (Shemot 11:24). Now when they saw that a plague came and struck their first-born, Moshe’s words, lest he fall upon us with pestilence, became clear. They therefore said, We are all dead men (Shemot 12:33). The Mitzrim then chased them out (Shemot 12:39) to go and sacrifice. They also let them have what they asked for (Shemot 12:36).

And the king of Mitzrayim said. The word tafri’u (ye cause to break loose) means ye cause to disrupt. Yifra (cast off restraint) in When there is no vision, the people cast off restraint (yifra) (Mishlei 29:18) is similar. Paroh included Moshe and Aharon in get you unto your burdens, for Moshe and Aharon represented all of Yisrael. Your burdens does not mean your affairs. And will ye make them rest from their burdens (v. 5) proves the aforementioned.

And Paroh said. Yefet says that the meaning of the people of the land are now many is, we are not concerned if pestilence or sword befalls them, for those who toil are many. However, according to my opinion its meaning is, you are seeking to cause a great amount of work to cease.
And the same day Paroh commanded. The taskmasters were Mitzri and the officers of the people were Bnei Yisrael.
Ye shall no more give. Tosifun (ye shall more) is spelled with an alef. However, it is usually spelled with a vav. Both of these letters interchange with the yod.
[Straw.] It is customary for those who build with soil to mix it with straw or chaff so that it will last.

To make brick. Lilbon (to make brick) comes from the same root as levenah (brick). A brick structure is stronger than a stone structure, because a structure made out of soil will be damaged by water and a stone structure will be harmed by fire. It is similarly written, And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for mortar (Bereshit 11:3). Note, there are nouns that are vocalized with a tzere, such as the word sefer (book), or a segol, i.e., tzedek (righteousness), whose status does not change at an etnach or at the end of a verse. The word teven (straw) falls into this category. We not know the reason for the this; however, such is the case.
And gather. Ve-kosheshu (and gather) comes from the same root as kash (stubble). comes from a double root.
And the tale. Matkonet means tale. It refers to a specified amount.

Let heavier work be laid. Saadiah Gaon says that al yishu (let them not regard) is like al yishanu (let them not rely) with the nun omitted, as it is in the word tet (to put) in I begin to put the dread of thee (Devarim 2:25). Pay no attention nor listen to the dreamer who says that the root of tet is tat. Because he found Scripture employing the word tattah (you put) in My enemies you put to flight before me (Shmuel II 22:41), he thought that tattah is like shattah (thou hast set) in Thou hast set our iniquities before Thee (Tehillim 90:8). Now he cannot deny that the second tav in the word tattah indicates the second person and the tav of the root is swallowed in the dagesh, even though the tav should receive a dagesh like the tav in ve-hishbatti (and I will cause to cease) in and I will cause evil beasts to cease out of the land (Vayikra 26:6). Since this is the case it is better for the nun to be swallowed as it is swallowed by the tav in the word va-amitto (and his truth) (Bereshit 24:27), for the word amitto should have been written aminto and the word bat (daughter), benat and the word tet, tenet. The missing first nun of the word tattah in tattah li is similar to the missing yod in rad (spent) in the day was far spent (Jud. 19:11) and to the missing nun in the word ga (touch) in Touch the mountains, that they may smoke (Tehillim 144:5). However, in my opinion the word yishu (regard) means slack off, as Paroh said, for they are idle (nirpim) (v. 8). Yishu is similar to hasha (let go) in Let go of me (Tehillim 39:14) and she’u (let go) in Let go of me (Is. 22:4), and to hasha (weaken) in And weaken their eyes (Is. 6:10), for when the eyes weaken they grow dim. Tishenah (shall be closed) in And the eyes of them that see shall be closed (Is. 32:3) is similar.
[Lying words.] Its meaning is, because of the lying words that Moshe and Aharon assure them with.
Went out. Of the king’s palace to the people who were working.
Go yourselves, get you straw where ye can find it. Close by or far off.
For nought of your work shall be diminished. Nigra (diminished) is a participle. It is therefore vocalized with a kamatz as is the rule.
Were scattered. Va-yafetz (were scattered) is a transitive verb. Paroh, who caused them to scatter, is the subject.
For straw. In place of straw. Compare, la-chomer (for mortar) in and slime had they for mortar (Bereshit 11:3).
And the taskmasters were urgent. Atzim (urgent) is a transitive verb. It is like the word shav (returned) and the word mash (moved), which is sometimes found transitive and at times intransitive.
[Saying.] Its meaning is, saying to them..
Daily. The phrase devar yom be-yomo (daily) is similar to And from one sabbath to another (Is. 66:23).
And the officers…over them. Over Bnei Yisrael.

[Both yesterday and to-day.] I have previously explained the use of the additional gam (both). Now, both yesterday refers to the day that Moshe did the signs before the eyes of the people and they consequently were not occupied with their work. To-day refers to the day that Moshe and Aharon came to Paroh. And thus it is written, And the same day Paroh commanded the taskmasters of the people (v. 6).
Wherefore dealest thou thus with thy servants? It was never your practice to do this.

But the fault is in thine own people. The word ve-chatat (but the fault is) is a verb in the perfect. However, the vav changes it into an imperfect in accordance with the rules of grammar. The word is similar to ve-chate’ah. Now when the alef was silenced, as it is in the word chata, it was not possible to place a heh after the alef. They therefore substituted a tav for the heh. There is no need to place a dagesh in the tet. The word ve-karat (will befall) in and evil will befall you (Devarim 31:29) is similar. The word am (people) is here a feminine. Compare, ha-am (the people) in the people that were therein, how they dwelt in security (Jud. 18:7) and ha-am (the people) in Why is this people of Yerushalayim slidden back (Yirmiyahu 8:5). Its meaning is, but the sin will be upon you. Moshe out of respect alluded to Paroh by saying that the sin would be on his people. That I and my son Shlomo shall be counted offenders (Melachim I 1:21), And our enemies mock us as they please (Tehillim 80:7), and Thus they exchanged their glory (Tehillim 106:20) are similar.
But he said. Your words did not avail, as Paroh was steadfast in the hardness of his heart.
Go therefore now, and work. Paroh said this to the officers, as they too were obligated to work.

Did see. This verse is connected to the verses that follow it. They saw themselves in dire straits because Paroh had said to them, Ye shall not diminish aught from your bricks, your daily task. Then they met Moshe and Aharon and complained to them. The word otam (they) means themselves, their very bodies. Otam (themselves) in But the shepherds fed themselves (Yechezkel 34:8) and oto (himself) in and he buried himself in the valley (Devarim 34:6) are similar. Rabbi Moshe ben Bilam says that oto (it) in he shall bring it (oto) unto the door of the tent of meeting (Bamidbar 6:13) is also similar. However, in my opinion its meaning is that the priest shall command to bring him.

And they met. The words “who were” are missing. Our text should be read as if written: who were standing. And Paroh dreams (Bereshit 41:1) is similar. Its meaning is, and Paroh was dreaming. Similarly, and behold he was standing by the river (Ibid.). There are many other such instances in Scripture.
And they said unto them: Hashem look. At the violence done to us, the responsibility for which falls upon you.

[Ye have made our savour to be abhorred in the eyes of Paroh.] Note that the five senses are perceived in one place located above the forehead. Hence one sense is substituted for another sense, as in And the light is sweet (Kohelet 11:7). However, Rabbi Merinus says that its meaning is, we are as disgusting and abhorrent in his eyes as a foul odor.

And Moshe returned. Now a question: Why did Moshe complain and say, Why is it that thou hast sent me? and Neither hast thou delivered Thy people at all after Hashem told him, And I know that the king of Mitzrayim will not give you leave to go (Shemot 3:19) until he performed all the signs that Hashem commanded him? The answer is, Moshe thought that Paroh would lighten Yisrael’s yoke as soon as he spoke to him. However, Paroh placed a heavier workload upon them. [WHEREFORE HAST THOU DEALT ILL WITH THIS PEOPLE?] Contrary to Your words, I have surely seen the affliction of My people (Shemot 3:7); And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Mitzrim (Ibid.). [WHY IS IT THAT THOU HAST SENT ME] To harm Yisrael. Behold, I have not found an answer to give the officers.
For since. From the day that I spoke to Paroh he hardened his yoke over them, as it is written, And the same day Paroh commanded the taskmasters of the people (v. 6).
[Neither hast thou delivered.] My very thought was that Paroh would begin to lighten their burden and You would begin to deliver them.
[He has dealt ill with this people.] The word hera (he has dealt ill) is a transitive verb. It is similar to here’u (they did worse) in they did worse than their fathers (Yirmiyahu 7:26).

And God said unto Moshe: now shalt thou see. When I bring the plagues upon Mitzrayim things will start getting better for Yisrael, as I will yet explain. God who is Almighty and also awe inspiring, placed before us the secret of the Torah. I will now begin to explain the Torah portion called, And I Appeared.

And Elokim spoke. Scripture reads, And the people believed (Shemot 4:31). The latter implies that not all of the people believed. Everyone including Paroh, as I will yet explain, admitted to the existence of Elokim. Scripture therefore says, And Elokim spoke unto Moshe, and said unto him: I am Hashem (v. 2); Wherefore say unto the children of Yisrael: I am Hashem (v. 6); and ye shall know that I am Hashem your Elokim (v. 7).
And I appeared. The patriarchs received their prophesies in visions of the night, hence the term And I appeared.

[Almighty.] It is difficult to explain the word Shaddai (Almighty). Saadiah Gaon says that the shin of Shaddai is a preposition, like the shin prefixed to she-attah (that it is thou) in that it is thou that talkest with me (Jud. 6:17). The meaning of Shaddai is: Who said to the world, enough. However, I cannot see any meaning in this interpretation. How can God be called by the name “Who is enough?” Shaddai therefore can only be taken as an adjective, like the words tov (good) and sallach (ready to pardon) in good, and ready to pardon (Tehillim 86:5) and davvai (faint) in My heart is faint within me (Yirmiyahu 8:18). Now Rabbi Shmuel the Nagid explains Shaddai with the Arabic word al kahar, which means victorious and mighty. He further notes that the yod in Shaddai is in place of the double letter, like the yod in dalyu (hang limp) in The legs hang limp from the lame (Mishlei 26:7) and the alef in baze’u (divide) in Whose land the rivers divide (Is. 18:2). Shaddai (mighty) in like a mighty voice (Yechezkel 1:24) and Shaddai (mighty) in And mighty shall he thy silver (Iyov 22:25) are similar. The Nagid explained it well.
[I made me not known to them.] The word nodati (I made Me known) is in the nifal. It is not like hodati (I made known) as Menachem maintains.

[But by my name yhvh.] Rabbi Merinus says that u-shemi YHVH (But by my name YHVH) is an oath, as in Arabic there is a vav which indicates an oath. Rabbi Merinus explains the meaning of I made Me not known to them as: I made Me not known to them as I made Me known to you. However, we never find a vav with this meaning in Scripture. This then is its grammatical explanation. There are words that are to be read as if written twice. The same applies to letters. For example, the mem prefaced to me’el (From the Hashem) in From the Hashem of thy father, who shall help thee, and the (ve-et) Almighty, who shall bless thee (Bereshit 49: 25) is also to be placed before ve-et (and the) and be read as if written u-me’et (and from the). Similarly the bet of be’el Shaddai (as Hashem Almighty). Our phrase is thus to be read as if written: but by My name YHVH (u-vi-shemi) I made Me not known to them.

Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that the word le-vado (only) has been omitted from the end of our clause. Our text should be read as if written: but I made Me not known to them only by My name YHVH. On the contrary, I at times appeared to them with the name El Shaddai (Elokim Almighty) and at other times with the name YHVH. In my opinion, thy name shall not be called any more only Yaakov, but Yisrael shall be used with it (Bereshit 35:10) is similar. Really, there is no need for Saadiah Gaon’s reconstruction because we know that El Shaddai and the blessed and glorious Hashem are one and the same, except that the term El Shaddai is an adjective and the glorious and revered name is, as I have explained, sometimes a noun and sometimes an adjective. Now we find it written with regard to Avraham, I am Hashem (YHVH) that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it (Bereshit 15:7). We similarly find with regard to Yaakov, I am Hashem (YHVH), the Elokim of Avraham thy father (Bereshit 28:13). Rabbi Yehoshua says that Avraham and Yaakov did not know the name YHVH. Moshe used it when writing the Torah. However, Rabbi Yehoshua is incorrect, for how would Moshe dare to write a name that Elokim did not utter. There is no doubt that the patriarchs knew the name YHVH as a proper name. However, they did not know it as an adjective.

I will now reveal to you part of the secret meaning of the name El Shaddai. We know that Hashem created the three worlds that I have previously noted. Everything in the lowest world receives power from the middle world according to the arrangements in the higher world. Due to the fact that man’s soul comes from above the middle world, if it is wise and recognizes the works of Hashem, both those done without an intermediary and those done via an intermediary and if the soul forsakes the pleasures of this lowest world and separates itself from them to cleave to Hashem the glorious, should there be at the time of the birth of such a person an arrangement of the stars indicating that evil will befall this man on a certain day, the Hashem to whom this man cleaves will set the chain of events in such a way that this man is saved from the evil that was destined to befall him. Similarly, if it is in the arrangement of the stars that this man be sterile Hashem will make him virile and he will sire children. Therefore our sages said that Hashem told Avraham, “Leave your astrological calculations.” The statement “Yisrael has no star” is close in meaning to the latter. I will yet explain this in the Torah portion Ki Tissa. Therefore, before Hashem said to Avraham, and I will multiply thy seed, he told him, I am Hashem Almighty (El Shaddai) (Bereshit 17:1), the meaning of which is: I overcome the upper arrangements. The aforementioned does not mean that the arrangements are destroyed. It rather means that the one who cleaves to Hashem knows that Hashem creates good things for him that are not in keeping with what the stars have determined for him. Yaakov therefore said, the angel who hath redeemed me from all evil (Bereshit 48:16), i.e., all evil that was destined to come upon me. This is, as I will explain, the secret of the whole Torah. Now the patriarchs did not reach the level where they were able to cleave unto Hashem as Moshe, whom Hashem knew face to face, did. Moshe was therefore able to change the laws governing the lower world and produce signs and wonders that the patriarchs were incapable of. Now Moshe said two things to Hashem. One, why is it that Thou hast sent me (Shemot 5:22)? Two, neither hast Thou delivered Thy people (Shemot 5:23). Hashem answered the latter with, Now shalt thou see what I will do to Paroh (v. 1). He answered the former with, I am Hashem (v. 2). The meaning is that via the patriarchs My name El Shaddai was publicized, but through you My revered name YHVH will be known in the world. As Hashem said, Wherefore say unto the children of Yisrael: I am Hashem (YHVH) (v. 6), the meaning of which is, behold, I have sent you to make this name known.
And I have also established. I have also sent you because I have established my covenant with the patriarchs to give the land of Kenaan to them or to their children who are their equivalent.
And moreover. I have also sent you because the children of Yisrael have repented and have cried out unto me.
Wherefore. As I live so will my word live. I will redeem you with an arm stretched from the heaven to the earth.
And I will take you to me. When you receive the Torah on Mount Sinai.
[Who brought you out.] Its meaning is that according to the great combination of the stars in heaven Yisrael was destined to remain in exile. This will be explained in the Torah portion Ki Tissa.
And I will bring you into the land. For many of those who left Mitzrayim entered Kenaan. Additionally, their children are their equivalent.

[Which I lifted up my hand.] This is to be understood figuratively. God is compared to a man who lifts up his hand to heaven and swears. It is like For I lift up My hand to heaven (Devarim 32:40) and when he lifted up his right hand and his left hand unto heaven (Daniel 12:7).
[I am Hashem.] Its meaning is, I will cause this to come about.

And Moshe spoke. Yisrael did not hearken nor pay attention to the words of Moshe, as their spirit was impatient because of the length of their exile and the hard labor which was recently put upon them.
And the Lord spoke…saying. To Moshe. Speak unto the children of Yisrael, and say unto them (Vayikra 1:2) is similar.
Go in. To the king’s palace.

And Moshe spoke before the Lord, saying. Behold, the children of Yisrael who are thy people have not hearkened unto me; how then shall Paroh who is a king, and is not a member of your people hear me. Furthermore, it is a great handicap for me who am of uncircumcised lips to speak before him. Before I went to see Paroh for the first time You promised me that You would instruct my mouth not to pronounce a letter which is too difficult for me. However, now I may stumble in my words before him. Furthermore, You said that Aharon shall be the intermediary between me and Yisrael.

And the Lord spoke unto Moshe and Aharon. God now included all the details. Aharon was also going to be the intermediary between Moshe and Paroh, as Scripture will go on to explain. God’s command was therefore directed to both of them.

And gave them a charge. To go unto the children of Yisrael, and unto Paroh king of Mitzrayim. However, Rabbi Yehoshua says that and gave them a charge means, and gave them a charge not to be angry at the children of Yisrael if they did not hearken unto them. This interpretation is unnecessary.

These are the heads of their father’s houses. Moshe and Aharon’s father, or it refers to the children of Yisrael who are mentioned above. The men mentioned were among those who descended to Mitzrayim. Scripture starts with Reuven because the only honor left to him was to be listed first in the genealogy. These four sons of Reuven descended to Mitzrayim.
And the sons of Shimon. The family of Ohad was destroyed in Mitzrayim or in the desert, as it is not mentioned in the Torah portion Pinchas.
Zerach. Zohar and Zerach are one and the same.

The sons of Levi. These two tribes were mentioned first because they were older than Levi. Here Scripture is mainly concerned with Levi, as the Torah has no other intention now than to list the genealogy of Moshe and Aharon. Gershon, Kehat, and Merari are mentioned in the order of their birth. They descended to Mitzrayim.

[These are that Aharon and Moshe.] Aharon is mentioned first because of his age. Scripture mentions how long Levi lived but does not do so for the other tribal patriarchs out of respect for Moshe and Aharon.
The sons of Gershon. He had no sons but these two.
And the sons of Kehat. Scripture mentions how long Kehat lived but does not do the same for Gershon and Merari out of respect for the messengers.

And the sons of Merari. His sons numbered two; there were no more. Scripture therefore says, These are the families of the Leviyim according to their generations, for those who descended to Mitzrayim did not sire any children except for these sons of Yaakov. Scripture also mentions how long Amram lived, out of respect for his sons.
And the sons of izhar. They are mentioned because of Korach who quarreled with Moshe.
And the sons of uzziel. Uziel is mentioned because of the honor given in the Torah to Mishael and Eltzafan. Scripture did not care to mention the sons of Chevron.

And Aharon took. Aharon’s wife is mentioned out of respect for Elazar. Scripture notes that Elisheva was the sister of Nachshon because of the honor of the priesthood. The sons of Korach are mentioned because they were righteous, as it is written, Notwithstanding the sons of Korach died not (Bamidbar 26:11). The prophet Shmuel was a descendant of Korach.

And Elazar. Elazar’s wife is mentioned out of respect for Pinchas, as the priesthood was given to him eternally. Hence, logically speaking, Putiel was a Yisraeli. We do not know the meaning of Putiel as we do not know the meaning of Mishael and Aharon and all the other names that are mentioned. If what happened to Moshe had not been recorded, we would not know why he was so called.
These are that Aharon and Moshe. Scripture mentions Aharon before Moshe because Aharon was older and also because he prophesied to Yisrael before the arrival of Moshe.

These. Now from the time that they spoke to Paroh, Scripture mentions Moshe before Aharon because of his great status. Indeed, Hashem spoke to him face to face and he alone drew near unto the thick darkness where Hashem was. This was not the case with Aharon. Scripture testifies with regard to Moshe, My servant Moshe is not so (Bamidbar 12:7). Furthermore, Aharon said, oh my lord twice. You will therefore not find in the entire Pentateuch starting from this verse Moshe not mentioned before Aharon. The same holds true for the Prophets and similarly for the Writings. There is no argument to the contrary from Now these are the generations of Aharon and Moshe (Bamidbar 3:1) or from, and she bore unto Amram Aharon and Moshe (Bamidbar 26:59), as Scripture lists them there in the order of their birth. The words generations and and she bore is proof of this.

And it came to pass. One may wonder why the arranger of the chapters did not connect this verse with what follows it when in fact it is dependent upon what comes next. Though we know no reason for the above, we do know that they are connected. On the day when Hashem spoke unto Moshe in the land of Mitzrayim (v. 28) what he told him was, I am Hashem; speak thou unto Paroh. (v. 29). Similarly, So, it came to pass, when all the men of war were consumed and dead from among the people (Devarim 2:16) is connected to that which follows it. Perhaps the one who arranged the places to stop knew why he did this, as his mind was much greater than ours.
That Hashem spoke. Scripture now goes back to the subject of And Hashem spoke unto Moshe and unto Aharon (Shemot 6:13), namely, Go in, speak unto Paroh king of Mitzrayim (Shemot 6:11).
I. and Hashem said. This was in response to, how then shall Paroh hear me, who am of uncircumcised lips (Shemot 6:12). Elokim answered Moshe, See I have set thee in Elokim’s stead to Paroh.

And the Lord said. Its meaning is: See, I have greatly elevated your status in that in Paroh’s eyes your stature is that of an angel. This is what Elokim’s stead means. Elokim speaks to the prophet and the prophet speaks to the men of his generation.

[And Aharon thy brother shall be thy prophet.] Those who say that the word navi (prophet) comes from the root of niv in niv sefatayim (the fruit of the lips) (Is. 57:19) err. Niv comes from a two-letter root according to the French sages and from a hidden ayin root according to the Spanish sages. However, navi comes from a three-letter root. That its alef is a root letter can be seen from the words nevi’im (prophets) (Bamidbar 11:29) and va-yitnabe’u (they prophesied). Furthermore, the word niv in niv sefatayim means fruit, for niv comes from the same root as tenuvah (fruitage) (Is. 27:6) and yenuvun (they shall bring forth fruit) in They shall still bring forth fruit in old age (Tehillim 92:15). Ve-nivo nivzeh okhlo (and the fruit thereof, even the food thereof, is contemptible) (Malachi 1:12) is true proof of this. Additionally, what meaning is there to, restore the man’s wife; for he is a prophet (Bereshit 20:7) if navi (prophet) means a speaker. Its only meaning is, he is a prophet to whom I reveal my secrets, as in But He revealeth His counsel unto His servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). He enjoys My presence therefore and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live (Bereshit 20:7).
Thou shalt speak. To Aharon.
All that I command thee; and Aharon thy brother shall speak unto Paroh. Even though Aharon is not mentioned every time that Moshe came to Paroh, we know that they always came together.

And I will harden Paroh’s heart. The question arises: “If Hashem hardened Paroh’s heart what was his transgression and what was his sin?” The answer is: Hashem granted wisdom to man and implanted in his heart the intelligence to receive power from on high to add to his good or to diminish his evil. I will explain this in the Torah portion Ki Tissa and when I comment on the verse Oh that they had such a heart as this alway (Devarim 5:26). Now the meaning of our verse is: I will harden his heart in order to multiply My signs and My wonders. Rabbi Yehoshua says that its meaning is: I will harden his heart so that he will be able to bear the plagues. However, he spoke incorrectly.
And I will lay my hand. That is, my blow, for a blow is struck with the hand. Scripture speaks anthropomorphically.
[My Hosts.] Its meaning is: as the angels are Hashem’s hosts in heaven so are Yisrael upon the earth.

Shall know. Rabbi Yehudah, the first grammarian, has already noted the difference between ve-yade’u (shall know) and ve-yede’u (shall know). The word ve-yade’u, which is vocalized with a long kamatz, is a verb in the perfect. Compare, shame’u (they heard). The vav prefixed to yade’u changes it to an imperfect as per the grammatical rules. On the other hand, the yod of the word ve-yede’u, which is vocalized with a tzere, is a future prefix. Compare, ve-yishmeru (they shall keep). The silent yod between the yod and the dalet is in place of the root yod. Behold, God noted why He brought the plagues upon the Mitzrim. He brought them so that His glorious name would be known in the world.
And Moshe and Aharon did so. Scripture now states generally that the signs were performed by Aharon and also by Moshe. It then goes on to explain each one of the signs.

And Moshe. The Pentateuch records the ages of Moshe and Aharon. Aside from these two, we do not find in all of Scripture prophets concerning whom the Bible says that they prophesied in their old age. Their status was greater than that of all the other prophets, and to them alone did Hashem speak in a pillar of cloud. Do not think that Shmuel is to be included among them because it is written, He spoke unto themin the pillar of cloud (Tehillim 99:7), since I have already explained in its proper place that the Torah was given only to these two. Now, behold, through Moshe and Aharon the righteous shall inherit the world to come, while all the other prophets are prophets who rebuke or predict the future.

And Hashem said unto Moshe and unto Aharon. Hashem now began to direct His words to the two of them. Hashem knew that at first Paroh would not ask for a sign but would merely say, I know not Hashem (Shemot 5:2). However, now Paroh would ask for a sign.

Take thy rod. The reference is to Moshe’s rod which Moshe had given to Aharon. Say unto Aharon: Take thy rod, and stretch out thy hand (v. 19); and he lifted up the rod (ba-matteh), and smote the waters (v. 20) is proof of this. Now by employing a bet that has a pattach beneath it Scripture is informing us that when He told him, Take thy rod, He was referring to the well-known rod. And thy rod, wherewith thou smotest the river, take in thy hand, and go (Shemot 17:5) is additional proof of the above.

And Moshe and Aharon went in. This too, namely, that the rod became a tannin (serpent), was a wonder. It was not like the wonder that he did for Yisrael, as there it only changed into a nachash (serpent). However, Yefet says that nachash (serpent) and tannin (serpent) are one and the same.
Then Paroh also called for the wise men. Astrologers.
And the sorcerers. Those who appear to change natural law.

The magicians. Those who know the secrets of nature. Chartumim (magicians) is a quadriliteral. It might be a Mitzri or Kasdi word, as we do not find this word used in Scripture except when dealing with them. Scripture indicates a difference between what Moshe did and what the magicians did. Moshe really changed the staff into a serpent. As for the magicians, Scripture reads, with their secret arts. Be-lahatehem (with their secret arts) comes from a triliteral root. It is derived from the same root as lahat (flame) in the flaming sword (Bereshit 3:24) and lohatim (them that are aflame) in I do lie down among them that are aflame (Tehillim 57:5) and lihat (ablaze) in And the day that cometh shall set them ablaze (Malachi 3:19). It refers to an illusion of lightning and passing fire.

For they cast down. This, the swallowing of the magicians’ rods by Aharon’s staff and their consequent disappearance, was a second wonder. Scripture refers to the staff as Aharon’s rod for it was so at first. Rabbi Yehoshua says that Aharon’s rod swallowed the rods of the magicians after it returned to its original form. And this was a great wonder.
And Paroh’s heart was hardened. By itself. Paroh saw that the magicians were able to do what Aharon did.

And Hashem said…Paroh’s heart is stubborn. Kaved (is stubborn) is a verb in the perfect. It is like the word zaken (was old) in when Yitzchak was old (Bereshit 27:1), chafetz (were pleased) in If Hashem were pleased (Jud. 13:23), ahev (he loveth) in such as he loveth (Bereshit 27:9). The mem of me’en (refuseth), which is a root letter, is vocalized with a tzere so that a dagesh is not placed in the alef which follows it. Cheref (jeoparded) in jeoparded their lives (Jud. 5:18) is similar.

Get thee unto Paroh in the morning. It is the custom of the king of Mitzrayim until this very day to go out in the months of Tamuz and Ab to see how high the water has risen. This is the time the river increases. Hashem commanded Moshe to go in the morning and stand before the river and perform the sign of the striking of the river in the presence of Paroh. He commanded Moshe to take and then give to Aharon the rod which he had turned into a serpent before coming unto Paroh (Shemot 4:3) and to wave it over the waters of Mitzrayim so that Paroh would see with his very eyes the river turn into blood at the moment that Aharon struck it.
And thou shalt say unto him. Say the following to him, because if he does not listen, this is the first plague. The rod which turned into a serpent (v. 10) was not a plague.

Thus saith the Lord. The messenger speaks the word of the one who sent him. Moshe was brief, for the term “His messenger” has been omitted. The statement should be understood thus: behold, I His messenger will smite with the rod that is in my hand.
[With the rod that is in my hand.] Moshe said, that is in my hand, even though the rod was in Aharon’s hand because they were equals and both participated in the performance of the sign.
And the fish. Fish is a general term for all things that swarm in the waters.
Shall loathe. Ve-nil’u (shall loathe) is a nifal from the same root as the word la’ah (weary). Its meaning is, will be unable.

And the Lord said. According to my opinion this is to be understood as follows. Aharon waved his hand and struck the Yeor. He also waved his hand toward all the sides of Mitzrayim to turn the waters of all the rivers in the land of Mitzrayim, that is, in the kingdom of Mitzrayim, into blood. The term the waters of Mitzrayim is a general term. Over their rivers is one of its particulars. The term ye’or (stream) refers exclusively to the Yeor. There are other rivers in Mitzrayim, for the blood was over all of their country.
Over their streams. The plural ye’orehem (their streams) is employed because the Yeor is found in many places.
Their pools. Pools of rainwater that form by themselves.

And over their ponds of water. This refers to fountains, wells, and cisterns. Saadiah Gaon says that the word meyeme (water of), which is the word me (water of) doubled, refers to sweet water while the word me refers to bitter water, as in me ha-yam (waters of the sea). Scripture therefore reads, ha-kore le-me ha-yam (that calleth for the waters of the sea) (Amos 5:8). Now the Gaon forgot that Scripture states, me ha-yarden yikkaretun (the waters of the Yarden shall be cut off) (Yehoshua 3:13). The word me is always doubled when connected to a pronoun, as in the word memai (my water) (Shmuel I 25:11) and in memekha (thy water) (Yechezkel 12:18). This mode comes exclusively in the plural form, as it is incorrect to say memi (my water) and memah (her water). We find me used in the singular in because the water of (me) sprinkling was not dashed (Bamidbar 19:13).
[Both in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.] That is, in water found in the homes in vessels made out of wood or basins made out of stone.
And Moshe and Aharon did. Scripture notes the smiting of the Yeor. However, it does not bother to mention the waving of the hand over all the waters of Mitzrayim.

And the magicians of Mitzrayim did in like manner with their secret arts. The word be-latehem (with their secret arts) comes from the same root as ba-lat (stealthily) in she approached him stealthily (Jud. 4:21). It means with secret things hidden from the eye. A heh has not been omitted from the word, for the heh is not an implied letter in the middle of a word. One may ask: If all the water in Mitzrayim was turned into blood by Aharon, where did the magicians find the water to turn into blood? The answer is: Aharon turned only water that is found above ground into blood. He did not transform any water that was below ground. The magicians dug and brought forth water from beneath the ground and openly turned it into blood. Now, there is a great difference between what Aharon did and what the magicians brought about. Aharon transformed all of the Yeor that was before him plus all the water that was in all the borders of Mitzrayim, which he did not see. Furthermore, he changed water that was not standing still but was continually running, with other water taking its place, into blood. Additionally, the plague lasted for seven days. The magicians, on the other hand, were only able to transform a little water standing in a vessel, for a moment, until Paroh returned to his house.
And Paroh turned. Scripture states even this because it first mentioned the sign of the rod which turned into a serpent and swallowed the other rods.

Digged. Many say that the water was as red as blood in the hands of a Mitzri and became clear in the hands of a Yisraeli. If this is so then why doesn’t the Torah record this sign? I believe that the plagues of blood, frogs, and gnats included both Mitzrim and Hebrews, for we shall follow Scripture. These three plagues caused little harm. However, Hashem differentiated between the Mitzrim and Bnei Yisrael with regard to the swarms, which was a very harmful plague. So too with regard to the plagues of murrain and hail because of their flocks. This was not the case with the boils and locusts, for they left Mitzrayim. Now as the Mitzrim digged, so did the Hebrews dig.
Were fulfilled. Scripture notes this because unlike the other plagues, this plague lasted many days.
And the Lord spoke…go in unto Paroh. With your brother Aharon and inform him of the second plague if he does not let my people go.

And if. The word ma’en (refuse) is a transitive participle. It is like the word ve-shabbe’ach (wherefore I praised) in Wherefore I praised the dead (Kohelet 4:2). The meaning of nogef (smite) is destroy. It is thus written, And frogs, which destroyed them (Tehillim 78:45). The commentaries are divided as to the meaning of the word tzefarde’im (frogs). Many say that it is a type of fish called al-timsach in Arabic that is found in Mitzrayim, that arises from the river and preys upon people. Others say that it is the well-known sound-producing creature which is found in the majority of rivers. This interpretation appears to me to be correct.
And the river shall swarm. Ve-sharatz (shall swarm) is a transitive verb. It is like yishretzu (swarm) in Let the waters swarm (Bereshit 1:20).
[Which shall go up.] The reason Scripture states this is that the river is always lower than the city.

Both upon thee, and upon thy people. Yefet says that Scripture reads, both upon thee, and upon thy people to hint that the frogs shall affect only Paroh and his people but not Yisrael. However, this is no proof. Since Scripture mentions that the frogs shall go up upon him and upon all of his people, there was no reason to mention Yisrael.

And the Lord said…stretch forth thy hand. Towards the four corners of heaven and the frogs will arise from the canals, from the rivers, and from the pools. However, they will not arise from all gatherings of water.

And Aharon stretched out his hand. Behold, Aharon merely stretched forth his hand but did not strike the water as he did the first time. He merely indicated that the frogs could arise from the moment that he stretched out his hand.

And the magicians did in like manner. In the little water. Paroh therefore saw that there was a difference between what Aharon did and what his magicians were able to do. He called Moshe because he saw that his magicians could add to the plague but were unable to mitigate it.

Then Paroh called. Paroh employed the plural form for entreat (hatiru) out of respect for Moshe and Aharon. This plague was worse than the first one, for we read, He sent among them…frogs, which destroyed them (Tehillim 78:45).
And Moshe said unto Paroh: have thou this glory over me. I will glorify you by entreating Hashem that He take away the plague on a day that you yourself shall designate.
[And remain in the river only.] The reason for mentioning the river is that this is where the frogs started from. Once Scripture notes the river there is no need to mention the canals and pools.

And he said: against tomorrow. Rabbi Shmuel ben Hofni says that people usually pray that a plague be removed from them immediately. Paroh, however, thought that the plague of frogs resulted from an unpropitious conjunction of heavenly bodies which Moshe knew about. He thought that the time for the removal of the frogs had now come. Therefore Paroh tested Moshe by asking him to extend the plague and said, Against tomorrow.

And the frogs shall depart. Ve-saru (shall depart) is ultimately accented, contrary to the rules of grammar. We find the same irregularity in the word samu (they put) in that they should put me into the dungeon (Bereshit 40:15).

And Moshe and Aharon went out. Moshe cried unto Hashem because he trusted that Hashem would not put him to shame. Out of his own accord and without the permission of Hashem, he had told Paroh, Be it according to thy word.
And Hashem did according to the word of Moshe. Which he had spoken of his own accord.
And they gathered. Va-yitzberu (and they gathered) is similar in meaning to the word va-yitzbor (laid up) in And Yosef laid up corn (Bereshit 41:49).
Heaps. Chomarim chomarim (heaps) is similar in meaning to chamor chamoratayim (heaps upon heaps) (Jud. 15:16).
But when Paroh saw that there was respite. The word harevachah (respite) is similar in meaning to ve-ravach (relief) in so Shaul found relief (Jud. 16:23).
He hardened his heart. Scripture employs an infinitive (hakhbed) in place of a perfect.

And the Lord said. Note that the first three plagues and signs which Aharon brought about pertained to the lowest elements, as I have explained previously, since two were related to water and one to the dust of the earth. However, the plagues brought about by Moshe with his rod related to a higher element. This was so because Moshe was on a higher plane than Aharon. Thus the hail and the locusts were brought by the wind, and the darkness was in the air. Moshe also brought about the plague of boils. However, three plagues came about without the use of the rod, namely, the swarms of beasts, murrain, and the death of the first-born. One plague, that of the boils, was brought about by Moshe with Aharon’s minor participation and without the use of the rod.

[That it may become gnats throughout all the land of Mitzrayim.] This is similar in meaning to And it shall become small dust over all the land of Mitzrayim (Shemot 9:9). The dust which Aharon struck gave birth, as it were, to gnats which went up over all the land of Mitzrayim.

And they did so. And they did refers to Moshe and Aharon. Moshe is included because he told Aharon to smite the dust with the rod. Our verse is similar to and thy rod, wherewith thou smotest the river, take in thy hand (Shemot 17:5).

And there were gnats. Kinnam (gnats) is a generic name. The mem of kinnam is either superfluous or in place of a heh. In any case, it is not a root letter. The mem sometimes serves as the sign of the feminine plural, as in the word tzefardi’im (frogs). This term is a feminine, for when referring to the singular Scripture reads, va-ta’al ha-tzefarde’a (and the frog came up) (Shemot 8:2). The term kinnim is proof of the aforementioned. According to this interpretation the word ha-kinnam is irregular because of its superfluous mem. It is similar to the word rekam (empty) and chinnam (gratuitous). However, Yefet says that the mem of kinnam is a pronominal suffix relating to the Mitzrim. He claims that the singular of kinnim (gnats) is kan, in the same way that the singular of pittim (morsels) is pat (morsel). He also says that the word ha-kinnam is similar to the word ha-oholi (my tent) (Yehoshua 7:21).
