Do not be amazed that Scripture records that after one spot was struck, all the dust of the earth became gnats throughout all the land of Mitzrayim. Its meaning is that the plague then started. The same is true regarding the plagues of the water and the boils.
And the magicians did so. They struck the dust of the earth.
To bring forth gnats. To cause the earth to bring forth gnats as Aharon did. However, they could not do so.
[And there were gnats upon man, and upon beast.] Scripture notes this a second time because the plague was also upon the magicians.

Then the magicians said. When the magicians saw that unlike the changing of the rod into a serpent and the plague of blood and frogs where they were able to duplicate Aharon’s actions they were now unable to imitate what Aharon had done, they said to Paroh that this plague did not come to liberate Yisrael but was a disaster sent by Elokim in keeping with the arrangements of the stars dealing with Mitzrayim’s fortune. I have previously explained that Paroh did not deny the existence of a Creator. He only denied the existence of the Elokim which Moshe revealed to him. Our verse is explained by, it is not His hand that smote us; it was a chance that happened to us (Shmuel I 6:9) from heaven. Hence Paroh’s heart was hardened. Our interpretation is supported by the fact that the magicians said, This is the finger of Elokim, and not, this is the finger of Hashem, meaning the Elokim of Yisrael, as Paroh did when he exclaimed, Entreat Hashem, with regard to the plague of frogs and then similarly used this term for Elokim in the latter plagues. Furthermore, Moshe told Paroh that the Yeor would be stricken before it was actually plagued, and he likewise informed him that the land would be inundated by frogs before they appeared. However, Moshe did not inform Paroh that a plague of gnats was about to strike.
And the Lord said. It is the custom of kings to go out to the river in the morning, for it is good for the eyes to see water.
I will send. The word mashli’ach (I will send) is in the hifil. It is irregular.
[Swarms of flies.] The word arov (swarms of flies) refers to a mixture of evil beasts such as lions, wolves, bears, and leopards.
[And also the ground.] Uninhabited places.

And I will set apart. Some say that the word ve-hifleti (and I will set apart) is missing an alef. However, I believe that it comes from a root ending in a heh. The meaning of ve-hifleti is, and I will set apart. It is logical to assume that Paroh now started to lighten Yisrael’s burden. When he saw that Hashem put a division between Yisrael and Mitzrayim he feared to harm them. He now saw the need to send them to offer sacrifices to Hashem, lest he fall upon us with pestilence (Shemot 5:3). Don’t you see that he now gave them permission to sacrifice to Hashem in the land of Mitzrayim?

[That I am Hashem in the midst of the earth.] This is a metaphor. It is the manner of kings to establish their residences in the middle of their kingdoms so as to be equidistant to their borders. Hashem similarly placed the heart, which is “king” over man’s body, in the center of the human corporeal frame. Man’s spirit too is located in the center of the body, as it is written, And (Hashem) formed the spirit of man in the midst of him (Zecharyah 12:1). There are many proofs from nature that this is so. Scripture states, Out of Tziyon, the perfection of beauty, Elokim hath shined forth (Tehillim 50:2) because Tziyon is in the center of the inhabited world and Elokim’s presence is seen in the inhabited world.
And I will put a division. The meaning of pedut is a division. The word pidyon (redemption) is always similar in meaning.
And the Lord did so. On the morrow, as Moshe had spoken.
[And there came grievous swarms.] By themselves. This plague was worse than any of the previous plagues.
And Paroh called. It was now clear to Paroh that the plagues came because the children of Yisrael did not offer sacrifices unto the Lord.
[In the land.] In his kingdom and not in any other place.

And Moshe said. Rabbi Yehoshua says that the clause the abomination of the Mitzrim was written to disparage idol worship. What Moshe actually said to Paroh was, “the god of the Mitzrim.” Rabbi Yehoshua further states that the god of Mitzrayim was shaped like a lamb because the Mitzrim believed that the constellation of the lamb ruled over their land. It is because of this that the Mitzrim did not eat meat. However, if the reason for the Mitzrim not eating meat was their worship of the lamb why did they also abstain from ox and goat meat? I believe that the ancient Mitzrim in the time of Moshe had the same belief currently held by the people of Hodu, who make up more than half of the world. All of them are descendants of Cham. They do not eat meat until this very day. These people also do not drink milk or blood or eat fish or eggs. In other words, they do not eat anything coming from a living creature. Furthermore, they abhor any person who eats any of the aforementioned. They consider shepherding to be an especially disgusting type of work. It is similarly written, for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Mitzrim (Bereshit 47:34). They also do not allow any meat-eating person in their country. If any of them goes to a foreign country he will flee from any place where flesh is eaten. They will not eat anything which a meat-eater has handled. They consider his very garments unclean. It is thus written, because the Mitzrim might not eat bread with the Hebrews (Bereshit 43:32). Behold, Potifar placed everything with the exception of the food which he ate under the care of Yosef, who was then living in his house. Potifar would not permit him to touch his food because Yosef was a Hebrew. There is no reason to ask, “If this is so, then why did the Mitzrim keep cattle?” We find the same to be the case in contemporary Hodu. Horses, asses, and camels were used to carry burdens and for riding. Cattle served to pull the plow and sheep were kept for their wool. I will yet speak on this when I discuss the Passover observed in Mitzrayim. Yefet says that an interrogative heh is missing in the phrase ve-lo yiskelunu, for its meaning is, will they not stone us. However, I believe that the word hen (lo) in hen nizbach (lo, we sacrifice) has the same meaning as the interrogative heh. The meaning of our verse thus is: if we sacrifice (hen nizbach) the abomination of the Mitzrim before their eyes, will they not stone us? The word hen in hen hayetah ka-zot (if there hath been such a thing) (Yirmiyahu 2:10) is identical.
We will go three days’ journey into the wilderness. We must remove ourselves from the Mitzrim.
[As he shall command us.] Regarding the type and number of animals to be selected as sacrificial victims.

And Paroh said. The phrase entreat for me should have been placed at the beginning of the verse, as the verse means entreat for me that this plague will be removed and I will let you go to sacrifice in the wilderness as you asked. However, this is on the condition that you go no further than three days’ journey into the desert.

And Moshe said…only let not Paroh deal deceitfully. The word hetel (deal deceitfully) is irregular. A dagesh should have been placed in the tav, for its heh is a root letter. It should have been vocalized like the word dabber (speak) in behold, I cannot speak (Yirmiyahu 1:6). We find the same irregularity in hatel tehatellu vo (mock, will ye mock him) (Iyov 13:9). The correct vocalization of this word is found in the clause va-yehattel ba-hem eliyahu (that Eliyahu mocked them) (Melachim I 18:27). Moshe said, only let not Paroh deal deceitfully any more, because he had promised to let the people go during the plague of the frogs and then didn’t.

And Moshe went out. There are words in Hebrew that have the same meaning in the kal and hifil. These words come in two forms with one meaning. Examples are: va-yetar (and entreated) in and entreated Hashem and ve-hatarti (and I will entreat) in and I will entreat Hashem (v. 25). Similarly moreh (shoot) and yarah (shot) in which I shoot and he shot an arrow (Shmuel I 20:36). However, such words are rare.

And the Lord did. The word va-yasar (and he removed) is grammatically irregular. Roots having a vav as their middle letter are vocalized with a kamatz beneath their first stem letter, i.e., va-yashav (and he returned) and va-yakam (and he got up). However, in cases where the last letter of the root cannot receive a dagesh, i.e., if it is a chet, ayin, or resh, then the first root letter is vocalized with a pattach, as in va-yanach (and rested) in and rested on the seventh day (Shemot 20:11); va-yana (was moved) in and his heart was moved (Is. 7:2); va-yasar (and he turned) in And he turned in unto her (Jud. 4:18). All of the aforementioned applies to words in the kal, because in the hifil roots having a vav as their middle letter are vocalized with a segol beneath their first stem letters in cases where their roots do not end in the letters mentioned above. An example of the aforementioned is va-yashev (and he brought back) in And he brought back all the goods (Bereshit 14:16). Now and he removed is written va-yasar rather than va-yaser. It is like va-yasar (and he took off) in And he took off their chariot wheels (Shemot 14:25). However, it appears that va-yasar is a kal and that va-yasar he-arov (and He removed the swarms of flies) means: and the swarms of flies departed.
And Paroh hardened his heart. He hardened his heart as he did at the plague of the frogs wherein it is written: he hardened his heart (v. 11).

Go in unto Paroh. To his palace. Rabbi Yehudah Ha-Levi says that two plagues were in the water: one, that it turned red and the fish died; two, that frogs arose from it. Two plagues were on the earth: one of gnats and the second the swarms, which were an assortment of wild animals. And it is written, Let the earth bring forth the living creature (Bereshit 1:24). There were likewise two plagues in the air. Murrain is nothing but a change from the normal in the air’s heat or cold. This change causes an untold number to die in an instant, as the spirit of life which resides in the heart depends on the air. The second plague was the boils. Scripture refers to the firmament which is above their heads as the heaven. The seventh plague was a mixture of the sphere of the whirlwind and the sphere of fire. It is thus written, and fire flashing up amidst the hail (v. 24). The eighth was the plague of locusts which the wind brought from afar. The ninth was a wonderful plague in that the light from the two great luminaries and the stars was absent from above the land of Mitzrayim. The tenth was the descent of the destroyer from the spheres of the glory to kill the first-born.
And will hold them still. The word hand or something similar has been omitted. One that holdeth a dog by the ears (Mishlei 26:17) is similar.

Behold, the hand of Hashem is upon. Observe, we find that a yod interchanges with a vav, as elsewhere we read, and thou wouldest be (hoveh) their king (Nechemyah 6:6). The opposite is the case with the vav of kovai (that wait for me) in For they shall not be ashamed that wait for Me (Is. 49:23) which interchanges with a yod in the word ve-kove (but they that wait) in But they that wait for Hashem shall renew their strength (Is. 40:31).

The word dever (murrain) is a collective noun. Its verbal form is found employed only once, in va-tedabber (she destroyed) in she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Yehudah (Divrei Hayamim II 22:10). The book of Melachim reads, va-te’abed (and she destroyed) (Melachim II 11:1). This interpretation is far-fetched. However, we know of no better one.

And Hashem shall make a division…nothing. The word davar (nothing) is used in reference to many words joined together, as in ha-davar (the word) in The word that Hashem spoke to Yirmiyahu (Yirmiyahu 46:13). It is also used in reference to a thing, as in our verse. Davar in thou hast not lacked a thing is similar (Devarim 2:7).
And the Lord appointed. He set a fixed time for the sign to begin.

And Hashem did. The meaning of and all (kol) the cattle of Mitzrayim died is, that most of the cattle of Mitzrayim died. For behold, it is written, Now therefore send, hasten in thy cattle (v. 19). We find the same with regard to the plague of hail. Scripture reads, and the hail smote every herb of the field (v. 25). The plague of locusts concerning which it is written, and they shall eat the residue of that which is escaped, which remaineth unto you from the hail (Shemot 10:5) is proof of this.

So much as one. Ad echad means, as I will explain in the song of Moshe, so much as one. The meaning of our verse is: even though Paroh sent agents and saw that Hashem loves Yisrael and on their account smote his flocks, he was not so bothered by the death of the flocks during this plague as to let Yisrael go. Perhaps the plague did not last a long time.
And it shall become. This was miraculous, that this small amount of soot turned into dust all over the land of Mitzrayim. This plague did not separate out Bnei Yisrael.

Blains. The alef of avabu’ot (blains) is superfluous, as avabu’ot comes from the same root as tiveh (to boil) in And the fire causeth the waters to boil (Is. 64:1). The word is doubled like the words teshasha’u (shall be dandled) (Is. 66:12) and tesagsegi (thou didst make it to grow) (Is. 17:11).

And they took the soot of the furnace. Each as earlier noted took handfuls of soot and Moshe threw all of it heavenward. It is possible that the magicians were not smitten with the plague of frogs and swarms. Through their wisdom and their knowledge of natural law they searched for a way to gain a small respite. However, their knowledge now failed them, as Scripture tells us. Paroh did not ask Moshe and Aharon to entreat the Lord because the plague did not last long. We cannot conclude from the plain meaning of the text that since the first plague lasted for seven days all the other plagues did so too. Additionally, we shall pursue the text of Scripture. It is known that the plague of murrain lasted for one hour and the plague of darkness for three days. There is no way to ascertain in which month Moshe came and the plagues commenced. However, if our holy sages received this via tradition we accept and abide by it.
And Hashem hardened the heart of Paroh. He therefore did not request Moshe to entreat Hashem.
And the Lord said. Scripture does not here note that Paroh went out unto the water. Perhaps he had another reason for rising early.

For. Scripture reads, all My plagues because thunder, hail, rain, and fire combined in this plague. We do not find Paroh to be as afraid of all the passing plagues as he was of this one. He also said, Hashem is righteous (v. 27).
[That there is none like me in all the earth.] This was said in accordance with Mitzri belief that their gods had the power to harm or to benefit.

And smitten. Va-akh (and smitten) is missing a nun. It is like the word ve-at (though I was offering) in Though I was offering them food (Hoshea 11:4). They are both the same. Their roots are nun, tet, heh and nun, kaf, heh.

[Pestilence.] Scripture reads, ba-dever (with pestilence) because it refers to the well-known pestilence. It means: I would have killed all of you along with your cattle with the pestilence with which I smote them.

But in very deed for this cause have I made thee to stand. Scripture goes on to explain the meaning of zot (this). It means to show thee My power. And out of the midst thereof as the color of electrum, out of the midst of the fire (Yechezkel 1:4) is similar. However, Yefet says that its meaning is, for this plague, the reference being to the plague of hail.

[And that my name may be declared throughout all the earth.] This does not refer to Paroh. On the contrary, the word sapper (be declared) is an infinitive like the word kabbed (promote) in for I will promote thee unto very great honor (Bamidbar 22:17). Its meaning is not that Paroh will go all over the world to declare Hashem’s glory, but rather that Hashem’s name would be declared from generation to generation because of the signs which He performed.

As yet exaltest thou thyself against my people. Mistolel (exaltest) means praises. It comes from the same root as the word salseleha (extol her) in Extol her, and she will exalt thee (Mishlei 4:8). Now even though its first root letter is doubled it still belongs among the double roots. It is similar to the word solu (extol) in Extol him that rideth upon the skies (Tehillim 68:5). Likewise ve-gilgaltikha (and roll thee down) (Yirmiyahu 51:25) is similar to mitgolel (wallowing) (Shmuel II 20:12) and golu (roll). However, Rabbi Merinus says that the meaning of mistolel (exaltest) is strengthens and comes from the same root as mesillot in And the king made of the sandalwood pillars (mesillot) for the house of Hashem (Divrei Hayamim II 9:11). Elsewhere it is written, And the king made of the sandalwood pillars (misad) for the house of Hashem (Melachim I 10:12).

I will cause it to rain. It is well known that even today neither rain nor hail comes down upon the land of Mitzrayim. There is no need to explain why this is so. The same is still true of many other places. It was because of this that the Mitzrim were greatly afraid, for with the exception of something resembling dew, nothing rains down there.
Send hasten. The word ha-ez (hasten) means make to flee or gather. He-izu (flee) in The inhabitants of Gevim flee to cover (Is. 10:31) is similar.
He that feared…made flee. On that very day.

And he that regarded not. There is a meaning in Arabic for the vav of va-ya’azov (left). However, it is not in our power to translate it into another language. Va-yissa (lifted up his eyes) in, On the third day Avraham lifted up his eyes (Bereshit 22:4) is similar. There are many other similar instances.

And the Lord said. From a strictly logical point of view it appears that the stretching forth of his hand was with his rod. Behold, it is written afterwards, And Moshe stretched forth his rod toward heaven, that is, in the air above. In the open firmament of heaven (Bereshit 1:20) is similar.
And fire ran down. Va-tihalakh (ran down) is a kal form. It expresses going.
Unto the earth. Contrary to its nature, which is to go up.
And fire flashing up amidst the hail. A miracle within a miracle.

And the hail smote. This was a very strong plague, for it killed man and beast and broke every tree of the field. However, Hashem pitied them and their cattle. Moshe did not mention this to Paroh because he saw that Paroh sent agents and learned that there was not even one of the cattle of Bnei Yisrael dead, and yet did not take this to heart.
And called. Paroh said, I have sinned, because he was greatly afraid that he, as was told to him, would be destroyed by the pestilence.

Entreat Hashem. Paroh made mention of the glorious name and referred to kolot Elokim (noises from Elokim) because he, as I have already noted, admitted to the existence of a Deity. Moshe combined the proper and adjectival names and said, “Hashem Elokim” (YHVH / Adonai Elokim) because Paroh did not employ the term kolot YHVH / Adonai. The meaning of YHVH / Adonai Elokim is: Hashem alone is Elokim. We never find Moshe employing this phrase in the entire Torah. The term Adonai Elokim in O Hashem Elokim, Thou hast begun (Devarim 3:24) does not refute the aforementioned, as Adonai is written there with an alef, dalet.
And Moshe said unto him: as soon as I am gone out of the city. The commentaries say that Moshe was unable to spread forth his hands in Mitzrayim because it was filled with idols.
That the earth is Hashem’s. Not yours.

But as for thee. Rabbi Shlomo says that the meaning of terem tire’un (ye will not yet fear) is: you do not fear. He interprets terem yishkavu (but before they lay down) (Bereshit 19:4) similarly. However, the meaning of this word is not as he imagined, as the subject always follows. Following terem yishkavu (but before they lay down) Scripture reads, the men of the city, even the men of Sedom, compassed the house round: its meaning is, at the time when they lay down they compassed the house round. The word terem (before) in before they call, I will answer (Is. 65:24) and terem (before) in Yea before the fat was made to smoke (Shmuel I 2:15) are similar. The same applies to all times the word terem is used. Thus terem never has the meaning of no. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon of blessed memory connected the whole subject. He explained it as follows. Moshe said to Paroh, I shall pray for the hail to be removed. However, what it destroyed, it destroyed.

The meaning of And the flax and the barley were smitten is, the flax and barley shall not return and I shall not pray for their recovery. Behold, its meaning is, before you fear Hashem and confess and say Hashem is righteous, the barley and flax shall already be smitten. This vav, as I have noted, is correctly used according to the Arabic. However, in my opinion a word has been omitted, its interpretation being: before I spread my hands you will fear Hashem, viz., you and your servants. Moshe was being polite. Its implication is, when the plague is removed you will rebel. Therefore Scripture notes afterwards, and (Paroh) hardened his heart, he and his servants. We do not find this in any other place.

And the flax and the barley. Scripture relates what happened. It is clear from the word nukkatah (were smitten) and also from the word nukku (were smitten) (v. 32) that the root of makkeh (smite) is nun, kaf, heh. It is similar to the words shuppu (corrode) and ru’u (unsightliness) in And his bones corrode to unsightliness (Iyov 33:21).
They ripen late. Afilot (ripen late) is an adjective. The word afel (darkness), as in, darkness, and not light, is close in meaning to it. It means that they were beneath the earth and unseen.

Poured. Nittakh (poured) is used in the same sense as ke-hittukh (as is melted) in As silver is melted in the midst of the furnace (Yechezkel 22:22). It is a nifal like the word niggash (drew near) in but Moshe drew near unto the thick darkness (Shemot 20:18).
And when Paroh saw. Scripture now mentions, he sinned yet more, because Paroh confessed and said, I have sinned this time (v. 27).
[And hardened his heart, he and his servants.] From this, Moshe’s words, But as for thee and thy servants (v. 30), become clear.
And the heart of Paroh was hardened. Though he feared this plague more than the earlier ones.

Go in unto Paroh. Go in unto him this time and do not be astonished that he has hardened his heart until now, For I have hardened his heart, and the heart of his servants. God mentioned the heart of his servants because their hearts would mellow with the coming of the plague of the locusts.

[For I have hardened his heart.] Its meaning is: I have hardened his heart that I might show these My signs in the midst of them. The Spanish scholars differ with regard to the word shiti (I might show). Some say that shiti is similar to binu (consider) (Devarim 32:7), simu (set) (Bereshit 43:21), and other such words. The same is the case with yashit (he will put), yasim (he will place), yavin (he will understand), and comparable words in all of their forms. Others hold that shiti is a hifil minus the sign of the form, because they found the words yasum (maketh) and la-sus (rejoice) in who maketh a man dumb (Shemot 4:11) and for the Lord will again rejoice over thee for good, as He rejoiced over thy fathers (Devarim 30:9), all of which are kals. Others say that yasis is similar to yasus (he will rejoice) and shiti to sumi (set). They are all kals. In Shemot 12:9 we find: “Behold, I the writer add to the words of this sage as I heard from his mouth.”

And that thou mayest tell. Hashem spoke to Moshe, who is equivalent to all of Yisrael. Similarly, that ye may know that I am Hashem means that all Yisrael shall know the aforementioned. The Torah speaks in human terms when it says, I have wrought, for it pictures Hashem as acting as a human being who arranges events in order to avenge himself upon another.

And Moshe and Aharon went in. We know that Moshe would not come in unto Paroh unless Aharon was with him, as Aharon was his spokesman. Scripture here mentions Moshe and Aharon because now, unlike any of the other instances of the plagues, they were both returned to and finally expelled from the presence of Paroh.
To humble. Le’anot (to humble) is a nifal. It comes from the same root as ani (humble).

Locusts. Arbeh (locusts) is the name of a type of locust. Perhaps it is so called because it is more numerous than other kinds of locusts. Scripture states, That which the palmer-worm (gazam) hath left hath the locust (arbeh) eaten (Yoel 1:4). Concerning it, Scripture states, My great army which I sent among you (Yoel 2:25). If this be the case then the alef of arbeh is superfluous.
And they shall cover. Metaphorically speaking.

That one shall not be able to see. The word ish (a man) has been omitted. Yefet says that many days passed between the plague of hail and the plague of locusts, for Scripture states: which groweth for you out of the field.

Shall be filled. This word is irregularly used in the Hebrew language. The meaning of u-male’u (shall be filled) is that the houses were full of locusts. However, we also find mile’u (fill) in Fill four jars with water (Melachim I 18:34) wherein mile’u is a transitive verb. It is as if it were vocalized with a pattach beneath the mem and a dagesh in the lamed and belonged to the conjugational form that receives a dagesh.

[And he turned.] Rabbi Yehoshua says that va-yifen (and he turned) refers to Moshe, who paid his respects to the throne by facing the king and walking out backwards. However, Yefet says that Moshe finished his duties. So too u-fanita (and thou shalt turn) in and thou shalt turn in the morning (Devarim 16:7). However, what shall Yefet do with the word va-yifen (and he looked) in And he looked this way and that way (Shemot 2:12)? Va-yifen is to be explained as coming from the same root as panim (face). It has the same meaning as va-yar (and he saw). Now Moshe left the presence of Paroh without his permission. Scripture notes this because Paroh asked that Moshe and Aharon be brought back. After they were returned Paroh, in anger, commanded that they be driven out.
And Paroh’s servants said. The meaning of ha-terem teda (knowest thou not yet) is: do you first want it to become clear to you that Mitzrayim is destroyed.

Were brought again. The word et indicates the thing itself. Now whether one says ha-adam ohavi (the man loves me), in which the yod is a first person pronominal suffix, or he says ha-adam ohev oti (the man loves me), the reference being to my very self, the meaning is one and the same. Therefore, if someone says re’uven harag et shimon (Reuven killed Shimon) he is telling us that Shimon has been slain. However, the same is the case if he says, re’uven harag shimon (Reuven killed Shimon). Ve-rav ya’avod tza’ir (and the elder shall serve the younger) (Bereshit 25:23) and asher bara Elokim adam (that Elokim created man) (Devarim 4:32) are similar. Do not think that et indicates the direct object because it is often found to be so used. It is also found before the subject, as in u-va ha-ari ve-et ha-dov (and when there came a lion, or a bear) (Shmuel I 17:34) and many other similar cases. Rabbi Yehudah the grammarian says that Scripture reads, va-yushav (were brought again) rather than va-yushevu (were brought again) because of the word et. However, I believe that Scripture reads, va-yushav because Moshe was the most important one. Scripture similarly reads, va-tedabber miriam ve-aharon (And Miriam and Aharon spoke) (Bamidbar 12:1) because Miriam was the main speaker.
For we must hold a feast unto Hashem. All of us are obligated to sacrifice unto Hashem.
So be Hashem with you. Whom you say is with you.

[See ye that evil is before your face.] The evil is close to you and is before your face. This meaning is also to be connected to for that is what ye desire (v. 11). Hence it is only right that I so act. At this point Paroh surmised that they wanted to flee. Note that our Master Moshe did not go so far as to lie and say that Yisrael would return. He merely said that they would travel a three days’ journey (Shemot 9:23). However, the Mitzrim thought that they would return. Hence they let them have what they asked. Moshe had another reason for acting in this manner. Had Paroh given Yisrael permission to go and Yisrael did not return, Paroh would not have pursued them. However, Hashem commanded Moshe to act in this manner so that Paroh would chase after them and drown. Behold, this is clearly stated, that they turn back and encamp before Pi Hachirot (Shemot 14:2). One should not question the acts of Hashem, as He does everything with wisdom, though it be hidden from the eyes even of wise men. We find a similarity in the account of David, viz., And it shall be, when thou hearest the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry-trees, that then thou shalt bestir thyself; for then is Hashem gone out before thee to smite the host of the Plishtim (Shmuel II 5:24).
Not so; go now ye that are men. The word gever (man), unlike the word adam (man), always refers to a man in Scripture.
For that is what ye desire. The above-noted evil.

For the locusts. Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that ba-arbeh (for the locusts) indicates that Moshe placed a locust on the rod. However, this is incorrect. The correct interpretation of ba-arbeh is: so that the locusts would come.

An east wind. Kadim (east) is an adjective, since kedemah mizrachah (the east side) is a noun. Kadim is so called because it is the first of the sides because the sun begins to shine there. Hence the west is termed achor (hinder side). Compare, Behold, I go forward (kedem), but He is not there, And backward (achor), but I cannot perceive Him (Iyov 23:8).
Brought the locusts. From its place and deposited them in all the kingdom of Mitzrayim.
Went up. Neither after them shall be such was prophetically written.
For they covered the face of the whole earth. The meaning of so the land was darkened is that the locusts intervened between the sun and the land. The land is always dark.
Then Paroh called for Moshe and Aharon in haste. Via his messengers. Paroh added, I have sinned, because he drove them away from his presence in disgrace.
Now therefore forgive, I pray thee. I will explain the term sa na (forgive, I pray thee) in the Torah portion Ki Tissa.
[Only this once.] Because I will not sin again by rebelling against Hashem. Paroh did not promise to free the people because Moshe was angry. Moshe went out of the city as was his wont and prayed.

And Hashem turned an exceeding strong west wind. West is termed yam in the holy tongue because the great sea which goes out from Spain and passes by the land of Mitzrayim and goes on to the Land of Yisrael lies in the west. This sea is not to be identified with the Atlantic Ocean because Yisrael did not inherit that much territory. The Spanish Sea is called the great sea because it is three hundred Parsi miles wide, whereas none of the seas in the Land of Yisrael such as the Sea of Reeds, the Kineret, and the Salt Sea is even thirty Parsi miles wide.
But the Lord hardened. This is to be understood à la the words of our sages of blessed memory who said, “The door is opened for one who comes to defile himself.”
And the Lord said. We may logically assume although it is not so stated that Moshe’s staff was in his hand.

Even darkness which may be felt. Yefet says that ve-yamesh (which may be felt) is like ve-yamish (and it shall depart); its meaning is: that the darkness to which they have become accustomed shall depart and another type of darkness, thicker than it, shall come. Others say that ve-yamesh is missing an alef. Now the word emesh in the holy tongue refers to the previous night, like emesh (yesternight) in spoke unto me yesternight (Bereshit 31:29). It is the same case with the Arabic ams, as the shin and samekh interchange in most of the words. Now their interpretation makes no sense. I believe that ve-yamesh comes from the same root as yemashesh (gropeth) (Devarim 28:29). One cannot argue that yemashesh comes from a double root because with regard to something very similar Scripture uses the term yemishun (handle) in They have hands but handle not (Tehillim 115:7). Ve-yamesh refers to Mitzrayim, Mitzrayim being in the singular, as in so Mitzrayim said I will flee (Shemot 14:25). Now the meaning of ve-yamesh choshekh (even darkness which may be felt) is that the Mitzrim will feel the darkness with their hands, for the darkness shall be so thick that neither a candle nor a fire shall give off light. They saw not one another (v. 23) neither by the light of day nor by candlelight is proof of the aforementioned.

And Moshe stretched forth. The Mitzrim had no way of knowing that three days passed except through Bnei Yisrael, who had light. Now there are times when a thick darkness comes over the Atlantic Ocean during which time it is impossible for a person to distinguish between day and night. The aforementioned occasionally lasts for as long as five days. I myself have been there many times.
Neither rose any from his place. From his house, as in abide ye every man in his place (Shemot 16:29). For where could they go without light?
And Paroh called. After three days when they saw light.

Only let your flocks and your herds be stayed. Paroh wanted to know what was in Moshe’s mind. He wanted to learn whether Moshe planned to escape. Paroh said, let your little ones also go with you because Moshe had earlier told him, We will go with our young and with our old (v. 9).
Thou must also give into our hand sacrifices and burnt-offerings. You are obligated to give into our hands sacrifices and burnt offerings to be brought on the altar on your behalf.

There shall not a hoof be left behind. Of any kind that are among our cattle, as we do not know which kind we are to choose and how many of them we will sacrifice. This is the meaning of we know not with what we must serve.
But Hashem hardened Paroh’s heart. In a manner similar to for Hashem thy Hashem hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate (Devarim 2:30).
Thou shalt die. You will deserve to be put to death for rebelling against the king.
Thou hast spoken well. Ken (well) here has the same meaning as ken (right) in The daughters of Tzelofchad speak right (Bamidbar 27:6).
I will see thy face again no more. For I will never come to you again.

And Hashem spoke. The chapter opening with the words, Thus saith Hashem (v. 4) should have been connected to the previous verse. However, the chapter stating, Yet one plague more was inserted between them. The reason for this is that Scripture wanted to teach us when Thus saith Hashem was told to Moshe. It was related to Moshe while he was yet in Midyan, viz., Behold, I will slay thy son, thy first-born (Shemot 4:23). Moshe was commanded on Mount Sinai that when the time came for the plague of the first-born to arrive, every man should ask jewels of his neighbor. I have already explained why it is there written, but every woman shall ask of her neighbor (Shemot 3:22) and here it is written, and let them ask every man of his neighbor. Now the meaning of And Hashem said unto Moshe: Yet one plague more will I bring is that Hashem had already told this to Moshe. There are many such cases in Scripture. Hashem said, he shall surely thrust you out, in keeping with His statement, and by a strong hand shall he drive them out of his land (Shemot 6:1).
Speak now. I have already explained that the word na means now.
And Hashem gave. Scripture relates that Hashem kept his promise to Moshe: of And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Mitzrim (Shemot 3:21).
[Moreover the man Moshe.] For many let them have what they asked out of respect for Moshe.
And in the sight of the people. The people of Mitzrayim.

About midnight. Some grammarians say that ka-chatzot (about midnight) is an infinitive. Its meaning is, when it shall be exactly one half of the night. They want to compare ka-chatzot ha-laylah (about midnight) to ba-chatzi ha-laylah (at midnight) in And it came to pass at midnight (Shemot 12:29). Now it is common knowledge that it is beyond the ken of a wise man to ascertain the exact moment of noon without great effort and the use of large copper instruments. It goes without saying that it is much harder to ascertain the more difficult time of midnight. I believe that there is no need for all of this since the meaning of ka-chatzot ha-laylah (about midnight) is, when the first half of the night has passed. The same is the case with ba-chatzi ha-laylah in And it came to pass at midnight (Shemot 12:29). It refers to the remaining half of the night. And it came to pass at midnight (ba-chatzi ha-laylah) (Rut 3:8) and At midnight (chatzot laylah) I will rise to give thanks to thee (Tehillim 119:62) are convincing proof of this.
[Will I go out.] The reference is to the decree that goes out from Hashem.

The first-born of Paroh that sitteth upon his throne. Who is fit to sit upon Paroh’s throne after him. Moshe mentioned the most honored of all the Mitzrim, namely, the son of their lord whom all of them serve and also the meanest of them all, namely, the first-born of the maid-servant, who is himself a slave.

[That is behind the mill.] Who grinds. Compare, And he did grind in the prison house (Jud. 16:21). I have already explained that the prophets are not careful in preserving the exact wording but are rather concerned with reproducing meanings. The words hagmi’ini (give me to drink) (Bereshit 24:17) and hashkini (give me to drink) (Bereshit 29:45); zakhor (remember) (Shemot 20:8) and shamor (observe) (Devarim 5:12); sheker (false) (Shemot 20:13) and shav (false) (Devarim 5:17); lo tachmod (thou shalt not covet) (Shemot 20:14) and ve-lo titavveh (neither shalt thou covet) (Devarim 5:18) have one meaning. I will yet discuss this when I comment on the prayer of Moshe (Shemot 32:9). Now, the first-born of the maid-servant means the same as the first-born of the captive (Shemot 12:29). The captive woman is a maid-servant who sleeps in the dungeon at night as prisoners do, as was noted by Yosef when he said, that they should put me into the dungeon (Bereshit 40:15).

And there shall be a great cry. We do not find Scripture elsewhere stating anything like kamohu lo nihyatah ve-khamohu lo tosif (such as there hath been none like it, nor shall be like it anymore). The word al (over) has been omitted from our verse and the clause should be understood literally as follows: such as over it there hath been none like it, nor such over it shall be like it a cry anymore.
Such as like it (kamohu) refers to havoc, calamity, death, and the like.

Shall not a dog whet his tongue. To frighten them. None whetted his tongue against any of the children of Yisrael (Yehoshua 10:21) is similar. Its meaning is that no dog shall bark at them or bite them. Now no dog shall whet his tongue at them or their cattle here on earth. How much more so when He sends a destroyer from heaven to smite their first-born?
And all these thy servants shall come down unto me…saying. On your behalf.

And all the people that follow thee. Be-raglekha (follow thee) means: who are under your dominion. For I will lead them to the place which I desire. And there went up ten thousand at his feet (be-raglav) (Jud. 4:10) is similar. Moshe went out in hot anger because Paroh had told him, see my face no more (Shemot 10:28).
And Hashem said. According to the manner of the Hebrews and the rules of language this is to be rendered: and Hashem had already said. There are many other such instances.

And Moshe. Even though Moshe and Aharon did all these wonders which are mentioned in Scripture, Paroh’s heart did not soften and he did not let them go, because Hashem hardened his heart. The chapter opening with the words, And it came to pass at midnight (Shemot 12:29) should by right have followed next so that the plagues would be described in order. However, the chapter dealing with, This is the ordinance of the Passover (chap. 12) was inserted in the middle to inform us how the first-born of Yisrael were saved when the destroyer came upon Mitzrayim.

And Hashem spoke. Scripture now mentions the first of the commandments given via Moshe and Aharon, as they alone were prophets of the law. After them, except for extenuating circumstances as in the case of Gidon and Eliyahu, no new precepts were revealed. Do not take the chanting of psalms in the house of Hashem instituted by David to heart, as the latter was an enactment and an institution established by David and Shlomo. Thus Scripture states, by their beliefs (Divrei Hayamim II 9:22), and not by their prophecies. However, Saadiah Gaon says that they had a tradition going back to Moshe that a king would arise and innovate musical compositions. Neither carry forth a burden out of your houses on the sabbath day (Yirmiyahu 17:22) is similar.

This month. Rabbi Yehudah Ha-Parsi says that Bnei Yisrael, like the uncircumcised, employed a solar calendar. He offers as proof, Thou shalt therefore keep this ordinance in its season (Shemot 13:10). But lunar years are not all equal, as the seasons of plowing and harvest are dependent solely on the movement of the sun as it travels to the north or the south. However, he did not speak correctly. I will now explain. We know that it takes the moon, moving in its sphere in a given point facing the sphere of the zodiac, close to twenty-seven and a third days to return to this very point. Now let us assume a starting point wherein the moon is in conjunction with the sun at the beginning of Aries. In such a case the moon would not find the sun at the head of Aries when it returned there because the sun, traveling in its mean motion, would by then have journeyed twenty-seven degrees. This is because, contrary to the movement above, the sun and the moon move from west to east. The sun and the moon would next be in conjunction at the end of twenty-nine and a half days, two-thirds and seventy-three parts of an hour, according to the way Bnei Yisrael divide the hour. Thus the moon would have traveled the very degrees that the sun journeyed, and the moon also would have had to travel two days and close to five hours in the parts in which the sun had moved. Actually, the year belongs only to the sun, as the sun gives birth to the four seasons of the year, cold, heat, summer, and winter. Now let us assume the sun to be at the beginning of Aries. It will then travel three hundred and sixty-five days plus close to a quarter of a day in its sphere until it returns a second time to where it started out. It is for this reason that a year is called a shanah. Now the moon has no year, as the sun has no month. Nothing new happens to the sun; only to the light of the moon does something new occur. It is because of this that a month is called a chodesh and also a yerach. It is so called because the light of the moon is renewed. We have conclusive proof that the moon has no light of its own, and that its light comes from the sun. The sun therefore does not darken except in the moment when it is in conjunction with the moon at the head or the tail of Aries. Similarly, the moon does not darken except when it is opposite the sun in the aforementioned places at night. Due to the fact that the year of the uncircumcised is close to a solar year and because they saw that the moon is renewed twelve times during a solar year, they divided the days of the year into twelve parts and called each part a month because it is close to the days of a lunar month. This arrangement of theirs is not in keeping with the laws of nature. Similarly the Moslems, because their festivals are contingent upon lunar months and a month starts from the night that the moon is first seen. They saw that there are twelve months in a solar year and they did not find a closer way of reckoning than this, as there is only a difference of eleven days between the two ways of numbering the year. They therefore made all of their years lunar. The time of their Passover recedes each year by eleven days until thirty-three solar years equal thirty-four lunar years. These things are not based on the laws of nature. Now Hashem commanded in His Torah that the festivals be kept in their seasons, for He said, Observe the month of spring and keep the passover unto Hashem thy Hashem (Devarim 16:1). Now if spring is not found by half of the month then we make Passover in the month close to it. Hashem similarly called the festival of Sha’vu’ot, the feast of harvest (Shemot 23:16) and the festival of Sukkot, the feast of ingathering (Ibid.). The harvest and the ingathering are dependent on spring. Furthermore, we see that Hashem said that we should not observe the Passover on any day but the midpoint of a lunar month. The same applies to the festival of Sukkot. Hashem thus commanded that we observe lunar months and that the seasons of the festivals be preserved. Moshe did not mention in the Torah that we should count twelve or thirteen months. He said only that we should begin the count in the month that we find spring. That month is to be called the first month whether the year has twelve or thirteen months. It is thus written, in the second month (Bamidbar 10:11) and In the third month (Shemot 19:1). All the other months are similarly written. Nisan, Iyyar, Sivan, and all the other names of the months are not Hebrew. They are Kasdi terms. We therefore do not encounter these terms in any book of Scripture except in the Scroll of Esther and in the prophecies of Zecharyah, Daniel, and Ezra, who were in the Diaspora. This then is its meaning: in the first month, which is called Nisan in the Kasdi tongue. However, we find three months called by other names in Hebrew, viz., in the month Ziv (Melachim I 6:1); in the month Ethanim (Melachim I 8:2); in the month Bul (Melachim I 6:7). If we pursue the literal meaning of the text the month of Ziv is not Nisan but Iyyar, for it is written, in the month Ziv, which is the second month (Melachim I 6:1), that is, which is known as the second to the first of the months of Yisrael. The words of Shlomo’s reign (Ibid.) are not connected to the word month but rather to the fourth year of Shlomo’s reign (Ibid.), as we do not find the months related in the account of any king. Scripture only reports the year that the king started his reign. In the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign recorded in Chronicles (Divrei Hayamim II 3:2) is proof of this. We can refute Yehudah Ha-Parsi with the argument that not all years are equal. The years differ, due to the effect of the planets, in that the rain increases or diminishes and the heat or cold increases or diminishes each month, making it different from the known norm. Spring is therefore not be found to have arrived when the sun returns to the spot that it was in at the beginning of the previous year although it was then spring. There is more than a year and two weeks between one spring and the next. Bnei Yisrael therefore relied on the spring found in their country in whatever month it occurred, as the time of the appearance of spring varies in all countries according to the distance of that land from the equator. I will now give you a general rule. Although Bnei Yisrael in the time of the Holy Temple watched for the arrival of spring, the establishment of a leap year was not in their hands. It rather depended on the Bet Din which, as is related in the Mishnah, looked for other things besides spring. Now Moshe did not explain to us in the Torah how we should establish years or months. Neither did he tell us what we should do if we do not find it to be spring. One can pose a difficult question from all this, namely, why did Moshe explain the laws of the plagues of the leper, which fall upon one person and do not last forever, and leave out of the Torah the laws of the festivals that all of Yisrael is obligated to keep at all times? Furthermore, eating leaven on Passover and eating on the Day of Atonement are punished with excision. If Moshe relied on the conjunction of the moon and sun he should have explained whether he meant according to the moon’s mean motion or its true conjunction, which takes place opposite the sphere of the constellations, because at times there are approximately fourteen hours between the calculated conjunction and the true conjunction. It is because of this that our holy fathers said, “At times it comes at longer intervals; at times it comes at shorter intervals.” Only one who knows his way in the science of astronomy can know this. Additionally, Moshe should have explained from which part of the earth we reckon the conjunction. For behold, between Yerushalayim and this city, whose name is Lucca, there is more than three hours. If Moshe relied on the time the moon is first seen he should have explained the place of its sighting, as the Arc of Vision changes in each place according to the earth’s latitude and according to the latitude of the moon from the line of the constellations, in addition to changes in visibility due to longitude, latitude, atmospheric conditions, and the height of elevation or lack thereof. All of these things require lengthy exposition. Now if it is cloudy, shall we out of doubt observe the new moon for two days? This proves that the establishment of the new moon is contingent on the declaration of the Bet Din in each generation. They had a tradition that the Bet Din establish seven leap years every nineteen years, totaling two hundred and thirty-five months or six thousand, nine hundred and thirty-nine and two-thirds days, plus five hundred and ninety-five parts of an hour. The aforementioned are nineteen solar years without addition or subtraction. Do not concern yourself with the hour and four hundred and eighty-five parts of an hour according to “Shmuel’s calendar.” We know that this was not hidden from him. Shmuel only used a number which was close in his time to the men of his generation. Today there is a difference of close to nine days between the true circuit and Shmuel’s circuit. Do not be amazed at this. For behold the Braita states that one who wants to know the place of the moon should calculate the year of the world and divide it into months and divide the months into twenty-nine and a half days and two-thirds of an hour, i.e., seven hundred and twenty parts of an hour. Now seventy-three parts are missing. They will add up to more than two-thirds of a day each cycle. There will thus be a difference of close to half a year between the calculation of the conjunctions from creation and our own calculation of the conjunction. It has thus been made clear to you that the sum of our years equals out every cycle of solar years, and our months are always lunar months. Blessed be Hashem who has guided me in the straight path. I will now offer you proof from Scripture that the festivals are dependent upon the Bet Din. Scripture states, For the kinghad taken counsel, and his princes, and all the congregation in Yerushalayim, to keep the passover in the second month (Divrei Hayamim II 30:2). Now if they had a tradition to look for spring, as those who argue with our rabbis of blessed memory claim, why did the king take counsel to establish the Passover in the second month? It will now be shown if their words are true. Chizkiyahu did three evils. First of all, he did not offer the Passover sacrifice in its time although he was ritually clean. Why did Chizkiyahu delay the observance of Passover because most of the congregation had not arrived? Such a thing is only found in the words of tradition, not in Scripture. Second, he ate and caused Yisrael to eat leaven in the first month. Third, on his own he decided to observe the festival of unleavened bread in the second month. Such a thing is not to be done. With the exception of eating the paschal lamb on one night, Hashem did not command the observance of the Passover in the second month, for all those who are unclean eat unleavened bread along with all of Yisrael in the first month. Far be it for Chizkiyahu to do such evil. Moreover, Scripture says of him that he did not turn aside to the right or left from the commandments of Hashem. Furthermore, Chizkiyahu himself said in his prayer, Remember now, O Hashem, I beseech Thee, how I have walked before Thee…and have done that which is good in Thy sight (Melachim II 20:3). I will now explain. Know that Chizkiyahu took counsel with the entire congregation at the start of the first month that they should observe the Passover in the following month because most of the people had not arrived and the priests had not sanctified themselves in sufficient numbers. He thus added a month to the year, and the Passover that he observed was the actual Passover in its proper season. The fact that Hashem plagued those who ate the paschal lamb in a manner contrary to what is written is proof of this. If the Passover observed by Chizkiyahu was not celebrated in its proper time and was therefore not acceptable to Hashem, why did He plague them? If Chizkiyahu sinned how is it that he prayed on their behalf and Hashem accepted his supplication and healed the people? The answer to one who would argue that the sages of blessed memory did not maintain that Chizkiyahu acted properly in adding another month during the month of Nisan is: they spoke the truth. It is the custom of every Bet Din to ascertain at the end of the month of Adar whether it is necessary to add another month to the year or not. Now Chizkiyahu did not do this; he committed a small error in adding another month to the year at the beginning of the month. Now since the additional month always comes before the first month, the latter is always the first of the months, and the festivals will fall in the seventh month from it. This is the meaning of it shall be the first month of the year to you (v. 2). We know that many commandments are in memory of the Exodus from Mitzrayim. Behold, it is therefore fitting that the Exodus be the first reference point in Yisrael’s calculations. Thus it is written, And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Yisrael were come out of the land of Mitzrayim, in the fourth year…in the month Ziv, which is the second month (Melachim I 6:1). The gentiles ask, if the year is made up of months and the month of spring is its foundation and beginning, why do you calculate your years from the seventh month and say that a new year begins on its first day? The answer is that our sages of blessed memory have already noted that there are four new year days. We clearly see that the sanctification of the jubilee year is on the tenth day of the seventh month (Vayikra 25:9). Furthermore, Hashem commanded that the Torah be read in the set time of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles (Devarim 31:10)…that they may hear, and that they may learn (Devarim 31:12). Now if the beginning of the year of release is reckoned from Nisan, why didn’t Hashem command that the Torah be read during the festival of unleavened bread? Now they were idle for half a year. Furthermore, Scripture states, and the feast of ingathering at the turn of the year (Shemot 34:22). Elsewhere it states, at the end of the year, when thou gatherest in thy labors out of the field (Shemot 23:16). Additionally, we can derive the aforementioned from the way the Torah speaks and from the way nature acts. The Torah first states, ye shall not sow and afterwards says, neither (shall ye) reap (Vayikra 25:12). The season of sowing is close to Tishrei, not Nisan. Furthermore, if we reckon the beginning of the year of release from Nisan he who sowed in the sixth year will not harvest in the seventh year, because the harvest falls after Nisan when the year of release has already started. He will also not sow in the year of release. We thus see that the words of our sages are correct.

The beginning of months. Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that there is no need to use the term rosh chodesh (new moon). The term chodesh suffices, since the meaning of chodesh is the day that the light of the moon is renewed. Scripture thus states, chodesh ve-shabbat (New moon and sabbath) (Is. 1:13); chodshekhem u-mo’adekhem (your new moons and your appointed seasons) (Is. 1:14); mi-de chodesh be-chodsho (from one new moon to another) (Is. 66:23). Others argued with him and asked, if this be the case, then why does Scripture state, ba-chodesh hashe’vi’i be-echad la-chodesh (And in the seventh month, on the first day of the month) (Bamidbar 29:1)? Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen answered, to remove doubt. They also quoted, u-ve-roshe chodshekhem (and in your new moons) (Bamidbar 28:11) against him. He answered that Scripture speaks of the month of Nisan throughout the years, for only Nisan is the chief new moon. They then asked him, if so, then what sacrifices are we to offer on other new moons? He answered that Scripture states in the very same portion, This is the burnt-offering of every new moon throughout the months of the year (Bamidbar 28:14). Scripture likewise states, Also in the day of your gladness, and in your appointed seasons, and in your new moons (u-ve-roshe chodshekhem), ye shall blow with the trumpets (Bamidbar 10:10) because it is the beginning of the year. However, we will not set aside the words of our rabbis of blessed memory because of our own opinions. Our sages said that we sound the trumpets on the new moon of every month. It is correct to say chodesh or rosh chodesh. It is written, ad chodesh yamim (but a whole month) (Bamidbar 11:20), the meaning of which is: until the days of the month are complete.
Speak ye unto all the congregation of the children of Yisrael. For all those who are obligated to observe the commandments are required to do this.

They shall take. Whoever has cattle shall take from his cattle, as Bnei Yisrael had a lot of cattle. Or yikchu (they shall take) means they shall buy. Yefet says that they should start preparing the lamb on the tenth day and do so till the fourteenth day. However, we do not know whether this is a command for all generations or pertained only to the Passover observed in Mitzrayim.
A lamb, according to their fathers’ houses. If they be few.

A lamb for a household. If they be many. After stating, a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, Scripture says a lamb for each and every household. I have already explained the meaning of bayit (household) at the beginning of this book.
And if the household be too little for a lamb. Too little to eat a lamb because the members of the household are few. Then he and his neighbor shall take a lamb.

According to the number of the souls. Mikhsat (number of) means a portion. The word mekhes (tribute) in And Hashem’s tribute (Bamidbar 31:37) in which mekhes refers to the portion which each one shall take, is similar. So too the word kosi (portion) in O Hashem, the share of mine inheritance and my portion (Tehillim 16:5). This is also the meaning of takhosu (ye shall make your count). It comes from a double root. The doubled letter is missing in the word be-mikhsat and also in mekhes. Scripture follows the paradigm of memer (bitterness) in And bitterness to her that bore him (Mishlei 17:25), which comes from a double root in its vocalization of mekhes.

Your lamb shall be without blemish. It shall be without any deformity. The word seh (lamb) also applies to the two kinds taken in by the term tzon (flock). Sehkhevasim ve-seh izzim (the sheep and the goat) (Devarim 14:4) is similar. Rabbi Moshe ben Amram Ha-Parsi says that the obligation to offer a lamb only pertains to the Passover brought in Mitzrayim. However, in the Land of Yisrael one could sacrifice a lamb or a bull. He offers as proof, And thou shalt sacrifice the passover-offering unto Hashem thy Elokim, of the flock and the herd (Devarim 16:2), which applies to the Passover to be offered in all future generations. However, he did not speak correctly. All future Passover offerings are in memory of the paschal lamb offered in Mitzrayim, and one should not deviate from it. The meaning of the aforementioned verse can only be: And thou shalt sacrifice the passover-offering unto Hashem thy Elokim of the flock as an obligation; and of the herd, bring peace offerings to be eaten cooked in water. Similarly, And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter (Devarim 16:14) means thou art obligated; thy son and thy daughter are permitted to do so. Proof of the above is found in the book of Divrei Hayamim. We read there that on the fourteenth day they slaughtered lambs and bullocks. It is written there that the lambs were for Passover offerings and the bullocks which served as peace offerings were cooked in pots and caldrons. Only those sacrifices which came from the flock were roasted in the fire according to ordinance. Rabbi Yehoshua says that there is a difference between ben shanah (of the first year) and ben shenato (of the first year). A ben shanah has lived a year and ben shenato means exactly what Scripture says. Now with regard to the sacrifices offered by the princes it first states, keves echad ben shenato leolah (one he-lamb of the first year, for a burnt-offering) (Bamidbar 7:15) and then states, kevasim bene shanah (he-lambs of the first year) (Bamidbar 7:87).
And ye shall keep it. Each one shall keep it in his house.

At dusk. Ben ha-arbayim (at dusk) is a difficult phrase. Rabbi Shlomo says that it refers to the moment after midday that the sun moves to the west. He does not explain why arbayim is in the dual form. Now, Scripture states, And when Aharon lighteth the lamps at dusk (ben ha-arbayim) (Shemot 30:8), and there is no doubt that Aharon is to light the lamps when the sun sets. Now, when we researched this phrase we found that Scripture refers to the moment of ben ha-arbayim as erev (evening). For it is clearly written, At dusk (ben ha-arbayim) ye shall eat flesh (Shemot 16:12), and it is there stated, when Hashem shall give you in the evening (ba-erev) flesh to eat (Shemot 16:8). Likewise, concerning the lighting of the lamps it is written: Aharon and his sons shall set it in order, to burn from evening (erev) to morning before Hashem (Shemot 27:21). It is similarly written, even burnt-offerings mornings and evening (erev) (Ezra 3:3), and it is stated, The one lamb thou shalt offer in the morning; and the other lamb thou shalt offer at dusk (ben ha-arbayim) (Shemot 29:39). Now concerning the Passover sacrifice, about which the term ben ha-arbayim (at dusk) is employed, we find that Scripture states, there thou shalt sacrifice the passover-offering at even (erev), at the coming (bo) of the sun, at the season that thou earnest forth out of Mitzrayim (Devarim 16:6). Rabbi Shlomo explains that the reference is to the time that the sun comes to the west. However, this is not the meaning of bo. It refers to the opposite of the sun’s going forth upon the earth since it is written, the sun went out (yatza) upon the earth (Bereshit 19:23), which means the time that the sun first begins to be seen on the earth. Similarly, And when the sun comes (ba) he shall be clean (Vayikra 22:7) means when the sun shall no longer be seen upon the ground. Now it is written concerning a nocturnal seminal emission, But it shall be, when evening cometh on, he shall bathe himself in water; and when the sun comes (u-khe-vo ha-shemesh) he may come within the camp (Devarim 23:12). If this is not so, then let Rabbi Shlomo explain what difference there is between “when the sun comes” with regard to Passover and “when the sun comes” with regard to a nocturnal seminal emission. It is the same with and when the sun comes he shall be clean (Vayikra 22:7). The Sadducees say that there are three evenings. Their proof is from a verse which they found to read, ha-erev ha-shelishit (the third evening) (Shmuel I 20:5). However, they do not recognize or understand the truth. It is written, Tomorrow is the new moon…And in the third day thou shalt hide thyself well (Shmuel I 20:18, 19), the meaning of which is: when close to evening of the third day starting from today comes, you shall hide yourself well in the field where you are presently hidden. It is because of this that Jonathan said, until the third evening. I will now backtrack and explain. Know that the word arbayim is always vocalized according to the paradigm of the dual forms like ovnayim (birthstool) (Shemot 1:16). Luchotayim (planks) (Yechezkel 27:5) is similar. So is derachayim (ways) (Mishlei 28:18), as But he that is perverse in his ways (derachayim) shall fall in one of them (Ibid.) proves. The same is the case with the word shamayim (heaven), as the heavens consist of two poles which are like fastened nails upon which the sphere leans. I have already explained in The Book of Hashem, the Glorious, that the word shamayim comes from the same root as the word sham (there) in There the upright might reason with Him (Iyov 23:7). The term shamayim alludes to these two places. We thus have two evenings: one when the sun sets, that is, the time when the sun descends beneath the earth; the second when its light disappears from the clouds. Now there is close to one and a third hours between them. It is at this time that one who experienced a seminal emission may enter the camp and Aharon kindles the lights. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon, of blessed memory, says that the altar of the burnt offering measured five cubits in length and five cubits in width. Such an area has room only for a small number of kohanim (priests), who are the ones that sprinkle the blood from the paschal lambs before it coagulates. Now in the days of Yoshiyahu, when the number of Bnei Yisrael were few, the kohanim were not able to sprinkle the blood of the Passover offerings and the peace offerings that they slaughtered; i.e., they were not able to sprinkle them on the altar in one and a third hours. How much more unable to do so were they when all the tribes were in their country. There was thus a tradition that they begin to slaughter from the moment that it became clear to a person that the sun turned to the west. Scripture speaks of ben ha-arbayim (at dusk) because most of the paschal lambs were slaughtered then, and that marks its time limit; for one should not wait until the going down of the sun’s light.
On the two side-posts. Of the door of the house. Moshe will go on to explain how they are to take the blood.

[Lintel.] The word mashkof (lintel) means a window. Compare, va-yashkef (looked) (Bereshit 26:8). This window was in the door. This is the custom in all Moslem countries. The practice of the uncircumcised differs from that of the Mitzrim even regarding food, an example being, Thou shalt break it in pieces (Vayikra 2:6). Similarly with regard to women’s jewelry such as the wearing of nose rings and earrings and all that the prophet Yeshayahu mentioned concerning the daughters of Tziyon (Is. 3:18-24). Likewise, all of their houses without exception are built in courtyards. One entrance is called the door to the house and the other the gate of the courtyard. Many say that the purpose of placing the blood on the window and on the two side-posts was to demonstrate publicly that they slaughtered the abomination of Mitzrayim, since by then the fear of Bnei Yisrael had fallen on the Mitzrim, and Bnei Yisrael were not afraid of being stoned. Now if this was the case then the blood should have been placed on the entrance to the courtyard. However, the blood was placed in secret, for they closed the gate of the courtyard. Furthermore, they slaughtered the lamb at dusk, which is close to night, so that no one would see them. Moreover, no man left his house until the morning when each one went on his way and each one closed the gate to his courtyard. The Mitzrim thought that Bnei Yisrael would return. The reason the blood was smeared on the window was to make atonement for all those eating in the house and to serve as a mark for the destroyer to see. It is to be understood in the same way as and set a mark on the foreheads of the men (Yechezkel 9:4).

[Houses.] The word battim (houses) is grammatically irregular, as it has a dagesh following a long kamatz. This is contrary to the rule whereby a dagesh is only placed after a short kamatz, as in ronnu (sing) in Sing, O ye heavens (Is. 44:23). Perhaps battim was vocalized with a kamatz because of the missing yod in the word bayit. This form would thus not be confused with the form battim (baths) in ten baths are a homer (Yechezkel 45:14) wherein battim, the plural of bat (bath) in The ephah and the bath (Yechezkel 45:11), is vocalized with a pattach in the plural. The word battim (houses) in upon the houses is indicative, for unlike the rule it is penultimately accented.

With bitter herbs they shall eat it. One of the Spanish wise men explained that it is well known that because of the Yeor and the lack of rain, the humidity in Mitzrayim is very high and the air is always moist. It was therefore their custom to eat all sorts of bitter herbs and mustards with their meals. A Mitzri always had bitters in which to dip his bread, even if he had but one loaf of bread, because the bitters are a cure for their climate. However, we will rely on the opinion of our ancients of blessed memory, who explained to us that the reason for the bitter herbs is to remind us that they made their lives bitter (Shemot 1:14).

Raw. Some say that the meaning of na (raw) is: as it is now, i.e., when the meat is raw. However, we do not find the word na used in such a way elsewhere in Scripture. Others say that it comes from the same root as heni (breaks) in But if her father breaks her vow (Bamidbar 30:6) and means broken. However, this is incorrect, as Scripture later states, neither shall ye break a bone thereof (v. 46). However, in my opinion the word na has no counterpart in Scripture. It means the opposite of cooked and is referred to as chai (raw). Compare, For he will not have sodden flesh of thee, but raw (chai) (Shmuel I 2:15). I have previously noted that most of Arabic is similar to Hebrew. Now in Arabic raw meat is called nayy, and the alef heh, vav, and yod interchange in the tongue of the Arvim as it does in our tongue.

Nor sodden. Bashel (sodden) is an adjective. Here its meaning is, that which is sodden with water. That which is roasted in fire is also called mevushal, for it is written, And thou shalt roast (u-vishalta) and eat it (Devarim 16:7) and, And they roasted (va-yevashelu) the passover with fire according to the ordinance (Divrei Hayamim II 35:13). It is possible that nor sodden at all with water means nor cooked, that is, cooked in water, as a royal dish is sodden in liquids. They place a wide copper utensil on the fire and fill half of it with water. When the water boils they place the pot with the meat in cold water above the boiling water. Thus is the meat cooked. This dish is better than one prepared close to the fire. I the writer add to the words of this scholar what I heard from his very own mouth. Bashel (sodden) is an adjective following the paradigm of kaved (heavy) and zaken (old). The term bashel here is similar, as its bet is vocalized with a kamatz and its shin has no dagesh. Bashel is not an infinitive like kabbed (promote) in for I will promote thee (Bamidbar 22:17) or hakkeh (smite) in thou shalt surely smite (Devarim 13:16), as the infinitive is not joined to a word unless it is a perfect or an imperfect. Compare, dabber yedabber (speak well) (Shemot 4:14), and hakdesh hikdashti (I verily dedicate) (Jud. 17:3). However, the infinitive is never joined with the po’el or pa’ul. Thus bashel (sodden) is similar to kaved (heavy). Its feminine form is beshelah, as in the shoulder…when it is sodden (beshelah) (Bamidbar 6:19). Do not ask what need Scripture had to use the two terms bashel and mevushal. As the scholar pointed out, there are two soddenings, one of which is the placing of the utensil with the meat in the midst of the boiling water. The plural of bashel mevushal is beshelim mevushalim. Compare, chakhamim mechukkamim (exceeding wise) in But they are exceeding wise (Mishlei 30:24). The singular form is chakham mechukkam. Compare, barukh u-mevorakh (exceedingly blessed). There is a difference in nuance from a grammatical standpoint between chakham (a wise man) and mechukkam (one who has become wise). There is, as the scholar explained, a similar difference between bashel (sodden) and mevushal (sodden).

Its head with its legs and with the inwards thereof. The word al has the meaning of with. The word al in And they came, both men and (al) women (Shemot 35:22) is similar. The head and the legs are to be washed in water as the ordinance requires.

But that which remaineth of it…burn with fire. If one was unable to eat one’s portion due to circumstances beyond one’s control. Yefet says that the reference is to the bones. However, Scripture only speaks of what is normal.

And thus shall ye eat it. The reference is only to the paschal lamb eaten in Mitzrayim. However, those in Argalon do the same today in memory of the Exodus. These spiritual errants all leave their land on the fifteenth day in memory of the Exodus.
And your staff in your hand. To lead the asses. Compare, and he smote the ass with his staff (Bamidbar 22:27).

[In haste.] Yisrael was not to delay. They were to hurry and eat the paschal lamb before the moment of destruction arrived, when Hashem would pass over their homes. Hashem therefore commanded that the lamb be roasted in fire, because food that is roasted cooks quickly. The holy patriarchs similarly said the paschal lamb may be eaten only until midnight and it may only be eaten roasted.
For I will go through the land of Mitzrayim. Hashem’s might and His power passed throughout the land. Hence it was as if Hashem Himself went throughout the land.

And against all the gods of Mitzrayim I will execute judgments. In the manner of Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground (Shmuel I 5:4). It is similarly written, upon their gods also Hashem executed judgments (Bamidbar 33:4).

And the blood shall be to you for a token. This shall be for you a token so that your hearts will be strong and will not weaken as you hear the cries of the Mitzrim when their first-born die via the destroyer. [AND WHEN I SEE THE BLOOD.] I will pass over you and there will be no plague among you because I will see the blood. The blood will be a sign to the destroyer.
And this day shall be unto you. It shall be a memorial for generations.

And ye shall keep it a feast. The reference is to the feast of Passover. Scripture says that it shall be kept a feast by an ordinance throughout your generations. However, it does not say that it is to be kept in all of your dwelling places, because this commandment is, as I will explain, contingent on dwelling in the Land of Yisrael.

Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread. The reason for shall ye eat unleavened bread is to recall the matzot eaten when they left Mitzrayim. They were not previously commanded to eat unleavened bread save for that which is to be eaten with the paschal lamb before midnight. However, God now commanded that they eat unleavened bread for seven days in memory of what happened to them when they left Mitzrayim, as it is written there, for it was not leavened (Shemot 12:39). Had the Mitzrim permitted them to tarry a bit, they would have leavened their dough. They ate unleavened bread for seven days until Paroh was drowned on the seventh day. The heavenly cloud led them day and night and they did not tarry very long even when they camped. It is similarly written when discussing the paschal lamb, seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith, even the bread of affliction (Devarim 16:3). Now according to its plain meaning, the text Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread is stating an obligation. That thou mayest remember the day when thou camest forth out of the land of Mitzrayim all the days of thy life (Devarim 16:3) is proof of this. It is because of this that Scripture states, Ye shall eat nothing leavened; in all your habitations shall ye eat unleavened bread (Shemot 12:20), as the latter is an obligation within the Land of Yisrael and outside of the Land of Yisrael.

[Howbeit the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses.] Now since Yisrael had a tradition of commencing the slaughter of the paschal lamb when the sun started going down towards the west, and it is written, Thou shalt not offer the blood of My sacrifice with leavened bread (Shemot 34:25), the rabbis of blessed memory interpreted the word ach (howbeit) to mean a part of. Mark the fact that ceasing an act is not an act. The meaning of And on the seventh day Elokim finished (Bereshit 2:2) is: when the seventh day started Elokim had already finished his work. Similarly, the meaning of the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses is: when the first day starts, all leaven shall already have been removed from the houses. Now the first day starts at the end of the fourteenth day at even, as it is written, from the first day until the seventh day. The meaning of the phrase then is that the seven full days are from the fourteenth day of the month at even, which is the end of the fourteenth day, until the twenty-first day at even. I will yet speak concerning this.
And in the first day. The day of the Exodus from Mitzrayim. The seventh day is, as I will explain, the day that the Mitzrim drowned.

No manner of work. We do not find the phrase kol melakhah (no manner of work) stated with regard to any of the festivals, with the exception of the Sabbath and the Day of Atonement. However, the phrase is employed with regard to Passover with the proviso that that which every man must eat is permitted. In all other places, be it Passover, Sha’vu’ot, the Day of Memorial, or the festival of Sukkot, Scripture employs the abridged form and states, ye shall do no manner of servile work. Only in one place with regard to Passover is it stated that you shall do no manner of work under the first stated conditions.
And ye shall observe. God here commanded that the matzot be watched from the time of the harvest.

[Have I brought.] Scripture reads, have I brought your hosts out of the land of Mitzrayim although they had not yet left Mitzrayim. This prophecy took place at the beginning of the month. It meaning is: you will say this in all of your generations.

In the first. Scripture uses an abridged form since it had already stated, it shall be the first month of the year to you (v. 2). The meaning of in the first thus is, in the first month. In the tenth, on the first day of the month (Bereshit 8:5) is similar.

Leaven. Se’or (leaven) refers to something which induces leavening. The substance is well known. Scripture then goes on to say, for whosoever eateth anything which is leavened (machmetzet). Note that from the first day until the seventh day (v. 15) is not connected to what is adjacent, i.e., to shall be cut off but rather is connected to for whosoever eateth leavened bread. It is similar to of Shlomo’s reign over Yisrael (Melachim I 6:1).
