Yefet says that some letters refer both to the word in which they are placed and to a word previously written, as in odem pitdah u-vareket (carnelian, topaz, and smaragd) (Shemot 28:17), which is to be interpreted as if written, odem u-pitdah u-vareket (carnelian, and topaz, and smaragd). The same is true of mi-yom ha-rishon ad yom ha-shevi’i (from the first day until the seventh day).

[Whether he be a sojourner.] Scripture already noted that whosoever eateth leavened bread from among Bnei Yisrael incurs the penalty of excision. Scripture now adds a sojourner who is a sincere proselyte.

Nothing leavened. Scripture first mentions the punishment and then the warning. In all your habitations shall ye eat unleavened bread is not optional as Six days shall work be done (Shemot 35:2) is. On the contrary, it is an obligation so that one will remember.
And Moshe called for all the elders of Yisrael. So that they would tell the people.
And take you lambs. On the tenth day, as he was commanded by Hashem.

[And kill the Passover lamb.] The grammarian says that ve-shachatu (and kill) in and kill the passover lamb is a pi’el. However, he spoke incorrectly. Ve-shachatu (shall kill it) in and the whole congregation of Yisrael shall kill it (v. 6) is a kal. It is properly vocalized with a kamatz beneath the shin because of the silent missing letter. However, ve-shachatu (and kill) in and kill the passover lamb is imperative in the kal. We do not find this root in the pi’el in any place in Scripture. The shin of ve-shachatu should have been vocalized with a chirik, as miskhu (draw) is. However, since the shin is followed by a guttural it was vocalized with a pattach, as is Hebrew practice. Compare, bacharu (choose) in choose you (Yehoshua 24:15). There are many other similar instances. The shin is therefore vocalized with a long pattach in the imperative. Both words are from the same conjugation.
And ye shall take. Moshe now explains the manner in which the blood is to be taken and placed on the lintel.

[A bunch of.] The word aguddat means a bunch (of). Compare, la-aggudah (band) in and became one band (Shmuel II 2:25). Rabbi Merinus says that the alef in aguddah is appended, as aguddah comes from the same root as gedud (troop). Others say that the alef in aguddah is a root letter like the alef in afuddato (skillfully woven) in and the skillfully woven band (Shemot 28:6).

[Hyssop.] Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that azov (hyssop) is a plant known in Arabic as zatr and in the vernacular as oregano. It is an herb distinguished by various kinds of flavors. However, this interpretation is incorrect, for Scripture states, even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall (Melachim I 5:13). I do not know the identity of the azov. However, logically speaking it is not a very mighty plant for it is the opposite of the cedar mentioned in Scripture.

[Basin.] Some say that they slaughtered the paschal lamb in the threshold of the gate, and they dipped the hyssop into it and then touched the side-posts with the blood. They say that the word saf (basin) is similar in meaning to the word saf (threshold) in and he measured the threshold (saf) of the gate (Yechezkel 40:6) and to sippim (thresholds) in and the posts of the thresholds moved (Is. 6:4). Others say that saf (basin) is similar to sappot (basins) in brought beds, and basins (Shmuel II 17:28) and that saf is a vessel over which they slaughtered the paschal lamb.
[Until the morning.] I will yet explain what this means.

And will not suffer. He will not suffer the destroyer. Yitten (will suffer) here is similar in meaning to netatikha (suffered I thee) in Therefore suffered I thee not (Bereshit 20:6). Now, the destroyer is under God’s power. If God allows him to come into their homes it is as if He gave him permission to do so.

And ye shall observe this thing. Many are of the opinion that the placing of the blood on the lintel and on the two side-posts is an obligation for all generations because this thing is connected to the taking of the hyssop and dipping it into the lamb’s blood. Furthermore, Scripture afterwards states, for that he passed over the houses of the children of Yisrael in Mitzrayim (v. 27). This interpretation would be correct from a logical point of view were it not for the true tradition which states otherwise. The correct interpretation is that this thing refers to and kill the passover lamb. The meaning of the children’s question is, when your children will see their family in a group eating an entire lamb, whose bones one is prohibited to break, with its head, with its legs, and with the inwards thereof, unlike the custom on all other festivals, and from which a gentile, an uncircumcised one, a sojourner, and a hired servant may not eat, they will question you.

And it shall come to pass. Moshe now explains that the slaughter of the paschal lamb is contingent upon dwelling in the Land of Yisrael. Do not be troubled by the Passover observed by Bnei Yisrael at Mount Sinai. That was a commandment from on high. They did not observe another Passover in the desert. At Mount Sinai they were in an inhabited land and were thus able to find unleavened bread. However, when they were in a land that no man passed through they only had manna.
And it shall come to pass…what mean ye by this service. The strange ritual that I noted.

That ye shall say: it is the sacrifice of Hashem’s Passover. The word pesach (passover) is to be rendered pity, as we find, paso’ach ve-himlit (He will pity it and He will rescue it) (Is. 31:5). The lamb is termed pesach (passover), as in and kill the passover (pesach) (v. 21), because Hashem had pity on the first-born of Yisrael because of the blood of the lamb. However, Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that the word pesach is derived from the word pi’se’ach (limp), since a lame person supports himself on his healthy leg. The destroyer acted in a similar manner. He exterminated the first-born in the Mitzri home and passed over the home of his Hebrew neighbor and did not destroy him. The term posechim (hopping) in How long will you keep hopping between two opinions (Melachim I 18:20) is similar.
And the children of Yisrael went and did so. They took a lamb on the tenth day of the month. They did as Hashem had commanded Moshe and Aharon: This is the ordinance of the passover (v. 43).
And it came to pass at midnight. The reference is to the second half of the night.

[Unto the first-born of the captive that was in the dungeon.] Yefet says that the captives who grind the millstone in prison during the day are put at night into a pit whose opening is covered with the millstone. This is the meaning of behind the mill (Shemot 11:5).
And Paroh rose up. He himself. But the Leviyim alone shall do the service (Bamidbar 18:23), meaning the Levi himself, is similar.
For there was not a house where there was not one dead. Scripture speaks of the majority of houses.

And he called. Logically speaking Moshe and Aharon were not in the land of Raamses with Bnei Yisrael on the night of the fifteenth. On the contrary, they were in that part of Mitzrayim in which was the royal seat where Paroh lived. Now Moshe and Aharon left the doors of their homes at midnight in accordance with Elokim’s dictate. After Paroh gave Bnei Yisrael permission to go and worship Elokim, Moshe went with the servants of Paroh to Raamses to bring Yisrael out of Mitzrayim. It is common knowledge in our time that there are six Parsi miles between ancient Mitzrayim, where Yosef’s treasures are known to be until this very day, and Raamses. Now Bnei Yisrael began to leave Mitzrayim in the morning, namely, at the break of dawn when the light of the sun is seen in the clouds. There is a full hour and a third between the moment that dawn breaks and sunrise. We find that it can be very dark and still be morning. Thus Scripture states, And she lay down at his feet till the morning (Rut 3:14), and then adds, before one could discern another. Now some Bnei Yisrael exited Mitzrayim at the break of dawn when, from the Torah’s standpoint, it is still night until sunrise. This group was close to Mitzrayim. Another group who were further from Mitzrayim exited that very day. Bnei Yisrael constituted a very large congregation. It is more than eight Parsi miles from one end of Raamses to another. Scripture therefore states in one place, Hashem thy Elokim brought thee forth out of Mitzrayim by night (Devarim 16:1), and elsewhere reads, This day ye go forth (Shemot 13:4). It is further stated, the children of Yisrael went out with a high hand in the sight of all the Mitzrim (Bamidbar 33:3), and it is there recorded, while the Mitzrim were burying them that Hashem had smitten. Now the Mitzrim buried their dead during the day. I have thus explained the meaning of morning.
Both ye…as ye have said. Our cattle also shall go with us (Shemot 10:26).
[And bless me also.] Paroh asked them to bless him and pray for him.
[Also.] Scripture reads also because Paroh, as Moshe had foretold, gave them sacrifices.
Were urgent. Va-techezak (were urgent) is in the feminine, because the state of Mitzrayim includes everything.
[We are all dead.] I have explained its meaning in my comments on lest he fall upon us with pestilence (Shemot 5:3).

Their kneading-troughs. Misheret (kneading-trough) is a wooden vessel. Compare, mishartekha (thy kneading-trough) in thy basket and thy kneading-trough (Devarim 28:5). Their asses were laden with garments which they asked of the Mitzrim.

And the children of Yisrael did. Each one asked in accordance with his status. Thus we find that only the princes donated precious stones, spices, and oil for the work of the tabernacle (Shemot 35:27, 28).

And they despoiled. We do not find the root nun, tzadi, lamed in the kal. We find it only in the hifil and the pi’el. They are both transitive verbs because there is no difference in meaning between va-yenatzelu (and they despoiled) and va-yatzel (hath taken away) in Thus Elokim hath taken away (Bereshit 31:9) except that in the hifil the object is mentioned and in the pi’el it is omitted.

And the children of Yisrael journeyed. The samekh in the word va-yisu (journeyed) should have received a dagesh to compensate for the missing nun, as the gimel in va-yiggeshu (and drew near) (Bereshit 44:18) and the tav in va-yittenu (and they gave) (Bereshit 35:4) do. It is possible that the dagesh was omitted to simplify enunciation.
From Raamses. Raamses is vocalized with a pattach beneath the resh and a sheva beneath the ayin. It is not a city but rather the name of a district.
To Sukkot. Sukkotah means: to Sukkot.
[Men.] Scripture mentions men. There was no need to mention the women because there were as many women as there were men, maybe even more.
Beside children. Taf (children) refers to those under the age of twenty.
And a mixed multitude. Of Mitzrim who intermingled with them. They are the asafsuf (mixed multitude) who joined them.
And they baked. The dough which they brought out of Mitzrayim had leaven in it. They did not bake it until they camped in Sukkot.

Now the time that the children of Yisrael dwelt in Mitzrayim was four hundred and thirty years. There are many calculations in Scripture whose point of departure is unknown to us. I will now mention a few of them. And it came to pass at the end of forty years, that Avshalom said unto the king (Shmuel II 15:7). Now Avshalom was not then forty years old. Furthermore, King David’s reign was not yet over. The commentaries tell us that the point of departure for this calculation is from the day that the ark abode in Kiryat Yearim (Shmuel I 7:2). It is stated, Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year (Yechezkel 1:1). Some say that Yechezkel was thirty years old when he began to prophesy. Others say that the reference is to the thirtieth year of the jubilee. Other say that its point of departure is the finding of the Torah which was discovered by Chilkiyahu the priest. However, I am uncertain, for they are opinions without foundation or support. It is written: And within threescore and five years shall Efraim be broken, that it be not a people (Is. 7:8). The latter prophesy was uttered during the days of Achaz, whose reign lasted for sixteen years. Shomron was exiled in the sixth year of his son Chizkiyahu’s reign. The commentaries were therefore forced to say that the sixty-five years start from the day that Amos prophesied, And Yisrael shall surely be led away captive out of his land (Amos 7:11). Others say that its point of departure is the earthquake. Now when we investigated the years starting with the time that Yisrael came to Mitzrayim in the days of Yosef and his brothers we found that they do not come to the number of years spoken of in Scripture. There is no doubt that Kehat was among those who descended to Mitzrayim. Let us imagine that Kehat begot his son Amram at the end of his life and that Amram similarly begot Moshe at the end of his life. Now the years of Kehat and Amram’s lives come to two hundred and seventy. Moshe was eighty years old when Bnei Yisrael went out of Mitzrayim. It all thus comes to three hundred and fifty years. We are missing eighty years. It is for this reason that the elders added, “dwelt in Mitzrayim and other countries.” The four hundred years in and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years (Bereshit 15:13) is not connected to and they shall afflict them but rather to thy seed shall be a stranger (Ibid.). There are many other such instances. We similarly find in our own chapter, from the first day until the seventh day (v. 15). Now we find it stated that Hashem told Avraham at the covenant made “between the pieces,” that thy seed shall be a stranger…four hundred years. We know that the number of years that Yisrael dwelt in Mitzrayim is contingent upon the “end,” which was told to Avraham. The author of the Seder Olam was compelled to say that after Avraham came to the land of Kenaan he returned to Charan. The commentaries were forced to say that the prophecy I am Hashem that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees (Bereshit 15:7) is not connected to the above-noted chapter but was said later. However, there is no need for all of this. Only the counting of the four hundred years is from the day that Yitzchak was born. The additional thirty years start from the day that Avraham left Ur of the Chaldees, the land of his nativity, and came with his father to Charan, as it is written, and they came unto Charan, and dwelt there (Bereshit 11: 31). Avraham lived in Charan with his father for five years. He came to the land of Kenaan at the age of seventy-five and never returned to Charan. Now thirty years passed from the time that Avraham left Charan till the day Yitzchak was born. Avraham was the important one, and to him was the land of the Kenaani given. The verse I am Hashem that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees (Bereshit 15:7) is connected to the entire chapter preceding and following it. The meaning of Now the time that the children of Yisrael dwelt in Mitzrayim is to be explained: they were strangers there, also their fathers were strangers, as it is written, Yea, very few, and sojourners in it (Tehillim 105:12); and as Avraham said, I am a stranger and a sojourner with you (Bereshit 23:4).
Four hundred and thirty years. From the day that their father Avraham left the land of his birth.

[And it came to pass at the end of four hundred and thirty years.] Scripture states this so that it be known that they did not exit Mitzrayim because of their cries to Hashem until the time that Hashem had decreed for them had come.

It was a night of watching unto Hashem. Since Scripture notes, it was a night of watching unto Hashem, and concludes by saying, this same night is a night of watching unto Hashem for all the children of Yisrael throughout their generations, the plain meaning of our verse appears to be: since Hashem watched them and did not suffer the destroyer to come into their homes to plague them, Hashem commanded that this night be a night of watchingfor all the children of Yisrael throughout their generations through the eating of the paschal lamb according to its ordinance and the ingesting of unleavened bread and bitter herbs on this night. Others say that watching here has the same meaning as the word watching in The watchers of the walls (Cant. 5:7); its meaning is that they should not sleep on this night but should praise Hashem and relate the might that Hashem displayed when they went out of Mitzrayim. Our sages hinted at the latter meaning when they said, The time for the reading of the morning shema has arrived.

And the Lord said…this is the ordinance of the Passover. Since Scripture mentioned that it was a night of watching (v. 42), the reference being to the night of the fifteenth wherein the paschal lamb is to be eaten, the Torah completes its explanation of the laws of the Passover that is to be observed in future generations. Now Scripture does not mention the lintel and the side-post. Neither does it mention that the lamb is to be eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, as they were previously mentioned with regard to the Passover observed in Mitzrayim. Its meaning thus is: you shall eat the Passover offering in the future as you ate it in Mitzrayim. Scripture then added other commandments. However, the commandments with regard to the lintel and the side-post have nothing to do with the eating of the paschal lamb. Do you not see that at the beginning of the chapter (i.e., v. 43) it states, there shall no alien eat thereof (bo)? The meaning of bo (thereof) is, of it. Its usage in this context is correct in Hebrew and also in Arabic. Ve-hanotar ba-basar u-va-lechem (and that which remaineth of the flesh and of the bread) (Vayikra 8:32) is similar.

But every man’s servant…when thou hast circumcised him. According to his wish, that he be converted to the law of Yisrael, if he is of the age when one is obligated to observe the commandments. The law dealing with someone that is bought for money and someone born in the house is the same. However, Scripture deals with that which is more prevalent.
A sojourner and a hired servant. Who are Bnei Yisrael shall not eat of the paschal lamb if a portion of the lamb has not been assigned to them, as is the law for the entire congregation.

In one house shall it be eaten. As the paschal lamb eaten in Mitzrayim was. Thou shalt not carry forth aught of the flesh abroad out of the house is proof of this. However, our sages of blessed memory said that in one house means in one company. The latter is the correct interpretation.

All the congregation of Yisrael shall keep it. All those of the age when one is obligated to observe the commandments are required to prepare a paschal lamb. When I researched the Torah, I found that the twenty-three times where karet (excision) is stated refer to negative precepts. However, I found only two dealing with positive precepts, namely, the paschal lamb and circumcision. Perhaps the reason for this is that there is an obligation to “remember” the Exodus from Mitzrayim, and there is no greater manifestation of “remembering” than eating the paschal lamb in its proper time. And the beginning of the decalogue states, I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Mitzrayim (Shemot 20:2).
And when a stranger shall sojourn with thee. The meaning of with thee is, with thee in the land of Mitzrayim.
[And will keep the Passover.] Its meaning is, and he wants to keep the Passover. Then let him first be circumcised.
[But no uncircumcised person shall eat there-of.] The reference is to uncircumcised Bnei Yisrael such as those born on the way in the wilderness.
One law. The stranger spoken of in this verse refers to a righteous proselyte, not to a stranger that dwells within the gates.

[Thus did all the children of Yisrael.] Scripture has already mentioned this above. Perhaps the reason it is noted again is that it refers to the Passover offering brought in the wilderness of Sinai, at which time the strangers were circumcised. Do not be surprised that this is written in this place. Scripture states in the chapter dealing with the coming down of the manna that they should take a jar and put manna therein and place it before Hashem (Shemot 16:33). However, Hashem had not yet commanded the making of the ark of the testimony. Have I brought your hosts out of the land of Mitzrayim (v. 17) is similar.

And it came to pass the selfsame day. I believe that this verse is connected to the verse which follows, in which Hashem told Moshe to sanctify the first-born. The plague of the first-born took place at midnight, and when Yisrael went out of Mitzrayim the next day Hashem immediately commanded that the first-born of Yisrael and the first-born of their cattle be sanctified.

And the Lord spoke. Scripture employs a short form, for Moshe stands in place of Yisrael. However, Yefet says that Moshe was commanded to verbally sanctify all first-born. The aforementioned is the reverse of then the priest shall defile him (Vayikra 13:8); the priest, being holy, defiles an individual by declaration.

Openeth. Peter (openeth) means the opening of. Peter is similar to peture (open) in and open flowers (Melachim I 6:18). Its meaning is, the son who first opens the womb. The word rechem (womb) is irregular, as according to the rules of Hebrew grammar the letter preceding a guttural is vocalized with a pattach.
And Moshe said. Remember this day was said by Moshe on the fifteenth day. It means the same as And this day shall be unto you for a memorial (Shemot 12:14).

[Out of the house of bondage.] This indicates that the Mitzrim forced them to work as if they were their slaves. Elsewhere Scripture reads, out of the iron furnace (Devarim 4:20), for the Mitzrim overpowered them. However, Hashem brought them out by strength of hand from the mighty.

This day. Moshe first mentions, there shall be no leavened bread eaten, its meaning being, do in future generations what you did on the day that you left Mitzrayim. As you left Mitzrayim at the time when the first ears (aviv) are found, so shall you do yearly in the future in the Land of Yisrael when the first ears come. The first ears refers to the first ears of barley. The word aviv (Aviv) means the first that ripens. Aviv comes from the same root as av (father), which means first to the one whom one begets, or sage to the student whom one teaches. Furthermore, it is written, for the barley was in the ear (aviv) (Shemot 9:31). Even of the first-fruits (bikkure) of wheat harvest (Shemot 34:22), which is written with regard to the festival of weeks, is proof of the above.
And it shall be. Scripture does not list all of the seven Kenaani nations because they have already been mentioned elsewhere.
The seven days. This is the service.

Unleavened bread. Now the stranger that is within the gate was exhorted by God to observe the Sabbath, as it is only on the condition that he do no work before the Lord on the Sabbath that he may dwell within the gates. Similarly on the Day of Atonement, for it is so written. The same applies to Passover, as a stranger is not permitted to eat leaven even on his own property. This is the meaning of in all thy borders.

It is because of that. Rabbi Merinus says that ba’avur zeh (it is because of that) should have been written, zeh ba’avur; i.e., this is because of what Hashem did for me. He cited what in his opinion are many other such instances. However, I do not think that he was right in even one instance. For how can we invert the words of the living Elokim? The meaning of the verse is just the opposite of what he understands it to be, because we do not eat unleavened bread “because of this.” Its meaning rather is: it is because of this, i.e., it is because of this service, namely, the eating of unleavened bread and the abstention from leavened bread, which are the first of the precepts that Elokim commanded us, that Hashem did signs for us and brought us out of Mitzrayim. Its meaning thus is: Elokim took us out of Mitzrayim only to serve Him, as it is written, when thou hast brought forth the people out of Mitzrayim, ye shall serve Elokim upon this mountain (Shemot 20:12). It is furthermore stated, I am Hashem your Elokim, who brought you out of the land of Mitzrayim, to be your Elokim: I am Hashem your Elokim (Bamidbar 15:41).

And it shall be a sign unto thee. There are those who oppose our holy patriarchs and say that for a sign…and for a memorial is to be understood in the manner of For they shall be a chaplet of grace unto thy head, And chains about thy head (Mishlei 1:9). They also say that And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand (Devarim 5:8) is like Bind them continually upon thy heart, Tie them upon thy neck (Mishlei 6:21) and also that And thou shalt write them upon the door-posts of thy house (Devarim 6:9) is like Write them upon the table of thy heart (Mishlei 3:3). They furthermore say that it shall be for a sign…and for a memorial means for with a strong hand hath Hashem brought thee out of Mitzrayim shall drop from your lips. However, this is incorrect, for at the beginning of the book of Mishlei it is stated, The Proverbs of Shlomo. Thus whatever Shlomo henceforth mentions is by way of parable. However, it is not, heaven forbid, written in the Torah that it is metaphoric. Hence it is to be taken only at face value. We thus will not interpret it except literally. It does not contradict reason if explained according to its plain meaning, like Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart (Devarim 10:16), which has to be interpreted according to the requirements of reason.

[Upon thy hand.] Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that the term yad (hand) in most of Scripture refers to the left hand, as in Yea, My hand (yadi) hath laid the foundation of the earth, And My right hand hath spread out the heavens (Is. 48:13); and Her hand (yadah) she put to the tent-pin, And her right hand to the workmen’s hammer (Jud. 5:26). However, the teachings of tradition are firmly established and do not require any support.

From year to year. Mi-yamim yamimah (from year to year) is similar to yamim tiheyeh ge’ullato (for a full year shall he have the right of redemption (Vayikra 25:29). The meaning of mi-yamim yamimah is, from year to year. The year begins when the Bet Din announces its commencement.
And it shall be. Moshe mentions only the Kenaani, because he was the father of them all.
[As he swore unto thee.] Its meaning is similar to for unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give this land (Bereshit 26:3).
That thou shalt set apart. Thou shalt set it apart unto the Lord so that it does not get mixed up with another. Now these two precepts were commanded on the fifteenth day.

Coming of. Sheger (coming of) follows the paradigm of eretz (land of) whose vocalization does not change in the construct. However, a number of irregular cases are found. They are: shegar (the increase of) in the increase of thy kine (Devarim 7:13), chadar (chamber of) in and in the chamber of thy bed (Shemot 7:28), havel (vanity of) in Vanity of vanities (Kohelet 1:1), hamatekha (thy venom) in That puttest thy venom thereto (Chavakuk 2:15), and delatekha (thy doors) in and shut the doors (Is. 26:20). I have not found any additional instances.
And every firstling of an ass. Which is unclean, thou shalt redeem with a lamb.

Thou shalt break its neck. Some say that va-arafto (thou shalt break its neck) means thou shalt write the word holy on its neck. However, I say that anyone who says this is himself a stiff-necked ass. For behold it is written, He will break down (ya’arof) their altars (Hoshea 10:2), and ve-arefu sham et ha-eglah ba-nachal (and shall break the heifer’s neck there in the valley) (Devarim 21:4), in which the meaning of ve-arefu is, as explained by the transmitters of the law, to cut off the neck. All firstlings that are not brought up on the altar or are not redeemed are required to be killed, as all the first-born of Mitzrayim both man and beast perished. Hashem did not save them from the decree which he had issued on the first-born of the Mitzrim except that they should be prepared for His service. Bnei Yisrael had no unclean animals except for asses. Therefore no other first-born is to be redeemed.
And it shall be. Rabbi Yehudah Ha-Levi of blessed memory says that the word machar (in time to come) is missing an alef, its meaning being that which comes after today.

And it came to pass. Moshe begins by saying, By strength of hand Hashem brought us out from Mitzrayim (v. 14) and backtracks and explains that what the strength of hand refers to is the plague of the first-born. It was because of this plague, and not because of the first plagues, that Yisrael went out of Mitzrayim. The poet similarly says, To Him that smote Mitzrayim in their first-born, For His mercy endureth for ever (Tehillim 136:10). Moshe wrote elliptically. When Moshe said, that Hashem slew all the first-born in the land of Mitzrayim, both the first-born of man, and the first-born of beasts, it was known that Hashem saved our first-born and the first-born of our cattle. It is to the latter, not to the slaying of the first-born, that therefore I sacrifice to Hashem all that openeth the womb is connected.
All that openeth the womb, being males. From a kind fit to be sacrificed to Hashem.

And it shall be for a sign. Scripture mentions, And it shall be for a sign upon thy hand with regard to two commandments. That which the sages of blessed memory transmitted, namely, that the chapters are to be written, is true.

And for frontlets. Totafot (frontlets) means a memorial. Others say that the tet of totafot is doubled, its meaning being to speak. They say that it comes from the same root as ve-hettef (and preach) in and preach toward the south (Yechezkel 21:2). However, in my opinion this is far-fetched.
Can a fool who rebels against his maker succeed? When at peace his liver an arrow shall split. Note and take heed, O recusant; All that the portion Be-Shallach records concerning Paroh.

And it came to pass when Paroh had let the people go. The vav in ve-lo nacham (led them not) is like an unaspirated fa in the Arabic tongue. It is known that the distance between Mitzrayim and Yerushalayim by way of the land of the Plishtim is not very great. It is about a ten-day journey by straight road. If this was not so, how did the tribes come as far as Mitzrayim upon their asses? If the distance was very great how much would have been necessary for them and their asses to eat? Furthermore, upon returning they brought back food for their households.

Although that was near. Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that ki karov hu means although that was near. In my opinion, ki am keshe oref hu (for it is a stiff-necked people) (Shemot 34:9); refa’ah nafshi ki chatati lakh (Heal my soul; for I have sinned against Thee) (Tehillim 41:5); and ki rekhev barzel lo (though they have chariots of iron) (Yehoshua 17:18) are similar. However, I see no need for this interpretation, for its meaning is: the reason Elokim did not lead them by way of the land of the Plishtim was that it was close. Elokim thus led them via a distant way so that they would not witness any war and say, Let us make a captain, and let us return to Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 14:4).

[Lest peradventure.] We know for certain that Hashem knows the future. Hashem knew that the people would repent if He led them by the way of the land of the Plishtim. Scripture reads, Lest peradventure the people repent because the Torah employed human terminology so that those who study will understand.

Led the people about. Va-yassev (led about) is a verb that comes from a double root. Its stem is samekh, bet, bet. Va-yassev also has an alternative vocalization. Compare, va-yasekh (shut up) in Or who shut up (Iyov 38:8) and va-yagel (and rolled) in and rolled the stone (Bereshit 29:10). Pay no heed to those who say that the root of va- yassev is nun, samekh, bet.

[The wilderness.] The word ha-midbar (the wilderness) is to be read as if written twice. The clause is to be understood as if written, by the way of the wilderness, wilderness of the Red Sea. Similarly, ha-aron ha-bebrit (the ark of the covenant) (Yehoshua 3:14) is to be understood as if written, the ark, ark of the covenant, and, ve-etz ha-da’at tov va-ra (the tree of the knowledge of good and evil) (Bereshit 2:9) as if written, and the tree of the knowledge, knowledge of good and evil. Likewise the terms ha-sefer ha-miknah (the deed of the purchase) (Yirmiyahu 32:12) and ha-yayin ha-chemah (the wine of fury) (Yirmiyahu 25:15). There are many other similar instances.

Red Sea. Suf (Red) is the name of a place. Others say that suf comes from the same root as sof (the end) in The end of the matter (Kohelet 12:13). It is so called because it lies at the end of the world. The reference is to the Atlantic, which I have already mentioned. However, this is a major blunder, because the yam suf (Red Sea) lies in the east, opposite Mitzrayim. The Spanish Sea is larger than it.

Armed. Some say that chamushim (armed) means full of wealth, possessing all that they need. Now Scripture states, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual (Shemot 12:39). Furthermore, what reason is there to mention this now? The only meaning of chamushim is, girded with weapons for war. Compare, chalutzim ta’avoru (ye shall pass over armed) (Devarim 3:18), the meaning of which is: ye shall pass over with girded loins. The fact that Scripture in one place reads, ve-attem ta’averu chamushim (but ye shall pass over before your brethren armed) (Yehoshua 1:14) and in another place refers to Bnei Yisrael as chalutzim (Devarim 3:18) is true witness to the aforementioned. What reason was there for them to carry food before their brethren? The reason Scripture at this point notes that the children of Yisrael went up armed is that it is previously stated, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Mitzrayim (v. 17). For Bnei Yisrael went out with a high hand (Shemot 14:8), with weapons of war and not like fleeing slaves.

And Moshe took the bones of Yosef. Scripture mentions above that the children of Yisrael who were alive in that generation went up out of the land of Mitzrayim. Scripture now notes that the children of Yisrael also brought up with them the most honored one of them, the one through whom they came down to Mitzrayim. The latter had made them swear before his death that they would tell their children, and their children would instruct their children about this. Now Moshe busied himself with fulfilling the oath so that no guilt would fall upon Yisrael. For we see that the princes of Yisrael swore an oath to the Givonim. Now they only took this oath on condition that the Givonim came from a distant place as they claimed. After it was found that the Givonim came from close by it was fitting that they not keep their oath so that they and all Yisrael not violate the injunction, thou shalt save alive nothing (Devarim 20:16). However, they kept their oath out of regard for Hashem’s glory so that they not desecrate it. Many years later Hashem punished the children of Yisrael because Shaul permitted the Givonim who were in Nov, the city of the priests, to be put to death.
[The bones of Yosef.] Scripture mentions the bones of for all of the flesh and skin breeds worms and putrefies, and after a few years only the bones remain.
And they took their journey…Etam. Etam is, as I will explain, the wilderness of Shur.

And Hashem went before them by day. We know that Hashem inhabiteth eternity and His name is Holy (Is. 57:15), and that He is enthroned of old. Selah (Tehillim 55:20). Scripture speaks in the language of men. It reads so because Hashem’s power went with Yisrael, as in That caused His glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moshe (Is. 63:12).

[In a pillar of cloud.] Scripture reads, in a pillar of cloud because it was not shaped like other clouds but was in the form of a pillar stretching from the sky upon the earth. A pillar is called an ammud in Hebrew because the base (ma’amad) of the house is on it.

[That they might go by day and by night.] Scripture reads, that they might go by day and by night because the camp was large and they could only journey a short distance. They therefore journeyed part of the day and also part of the night. These two pillars were, as I shall explain, before Bnei Yisrael until they came to the sea.
Departed not. Yamish (departed) is a transitive verb. For Hashem mentioned above did not cause the pillars to depart from before the people.

[By day.] The word yomam (by day) is not found employed in Scripture except for the time when the sun shines upon the earth. The word yom (day) found in the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings refers also to nighttime, for it is written, on the day (yom) that I smote all the first-born in the land of Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 8:17). Now the slaying of the first-born took place at night. It is also written, this day (ha-yom) is a day (yom) of good tidings (Melachim II 7:9). Now it was then night, for we read there, if we tarry till the morning light (Ibid.). Scripture also reads, The day (yom) I cry in the night before Thee (Tehillim 88:2).

And Hashem spoke. It is truly not proper for an intelligent person to scrutinize Hashem’s actions and ask, why did Hashem act thus? For all of Hashem’s actions are done wisely. Man’s wisdom is as nothing before Hashem. I mention this because you will read in this Torah portion that Hashem guilefully commanded Bnei Yisrael to turn back so that Paroh would go out and pursue them, and drown in the sea. Hashem’s thoughts are very deep.
Pi Hachirot. Pi Hachirot is elsewhere called Pene-hahiroth (Bamidbar 33:8). It is so called because the mouth (peh) is on the face (panim). It is the name of a place.

Before baal-zephon. Some say that the Mitzri magicians made bronze images which drew power from the stars, and that Ba'al Tzfon was a statue that no slave fleeing Mitzrayim was able to pass by. It is because of this that Scripture reads, that the people were fled (v. 5). However, in my opinion because Moshe said to Paroh, We will go three days’ journey into the wilderness (Shemot 8:23), it appeared to Paroh from these words that Moshe knew the road that they would take to the place where they intended to sacrifice. Thus when Paroh heard that Bnei Yisrael started to go by way of the wilderness, and when they had traveled some distance backtracked to go in another way, Paroh surmised that everything that Moshe had told him was said in guile, that he did not intend to sacrifice but to flee. For one who flees becomes confused on the way and does not know which road to take.

Over against it. The word nikhcho (over against it) is vocalized with a chirik. It is similar to the word niflo (was fallen) in after that he was fallen (Shmuel II 1:10). There are many other such instances.
And Paroh will say of the children of Yisrael. This is similar to say of me (Bereshit 20:13).

Entangled. Nevukhim (entangled) is vocalized with a shuruk in place of a cholam. It is similar to the word ta’avuri (pass) in neither pass from hence (Rut 2:8), for nevukhim is a nifal as the word nekhonim (ready) (Shemot 19:11) is. Now navokhu (perplexed) (Yoel 1:18) and also navokhah (perplexed) in but the city of Shushan was perplexed (Est. 3:15) are like nakhonah (established) in And the kingdom was established (Melachim I 2:46). Its meaning is, they are like a person who cannot find anyone to advise him and does not know what to do. The nun in nivkhe (depths of) in the depths of the sea (Iyov 38:16) is a root letter. The meaning of nivkhe yam (the springs of the sea) is the depths of the sea. Nivkhe has no place here.
The wilderness hath shut them in. The ways of the wilderness are closed to them, and like fugitives they do not know where to go.
And I will harden Paroh’s heart. As if he forgot the plagues with which the Mitzrim were smitten because of Yisrael.
And I will get me honor upon Paroh. My glory shall be manifest in the world when I drown Paroh and his army.
And the Mitzrim shall know. The remnants and those who drowned prior to their death shall know that I am Hashem.
And they did so. Scripture’s short way of saying that they turned backwards.
And it was told the king of Mitzrayim. That they are not going for any purpose but to flee.
And he made ready his chariot. By command. It is like So Shlomo built the house (Melachim I 14:4).
And he took six hundred chosen chariots. The chosen chariots of all the chariots that he had.

And captains. Note that the king is like the number one. Therefore the one who is next to him in rank is called the mishneh (the second), which is derived from the same root as shenayim (two). The third in rank is called the shelishi.
With a high hand. They had all the weapons of war and so did not go out like fugitives.

And the Mitzrim pursued after them. This is in keeping with linguistical style. It is similar to and the people saw, and they trembled and stood far off (Shemot 20:15), the meaning of which is, when they saw this, they trembled and stood far off. The meaning of and the Mitzrim pursued after them thus is: when the Mitzrim pursued them, they overtook them as they were encamping by the sea.
[All the horses.] Scripture notes this to inform us that they did not come upon them scattered.
And his horsemen. Parashav means his horsemen.
And his army. Chelo (his army) means his foot soldiers.
And when Paroh drew near. When Paroh caused his camp to draw near. The verb hikriv (drew near) is always transitive in Scripture.

And they said. We find that the holy tongue employs two words with one meaning back to back when one would suffice. Now the phrase ha-mibbeli en kevarim (because there were no graves) is similar to ha-rak akh be-mosheh (only with Moshe?) (Bamidbar 12:2).
To bring us forth. Le-hotzi’anu (to bring us forth) is vocalized with a long kamatz in place of a tzere. It is similar to ro’ani (seeth me) in Thou hast said: None seeth me (Is. 47:10).

Is this not the word. This is not stated. However, we know that this was the case, for how could they say to his face something that was not true? This remark was included in but they hearkened not unto Moshe (Shemot 6:9).

Stand still, and see the salvation of Hashem. For you will not wage war but you shall see the salvation which Hashem will work for you this day. One may ask: How is it that a large camp comprising six hundred thousand armed men were afraid of those who pursued them? Why did they not stand and fight for their own and their children’s lives? The answer is: The Mitzrim were masters over Yisrael. The generation that left Mitzrayim were trained from their youth to bear the yoke of the Mitzrim. They were of humble spirit. How then could they now wage war against their masters? Bnei Yisrael were lazy and not learned in war. Can you not see that were it not for the prayers of Moshe, the Amaleki, who came with a small number of men, would have defeated Yisrael. Hashem alone, Who doeth great things (Iyov 5:9); And by Him actions are weighed (Shmuel I 2:3), so arranged events that all Yisraeli males who left Mitzrayim died out, for they had no spirit to fight the Kenaani; and a new generation with a noble spirit, who had never tasted exile, arose after the generation of the wilderness. I have noted the aforementioned in the account of Moshe recorded in the Torah portion Ve-Eleh Shemot.

Hashem will fight for you. Lakhem means for you. Similarly, whenever the word war (milchamah) is followed by a lamed it indicates aid. Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen therefore explains li (me) in For there are many that fight (lochamim) me (li) on high (Tehillim 56:3) to mean for me. The meaning of on high is, a war on high, as is the case with all that sit.
And ye shall hold your peace. In contrast to and the children of Yisrael cried out (v. 10).

Wherefore criest thou unto me. Some say that Moshe was crying out unto Hashem. However, this is incorrect, for Hashem had already told Moshe, and I will get Me honor upon Paroh (v. 4). On the contrary, this was told to Moshe who stood in Yisrael’s stead because the children of Yisrael cried out to Hashem.
That they go forward. Little by little until they reach the edge of the sea.

And lift thou up. Hashem told Moshe to lift up his rod and divide the sea before the children of Yisrael went forward. Hashem did not tell Moshe to strike the sea. He told him to stretch out his hand toward the sea in the manner of And Moshe stretched forth his rod toward heaven (Shemot 9:23). We know that the rod did not divide the sea but that from the moment that Moshe stretched his hand toward the sea Hashem caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind and the waters then split. For it is so written.

And I. We know that the Red Sea is not situated between Mitzrayim and the Land of Yisrael. There was no reason for them to enter the sea. However, Hashem commanded them to do so, so that the Mitzrim would enter behind them and drown. The children of Yisrael, as I will explain, entered the sea from the wilderness of Etam and exited the sea to the wilderness of Etam.
And the Mitzrim shall know. Those that remained.
When I have gotten me honor upon Paroh. Who will drown along with his chariots and horsemen.

And the angel of God. This took place before speak unto the children of Yisrael, that they should go forward (v. 15). It’s meaning thus is, and the angel of God had already removed. I have already showed you many such instances. Now because these three verses are connected to each other and each one has seventy-two letters we find in them, as stated in the books, the sign of the secret of God’s explicit name. However, in my opinion it is so written because, as I will explain in the Torah portion Ki Tissa, the numerical value of God’s glorious name comes to seventy-two. The Book of Raziel states that one who wants to query the heavenly powers in a dream should read the verse, Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year, etc. (Yechezkel 1:1), for it contains seventy-two letters.

The angel of Elokim. The reference is to the great prince who goes in the cloud, concerning whom it is written, And Hashem went before them by day (Shemot 13:21). When this angel, who went before the camp of Yisrael, moved and went behind them, the pillar of cloud moved with him. Let the one who identifies the angel of Elokim with the cloud show us where we find the pillar of cloud called the angel of Elokim. Furthermore, if the angel and the pillar are one and the same, why is and the pillar of cloud removed from before them repeated? If he should answer that Scripture repeats the same idea in different words, then we respond that it is not the manner of Scripture to repeat itself except in prophecy or reproof. Moreover, it is unfit to repeat oneself when reporting how something happened.
And it came. And the angel came.
And there was the cloud and the darkness here. Between the camps.

And it lit up the night. As was the manner on all the nights, so that Yisrael could cross the sea. They crossed it at night. Rabbi Merinus says that the meaning of va-ya’er (he lit up) is, he darkened. And the night shall be light about me (Tehillim 139: 11) is similar. Furthermore, we find, On the light of the fourteenth day in rabbinic literature. However, the one who interprets thus turns darkness into light and light into darkness, for it is impossible in any language for a word to mean both a thing and its opposite unless it is euphemistically used, as in Navot did bless Elokim and the king (Melachim I 21:13). The word light in shall be light about me refers to the light itself, as I have explained. Similarly, the sages said that On the light of the fourteenth is a refined language, which is similar to a euphemism. Furthermore, what reason was there for Scripture to say, and he darkened the night? It is dark every night. The only meaning of va-ya’er et ha-laylah is that he lit up the night as he did from the day that Yisrael went out of Mitzrayim, for the pillar of fire was seen every night. Now if Yisrael had no light how did they cross the sea? For behold, by the time Paroh came into the sea and Hashem looked forth upon him in the morning watch, most of Bnei Yisrael had already crossed.
And Moshe stretched out his hand…all the night. Even while Yisrael was crossing, the wind did not cease.

And the children of Yisrael went into the midst of the sea. Do not think that because Scripture reads, in the midst of the sea that Bnei Yisrael reached the middle of the Red Sea. On the contrary, even if they entered the sea for even half of a Parsi mile one may say that they came in the midst of the sea. It is like And the mixed multitude that was in the midst of them (Bamidbar 11:4), for the mixed multitude was not in the middle of the camp. The meaning of the midst of the sea is, the place where there was water at the beginning of the night.

And the waters were a wall unto them. The waters froze. It is also written, The floods stood upright as a heap (Shemot 15:8). After most of Yisrael crossed, the waters which formed a wall for them melted. This is the meaning of that the waters may come back upon the Mitzrim (v. 26). These waters separated between the Mitzrim and the dry land. It therefore states, and the Mitzrim fled against it (v. 27), as the Mitzrim thought that they would go out onto dry land. But the walls of water melted and separated them and dry land. There is no doubt that those who pursued Yisrael saw the light by which Yisrael crossed.
And it came to pass in the morning watch. The alef of ashmoret (watch) is a superfluous letter.

That Hashem looked forth. The reference is to the angel of Hashem mentioned earlier. The same is the case with Gidon, where the messenger is called by the name of the sender. Since the sender commands his agent to commit an act, it is as if the sender himself had executed it.
Through the pillar of fire and of cloud. Between these two pillars.

And discomfited. Possibly because of this the poet says, The voice of Thy thunder was in the whirlwind (Tehillim 77:19). Similarly And He shot forth lightnings, and discomfited them (Tehillim 18:15). Elsewhere it is written, And He sent…Lightning, and discomfited them (Shmuel II 22:15).
And he took off. Va-yasar (and He took off) is a hifil. It should have been vocalized va-yaser with a segol beneath the samekh. I have already noted its grammatical explanation.

[And he took off their chariot wheels.] Some say its meaning is that they untied the knot of the wheel from the horses so that, being lighter, they could flee more easily. However, the above-mentioned divine discomfit fell upon them and their horses, and they could only drive them with great difficulty. Others say that va-yasar comes from the root of sorer (rebellious) (Devarim 21:18). He who went before them wanted to turn the chariot around.

For Hashem fighteth for them against the Mitzrim. Lahem means for them. It now becomes clear that Hashem’s word, and the Mitzrim shall know that I am Hashem (v. 4), which He spoke earlier meant: and the Mitzrim shall know before their deaths.
That the waters may come back. The waters which served as walls for them should return to their previous state.
When the morning appeared. Lifnot boker (when the morning appeared) means toward morning.
To its strength. Le-etano means to its strength. It is a noun, like etan in mighty rivers (Tehillim 74:15).

Fled against it. I have already explained that the Mitzrim in fleeing thought that they were returning to dry land when in actuality they were going toward the sea. May the bones of Chivi the dog be crushed. Chivi said that Moshe knew the time of low tide, when the level of the sea goes down, and the time of high tide, when the sea comes in and its level rises, and so brought his people across the sea when the tide was normally low. However, Paroh did not know the manner of the sea and therefore drowned. This interpretation is sheer madness, as the sea is not normally dry in any place when its level goes down. However, all was dry. Neither do walls of water remain on the right or the left. Furthermore, the end of low tide and the beginning of high tide do not become clear until some hours have passed. Moreover, Bnei Yisrael had not yet finished crossing before Paroh and his army drowned.

And Hashem overthrew. Va-yena’er (overthrew) is a pi’el. Na’arti (I shook) in Also I shook out my lap (Nechemyah 5:13) is similar to it. Va-yena’er is to be understood in the manner of hath He thrown into the sea (Shemot 15: 1).
And the waters returned. The waters that were walls returned.

So much as one of them. Even one of them did not escape. Similarly ad echad in and, behold, there was not so much as one (ad echad) of the cattle of Bnei Yisrael dead (Shemot 9:7). Indeed, the poet says, There was not one of them (echad me-hem) left (Tehillim 106: 11).

But the children of Yisrael. The reason this is noted a second time is that there remained some Bnei Yisrael who were still crossing the sea while Paroh was drowning. This was a miracle within a miracle, for in the place where Bnei Yisrael were crossing the sea there was a strong east wind drying and where Paroh and his host were, Hashem brought another wind to melt the waters that were frozen and formed walls. There were thus two winds in two places in the sea close to one another. True proof that this interpretation is correct is offered by the statement in the Song of Moshe, And with the blast of Thy nostrils the waters were piled up (Shemot 15:8), which speaks of the wind that blew for Yisrael; and the statement, Thou didst blow with Thy wind, the sea covered them (Shemot 15:10), which speaks of the wind that caused the Mitzrim to drown. It is because of this that the end of the song reads, and Hashem brought back the waters of the sea upon them; but the children of Yisrael walked on dry land in the midst of the sea (Shemot 15:19). Do not ask, how could all of Yisrael cross in one night? Did not the six hundred thousand men on foot make up only a quarter of the camp? Perhaps they passed over some other way. Or perhaps the sea split into twelve parts, as the sages of blessed memory say. Now Bnei Yisrael did not cross the width of the sea. On the contrary, they moved along its length and came out in the wilderness of Shur from wherein, as I will explain, they entered the sea.

Thus the Lord saved. Now Bnei Yisrael were saved from the hand of the Mitzrim. Until now the fear of Paroh was upon them. Scripture tells us that the Mitzrim drowned in the sea. The sea did not cast their bodies out upon the dry land, for it is clearly written, The earth swallowed them (Shemot 15:12). The meaning of and Yisrael saw the Mitzrim dead upon the sea-shore therefore is: when the Mitzrim drowned, Bnei Yisrael, who were on the shore, saw their dead bodies.
Feared. When Yisrael saw this great blow they feared Hashem, as in And David was afraid of Hashem that day when Uzah who put forth his hand to the ark of Hashem died (Shmuel II 6:9).
And they believed in Hashem. They believed that Hashem is truth and that Moshe is His servant and will do only that which Hashem commands him to do.

Then sang Moshe. It is Hebrew style to employ an imperfect preceded by the word az (then) in place of a perfect. Compare, Az yivneh shelomoh (then did Shlomo build) (Melachim I 11:7); az yedabber yehoshu’a (then spoke Yehoshua) (Yehoshua 10:12); az yavdil mosheh (then Moshe separated) (Devarim 4:41). The same is true in Arabic. Moshe composed the song by himself. He then taught it to all of Yisrael, each one of whom then sang and said, I will sing unto Hashem. And Moshe and the elders of Yisrael commanded the people (Devarim 27:1) is similar. The commandment was first spoken only by Moshe. The elders of Yisrael then repeated it to everyone.
And spoke, saying. Each one of Bnei Yisrael was to say the following, or the following was to be said in every generation.

For he is highly exalted. He demonstrated His exaltation by casting both the mighty rider and his exalted and powerful steed into the sea as one casts an arrow. The meaning of ramah (thrown) in ramah va-yam (hath He thrown into the sea) is similar to the word rome (throws) in armed with that which a bow throws (Tehillim 78:9).

Hashem is my strength and song. Rabbi Shlomo of blessed memory says that there is a difference between ozzi (my strength), which is vocalized with a furtive kamatz, and uzzi, which is vocalized with a kubbutz. He therefore says that the yod in ozzi (my strength) in Hashem is my strength and song is superfluous. However, Rabbi Shlomo does not offer another such instance. Rabbi Shlomo goes on to say that ve-zimrat (and song) is in the construct with Kah (Hashem). He interprets our verse as if it read: The strength and vengeance of Hashem became my salvation. Rabbi Shlomo thought that our verse is similar to va-yehi ba-yom ha-shelishi va-yissa avraham et enav (on the third day Avraham lifted up his eyes) (Bereshit 22:4). However, one who knows Arabic knows the difference between the two verses. It is neither correct Hebrew nor Arabic form to say ozzi ve-zimrat Kah va-yehi li li-shu’ah. There is no difference between ozzi vocalized with a furtive kamatz and the same word vocalized with a kubbutz. For while Scripture reads, chukki (mine allotted) in Feed me with mine allotted bread (Mishlei 30:8) it elsewhere reads, chokkha ve-chok ba-nekha (thy due, and thy son’s due) (Vayikra 10:13). Now we find the word ve-ozzekha (in Thy strength) (v. 13) vocalized with a furtive kamatz, later on in this song and similarly in O Hashem, in Thy strength (be-ozzekha) the king re-joiceth (Tehillim 21:2). The yod of ozzi is thus a first person suffix. Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that the meaning of ve-zimrat Kah is, Hashem is my song, for the resh of ve-zimrat (and song) is vocalized with a kamatz. Similarly, the meaning of shenat in I will not give sleep (shenat) to mine eyes (Tehillim 132:4) is, my sleep, as shenat is vocalized with a kamatz. Likewise, the meaning of nachalat, which is vocalized with a kamatz in Yea, I have a goodly heritage (nachalat) (Tehillim 16:6) is my heritage. Similarly, the meaning of menat, which is vocalized with a kamatz in, O Hashem, the portion (menat) of mine inheritance and of my cup (Tehillim 16:5), is my portion. However, what will Rabbi Moshe do with the word menat (portion) in the king’s portion (Divrei Hayamim II 31:3) in which menat is vocalized with a kamatz and is in the construct. It is the same case with the word yam (sea) in the salt sea (Bamidbar 34:3) and in the sea (yam) of Kineret (Bamidbar 34:11). Should one respond that the latter are irregular, we would tell him to place ozzi ve-zimrat Kah among them. I believe that the word ozzi (my strength) is, as is the style of the Hebrew language, to be read as if written twice. Our clause is to be read as if written, ozzi, ve-zimrat ozzi Kah (Hashem is my strength and the song of my strength). The reason behind this verse is that Moshe earlier mentioned, The horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea (v. 4). Moshe now states that this was not through his own majesty and strength. On the contrary, he confesses, my strength and the glory of my strength is Kah alone who is Hashem. Kah is, as I have explained, one of the three proper names of Hashem. All three come from one root. Since the word eheyeh is frequently employed in speech it was necessary to substitute a vav for a yod in Hashem’s glorious name. The word Kah is likewise known. Its yod was vocalized with a pattach because of the guttural and the silent yod was dropped because it has another secret numerical meaning. We find Kah combined with Hashem’s glorious name in ki ozzi ve-zimrat Kah YHVH (for Hashem Hashem is my strength and song) (Is. 12:2). I have already explained that the name YHVH is at times a proper name and at times an adjective.
This is my God. My power.
And I will glorify him. I will place Him in a building.

[This.] The word zeh (this) is to be read as if written twice. The last clause of our verse is to be read as if written: And this is my father’s Elokim, the reference being to the Elokim of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov.
And I will exalt him. For I will recount His might.
Hashem is a man of war. Hashem supports those who love Him and cleave unto Him and He is a man of war to their enemies.

[Man.] The word ish (man) means a being. Scripture thus states in reference to the stars, ish lo nedar (not one faileth) (Is. 40:26); and in reference to the living creatures, ish el ever panav yelekhu (they went every one straight forward) (Yechezkel 1:9); and in reference to the angels, ve-ha-ish gavriel (the man Gabriel) (Daniel 9:21). The meaning of ish milchamah (a man of war) thus is, a being who wages war. It is similar to the term ish emunim (a faithful man) (Mishlei 20:6), the meaning of which is, a being imbued with faith.

Hashem is his name. His name will now be known. Compare, That calleth for the waters of the sea, And poureth them out upon the face of the earth; Hashem is His name (Amos 5:8). He alone can do such a thing.
Paroh’s chariots. God, as it were, cast Paroh’s heavy chariots and their hosts as if they were a light arrow.
[And his chosen captains.] Moshe made mention of his chosen captains “who were over all them” because he had previously spoken of Paroh’s hosts.

[The Red Sea.] Yefet says that suf in yam suf (the Red Sea) has the same meaning as the word suf (flags) in The reeds and flags shall wither (Is. 19:6) and the word suf in and laid it in the flags (Shemot 2:3). For reeds and rushes grow around the yam suf, and not around other seas. However, Rabbi Yehoshua says that suf is the name of a city. It is like yam kinneret (the sea of Kineret) (Yehoshua 13:27).
The deeps. The deeps of the earth. Compare, The earth swallowed them (v. 11).
[Cover them.] A shuruk has been substituted for a cholam in yekhasyumu (cover them). Compare, ta’avuri (pass) in neither pass from hence (Rut 2:8).
The depths. Metzolot (the depths) means the deep waters. Similarly va-tashlikheni metuzlah, (for thou did cast me into the deep waters) (Yonah 2:4).
Glorious. The yod of nedari (glorious) is superfluous. It is like the yod of akhzari (cruel).

[Thy right hand.] The repetition of the phrase Thy right hand, O Hashem indicates the same as the repetition of For, lo, Thine enemies, O Hashem (Tehillim 92:10) and The floods have lifted up (Tehillim 93:3). It indicates time and time again. Its meaning is: your right hand dashes the enemy in pieces times without number.
[Glorious in power.] Glorious in power refers to Hashem. However, there are those who say that it refers to Hashem’s right hand.

And in the greatness of thy excellence. Which is superior to all who exalt themselves. You are able to shatter (overthrow) those that rise up against You. You need no iron weapons to shatter them. All You have to do is send forth Your wrath and it consumeth them as stubble, for God’s wrath is as hot as fire.
And with the blast of thy nostrils. You rebuke the waters and they congeal. Compare, By the breath of God they perish (Iyov 4:9).
The waters were piled up. The word ne’ermu (were piled up) is similar to the word aremat (a heap of) in a heap of wheat (Cant. 7:3).

The floods stood upright as a heap. The waters, whose nature is to flow and descend, turned into a heap (ned), as in And rose up in one heap (ned) (Yehoshua 4:16). The meaning of ned (heap) is a wall.
The deeps were congealed. Kafe’u means were congealed. Compare, ve-kippa’on (frost) (Zecharyah 14:6).
In the heart of the sea. The heart lies in the middle of the body from the point of view of the body’s width.
The enemy said. The reference is to Paroh.

[Shall be satisfied upon them.] The word timla’emo (shall be satisfied upon them) is difficult. Rabbi Merinus explains that timla’emo nafshi (my lust shall be satisfied upon them) means: my person shall be full of them; i.e., I will take all of their wealth. The term timla’emo is to be understood like the term yetza’uni (gone forth of me) in My children are gone forth of me (Yirmiyahu 10:20). Its meaning is connected to I will divide the spoil. Others say that timla’emo is used in the same sense as the word me’lo’o (presume) in that durst presume in his heart (Esther 7:5).
[My hand shall destroy them.] After doing the latter I shall destroy them.
My hand shall destroy them. Torishemo means shall destroy them. Similarly the word torishu (you will destroy) in But if you will not destroy (Bamidbar 34:55).

Thou didst blow with thy wind. Nashafta (Thou didst blow) comes from the same root as neshef (night). The meaning of nashafta ve-ruchakha (Thou didst blow with Thy wind) is: You brought a wind at night that drowned them.
They sank. Tzalelu (they sank) comes from the same root as metzolot (depths). Compare, My lips quivered (tzalelu) at the voice (Chavakuk 3:16).
In the mighty waters. This is connected to they sank. Our verse is to be read as if written: they sank as lead in the mighty waters.

As lead. Oferet (lead) comes from the same root as afar (dust). If one puts any of the six kinds of metal in the ground each will lose one of its familiar elements in a given number of years. However, lead will always maintain itself.

Who is like unto thee, o Hashem, among the mighty. Eilim (the mighty) refers to the holy angels in the celestial heights. The sons of the mighty (bene elim) refers to the stars. I will explain this further in the Torah portion Ki Tissa.
Glorious in holiness. The reference is to the Throne of Glory.

[Fearful in praises, doing wonders.] For all who want to acclaim God are afraid to praise His name because who can recite all of His praises. However, they are obligated to praise Him because He alone does wonders.

Thou stretchedst out thy right hand. Your wonders were manifest when You stretched forth Your hand from the highest realm of the celestial heights where Your name is exalted, and the ground which is beneath all earthly creatures swallowed up the enemy of Yisrael. Your right hand, which is above the heaven of heavens, reached, as it were, in a moment to the bottom of the sea.
[Thy right hand.] Its meaning is, Thy strength.
Thou in thy love hast led. Moshe used the perfect nachita (led) in place of the imperfect, as is the style in prophecy.
[In thy love.] The reference is to the pillars of cloud and fire, for God led them. On the other hand, it might allude to the fact that God led them up till now.
Thou hast led. Nehalta (thou hast led) is similar to etnahalah (I will journey) in I will lead on gently (Bereshit 33:14).
In thy strength. Not by their strength.
To thy holy habitation. The reference is to Mount Sinai where God’s Glory dwelt. It is similarly written, and brought you unto Myself (Shemot 19:4).
The peoples have heard. The reference is to the peoples round about them and also to the peoples whom they would pass by.
Pangs have taken hold on the inhabitants of philistia. The inhabitants of the land of Peleshet. The word inhabitants indicates this.
The mighty men. Ele (mighty men) spelled with a yod means sheep, for the sheep have leaders.
[Then were the chiefs of Edom affrighted…the mighty men of Moav, trembling taketh hold upon them.] The Plishtim, the Edomim, and the Moavim did not wage war with Bnei Yisrael in the wilderness.

All the inhabitants of Kenaan are melted away. Because of the reports which they received, as in And as soon as we heard it, our hearts did melt (Yehoshua 2:11). The inhabitants of Kenaan is also to be interpreted as the inhabitants of the land of Kenaan.

Terror and dread falleth upon them. This refers to Edom and Moav even though Kenaan is mentioned above. He spoke unto them in a pillar of cloud (Tehillim 99:79) is, as I have explained, similar. Likewise, and shed the blood of war in peace (Melachim I 2:5) only refers to Avner. So too, and Hashem healed Avimelech, and his wife, and his maid-servants; and they bore children refers to Avimelech’s wife and handmaids. All of this because Scripture reads, Till thy people pass over, O Hashem. For Yisrael passed them before they came to the land of Kenaan. Moshe repeated Till Thy people pass because they circled Mount Seir for many days.
[Thou hast gotten.] Its meaning is: they were slaves in Mitzrayim and Thou hast gotten them to be Your servants.

Thou bringest them in, and plantest them in the mountain of thine inheritance. A prayer that Yisrael remain long in the land and not be exiled from it. Our verse is like in the mountain of the height of Yisrael will I plant it (Yechezkel 17:23).

In the mountain. The goodly hill country and Levanon (Devarim 3:25) is similar. Or it alludes to Mount Moriyah. It is therefore followed by The place, O Hashem, which Thou hast made for Thee to dwell in.

[Which thou hast made.] Its meaning is: which Thou hast prepared as a place for a sanctuary for Thyself. The place mentioned lies opposite the glorious celestial place, for the places on earth vary in accordance with the star that is over them. Those who are versed in the science that deals with the constellations will understand this.

[The Sanctuary.] The word mikkedash (sanctuary) has the same meaning as mikdash (sanctuary). The word mittoharo (his brightness) in Thou hast made his brightness to cease (Tehillim 89:45) is similar, as the dagesh in the tet is superfluous, like the dagesh in the kof of mikkedash. The dalet does not receive a dagesh because the kof is vocalized with a mobile sheva. With the exception of the form shetayim we do not find it to be the way of Scripture to place a dagesh in a word which follows a mobile sheva. I have already noted its grammatical uniqueness.
Which thy hands have established. Its meaning is similar to thou hast made, for Scripture repeats itself.
Hashem shall reign. Hashem’s Kingship will be seen when the Holy Temple which will be dedicated to His name shall be built.

[For ever and ever.] Le-olam va-ed (for ever and ever) is an abridgment. The full form is le-olam ve-ad olam (for ever and until ever). Do not be amazed that the word ed is not in the construct, for we find, shokhen adve-kadosh shemo (That inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy) (Is. 57:15). It is the custom of Hebrew to vocalize a vav with a pattach when the syllable which follows it is accented. Compare, va-ez (or goat) in of ox, or sheep, or goat (Vayikra 7:23). It is for this reason that va-ed is vocalized with a pattach. Now Scripture reads, va-okhal mi-kol (I have eaten of all) (Bereshit 27:33). However, at the end of a verse it reads, ha-nachash hishi’ani va-okhel (the serpent beguiled me, and I did eat) (Bereshit 3:13). Hence the statement, le-olam va-ed.
For the horses of Paroh. This verse is, in my opinion, part of the song. Its purpose is to recall the wonder within the wonder, which I have noted.

[Upon them.] Upon them refers to the horses of Paroh…his chariots and his horsemen. It also includes Paroh. For Scripture clearly states, The enemy (Paroh) said (v. 9) and then goes on to say, The earth swallowed them (v. 12). Furthermore, it is explicitly written, But (God) overthrew Paroh and his host in the Red Sea (Tehillim 136:15).

And Moshe led. I believe that the pillar of cloud, and likewise the pillar of fire, that went before the people when they left Mitzrayim was to ensure that Yisrael was able to go by day and by night (Shemot 13:21). After Paroh and his hosts drowned, Yisrael was no longer frightened and did not travel at night. Indeed, we do not find it recorded in the Torah portion Be-Halotekha that Yisrael journeyed at night. Behold, Moshe now led the people according to Hashem’s command. There are only six journeys from the Red Sea until Mount Sinai lasting less than forty days. The air is then good. It is neither humid nor cold. He who does not have a tent can live outdoors without harm. When Yisrael came to the wilderness of Sinai they all erected booths, as they camped there for about year. Moshe informed them that they would tarry there until they constructed the Tabernacle. It was for this reason that, as I will explain, Yisrael brought out acacia wood from Mitzrayim. The festival of booths was established in commemoration of the booths that Yisrael made there, for Scripture states, that your generations may know that I made the children of Yisrael to dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Mitzrayim (Vayikra 23:43). How can one maintain that Yisrael dwelt in clouds? For the booths do not resemble clouds. I will yet explain why the festival of Sukkot is observed in the seventh month. When the Tabernacle was erected Hashem descended upon it in a pillar of cloud, as it is clearly written, and there was fire therein by night (Shemot 40:38). When the cloud journeyed the children of Yisrael went onward (Shemot 40:36). It is because of this that Scripture reads, and thou goest before them, in a pillar of cloud by day (Bamidbar 14:14). There were thus two interchanging pillars over the Tabernacle. If the statement to the effect that there were seven interchanging pillars over the Tabernacle is based on tradition, then we will rely on tradition and set aside our own opinions.

Into the wilderness of Shur. This is the very wilderness of Etam. Perhaps there were two cities in the wilderness that were so called. Or the wilderness had two names. And they went three days in the wilderness, the reference being to the wilderness of Shur, is proof of this. Therefore to indicate this the bet of ba-midbar (in the wilderness), which precedes and found no water, was vocalized for emphasis with a pattach.

And when they came to Marah. It is elsewhere written, And they journeyed from the Red Sea (Bamidbar 33:11). The latter is similar to And Moshe led Yisrael onward from the Red Sea, (and they went out into the wilderness of Shur and came to Marah) (v. 22). We similarly find, and they went three days’ journey in the wilderness of Etam, and pitched in Marah (Bamidbar 33:8).
Therefore the name of it was called Marah. Someone called it Marah. Who was born unto Levi in Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 26:29) is similar.

And the people murmured. Va-yillonu (murmured) is a nifal. It is similar to ve-yikkonu (shall be established) in And thy thoughts shall be established (Mishlei 16:3), which comes from the same root as nakhonu (prepared) (Mishlei 19:29). It comes from a double root or from a root in which the middle letter is missing. If it came from a root which begins with a nun it would have followed the paradigm of va-yiggashu (came near) (Bereshit 45:4).

And he cried unto the Lord; and the Lord showed him a tree. We do not know what type of tree this was. What happened can only be described as a miracle. If the waters were stationary then we would say that they were medicinally sweetened. What the sages said is correct.
There he made for them. Hashem for Yisrael.
A statute and an ordinance. To discipline them and to instruct them.

[And there he proved them.] This is to be understood in the manner of for Hashem your Elokim putteth you to proof, to know whether ye do love Hashem your Elokim with all you heart and with all your soul (Devarim 13:4). Scripture similarly states, And He afflicted thee, and suffered thee to hunger (Devarim 8:3); and that He might prove thee, to do thee good at thy latter end (Devarim 8:16), that is, to do good to those who did not murmur against Moshe.

And he said: if thou wilt diligently hearken. I have already noted that when the word shema (hearken) is followed by a lamed or a bet it does not mean to hear the words being spoken but rather to understand the subject which is being verbalized. Shema in our verse thus means to understand what the Lord commands us to do.
And wilt do that which is right in his eyes. This refers to the positive commandments.
And wilt give ear to his commandments. To understand what the negative commandments consist of.
And keep all his statutes. Not to violate them. Compare, And ye shall not walk in the statutes of the nation (Vayikra 20:23). It is Hashem’s statute not to imitate the practices of the nations.

[None of the diseases.] Its meaning is, the diseases you should remember. For you saw with your own eyes the diseases, the strokes, and the plagues which I put upon the Mitzrim because they rebelled against Me. Now if you will hearken to My statutes you will be saved from these plagues, for I will not do to you what I did to them. Additionally, you have no need of a physician for I am Hashem that healeth thee from all disease which I have decreed to be upon the earth. I will heal you as I healed the bitter waters which no physician has the ability to heal. Behold, what happened at Marah was the opposite of what occurred when the first plague struck, for the waters of the Yeor were sweet but the Mitzrim could not drink from them. However, here the bitter waters turned sweet. You should therefore love Hashem and keep yourself from rebelling against Him, for He will do good for you.

And they came to elim. Saadiah Gaon says there were seventy species of palm trees there. Others added, for each and every tribe. Others said, for each and every person. However, there is no need for these interpretations, for the springs of water, of which there were twelve, and the seventy palm trees did not come into being now because of Yisrael. Additionally, this was not the time for the ripening of palms. I believe that Yisrael tarried in Marah for only one day and that they stayed in Eilim for about twenty days. Scripture therefore says, and they encamped there by the waters. The next verse therefore informs us that Yisrael journeyed from Eilim on the fifteenth day of the second month. Now Yisrael camped in the following four places in fifteen days: the wilderness of Sinai, Dofkah, Alush, and Refidim, for they came to the desert of Sinai at the beginning of the third month. Scripture mentions the palm trees to let us know that contrary to the waters of Marah the waters here were sweet, for palm trees cannot flourish in a land of bitter waters.

And they took their journey. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that the reason Scripture mentions the fifteenth day of the second month is to inform us that Yisrael left Mitzrayim on the fifth day of the week. Now, the first day of Nisan fell on a Thursday and Iyyar on a Friday and on a Sabbath. Yisrael came to the wilderness of Sin on a Sabbath and complained upon camping. Moshe then told them that they would eat meat at even and that manna would come down in the morning. Now it is logical to assume that the manna first came down on a Sunday because Scripture states, And it shall come to pass on the sixth day (v. 5), the reference being to the sixth day of the week and the sixth day from the day on which the manna began to descend. We will accept that which the Gaon says because of tradition, not because of his explanation, for who told the Gaon that the manna came down on the morning following the coming of Bnei Yisrael to the wilderness of Sin? Bnei Yisrael may have camped there for four or more days but the manna started to come down on Sunday. The latter is so because we start the count from the day that the manna began to fall, for all the nations rely on Yisrael with regard to this numeration. Observe, the Christians named the days of the week after the stars. However, they did not do the same with the Sabbath day. The first five days of the week in Arabic are numbered.
