The sixth day is called al juma because it is the most honored day of the week for the Arvim and they congregate on this day. The Arvim refer to the day of shabbat as sabbat because the shin and samekh interchange in their script. They learned this from Bnei Yisrael. Behold, the natives of Hodu, who do not have the belief of six days of creation, begin the week on Wednesday because the sun is the star of that day and according to their beliefs it rules over them.

And the whole congregation of the children of Yisrael murmured. Bnei Yisrael murmured only against Moshe at the waters of Marah (Shemot 15:23) because it was he alone who led Yisrael onward. Only a part of Yisrael and not the whole nation complained. Scripture therefore reads, And the people murmured against Moshe (Shemot 15:24). However, in the wilderness of Sin we find that Scripture states, And the whole congregation of the children of Yisrael murmured against Moshe and against Aharon because both of them had brought them out of the land of Mitzrayim. In Marah they complained because of the water. However, they now complained about a lack of bread and meat because they had already consumed most of their cattle, for thirty days had passed since they left Mitzrayim. A congregation as large as Yisrael could only buy food at very great expense.
Behold, I will cause to rain bread from heaven. The bread will come down like rain from the sky.

[Bread.] The word lechem (bread) means food. It is found used for bread itself and also for meat, as in lechem isheh (food of the offering made by fire) (Vayikra 3:11). It is also used for fruit, as in Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof (be-lachmo) (Yirmiyahu 11:19).
[That I may prove them.] For they will daily need Me.
[Twice.] The meaning of mishneh (twice) is two omers per person, for it is so written.

And Moshe and Aharon said. Moshe and Aharon said, then shall ye know that Hashem hath brought you out from the land of Mitzrayim because Bnei Yisrael charged, for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness (v. 3). They answered, “Observe, we will perform two signs for you, one at the evening of this very day and one on the morning of the morrow so that you will know that Hashem hath brought you out from the land of Mitzrayim.” Scripture should have read: at even and in the morning ye shall know because and in the morning is not connected to then ye shall see the glory of Hashem. For as Scripture goes on to say, Yisrael saw Hashem’s glory on that very day.
And in the morning. I have already explained this.
For that he hath heard your murmurings. This is connected to then ye shall see the glory of Hashem.
And what are we. What can we do? We only did what we were commanded to do. The word ve-nachnu (and we) is missing an alef.
And Moshe said. Moshe now told them what the two signs would consist of.
Come near before Hashem. Turn to the wilderness.
And it came to pass. It became clear to them that when Aharon spoke to them, they came near before the Lord. The cloud came immediately and God’s glory was seen in it.
And Hashem spoke. Bnei Yisrael saw that Moshe went to the glory of Hashem and spoke to Hashem.

I have heard. The word telunnot is irregular in that its nun has a dagesh. This prophecy is repeated. Scripture had already noted, Hashem shall give you in the evening flesh to eat, and in the morning bread to the full. It was only repeated so that Yisrael would see the glory of Hashem.

[At dusk.] The term ben ha-arbayim means, as I have already explained, at dusk. This verse proves my interpretation of and in the morning, then ye shall see the glory of Hashem. (v. 7). For the verse states, At dusk ye shall eat flesh, and in the morning ye shall be filled with bread.
And it came to pass at even. At the end of that very day.
That the quails came up. Possibly from the direction of the sea.

A layer of dew. Shikhvat (a layer) is similar to yashkiv (bring down) in Or who can bring down (yashkiv) the bottles of heaven (Iyov 38:37). It means a descent. Scripture elsewhere writes, u-veredet ha-tal (And when the dew descended) (Bamidbar 11:9). May the name of Chivi rot for saying that the manna is to be identified with what is known in the Parsi tongue as tarnagbin, in Arabic as man, and in the vernacular as manna. There are many questions raised against him. First of all, no manna falls today in the wilderness of Sinai, for we know the location of the mountain. Now I have seen that which resembles manna in the kingdom of Al tzakir, and it only comes down in Nisan and Iyyar and in no other months. Additionally, if you place it in the sun it does not melt. Furthermore, it does not rot in the evening. Moreover, it is not very hard and one does not have to grind it in a pestle if one wants to make cakes out of it. Furthermore, it melts when placed upon the tongue. In addition, it does not satisfy because it does not produce good blood. It is only used as a medical ingredient. Furthermore, a double portion of manna came down on Friday. Moreover, the manna did not come down on the Sabbath. Furthermore, the manna came down wherever Yisrael camped. In addition, the manna crossed over the Yarden with Bnei Yisrael and did not cease to descend, according to the plain meaning of Scripture, until half the month of Nisan, had passed.

And when the layer of dew was gone up. The meaning of va-ta’al (was gone up) is ceased. It is similar to alah (went up) in Then defiledst thou it — my couch went up (alah) (Bereshit 49:4). The meaning of the latter verse is: from the time that you defiled my couch it was removed from me and ceased to function. Ta’aleni (take me away) in O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days (Tehillim 102:25) is similar. The dew came down first to clean the earth. When the dew was gone the manna descended. The latter is clearly written, viz., And when the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell upon it (Bamidbar 11:9).

A fine, scale-like thing. Mechuspas (scale-like thing) means round shaped. It has no cognate. The one who says that mechuspas is similar to machsof (uncovering) (Bereshit 30:37), which is spelled with a sin, is incorrect. For it is the manner of Hebrew to double the first and second root letters, as in the word yafyafita (thou art fairer) (Tehillim 45:3), or to double the second and third stem letters, as in the word yerakrak (greenish) (Vayikra 13:49), or to double only the third stem letter, as in sagrir (a very rainy day) (Mishlei 27:15). However, we never find the second root letter doubled except for instances when the heh is silent, as in hagigi (my meditation) (Tehillim 5:2) in which the gimel appears to be a third root letter after the heh is dropped. Hence it was doubled. However, we do not find the middle root letters to be doubled in words where all root letters are sounded.

And when the children of Yisrael saw it. Rabbi Shlomo says that the meaning of man hu (what is it) in Arabic is, what is it? However, someone misinformed him, because the Arabic phrase for “what is it” is mah huwi, as the term man is used in Arabic exclusively in reference to people. The way to explain man is to note that it comes from the same root as minnah (appointed) in who hath appointed your food and your drink (Daniel 1:10).

[And Moshe said unto them.] Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that we know that the Torah is not written in chronological order. Thus the meaning of And Moshe said unto them is: and Moshe had previously said unto them. There are many similar instances. Indeed, we find that Scripture states in this very portion, and it bred worms and rotted, the meaning of which is: and it bred worms and had previously rotted. Indeed, Scripture states, and it did not rot, neither was there any worm in it (v. 24). Scripture delayed reporting the words of Moshe because it had to elaborate and go on to say, This is the thing which Hashem hath commanded, etc. (v. 16).
[Gather ye of it every man according to his eating.] This was to be done by logical estimate. An omer for a head was for someone fully grown, for minors gather according to how much they consume.

And the children of Yisrael did so. According to the plain meaning of the text some gathered more and some less according to the number of people in their tents. However, our sages said that our verse speaks of a miracle.
And when they did mete it with an omer. Each one found that he had the amount that he had estimated.

And Moshe said unto them: let no man leave of it till the morning. Its meaning is, do not leave some of the manna over to eat on the next morning. Rather, trust in the Lord that it will descend on the following day. There was no command to eat the entire omer. However, that which a person did not consume was to be thrown outside of his tent.

Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moshe. The word anashim (some of them) is connected to Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moshe. They were few in number. Rabbi Merinus says that va-yarum (and it bred worms) comes from the same root as rimmah (worms).
And they gathered it morning by morning. The meaning of ve-cham ha-shemesh (and as the sun waxed hot) is: and when the day waxed hot. For the sun does not wax hot.
It melted. Namas (melted) comes from a double root and is in the nifal.

And it came to pass. More than the usual amount of manna descended on this day, as Scripture goes on to note. Yisrael gathered twice as much food on this day because Moshe had commanded them to do so. However, they did not know why. Also, Scripture states, they gathered, not they found. The rulers of the congregation came and told Moshe that Yisrael did as he commanded them. They then asked Moshe: What should be done with the extra portion? Why did he command them to gather twice as much food? How could they consume such a large amount of food?

And he said unto them. Hashem has already told me that you are obligated to rest tomorrow and not do any work including the preparation of food, for tomorrow is a Sabbath day unto Hashem. This is Hashem’s day because He rested from all His work on the seventh day. We find the same with regard to the Sabbatical year, viz., then shall the land keep a sabbath unto Hashem (Vayikra 25:2).

[Sabbath.] The word shabbat is grammatically difficult. It does not belong in the paradigm of gannav (thief) because the tav of shabbat is a feminine suffix, as is proven by the phrase shabbat hi la-Adonai (it is a sabbath unto Hashem) (Vayikra 23:3). The word shabbat is a noun meaning cessation. The following is its grammatical explanation. The word should have been spelled and vocalized shabbetet according to the paradigm of dalleket (inflammation) (Devarim 28:22). When one of the tavs was dropped the bet was vocalized with a kamatz to indicate that the word is feminine. It is the same, as I will explain, with the word achat (one).
[Bake.] The word efu (bake) is irregular. It should have followed the paradigm of asu (do). Behold, Moshe told the rulers of the congregation what they should do.

Bake that which ye will bake. Bake as you normally do so that you will have what to eat on this day. And see the that which ye will seethe has a similar meaning. Behold, prepare and cook all this according to your heart’s desire from one omer and eat as much as you need.

And all that remaineth. Lay it up till the morning and I will tell you what to do. Now Moshe did not inform them that no manna would descend on the Sabbath day. It was only in the morning that he revealed this secret to them

And Moshe said. Many lacking in faith erred because of this verse and said that a person is obligated to keep the Sabbath day plus the night which follows it, because Moshe said, for to-day and not the night before is a sabbath unto Hashem. Additionally, Moshe said, Tomorrow is a solemn rest (v. 23). They interpreted, in accordance with their view, And there was evening and there was morning one day (Bereshit 1:5) to mean that the first day was not finished until the morning of the second day. However, they spoke incorrectly. As I have already made mention to you, Moshe spoke to Yisrael only in accordance with their practice. Now the manner of the land of the uncircumcised with regard to their food, their dress, their buildings, and affairs is not the same as that of the Land of Yisrael. It is the practice in the Land of Yisrael that no one bakes, cooks, or does any other work, both in summer or winter, at any time but during the day. Hence Moshe said, Tomorrow is a solemn rest. Now pay close attention to understand the stupidity of those who explain and there was evening and there was morning in the manner which I noted above. For Scripture says, And Elokim called the light day (Bereshit 1:8), the reference being from the time that the sun rises until the time that it sets; and to the darkness He called night, the reference being from the time that the sun sets until the time that it rises. The night is thus the opposite of day, as the darkness is the opposite of the light. This being the case, how can Scripture refer to the evening, which commences at the time that the sun sets and lasts until the morning, as “day” when it is then night? Behold, concerning such people Scripture states, They change the night into day (Iyov 17:12). Now note that the word day is used in Hebrew in two ways. I have already mentioned one of them, viz., as long as the light of the sun is over any place on the earth. Therefore Scripture states, three days, night and day (Esther 4:16) and, and night and day (Bereshit 8:22). Now if the measure of the day includes the night in it, why mention night? It is also incorrect from the point of view of the science of linguistics for a noun to refer to two things which are the opposite of each other. The word day is used secondarily in the sense of close or far-off time, as in on the day that I smote all the first-born in the land of Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 3:13); thou art to pass over the Yarden this day (Devarim 9:1); and cast them into another land, as it is this day (Devarim 29:27); And it shall come to pass in that day (Is. 7:21). There are many other similar instances. Now let us leave all these things aside and seek, as I have said, only after the day of the Torah, for our years are not established according to the movement of the sun and moon but rather according to what the Bet Din decrees. Now we find that Scripture states, Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread (Shemot 12:15). Scripture then goes on to explain that this number begins on the evening of the fourteenth of the first month (Shemot 12:18). Scripture also states, from even unto even, shall ye keep your sabbath (Vayikra 23:32). Furthermore, a man who has a seminal emission during the night or day, for it is so written, viz., that which chanceth him by night (Devarim 23:11), does not become “clean” until sunset, which is the end of the first day. Now if it were so, namely, that the first day ends on the morning of the next day, then it is only fit for the one who experienced an emission to immerse himself in the morning. For if we say that the day and the night which follows it make up one day then the one who experienced an emission will be “unclean” for half a day and clean for half a day. And one who experienced an emission at the beginning of the night will be unclean for half of a day that passed and also for half of the coming day. This is the opinion of those who err. I have already explained to you the meaning of and there was evening and there was morning (Bereshit 1:5) in its place.

And Moshe said. Moshe now explained to them what they should do with the additional manna which was laid up, and he revealed to them its secret, that they would not find it this day because it did not come down.
Six days shall ye gather it. It shall always be as it is now for as long as you are in the wilderness; that is, ye shall gather it for six days but on the seventh no manna shall come down.
[In it there shall be none.] The word bo (in it) is added for additional clarification. It is similar to but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it (Bereshit 2:17).
And it came to pass on the seventh day. Of the manna’s appearance.
That there went out…to gather. To see whether Moshe’s words would stand up.
And Hashem said unto Moshe. Moshe was Yisrael’s representative. The meaning of our verse is: Hashem said unto Moshe, tell the following to Bnei Yisrael.
[My commandments.] This was said in reference to the people who left some of the manna over until the morning.

[My laws.] For Hashem taught them the reason for the Sabbath. They therefore gathered twice as much bread on the sixth day. There is a reason why Scripture employs the plural, namely, My commandments and My laws. All the commandments and laws are, beyond any doubt, to be taken literally. However, they have secret meanings pertaining to the soul that only the enlightened can understand. Thus every commandment has two meanings.

See. Its meaning is: see the wonder that Hashem will perform for you so that it shall become clear to you that Hashem commanded you to rest as He rested when He made all things in the beginning. Hashem is therefore permitting twice as much manna to come down today as normally comes down every day.
Abide ye every man in his place. In one’s tent.
[Let no man go out of his place.] It meaning is: let no man go out of his place on the seventh day to gather manna as the men who went out to gather did.
So the people rested. Scripture tells us that from that day on, no man went out on the Sabbath to gather.
And the house of Yisrael called the name thereof manna. Behold, Scripture previously noted the miracles associated with the manna. It now turns to relate its praises.

[And it was like coriander seed, white.] Some say that gad (coriander) refers to kosbarta, in Arabic, kusbar. Others say that it means mustard. However, I do not know, as it is not found in any other context save in reference to the manna. The same is the case with the word tzappichat (wafers), which Saadiah Gaon says means an unleavened wafer. Now when the manna was eaten as it was when it came down, it had the taste of a wafer made with honey. However, when cooked it had the taste of a cake baked in oil (Bamidbar 11:8). Scripture mentions these two delicacies.

And Moshe said. This chapter should have followed the account of the construction of the Tabernacle. It was placed here to relate the miracle of the manna lasting for generations. Now Moshe told this to Yisrael. He therefore said, wherewith I fed you.
A jar. A clay or copper utensil. The word is not found elsewhere.
[Before Hashem.] Its meaning is, before the divine glory which is upon the cherubim.

As Hashem commanded Moshe. Scripture here explains that before Hashem means: before the Testimony, the reference being to the ark. The ark is referred to as the Ark of the Testimony because of the tablets of the covenant that were in it.

And the children of Yisrael. This miracle was greater than all the other miracles that were done via Moshe, for many miracles were connected with the manna. These miracles, unlike all other wonders, lasted for forty years.

[Until they came to a land inhabited.] Scripture says this for they were in the wilderness, in a land that no man passed through (Yirmiyahu 2:6). Now once Yisrael crossed the Yarden they ate the grain that they found there. The reason Scripture found it necessary to say, they did eat the manna, until they came unto the borders of the land of Kenaan is that the manna accompanied them until they came to Gilgal, which lies on the border of the land of Kenaan. The manna then ceased to fall, for now they had new grain.
Now an omer is the tenth part of an ephah. Scripture mentions this measurement because one omer per person was sufficient for satiation.
Journeyed. Scripture is being brief in saying by their stages. For from the wilderness of Sin Yisrael journeyed to Dofkah; from there to Alush, and from Alush they went to Refidim.
[According to the commandment of Hashem.] Its meaning is, as I have already noted, via the hand of Moshe.

Wherefore the people strove. Scripture mentions the people, not all of the people as it does with regard to the manna, for there were two parties. One had no water to drink. This is the group that strove with Moshe. The second group had water which they brought from Alush. This group, as Scripture goes on to say, wanted to test Hashem and see if He would provide water.

Give us water. They spoke to Moshe and Aharon. There was no need to mention Aharon, for I have already explained that Moshe spoke to Yisrael only through Aharon. [WHY STRIVE YE WITH ME?] Moshe answered them, Why strive ye with me? Let us all cry out unto Hashem. He said, wherefore do ye try Hashem? to those who wanted to test Hashem.
And the people thirsted. When the thirst overpowered them they raged against Moshe and accused him of doing them evil in bringing them out of Mitzrayim.
And the people cried…they are almost ready to stone me. Scripture speaks metaphorically. Its meaning is: they have striven with me and they rage against me. If they had the power they would stone me.
And Hashem said. Some say that because Moshe said, they are almost ready to stone me, Hashem told him, Pass on before the people who strive with you and inform them that you will now give them water.
And take with thee of the elders of Yisrael; and thy rod, wherewith thou smotest the river. By command.
Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Chorev. Its meaning is, you will find Me there, the idea being you will encounter My strength and power on Chorev.
And thou shalt strike the rock. Which contains no water.
[And Moshe did so.] Scripture is being brief, for it does not mention, and the congregation drank, and their cattle (Bamidbar 20:11).
Called. Moshe or someone.

Massah and Merivah. Because of the two reasons noted. It is the style of the Hebrew language to begin its comments with the second of two items when two particulars are listed, as the second item is at hand. Compare, And I gave unto Yitzchak Yaakov and Esav (Yehoshua 24:4), which is followed by and I gave unto Esav (Ibid.). Scripture similarly first mentions Massah and then Merivah and turns to explain that the name of the place was called Merivah because of the striving of the children of Yisrael with Moshe. It then explains that the place was called Massah because they tried Hashem. Now “trial” refers to Yisrael’s asking, Is Hashem among us to provide for all of our needs? This second party angered Elokim more than the first. Scripture therefore says, Ye shall not try Hashem your Elokim, as ye tried Him in Massah (Devarim 6:16).
Then came Amalek. The reference is to the nation of Amalek, which dwelleth in the land of the South (Bamidbar 13:29).

And Moshe said unto Yehoshua. Yehoshua was the grandson of Prince Elishama ben Amihud, the possessor of the banner of the tribe of Efraim. Scripture refers to him here as Yehoshua, which is the name by which Moshe called him in the account of the spies.
Choose us out. It is Hebrew style to speak in this manner. Compare, choose thee (Shmuel II 24:12); Tarry ye here for us (Shemot 24:14).
Men. Renowned, powerful men and men of war, as in all of them men (Bamidbar 13:3).
And go out, fight with Amalek. Go out from the camp of Yisrael to fight against Amalek.
I will stand on top of the hill. Chorev, which is the same as Mount Sinai.
With the rod of Elokim in my hand. With which I will lift my hand to pray.
So Yehoshua did. Aharon and Chur are mentioned because of the need to explain (they) stayed up his hands (v. 12).

And it came to pass. Some say that Moshe held his hand up in a manner similar to one holding up a banner in war. However, if this was the case then Aharon or Chur would have lifted the rod up or they would have placed it on a high place on the mountain so that the people would see it standing. The correct interpretation is the one offered by the ancient sages.

But Moshe’s hands were heavy. We know that a human being does not have the strength to hold his hands up for an entire day. One cannot even hold them up for a few hours, certainly not until the going down of the sun. Now Scripture notes that Moshe’s hands were heavier than the hands of other old people. Moshe thus could not continually hold his hands up.
[And put it.] Its meaning is, they strengthened his place because he was not able to stand up.

And Aharon and Chur. Stood. Scripture employs the masculine kevedim (heavy) and similarly reads, mi-zeh echad u-mi-zeh echad (the one on the one side, and the other on the other side). Ve-hinneh yad sheluchah elai, ve-hinneh vo megillat sefer (behold, a hand was put forth unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein) is similar (Yechezkel 2:9).

And his hands were steady. Each one of his hands. The phrase is grammatically similar to Its branches run over the wall (Bereshit 49:22) and But the righteous are secure as a young lion (Mishlei 28:1).

Steady. Emunah (steady) is a noun meaning something lasting and permanent. Others say that emunah comes from the same root as the word omen (brought up) in And he brought up Hadassah (Esther 2:7). Aharon and Chur were like nursemaids who lifted up his hands.

And Yehoshua discomfited Amalek. There is no difference between va-yachalosh (discomfited or weakened) and va-yechelash (weakened) (Iyov 14:10). Likewise, the word yitrof (tear) (Tehillim 7:3) means the same as yitraf (tears) (Bereshit 49:27). The same is the case with the words tiddor (voweth) in voweth a vow (Bamidbar 30:4) and va-yiddar (vowed), which is vocalized with a pattach in and Yaakov vowed a vow (Bereshit 28:20). However, this root, like the word shav (returned), is sometimes transitive and sometimes intransitive. Or, va-yechelash (weakened) in a man (gever) dieth, and is weakened (Iyov 14:10) means he was already weakened, like the word va-yivash (and rotted) in and it bred worms, and rotted (Shemot 16:20). Scripture therefore employs the term gever (man), which indicates a mighty man.

Write this for a memorial in the book. This chapter was said in the fortieth year. The fact that Scripture reads ba-sefer (in the book) with a pattach beneath the bet is proof of the aforementioned. For ba-sefer refers to the well-known book, that is, the book of the Torah. It is also possible that they had another book known as The Book of the Wars of Hashem which was lost to us, as were the Sefer Ha-Yashar and the Midrash of Ido and the Chronicles of the Kings of Yisrael and the works of Shlomo.
[In the ears of Yehoshua.] For Hashem knew that Yehoshua was destined to wage war with the kings of Kenaan.

[For I will utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek.] Because Amalek angered Elokim. For the chiefs of Edom and similarly those of Moav and of Peleshet feared and trembled before Elokim because of the signs which Hashem displayed in Mitzrayim and at the sea. Now this very Amalek heard of the might that Elokim displayed on behalf of His people Yisrael. Behold, he came from a distant place to wage war against Yisrael. He did not fear Elokim. Indeed, Scripture explicitly states, and he (Amalek) feared not Elokim (Devarim 25:18). Some say that Amalek was the name of a king. They say this because Scripture reads, Amalek and his people. On the other hand, it is possible that another nation joined Amalek.
And Moshe built an altar. On Chorev. The word mizbe’ach (altar) is to be read as if written twice. Our verse is to be read as if written, mizbach Adonai (the altar of Hashem).

The hand upon the throne of Hashem. It is as if Hashem put His hand upon His throne. This was the taking of an oath. It is similar to For I lift up My hand to heaven (Devarim 32:40). Rabbi Yehoshua says that its meaning is that the first one to sit upon the throne of Yisrael, the reference being to Shaul, will have a mighty hand. We similarly find it said concerning Shlomo: Then Shlomo sat on the throne of Hashem (Divrei Hayamim I 29:23).
The word of Avram, the prisoner of hope; Who loosened his bowstring (yitro).

For He hath loosed my cord, and afflicted me (Iyov 30:11). The bow is a symbol of power. I.E. here indicates that he himself has passed the prime of life and has grown weak and weary. Half of his courage is forever gone; And the rest (yitro) was dissipated by his tortuous wanderings.
This is a comment upon the chapter Which opens with the word Yitro (Yitro).

Now Yitro heard. Scripture notes above the incident of Amalek because Amalek came to Refidim. Now the chapter that opens with the words In the third month (Shemot 19:1) should have followed the incident of Amalek, for Scripture states there, And when they were departed from Refidim, and were come to the wilderness of Sinai (Shemot 19:2). This being the case, why was the account of Yitro inserted between these two chapters? Saadiah Gaon says that Yitro came to the wilderness of Sinai before the giving of the Torah. However, I believe that Yitro came to Sinai in the second year, after the erection of the tabernacle. For the chapter speaks of a burnt-offering and sacrifices for Elokim (v. 12), and it does not mention that he built a new altar. Furthermore, Scripture writes, and I make them know the statutes of Elokim, and His laws (v. 16). Now this took place after the giving of the Torah. True proof that my words are correct is the fact that Scripture clearly states, where he was encamped, at the mount of Elokim (v. 5). Now Moshe spoke to Chovav, the latter being Yitro as I explained in the Torah portion These Are The Names. For Moshe’s father-in-law does not refer to Reuel, which precedes the term father-in-law, but refers to Chovav. Scripture clearly states, from the children of Chovav the father-in-law of Moshe (Jud. 4:11). Moshe told Chovav, [Leave us not, I pray thee] forasmuch as thou knowest how we are to encamp in the wilderness (Bamidbar 10:31). Now we know that Yisrael camped around Sinai for about a year. Lo and behold, Moshe’s very words prove this to be so. For Moshe is quoted in the Torah portion, These are the words as saying, Hashem our Elokim spoke unto us in Chorev, saying: …turn you, and take your journey (Devarim 1:6,7). Now this was said close to their time of journey. Moshe continued, And I spoke unto you at that time saying: I am not able to bear you myself alone (Devarim 1:9); for Hashem your Elokim hath multiplied you, and, behold, ye are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude (Devarim 1:10). The reason Moshe mentioned this to them was that Elokim told Yaakov, Behold, I will make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, and I will make of thee a company of peoples; and will give this land to thy seed after thee for an everlasting possession (Bereshit 48:4). Now the meaning of the latter is: when your seed increase I will give them the land. Moshe therefore said, Hashem your Elokim hath multiplied you and the time for you to inherit the land has come. However, since you are so numerous I was not able to carry you alone, and I had to place over you captains of thousands and captains of hundreds. Now this was the advice given to Moshe by Yitro on the morrow following his coming to the wilderness of Sinai. Moshe therefore said to Chovav, who, as we explained, is to be identified with Yitro, We are journeying (Bamidbar 10:29). Chovav responded, I will not go; but I will depart to mine own land, and to my kindred (Bamidbar 10:30). This is what And Moshe let his father-in-law depart; and he went his way into his own land (v. 27) refers to. I will now explain why the chapter dealing with Yitro was inserted here. It was placed here because Scripture had just mentioned the evil that Amalek did to Yisrael. The Torah wants to contrast it with the good that Yitro rendered Yisrael. Scripture notes, And Yitro rejoiced for all the goodness which Hashem had done to Yisrael (v. 9) and that he gave proper and correct counsel to Moshe and Yisrael. Moshe told Yitro, and thou shalt be to us instead of eyes (Bamidbar 10:31), meaning that he enlightened their eyes. King Shaul similarly said, for ye showed kindness to all the children of Yisrael (Shmuel I 15:6). Now because Scripture states in the preceding chapter, Hashem will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Shemot 17:16), namely, that when Elokim gives Yisrael rest they are obligated to wage war against Amalek, the Torah mentions the account of Yitro. For the descendants of Yitro lived in proximity to the nation of Amalek, and the Torah wants Yisrael to remember the kindness that Yitro demonstrated so that they do not harm his seed. Thus we find the Rechavim, who were descended from Yitro, living among the children of Yisrael in Yerushalayim. We find Yonadav the son of Rechav in the time of Yirmiyahu (Yirmiyahu 35:19). There is another chapter similar to the one above.
All that God (ELOHIM) HAD DONE. Scripture employs the name of God that was known in the world before the appearance of Moshe, for all admitted that God existed.

And for Yisrael his people. Hashem’s people, or the people of Moshe. It is possible that the lamed should be translated as “because,” that is, because of Moshe and Yisrael, the reference being to the plagues and the drowning of Paroh.
How that Hashem (YHVH) HAD BROUGHT. Scripture employs the divine name revealed to Moshe, since it was through the miracles that Yisrael went out of Mitzrayim.
And Yitro took. Scripture reads, Moshe’s wife, and not Yitro’s daughter, because Moshe was more important than her father’s house.

After he had sent her away. Some say that Moshe gave her permission to return to her father’s house, at the lodging place, prior to his returning alone to Mitzrayim. Other say she sent gifts to Moshe. Compare, shilluchim (gifts) in gifts unto his daughter (Melachim I 9:16).

And. Note that those who speak the holy tongue preserve the verbal forms in all conjugations. However, they are not careful to do so with proper nouns. Therefore do not be amazed that Moshe called his son Gershom because he lived (gar) there (sham). For look, kayin (Kayin) was so called because Chavah said, kaniti (I have gotten) (Bereshit 4:1). However, this is grammatically incorrect. The name Noach, which Scripture derives from yenachamenu (shall comfort us) (Bereshit 5:28), is even more difficult. Scripture at times inverts a name. Thus Chushim (Bereshit 46:23) and Shucham (Bamidbar 26:42) are one and the same. Yabetz (Yabetz) was so called because his mother bore him in pain (otzev). Sometimes a letter is dropped in a name, as in the case of Ma'achah which is a variant of Michah. The reverse is true of Yov (Iob) (Bereshit 46:13), which is the same as Yashuv (Yashuv) (Bamidbar 26:24). Many say it is the same with Shemu’el (Shmuel), which is derived from she’iltihu (I have asked him) (Shmuel I 1:20). However, in my opinion a shuruk has been substituted here for a cholam, as in the case of Tohu (Shmuel I 1:1) and Toach (Divrei Hayamim I 6:19); Tzuf (Shmuel I 1:1) and Zophai (Divrei Hayamim I 6:11); Nun (Shemot 33:11) and Non (Divrei Hayamim I 7:26). Now Shemu’el (Shmuel) comes from shemo el (his name is Hashem). Shmuel’s mother called him by Hashem’s name because Hashem answered her request. Do not be amazed that a human being should be called by Hashem’s name, for, observe, we find this to be the case with the name Tzurishadai (Bamidbar 7:36). There are many other similar instances. In my opinion the altar which Moshe built was similarly called Adonai-nissi (Hashem is my banner) (Shemot 17:15). Likewise, the name of the Messiah will be called Adonai-tzidkenu (Hashem is our righteousness) (Yirmiyahu 23:6). However, Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that Hashem’s name is connected to the word yikre’o (shall call him) and the name of the Messiah will be tzidkenu (our righteousness). Now its correct interpretation is in keeping with the opinion of the master of the cantillical notes, who placed a tircha in the word yikre’o. For there is a great difference between va-yikra be-shem Adonai (and called upon the name of Hashem) (Bereshit 12:8), written in connection with Avraham with a tircha beneath the word va-yikra, and vayikra ve-shem Adonai (and proclaimed the name of Hashem) (Shemot 34:5) which is written in the Book of Moshe as I will explain in its place.

And the name of the other was. It is the custom in Hebrew to say, “This is how the second one was called.” At other times it uses the term “the one,” as in and the name of one was Botzetz, and the name of the other was Sene (Shmuel I 14:4).

[For the Elokim of my father was my help.] The word amar (he said), which should have followed the word ki (for), has been omitted in for the Elokim of my father. Scripture does not read, “for he said the Elokim of my father was my help” because the phrase refers to for he said: I have been a stranger (v. 3), which is written above. It is similar to for Elokim hath made me fruitful (Bereshit 41:52). I have already explained why Moshe named his younger son Eliezer.
And came. Scripture notes that Yitro followed etiquette when he came to Moshe. Yitro went first, the sons of Moshe went behind him, and after them Moshe’s wife, as is the custom.
Where he was encamped. He encamped there for many days.

And he said unto Moshe. He had already said unto Moshe prior to his coming, via an agent or by a written message: I thy father-in-law Yitro am coming unto thee, and also thy wife, who is uppermost in importance, and her two sons who are coming with her.

And Moshe went out to meet his father-in-law. Out of regard for Yitro and his wisdom, but not out of regard for his wife and children, for it is not customary for a respected person to go out to meet his wife or children.

And bowed down. Va-yishtachu (and bowed down) is grammatically difficult. We know that it comes from a root ending in a heh. The vav in va-yishtachu is in place of a heh, like the vav of shalev (at ease) in I was at ease (Iyov 16:12), from whose root we get the word shalavti (at ease) in I was not at ease (Iyov 3:26). Now the term va-yishtachaveh should have been employed in the singular, rather than va-yishtachu, for the tav is a sign of the hitpa’el conjugation. It is like the tav in mishta’eh (steadfastly) in And the man looked steadfastly on her (Bereshit 24:21). For the rule relating to the dentals states that if the first letter of a root before which the tav of the hitpa’el conjugation is placed is a dental, then [the tav is placed after the first root letter]. Now because the heh has been changed into a vav in va-yishtachu Hebrew allows the first vav, which is not a plural suffix, to remain in place of the root heh and silences the vav. Hence the word reads va-yishtachu. Now a vav at the end of a word is the sign of the plural suffix when silent as in titra’u (look one upon the other) in Why do ye look one upon the other (Bereshit 42:1). Thus the word va-yishtachu, ending in a silent vav, would appear to be in the plural. Va-yishtachu was therefore penultimately accented to differentiate between it and the customary way of vocalizing plurals.
[And bowed down.] Logically speaking, the one who goes out is the one who bows to his counterpart.
[Each other.] Scripture refers to Yitro as Moshe’s friend because of his greatness in wisdom.
And they came into the tent. Which was known as Moshe’s tent.
And Moshe told. This verse indicates that the meaning of for Moshe, and for Yisrael (v. 1) is: because of them.

The travail. Tela’ah (travail) comes from the same root as ve-nilu (shall loathe) in and the Mitzrim shall loathe (Shemot 7:18). The tav is superfluous. Its meaning is, an affliction which a person is unable to bear or verbalize. It refers to Mitzrayim’s pursuit of Yisrael at the sea, the war with Amalek, and the thirst and hunger which the congregation suffered. Hashem delivered them from all of these.

And Yitro rejoiced. Va-yichad (rejoiced) comes from the same root as the word chedvah (rejoicing). It should have been vocalized like the word va-yift (enticed) in And my heart hath been secretly enticed (Iyov 31:27) and va-yishb (and took captive) in and took some of them captive (Bamidbar 21:1). However, the chet was vocalized with a pattach because it is a guttural, and the dagesh remains in the dalet as it was. I am not aware of a letter having a dagesh at the end of a word in all of Scripture except in the case of a bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, peh, tav at the end of a word when two sheva’im come together, as in the word va-yishb (and took captive) in and took some of them captive (Bamidbar 21:1) and va-yesht (and he drank) in And he drank of the wine (Bereshit 9:21). However, we never find a dagesh at the end of a word when preceded by a vowel except in the case of a pattach. In the latter case we find two such words namely, va-yichad (rejoiced) in And Yitro rejoiced and yichad (rejoice) in Let it not rejoice among the days of the year (Iyov 3:6).

And Yitro said: blessed be Hashem. Give your attention to the grammatical explanation of the word barukh (blessed). Note that the pa’ul can only be formed from transitive verbs. If you find a verb following the pa’ul form, look around; if you find it has a transitive po’el form, then the word is a real pa’ul. However, if you do not find it to be so, then the word is an adjective. Similarly, if a word is in the po’el form and its root does not come in the pa’ul in the same conjugation, then the word is also not a po’el but an adjective. For example, the po’el and pa’ul forms of shamar (kept) are shomer (keeps) and shamur (kept). Compare, shamur in riches kept by the owner thereof to his hurt (Kohelet 5:12). Now we encounter holekh (goes), omed (stands), yotze (goes out). All these words appear to be verbs in the po’el, for they follow the form of shomer. However, since these roots form intransitive verbs, for one cannot say halukh (wented), amud (stooded up), yatzu (wented out), these words do not come in the pa’ul. Therefore when Scripture uses the term holekh (went) in because he went (Bamidbar 22:21), it employs an adjective, not a verb. We find [Scripture using] the word atzum (mighty). The word appears to be a pa’ul because it follows the paradigm of shamur (kept). However, when we investigated this root we found the word va-ya’atzmu (waxed mighty), in and multiplied, and waxed exceedingly mighty (Shemot 1:7), to be among the intransitive verbs. For its transitive form comes in the hifil as in va-ya’atzimehu (and made them too mighty) in and made them too mighty for their adversaries (Tehillim 105:24). Now we cannot say that otzem (strengthens) following the paradigm of shomer (keeps) means strength, for in this case it has a different meaning, as in otzem (shutteth) in And shutteth his eyes from looking upon evil (Is. 33:15). Now we find the word barukh, which follows the paradigm of shamur (kept). We searched all of Scripture and we did not see this root used with this meaning in all of the kal conjugation. We found it used only with another meaning, namely, to kneel, as in va-yivrakh (kneeled) in and kneeled down upon his knees (Divrei Hayamim I 6:13), which is also intransitive and does not have a pa’ul form. The word barukh (blessed) is thus like the word atzum (might), a kal adjective. Rabbi Merinus says that barukh (blessed) is an adjective in the pi’el. Its resh should have received a dagesh like all other such roots, such as berekh (curse) in Navot did curse (Melachim I 21:13). Barukh follows the paradigm of shakkul (bereaved) in as a bear that is bereaved of her whelps (Hoshea 13:8). However, Rabbi Merinus spoke incorrectly, for all adjectives such as shakkul (bereaved), gibbor (warrior), shikkor (drunk) do not undergo any change by having the vowel that precedes the dagesh change in the singular construct or in the plural. Compare, gibbor (mighty man) in And Zichri, a mighty man of Efraim (Divrei Hayamim II 28:7), and gibborim (mighty) in Woe unto them that are mighty (Is. 5:22). Now the word berukh (blessed of), in Come in, thou blessed of Hashem (Bereshit 24:31) and berukhim (blessed) in, Blessed be ye of Hashem (Tehillim 115:15), argue against Rabbi Merinus.

Who hath delivered you. He said this to Moshe and Aharon, who were Hashem’s messengers and through whom the plagues came upon Paroh and Mitzrayim. Yitro therefore said, out of the hand of the Mitzrim, and out of the hand of Paroh. After this he blessed Hashem, who hath delivered the people from under the hand of the Mitzrim in Mitzrayim and at the splitting of the Red Sea.
Now I know. I have explained the meaning of now I know in the Torah portion Shemot, in the verse and they shall say to me: What is His name? (Shemot 3:13).

[Yea, for that.] Because of the fact that the Mitzrim dealt willfully with Yisrael. Yitro similarly, noted above, I know that Hashem is greater than all gods in that he punished the Mitzrim because they made Yisrael work with rigor. It is similarly written, Thou knewest that they dealt proudly (hezidu) against them (Nechemyah 9:11) that is, they behaved like a person who does whatever he wants to. Scripture already stated, for I know their pains; and I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Mitzrim (Shemot 3:7,8).
And Yitro, Moshe’s father-in-law, took a burnt-offering and sacrifices. The latter refers to peace-offerings.
[For Elokim.] The meaning of for Elokim is that henceforth the revered Hashem shall be his Elokim.
And Aharon came, and all the elders of Yisrael. There is no need to mention Moshe, as they were in Moshe’s tent.
To eat bread. Peaceofferings.
[Before Elokim.] Scripture reads thus because Moshe’s tent was on the east side of the tabernacle.
And it came to pass on the morrow. Of Yitro’s coming.
That Moshe sat. As was his custom.

From the morning unto the evening. Note that true morning begins with sunrise. The term morning is, as I have previously noted, also applied to the breaking of dawn, when light begins to be seen in the clouds. In the latter instance the term is artificially used. Similarly, true evening begins when the sun sets. The term is also artificially applied up to the time that the light sets. David similarly said, The sun ariseth, they slink away (Tehillim 104:22). Scripture then states, Man goeth forth unto his work, And to his labor until the evening (Tehillim 104:23). It is therefore fitting to interpret from even unto even, shall ye keep your sabbath (Vayikra 23:32) to mean: from the true evening to the true evening. However, our sages of blessed memory “added from the weekday to the holy day” and said that the Sabbath does not end until the stars come out. It is thus fitting from the Torah’s point of view to start the Sabbath at sunset. All scientists and astronomers admit that the day’s boundary is the moment when the circle of the sun faces all over the area of the earth. This starts at sunrise and ends at sunset.
And…saw all that he did to the people. That he caused them to stand from morning to evening.

Rabbi Shlomo says that Yitro reacted in this manner because Moshe alone sat and Yisrael stood, the latter being improper. There can be no doubt that Moshe’s station was too great for Yitro to say this. For behold, Aharon, who was a great man in the eyes of Yisrael and was older than Moshe, said to Moshe, Oh my lord (Bamidbar 12:11). Moshe acted in the proper manner, for the judge sits and the litigants stand. We thus read, then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand (Devarim 19:17). Yitro said, why to Moshe for no reason other than that Moshe was sitting alone and had no other judges to assist him. [WHY.] Rabbi Merinus says that the word maddu’a (why) is similar to mallakhem (what mean ye) (Is. 3:15) and to mazzeh (what is that) in what is that in thy hand (Shemot 4:2), each of which is a compound of two words. The same is true of maddu’a, which means: what is in your mind that you do this?

And Moshe said. Moshe answered, I do two things. One, Because the people come unto me to inquire of Elokim, that is, to inquire of Elokim’s law. The other, when they have a matter, it cometh unto me (v. 16). Moshe explained the second task first, namely, and I judge between a man and his neighbor (ibid.); and, he then said, to one who inquires, I make them know the statutes of Elokim.

And…said…the thing that thou doest is not good. In my eyes. Yitro then explained himself, Thou wilt surely wear away. Navol tibbol (thou shalt surely wear away) comes from the same root as yibbol (wither) in And whose leaf doth not wither (Tehillim 1:3) and novelet (fadeth) in For ye shall be as a terebinth whose leaf fadeth (Is. 1:30). Its meaning is, you shall, as it were, drop like a withered leaf. The word gam (both) is to be prefaced also to for the thing is too heavy for thee.
To perform it. Asohu (to perform it) is grammatically inconsistent. It follows the form of lishmerehu (to preserve him), for we do not find the heh to be visible in the root ayin, sin, heh.
Hearken now unto my voice, I will give thee council. I’atzekha, means I will give you council.

[Elokim.] Note that the term Elokim (Elokim) is, as I have noted, an adjective. It is only because the word is used often that this adjective is considered as if it were a proper noun. Examples of the latter are: Elokim (Elokim) in Elokim will let me gaze upon my adversaries (Tehillim 59:11); In the beginning Elokim (Elokim)created the heaven and the earth (Bereshit 1:1), and many other instances. It is for this reason that our sages of blessed memory placed Elokim among the names that are not erasable.

[And Elokim be with thee.] Its meaning is, Hashem will help you if you act in this manner. At the close of his words, Yitro told Moshe to ask permission of Hashem to act in accordance with Yitro’s counsel. This is what Yitro meant by and Elokim command thee so (v. 23). There is no doubt that Moshe did so.
[Be thou for the people.] The meaning of la-am is, for the people.
Before Elokim. From Hashem’s side.

And bring thou the causes unto God. If they be difficult. These are the things that Moshe mentioned at first, viz., when they have a matter, it cometh unto me (v. 16). Yitro then explained this to him, viz., the hard causes they shall bring unto thee.

And thou shalt teach them. As to the second thing you spoke of, you are obligated to teach and instruct them only those things that they are uncertain of. For it takes great effort to teach all, the work that they must do. Now as to the meaning of ve-hizharta (and thou shalt teach): ve-hizharta comes from the same root as nizhar in and took not warning (Yechezkel 33:5). Nizhar means took warning.
Them. Ethem (them) is a compound of two words.

[And thou shalt teach them.] You shall warn them to observe the positive and negative commandments that are tied to the heart, such as, to love Hashem, to cleave unto Hashem, to fear Hashem, to walk after Hashem, to circumcise the foreskin of the heart, not to hate one’s brother, not to take revenge, and not to bear a grudge. They are the most important commandments. Moshe similarly said, [But the word is very nigh unto thee] in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it (Devarim 30:14). There many such precepts.
They must walk. Yelekhu bah means wherein they must walk.

And the work that they must do. The reference is to positive precepts which are observed by action. Most of them are not positive commandments that stand by themselves but serve as a reminder, such as the Sabbath, the Festivals, the redemption of the first-born, loving the stranger, the fringes, the tefillin, the mezuzah, and also the prohibition against mixing linen and wool, and many others. I will explain them in their place.

Moreover thou shalt provide. I have already informed you that the speakers of Hebrew do not preserve exact wording. They only preserve meanings. Hence, as I will yet explain, we will not pay attention to whether the text is full or deficient. Now when Moshe recounted this incident, in place of able men he said, Get you…men (Devarim 1:13). Men in the latter verse has the same meaning as men in Choose us out men (Shemot 17:9) and in all of them men (Bamidbar 13:3). Yitro said appoint men.

Such as fear Elokim. Who do not fear men but fear only Hashem. It was to them that Moshe was referring when he said, wise…and understanding (Devarim 1:13). For it is not possible for one to be a fearer of heaven unless one be wise.

Yitro continued: MEN OF TRUTH. Who do not lie. HATING UNJUST GAIN (betza). Money. People who appear so, and are known as such by the community. It was in reference to these that Moshe said, and known (Devarim 1:13).

Rulers of thousands. One may wonder: If the meaning of the term rulers is here to be taken literally, then their number comes to more that seventy-nine thousand. Now, it is extremely far-fetched for there to have been so many rulers. Indeed, Scripture states, For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof (Mishlei 28:2). Furthermore, how is it possible for an eighth of the camp to be heads of the tribes? For this is what Moshe said, that is, So I took the heads of your tribes (Devarim 1:15). Additionally, how is it possible that all of the above-mentioned virtues were found in these people who came out of Mitzrayim and learned their ways? Indeed, Scripture states, After the doings of the land of Mitzrayim, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do (Vayikra 18:3). Now the desert generation, who were taught by Moshe for forty years, did not have to work, for their bread was freely given and their water faithfully delivered. The manna, which they were not in the habit of eating in Mitzrayim, in contrast to the types of food which they desired, instilled wisdom. Nevertheless, Moshe told this generation at the end of forty years, but Hashem hath not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day (Devarim 29:3). We are thus amazed as to how it was possible to find the above-noted number of wise and understanding men. It appears to me that the rulers of thousands were men who had under them a thousand people, namely, slaves, young men, or hired hands. It is possible that these were the heads of the tribes and that they numbered twelve. The rulers of hundreds were many. The rulers of fifties were so called after the manner of and fifty men to run before him (Shmuel II 15:1).
And let them judge the people. When the people have a matter. What they do not know how to judge you will judge. If you do not know it, then bring thou the causes unto Elokim (v. 19).

Then thou shalt be able. The vav of ve-yakholta (then thou shalt be able) is like the Arabic fah. If you do this thing, and Hashem grants you permission to do it, then you will be able to endure. Now the word amod (endure) is an infinitive. It is like the word amod (stand) in Stand in the door of the tent (Jud. 4:20). Peshotah (strip you) ve-orah (and make you bare), va-chagorah (and gird) in Strip you, and make you bare, and gird sackcloth upon your lions (Is. 32:11) are also infinitives.

[And all this people also shall go to their place in peace.] Its meaning is, when some the disputants who were standing before Moshe were not able to present their cases before him for adjudication, their conflict intensified when they returned to their tents. However, now each one would return to his place, that is, his tent, in peace.

[So Moshe hearkened.] Scripture mentions Yitro’s council but does not mention Moshe’s council. Moshe added to Yitro’s council: that is, Moshe placed officers over the tribes to enforce the decrees of the judges. Scripture thus reads, and officers, tribe by tribe (Devarim 1:15), and Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates (Devarim 16:18).

And Moshe chose able men. This thing was ascertainable. Such as fear Elokim is not mentioned, for only Elokim knows what is in a person’s heart. Moshe said that he chose wise men for us, for he was able to ascertain this. However, there are wise men who are not Elokim-fearing. Moshe mentioned men who are known (Devarim 1:13), that is, men whom people recognize. He did not mention them here because he was being brief.

They judged themselves. Yishputu (judged) means the same as yishpotu (judged). A shuruk has been substituted for a cholam in yishputu. It is similar to lo ta’avuri (neither pass) in neither pass from hence (Rut 2:5), which has the same meaning as ve-lo ta’avori (and neither pass). However, Rabbi Shlomo wanted to distinguish between them but was unable to do so. Now from a grammatical standpoint the following may be said. We find the terms chadelu (ceased) and chadellu (ceased) with a dagesh in the lamed because it is marked with an etnach in The rulers ceased (chadelu) in Yisrael, they ceased (chadellu) (Jud. 5:7). We similarly find the word nazollu (quake) at the end of a verse in That the mountains may quake (Is. 63:19). Scripture likewise reads, tehatellu vo (will ye mock him) (Iyov 13:9) since tehatellu is considered to be the last word in the sentence because it is connected to the word vo, which has only one vowel. Similarly, yishpetu hem is like yishputu (hem), for one can say that the etnach does not have the same power that the end of the verse has. Observe the word yippelu (fall) in The peoples fall under thee (Tehillim 45:6); yeminekha (thy right hand) in Hashem at thy right hand (Tehillim 110:5); avdekha (thy servant) in Thou hast dealt well with Thy servant (Tehillim 119:65) and many other such instances. We do not find this to be the case at the close of a verse.
And Moshe let his father-in-law depart. With respect, as in and Avraham went with them to bring them on the way (Bereshit 18:16).

In the third month. We do not know the meaning of the same day (ba-yom ha-zeh) unless the interpretation of Rabbi Moshe to the effect that it refers to the new moon is correct. It is like Tomorrow is the new moon (Shmuel I 20:18). Scripture notes this because the Torah was given a few days after Yisrael camped. Perhaps Moshe went up to Hashem on day one and then came down and spoke to Yisrael. Then on the third day of the month he went up again to report the words of the people to Hashem. It was then told to Moshe that the giving of the Torah would take place on the third day. All of this is by way of logical exegesis because we accept the tradition that the Torah was given on the sixth day of Sivan. According to the rules of the calendar, if a day was not added to the month of Iyyar, then the Torah was given on a Friday. It is possible that Scripture reads, the same day because the distance from Refidim and Mount Sinai was greater than the distance between each journey.
And when they were departed from Refidim. Its meaning is, they had already departed from Refidim. I have pointed out to you many other such instances.
They encamped in the wilderness. The previously mentioned wilderness of Sinai.

[And there Yisrael encamped.] Scripture reads, and there Yisrael encamped, after stating, they encamped in the wilderness, because the heads of the tribes and the elders camped before the mountain due to their respected positions. As I will explain, Yisrael stood around the mountain, in accordance with their status, on the day the Torah was given. Scripture uses the singular form va-yichan (encamped) because they were few in number. Rabbi Shlomo says that before (mi-neged) the mount means on the eastern side of the mountain. However, Scripture states, a good way off (mineged) shall they pitch, round about the tent of meeting (Bamidbar 2:2), namely, on all sides of the tent of meeting. For as the standards journeyed, so did they camp.
And Moshe went up unto Elokim. Scripture above reads, before the mount (v. 2). Its meaning thus is: and Moshe went up to the mount of Elokim.
[And Hashem called unto him.] Its meaning is, and Hashem had already called him. For Moshe would not have ascended without permission.

[Out of the mountain.] Scripture says this becauce Moshe did not ascend above the mountain. For Hashem spoke to Moshe on the mountain. Do not be bothered by the fact that Scripture afterwards states, And Hashem came down upon mount Sinai (v. 20), for the Torah says this from the point of view of Yisrael when they beheld the cloud and fire. Scripture explicitly states, and thou didst hear His words out of the midst of the fire (Devarim 4:36).

[Saying.] Its meaning is that Hashem called Moshe to tell him: Thus shalt thou say to the house of Yaakov). The meaning is, say something relating to all of the house of Yaakov, to those alive today and to their children after them.

[And tell the children of Yisrael.] The reference is to the elders. The elders will then tell all of the people. We thus read, And Moshe came and called for the elders of the people (v. 7), and it is then written, And all the people answered together (v. 8).
[House.] I have previously explained the meaning of the word house (Shemot 1:1).

Ye have seen. The vengeance that I executed upon the Mitzrim on your behalf, and that I bore you out of Mitzrayim as if you were carried on the wings of eagles. For an eagle flies higher in the air than any other bird. All birds are afraid of him and he fears no bird. [I BORE YOU ON EAGLES’ WINGS.] Moshe employed a similar metaphor later on when he said, As an eagle that stirreth up her nest (Devarim 32:11), that is, it slowly leads its young. Moshe similarly referred to the clouds when he said, Spreadeth abroad her wings (Ibid.).

And brought you unto myself. In that Elokim’s glory came down upon this mountain. This is the holy mountain referred to by Moshe. Now Moshe said, ye shall serve Elokim upon this mountain (Shemot 3:12). The latter is the same as Thy holy habitation (Shemot 15:13).

Now therefore, if ye will hearken unto my voice. To observe my commandments and keep the covenant which I will make with you. The reference, as I will explain with irrefutable proofs in the proper place, is to the covenant made by Moshe with Yisrael after the giving of the Torah, when he built the altar.
[Treasure.] The word segullah (treasure) means something precious, lovely, and unique.

[For all the earth is mine.] This is connected to all peoples. The clause is to be interpreted: for all the peoples of the earth are mine. This is what Scripture means by and [I] set you apart from the peoples, that ye should be Mine (Vayikra 20:26). Rabbi Merinus says that ki li kol ha-aretz (for all the earth is mine) means: even though all the earth is mine. I believe that this is the case with ki am keseh oref attah (it is a stiffnecked people) (Shemot 32:9) and refah nafshi ki chatati lakh (Heal my soul; for I have sinned against Thee) (Tehillim 41:5).
And Moshe came. To the camp of Yisrael. There is no need to mention that Moshe descended.

And set before them. As in And this is the law which Moshe set before the children of Yisrael (Devarim 4:44). However, the Gaon says that the word set is used here in the same way as the word set in set it in their mouths (Devarim 31:19). The reference is to the oral law which explains the written law.
Together. The word yachdav (together) is grammatically unique in Scripture because of the added vav. Yefet explains it to mean alone, by oneself, without anybody else there.
[Reported.] Scripture mentions, and Moshe reported, but has no need to mention that Moshe went up because Scripture is being brief.

And Hashem said. What reason is there for saying, And Moshe told the words of the people unto Hashem (v. 9) after having said, And Moshe reported the words of the people unto Hashem? Note that there are many verses in the Torah that should have come earlier. Their meaning is that such and such already took place. For example, the meaning of va-yitzar (formed) in, Then Hashem Elokim formed (Bereshit 2:7) is, He had already formed; the meaning of va-yatzmach (made to grow) in And out of the ground made Hashem Elokim to grow (Bereshit 2:9) is, He had already made to grow; the meaning of va-yomer (and said) in and said: Whose daughter art thou? (Bereshit 24:23) is, and he had already said. Indeed, Scripture explicitly states, And I asked her, and said (Bereshit 24:47), and then, I put the ring upon her nose (Ibid.). Similarly, the meaning of And she said unto the servant (Bereshit 24:65) is, and she had already said unto the servant, and then, she alighted from the camel (Bereshit 24:64). There is no need to elaborate. Now the meaning of And Moshe told here is, and Moshe had already told. Scripture does not mention what Moshe told. The word higid (told) always refers to something new that has not previously been mentioned. It is thus not connected to and Moshe reported. From Elokim’s answer to Moshe, “Lo, I come unto thee in a thick cloud” (v. 9), we learn what Moshe told. Furthermore, as I will explain, we find this clearly stated in Moshe’s very words. Note that the Mitzrim and the Indians are from the children of Cham. Each one relies on the other. The people of Hodu do not eat meat. The Mitzrim used to do the same. They changed their practice only because the kingdom of Yishmael overpowered them and they accepted the religion of the Yishmeelim. The Indian sages offer proofs in accordance with their thinking that it is impossible for Elokim to talk to a person and for that person to live. Now Bnei Yisrael were in Mitzrayim. There were among them people who followed this belief. They were in doubt about Moshe’s prophecy. And they believed in Hashem, and in His servant Moshe (Shemot 14:31) does not dispute this. For Scripture reads, And Yisrael saw (Ibid.). It does not say: and all Yisrael saw. Even if it read, all of Yisrael, it would speak of the majority as is the style of the language, as in and all the cattle of Mitzrayim died (Shemot 9:6), which is followed by Now therefore send, hasten in thy cattle (Shemot 9:19).
[Lo, I come unto thee.] This is to be understood as an answer to Moshe, who told this to God.
[In a thick cloud.] When Hashem will descend upon the mountain.
When I speak with thee. The Decalogue. They will then believe that Hashem in truth speaks with a person and he lives.

[And may also believe thee.] That you are a prophet. All doubt will be removed from their minds. It is explicitly written, we have seen this day that Elokim doth speak with man, and he liveth (Devarim 5:21). It is also written there, For who is there of all flesh, that hath heard the voice of the living Elokim speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived? (Devarim 5:23). And it is there written, Go thou near, and hear (Devarim 5:24). This is what Scripture means by and may also believe thee for ever.
And the Lord said…sanctify them to-day and tomorrow. Observe, God enlarged the time allotted for Yisrael’s sanctification by giving them the rest of this day and the morrow.

[And sanctify them.] By washing in water. This is indicated by and let them wash their garments. Our verse is to be interpreted after the manner of But if he wash them not, nor bathe his flesh (Vayikra 17:16). Moshe therefore said, starting from now, come not near a woman (v. 15) so that they would be sanctified and not be unclean. One who drew near to a women should sanctify himself, as in for she was purified from her uncleanliness (Shmuel II 11:4).
And be ready. Its meaning might be that no person among them should sleep during the night, after the manner of the high priest on Yom Kippur, as Yisrael would hear Hashem’s voice in the morning.

And thou shalt set bounds. Place a border on the mount. Set bounds about the mount, and sanctify it (v. 23) is therefore similar. I dwell on this because the crazy one who inverted the words of the living Elokim in his book said that Moshe intended to say, set bounds about the people, but what came out of his mouth was “the mount” rather than “the people.”
Whosoever toucheth the Mount. With his body.

No hand shall touch him. The word bo (him) refers to the person who touches the mount. It means that no one shall enter after him to grab him. On the contrary, those who see him shall immediately stone him from where they are standing or shall shoot him through with arrows if he be distant.

[Shot through.] The word yiyareh (shot through) differs from its counterparts. For the rule pertaining to roots that have a yod as their first letter is that the yod changes to a vav in the nifal imperfect, as in the word yivvada (be known) in and the plenty shall not be known (Bereshit 41:31) and va-ivvaser (and I was chastised) in Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised (Yirmiyahu 31:18). Perhaps they did this so that this root not be confused with the root of tivvare (thou mayest be feared) in That Thou mayest be feared (Tehillim 130:4). For the alef and the heh are silent at the end of the word and there is no difference in pronunciation between them.
Whether it be beast or man, it shall not live. Not so a bird as it cannot be taken, for it immediately flies away.

When the ram’s horn soundeth long. Yovel (ram) is a lamb. Jubilee (yovel) is so called because Scripture states, Then shalt thou make proclamation with the blast of a shofar (Vayikra 25:9), and the shofar is made from the horns of a lamb. It is similarly written, And it shall be, that when they make a long blast with the horn of the yovel, and when ye hear the sound of the shofar (Yehoshua 6:5). One must wonder at those who say that And when the voice of the horn waxed louder and louder, Moshe spoke (v. 19) refers to when the ram’s horn soundeth long. For the voice of the horn was a great wonder; there was no greater wonder at that assembly around Mount Sinai. For sounds of thunder, lightning, and a thick cloud are also visible in the world. However, the voice of the horn was unheard of until the day of the Decalogue. Behold, the sound was not from the horn of a lamb.

[When the ram’s horn soundeth long, they shall come up to the Mount.] The Gaon says that when Moshe sounds the horn it will give them permission to ascend. This took place after Moshe descended on the Day of Atonement and commanded that the tabernacle be constructed

They shall come up to the Mount. Rabbi Shmuel ben Hofni says that “they” refers to Aharon, Aharon’s sons, and the seventy elders concerning whom it is written, And unto Moshe He said: Come up unto Hashem, thou, and Aharon, Nadav, and Avihu, and seventy of the elders of Yisrael (Shemot 24:1). However, Moshe did not give permission to the rest of the people to ascend Mount Sinai. He therefore said “they” and not others. His words appear good in my sight. For the glory was continually on Sinai until the tabernacle was erected, as it is written, and the glory of Hashem filled the tabernacle (Shemot 4:34). Hashem then spoke with Moshe in the tent of meeting. Perhaps Moshe then sounded the horn and now that the glory was gone, Hashem gave him permission to ascend.
And Moshe went down…and sanctified the people. As I have already explained.

Be ready against the third day. The meaning of li-sheloshet yamim is, for the third day. According to the plain meaning of the text, Moshe did not add a day by himself. I will bring two faithful witnesses, both of which are found in this book. Now it is written, And he put them all together into ward three days (sheloset yamim) (Bereshit 42:17). It is then written, And Yosef said unto them the third day (yom ha-shelishi) (Bereshit 42:18). Scripture also states, within yet three days (sheloshet yamim) shall Paroh lift up thy head from off thee (Bereshit 40:19). It is then written, And it came to pass the third day (ba-yom ha-shelishi) (Bereshit 40:20). Similarly here, heyu nekhnim li-sheloshet yamim [means be ready for the third day].
And a thick cloud upon the Mount. Upon the mount alone. The same applies to the thunder and lightning.
[Exceeding loud.] Its meaning is, louder than the voice of any shofar (horn) that they ever heard.
And all the people that were in the camp trembled. Because of the sound of the shofar (horn).
And Moshe brought forth. Its meaning is: and Moshe brought forth the people out of their tents to meet Elokim and to accept Hashem who came down on Mount Sinai as their Elokim.

And they stood at the nether part of the Mount. Outside of the boundary that Moshe set for them. Now they stood at Mount Sinai in a manner similar to that in which Moshe made their children stand at the end of forty years when he made a covenant with them. The first-born that [came] near Hashem were first, after them the heads of the tribes, namely, the princes, after them the elders, after them the officers, after them all the men of Yisrael; after them came the little ones, after them the women, and after them the proselytes. Moshe and Aharon passed over the boundary and were on the mount close to the priests. This was so even though Scripture does not explicitly say so, as Scripture was brief. We know that they did not rebel against the word of Hashem for, behold, it is written, Go, get thee down, and thou shalt come up, thou, and Aharon with thee (v. 24). Moshe similarly said, I stood between Hashem and you (Devarim 5:5).

Now Mount Sinai was altogether on smoke. The shin of ashan (smoke) is vocalized with a long pattach because it is a verb in the perfect. Do not be surprised at the word for smoke since Scripture reads, ke-eshen ha-kivshan (as the smoke of the furnace) after saying, va-ya’al ashano (and the smoke thereof ascended). Note that ashano follows the form of shelalo (his spoil) and zehavo (his gold), for nouns come in various forms each of which has a different name. Thus Scripture reads, shegar alafekha (the increase of thy kine) (Devarim 7:13), but elsewhere it reads, ve-khol peter sheger be-hemah (every firstling that is male) (Shemot 13:12). Scripture reads, ve-et ha-bosem ve-et ha-shemen (and the spice, and the oil) (Shemot 35:28). However, we also find, ve-kinneman besem (and of cinnamon spice) (Shemot 30:23). Furthermore, Scripture reads, ariti mori im besami (I have gathered my myrrh with my spice) (Cant. 5:1). Now, if besami (my spice) was derived from bosem, the word should have been vocalized with a chataf kamatz and be pronounced bosmi like the word kodshi (my holy object), which is derived from kodesh (holy). Similarly, if besami was derived from besem (sweet) in and of cinnamon spice (Shemot 30:23), then besami should have been vocalized with a pattach like the word shamni (my oil), which is derived from shemen (oil), or with a chirik like the word tzidki (my righteousness), which is derived from tzedek (righteous). The word besami minus the yod is thus vocalized with two kematzim and pronounced basam (spice), like the word shalal (spoil) and the word zahav (gold).
And the whole Mount quaked greatly. The reverse of the usual, for mountains do not move. It is only by way of parable that Scripture states, And the hills did tremble (Is. 5:25).

And when the voice of the horn waxed louder and louder. The normal thing is for the sound of the shofar to be stronger when first sounded. However, the reverse was the case here. Perhaps Hashem made it sound weaker at the beginning so that Yisrael would not lose heart out of fright.

Moshe spoke. According to Saadiah Gaon, Hashem periodically stopped the sound of the shofar, at which time Moshe spoke with a loud voice. Hashem then answered Moshe with a voice, as in then he [Moshe] heard the Voice speaking unto him (Bamidbar 7:89). It is concerning this that Scripture states, that the people may hear when I speak with thee (v. 9). However, I have already told you that in my opinion, when I speak with thee refers to the Decalogue.

Moshe spoke is to be explained by connecting it to the voice of the horn (shofar). Moshe’s soul cleaved unto Hashem. Moshe spoke with Hashem from the foot of the mountain and asked something of Hashem. However, Scripture does not reveal what Moshe asked. Hashem answered Moshe with a voice audible to Moshe. The sound of the shofar, although very loud, did not prevent Moshe from hearing the voice. Because of this, Scripture states afterwards, and Hashem called Moshe with the sound of a voice and told him to ascend the mountain where the glory of Hashem was.

And Hashem came down. I will now convey a general principle that will satisfy you until, with Elokim’s help, I will come to the Torah portion Ki Tissa, where I will explain extremely deep things to you very clearly. Know that man’s soul is extolled and glorious. It comes from the middle world. However, man’s body comes from the inferior world. The only one in this inferior world who has the ability to speak is man. Likewise the hearer, that is, the person to whom the speaker wants to convey what is in the speaker’s heart. An intelligent person cannot invent speech. He must employ the language that is known and used. All languages are built upon the arrangement of the human form, which is made up of an incorporeal soul and a body made out of four elements. Now when a person speaks to a fellow human being in a language that the latter knows, he understands the speaker’s words and their forms in their arrangements. If one wants to speak of things that are on a lower level than human beings, he has to raise their level and give them human form so that anyone who hears him will understand his words. Hence they attributed a head to the earth, as in The head of the dust of the world (Mishlei 8:26), a mouth to the earth, as in And the earth opened her mouth (Bamidbar 16:32), and a side, as in from the sides of the earth (Yirmiyahu 6:22). We similarly find, the head of the Yarden (Bamidbar 13:29) and in the heart of the sea (Shemot 15:8). There are many such instances. Now they are all metaphoric, for the sea has no heart. Furthermore, they picture one part of the body as if it had the form of the entire body. Thus Scripture says, Death and life are in the hand of the tongue (Mishlei 18:21). There are many such cases. Similarly, when a person wants to speak of things more important than he, namely, of things from the upper world, he brings them down to his level and anthropomorphizes them, speaking of them as if they had human form. All this is done so that the hearer can be understood. Scripture thus reads, the man Gabriel (Daniel 9:21). Scripture similarly speaks of his arms and his feet (Daniel 10:6) and tells us, and the voice of his words [was] like the voice of a multitude (Ibid.). They [the writers of Scripture] took hold of this style of speech when describing the Most High. Scripture thus states, And a helmet of salvation upon His head (Is. 59:17); For the mouth of Hashem hath spoken (Is. 1:20); The eyes of Hashem are toward the righteous, And His ears are open unto their cry; The face of Hashem is against them that do evil (Tehillim 34:16,17); and and there was under His feet (Shemot 24:10). This is the way to understand And Hashem came down (Bereshit 11:5) and, and Elokim went up (Bereshit 17:22), for everything is full of His glory. I will present a parable in the Torah portion Ki Tissa through which you will be able to understand what Scripture means by Elokim ascending and descending.

[And Hashem called Moshe to the top of the Mount.] The reason Hashem called Moshe was so that Yisrael would see Moshe’s greatly elevated state, namely, that he reached the top of the mountain where there was the glory of Hashem, whose words the people would hear from the fire that was there.

Go down, charge the people, lest they break through. Each one from the place where he stands, thinking that they are rendering Me honor because of their great desire to gaze at My glory. Moshe therefore said, to gaze.
