Now the portion opens with the prohibition against making other gods alongside Hashem and concludes with the commandment to uproot the memory of idols and molten gods which were made in the land of Kenaan.

If thou buy. Before I begin to explain let me give you a general rule. Each ordinance or commandment is an independent unit. If we are able to find a reason that two ordinances or commandments are connected to each other, then we will expend all of our efforts to connect them. If we are not able to do so, we will conclude that the reason this cannot be done is our intellectual deficiency. There is nothing in the world more difficult for a human being to bear than to be under the control of another person like himself. Scripture therefore began with the law of the Hebrew servant. Our sages said that the Hebrew servant is a Yisraeli. The same applies to And if a man sell his daughter to be a maid-servant (v. 7). However, our sages maintain that And if a man smite the eye of his bondmen (v. 26) refers to a Kenaani. Similarly, If the ox gore a bondman (v. 32). And they said that then he shall be sold for his theft (Shemot 22:2) refers to a Yisraeli. Those who dispute with our sages say that the Hebrew slave is not a Yisraeli but rather someone of Avraham’s family. The same is true of the daughter sold into slavery and of all the slaves mentioned afterwards. They are to be understood in the same way. Their proof is from the wife and her children (v. 4), for they say that family identity is established by the father. They offer additional proof from and he shall serve him for ever (v. 6), for they say that the latter means all of the slave’s life. It was difficult for them to accept that a Yisraeli would have his ear pierced. Let us now seek the plain meaning of the words. If the Hebrew slave is not a Yisraeli, then why did Scripture state, If thy brother, a Hebrew man…be sold unto thee (Devarim 15:12)? Do we not know that brother in Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart (Vayikra 19:17) means a Yisraeli? It is the same case with between a man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him (Devarim 1:16). There are many such cases. Now there is no doubt that the meaning of Avram the Hebrew (Bereshit 14:13) is: Avram of the children of Ever, about whom Scripture says avi kol bene ever, (the father of all the children of Ever) (Bereshit 10:21), in contrast to and Cham is the father of Kenaan (Bereshit 9:18). On the other hand, it is possible that Avram was called the Hebrew because he came from beyond the river, although in this case the term used should have been ivri nahari rather than ivri. Let us assume that Scripture was being brief, because we find that the Bible states, And I took your father Avraham from beyond the River (me-ever ha-nahar) (Yehoshua 24:3). The Hebrews are also called Bnei Yisrael, for we see that Moshe told Paroh, Thus saith Hashem, the Elokim of Yisrael (Shemot 5:1). However, when Paroh asked Moshe, “Who is this Elokim?” Moshe answered him, The Elokim of the Hebrews (Ibid.). The Elokim of the Hebrews thus means the same as the Elokim of Yisrael. Now if Bnei Yisrael are called Hebrews because they are related to Ever, then the children of Yishmael and the children of Keturah and the children of Esav should be joined to us. However, we do not find Scripture referring to any people as our brothers except for Edom, who shared one womb with Yaakov. We also do not find Scripture referring to Esav as our brother in commandments. We find him referred to as a brother only in the account of the messengers. The same applies to Thou shalt not abhor an Edomi, for he is thy brother (Devarim 23:8) wherein Scripture mentions he is thy brother after first mentioning the term Edomi. The same is true of Because he did pursue his brother with the sword (Amos 1:11). Now we do not find in all of Scripture the word Hebrew employed except in regard to the children of Yaakov. Scripture thus states: And there was with us there a young man, a Hebrew (Bereshit 41:12); because the Mitzrim might not eat bread with the Hebrews (Bereshit 43:32); a Mitzri smiting a Hebrew (Shemot 2:11); two men of the Hebrews were striving together (Shemot 2:13). Yonah said, I am a Hebrew (Yonah 1:9) because he was asked, and of what people art thou (Yonah v. 1:8). If the term Hebrew had referred to many nations, Yonah would not yet have told them of what people he was. Scripture also states, that ye be not servants unto the Hebrews (Shmuel I 4:9); Now the Hebrews that were with the Plishtim (Shmuel I 14:21). The book of Yirmiyahu states: that every man should let his man-servant, and every man his maid-servant, being a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, go free (Yirmiyahu 34:9). The latter closes by explaining, that none should make bondmen of them, even of a Yehudi his brother (Ibid.). Now it is known that an Edomi is not called a Yehudi. Those who disagree with our sages say, look, it is written: And many from among the peoples of the land became Yehudim (mityahadim) (Esther 8:17) in reference to those who were not Yehudim. This is blindness. For according to their opinion, whether the meaning of the word mityahadim (became Yehudim) is that they claimed to be Yehudim or that mityahadim means they accepted Judaism, Scripture should have read, “even of one of his brothers who became Jewish.” Furthermore, the word mitabber (becoming a Hebrew) should be formed from the word ivri according to this interpretation. One who says this, meddleth (mitabber) with strife not his own (Mishlei 26:17). It has thus been clearly shown that the words of our sages are correct. We will rely upon them with regard to all of the commandments in accordance with their tradition, which they received from their fathers. Furthermore, how can one think that a Yishmeeli and an Edomi shall serve for six years and a Yisraeli until the year of jubilee.

Six years he shall serve. And no longer. It is like Six years thou shalt sow thy field (Vayikra 25:3). At the start of the seventh year of his being sold he shall go free no matter what year it be. Do not be amazed that Yirmiyahu writes, At the end of seven years (Yirmiyahu 34:14), because everything has two ends and sometimes the end is found at the beginning and sometimes it is at the end. Our verse deals with a servant whom the law courts have sold, namely, an individual concerning whom it is written, then he shall be sold for his theft (Shemot 22:2). However, And if thy brother be waxen poor with thee, and was sold unto you (Vayikra 25:39) or to a stranger (Vayikra 25:47) refers to a slave who sells himself according to the years remaining to the year of jubilee, for such a servant goes out when the Jubilee comes. Yisrael has a tradition that males but not females are sold because they stole. I will finish the matter in the chapter which follows. Rabbi Merinus says that the yod of the word la-chofshi (tree) is superfluous. It is like the yod of le-mishi (for cleansing) (Yechezkel 16:4) and the yod of akhzari (cruel) (Mishlei 11:17). However, Rabbi Yehudah the grammarian says the lamed of la-chofshi (free) is superfluous because its meaning is similar to chofshi (free) in And when thou lettest him go free (Devarim 15:13). Its yod is, as it were, the yod of relationship, like the yod of ha-kadmoni (of the east gate) (Yechezkel 19:19). The lamed of la-chofshi is like the lamed of la-avshalom (Avshalom) in the third, Avshalom the son of Ma'achah (Divrei Hayamim I 3:2). However, in my opinion the lamed and the yod in la-chofshi are both prepositions, even though one would have sufficed. Chofshi is similar to ha-oholi (of my tent) (Yehoshua 7:21) in in the midst of my tent. Chofshi (free) is an adjective.

[For nothing.] The word chinnam (for nothing) comes from the same root as channunu (grant) in grant them (Jud. 21:22). It means a gift. We do not know why chinnam has a mem. Its mem is like the mem of rekam (empty) (Bereshit 31:42).

If he come in by himself. Some say that the word be-gappo (by himself) has the same meaning as be-gufo (with his body). Now we find the phrase gufat sha’ul (the body of Shaul) (Divrei Hayamim I 10:12) in Scripture. However, the forms of nouns change. Others say that gappo (himself) has the meaning of wing. Wings are referred to as gappin in Aramaic. It is as if Scripture read, if he came in bondage possessing only the wing of his garment. However, this is out of context, for the context requires us to explain be-gappo as meaning that he carries no other body on his back. Gappo is like gabbi (my back) in The plowers plowed upon my back (Tehillim 129:3). Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that Scripture had to say, If he come in by himself, he shall go out by himself while saying he shall go out free because of his wife, that is, the Torah had to say, if he be married. Now if a Yisraeli women is not sold by a law court for theft, why does Scripture say, then his wife shall go out with him? It states this to teach us that the one who acquires a Hebrew slave is obligated to support his [the slave’s] wife. She is with him until they go out together.

If his master give him a wife. We find that those who employ the holy tongue render honor with various nouns but not with verbs. They use the terms adon (lord) and also adonim (lords). They employ the latter as a singular in a cruel lord (adonim) (Is. 19:4). They employ the term adonav (his lord) in the construct. They do not use the term adono (his lord), for we do not find the word adono in Scripture. However, Adoni (my lord), as in My lord asked (Bereshit 44:19), is employed in the first person. It is prohibited to use the plural form so that it not be confused with God’s glorious name. It is similarly unfit to use the singular declensional form adoni (my lord) in My lord asked (Ibid.) when God is spoken of. The same applies to the term Elo’ah (God). Rabbi Merinus says that eloho (their god), rather than elohav (their god), in their might unto their god (Chavakuk 1:11) is used in a disparaging manner.

If his master give him a wife. A Kenaani woman according to our sages. It is possible that the meaning of a Kenaani women is in keeping with Moreover of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you (Vayikra 25:45) conceming whom it is written, of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids (Vayikra 25:44). The same applies to all Kenaani slaves, for Scripture states, thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth (Devarim 20:16) with regard to the seven nations. Scripture states with regard to Shlomo, of the nations concerning which Hashem said unto the children of Yisrael: They shall not come among you, neither shall you go among them (Melachim I 11:2). Now this is written with regard to Zidonians and Chiti, not Moavim and Bnei Amon.

But if the servant shall plainly say. Our sages have already explained that his ear is not pierced unless all these conditions, including because he loveth thee and thy house (Devarim 15:16), have been fulfilled.

Then his master shall bring him unto Elokim. The term Elokim (Elokim) means those who establish Elokim’s laws in the land. It is customary for the judges to sit in the gate of a city that has doors and a bolt. To the door or the door-post means that what Scripture deals with in this verse is to be performed before those who sit in the gate.

And he shall serve him for ever. We know that the word le-olam (for ever) in Hebrew refers to time, as in it hath been already, in the ages (le-olamim) which were before us (Kohelet 1:10), wherein olamim means ages. Similarly, ve-yashav sham ad olam (and there abide for ever) (Shmuel I 1:22) means: and he will there abide until he grows up. Va-avado le-olam (and he shall serve him for ever) likewise means: and he will serve him until the year of jubilee, for there is no season of Yisrael that is longer than it. Going free is comparable to a renewal of the world. It is also possible that its meaning is that he should be as he was in former times.

And if a man sell his daughter to be a maid-servant. Scripture speaks of a minor who is under her father’s control, like the daughter whose oaths a father may annul. The phrase unto a foreign people (v. 8) is connected to this verse. For unto a foreign people speaks of the father.

To sell her unto a foreign people he shall have no power, seeing that he hath dealt deceitfully with her. Bi-vigdo (that he hath dealt deceitfully) is similar to the word nivgad (we deal treacherously) in Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother (Malachi 2:10). It is true and correct that the master has no right to sell her to a Yisraeli. We know this from tradition. The sages used this verse as a peg and as a support. Do not be surprised at the distance between unto a foreign people and the verse to which it is connected, for as I will explain, it is the same case with he shall make restitution (Shemot 22:2). Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that unto a foreign people means to a stranger. The same is true of wilt Thou slay even a righteous nation (Bereshit 20:4). However, it is impossible that Scripture would refer to an individual by one of these terms. It is correct for Scripture to say, “and Yisrael said,” because Yisrael is a collective noun, like Mitzrayim in and Mitzrayim said (Shemot 14:25). However, it is impossible for a noun which refers to a group, such as the terms people, nation, company, and congregation, to be used for an individual. The meaning of wilt Thou slay even a righteous nation is explained by that thou hast brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin (Bereshit 20:9).

[She shall not go out as men-servants do.] Its meaning is, she shall not go out as men-servants who always go out after six years. The maid-servant also goes out after six years of servitude, as Scripture states, If thy brother, a Hebrew man, or a Hebrew women, be sold unto thee, he shall serve thee six years (Devarim 15:12). However, the maid-servant goes out if she reaches the onset of puberty before six years pass.

If she please not her master. If she does not find favor in the eyes of her master after he bought her in order to take her for a wife. This is the meaning of who hath espoused her to himself; he espoused her to be his wife or he espoused her to be the wife of his son. Note that the word lo (himself) is spelled lamed alef in the text and is read as if written with a vav and so spelled in the margin. The Gaon says that the word lo has two meanings. It is similar to It is He that hath made us, and we are His (lo) (Tehillim 100:3). One meaning is, we have not made ourselves. The second meaning is, we are His. However, in my opinion only the second is the correct meaning. The same applies to all of them. Rabbi Yehudah the grammarian says that we cannot distinguish in pronunciation between lo spelled with an alef and lo spelled with a vav or a heh, as in is it not (ha-loh) in Rabbah of the children of Amon (Devarim 3:11). All cases where the text has an alef and the margin a vav are to be interpreted the way they are read. Note that the word ve-hefdah (then shall he let her to be redeemed) is a transitive verb. It is similar to ve-happodekha (and redeemed thee) (Devarim 13:6); padah (redeemed) in who hath redeemed my soul (Shmuel II 4:9); peditem (redeemed them) in For I have redeemed them (Zecharyah 10:8). Now vehefdah is a hifil. It is like ha-matzmi’ach (maketh to spring) in Who maketh the mountains to spring with grass (Tehillim 147:8) or like the word he’ekhil (fed) in saying Reuven fed (he’ekhil) Shimon bread. The meaning of ve-hefdah thus is, he shall seek her redemption and accept it whether she redeems herself, or her father or one of her relatives redeems her. If she is close to the end of her years of servitude, they shall compute how many years she has served and how many remain till the seventh year or to the time that she reaches the onset of puberty. The redemption money will be in accordance with the aforementioned computation.

Unto a foreign people. I have already explained it. Note that the term nokhri (foreign) applies to all people who are not Bnei Yisrael. The word nokhri does not have the same meaning as the word zar (stranger), as the term zar refers to one who is not of the same tribal family. Now if we say that Bnei Yisrael are called Hebrews because of Ever, who worshipped Hashem, then whoever is descended from Ever and follows Ever’s faith is called a Hebrew. However, if we say that one is called a Hebrew because of Avraham, then Scripture states, for in Yitzchak shall seed be called to thee (Bereshit 21:12). Now even though Scripture writes with regard to Yishmael, because he is thy seed (Bereshit 21:13), the land was given only to Yitzchak. Yaakov and Esav were sons of Yitzchak. However, Scripture states with regard to Yitzchak, for unto thee, and thy seed, I will give all these lands (Bereshit 26:3). Now Yitzchak’s seed was “called” only in Yaakov, to whom the land was given. Thus the children of the concubines along with the children of Esav are considered foreigners.
And if he espouse her unto his son. Yi’adennah (espouse her) follows the paradigm of yirashennah. The word mo’ed (season) is similar to the word moked (altar).
[After the manner of the daughters.] The reference is to virgin daughters who were not sold.
He shall deal with her. The son, and also the father if he took her.
If he take him another wife. Be she a daughter of Yisrael who was sold, or be she a daughter of Yisrael that was not sold.
Her food. She’erah refers to her food. He must sustain her flesh, which is what she’erah means.

And her conjugal rights. Some say that ve-onatah (and her conjugal rights) means: and the place of her dwelling. According to them, the word ve-anah (shall howl) in and jackals shall howl (Is. 13:22) and ve-anetah (and she shall respond) in and she shall respond there (Hoshea 2:17) have a similar meaning. However, I believe that ve-anah iyyim (and jackals shall howl) is to be taken as it implies. Ve-anah is similar to ve-anita (and thou shalt speak) in and thou shalt speak and say (Devarim 26:5). Ve-anah is used metaphorically, for Scripture there metaphorically states, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow (Is. 34:14). Similarly, ve-anetah in and she shall there respond means she shall make music. Ve-anetah is similar to enu (sing) in Sing unto Hashem with thanksgiving (Tehillim 147:7). Onatah refers to sexual activity, also known as the time of lovemaking. The word et (time) is missing a nun. It is similar to the word emet (truth). Hence the tav of ittekh (thy time) in and, behold, thy time (Yechezkel 16:8) receives a dagesh. Likewise, itto (his time) is similar to amitto (his truth). The word attah (now) is also similar. Note, onatah comes from the same root as et. The word attah (now) means this time.

And if. Scripture employed an abridged form in saying shelosh eleh (these three). It is similar to shelosh se’im (three measures) (Bereshit 18:6), for Scripture should have read, ha-shelosh ha-eleh. Many think that these three refers to her food, her raiment, and her conjugal rights. However, this is impossible. After Scripture stated, he shall deal with her after the manner of daughters (v. 9), and one is obligated to give these three things to all daughters there is no need to mention this here. Furthermore, Scripture writes concerning the beautiful woman who is a foreigner, but thou shalt not sell her at all for money (Devarim 21:14). How much more so is this maid-servant not to be sold for money. Its correct interpretation thus is: and if he does not do one of these three things, namely, if he does not marry her, or espouse her to his son, or redeem her, she shall go out for nothing when she has the onset of puberty. If any that is unclean by a dead body touch all of these, which means one of these, shall it be unclean (Chaggai 2:13) is similar. There are many other similar instances. The Gaon asks, what reason was there for Scripture to say, without money after stating for nothing? He answers: If she took ill in her master’s house and he spent money on medicine, then she did not have to pay him back anything. However, in my opinion there is no need for all of this, for Scripture offers additional explanation, such as for thou shalt die, and not live (Melachim II 20:1).

He that smiteth a man. The reason this follows the laws dealing with the man- and maid-servant is that Scripture wanted to go on and explain how to deal with one who strikes his man- and maid-servants. [A MAN.] The reference is to a Yisraeli.
He shall surely be put to death. By a court of law. This is the case whenever the term mot yumat (he shall surely be put to death) is employed. The one exception to this will be shown shortly.

And if a man lie not in wait. Tzadah (lie in wait) is similar to the word bi-tzediyyah (lying in wait) (Bamidbar 35:20) and tzodeh (layest wait) in though thou layest wait for my soul to take it (Shmuel I 24:12). Observe, it involves laying in wait and acting presumptuously.

But Hashem cause it to come to hand. Innah (cause it to come) is similar to mitanneh (seeketh an occasion) in he seeketh an occasion against me (Melachim II 5:7), the meaning of which is, he looks for reasons and excuses. The meaning of our clause is that Hashem caused and arranged things so that this person would die at this individual’s hand even though he had never intended to kill him. Hashem caused this to happen to him so that he would be exiled from his place because of some other sin which he committed. Scripture explicitly states, There shall no mischief befall the righteous (Mishlei 12:21).

And if a man come presumptuously. To slay him is to be understood as if written, and slew him with guile. Similarly If she profane by playing the harlot (Vayikra 21:9), the meaning of which is, if she profane herself by playing the harlot and therefore she profaneth her father (Ibid.). It is known that the term chillul (profanation) and the word techillah (beginning) come from a double root. However, they differ in meaning. It was therefore necessary to differentiate between them. Scripture therefore reads, techel li-zenot (profane by playing the harlot) (Vayikra 21:9), for if it had the meaning of beginning, it would read tachel (thou shalt begin), as in tachel lispor (shalt thou begin to number) (Bamidbar 16:9).

From mine altar. This is the reverse of the previous verse. It is there stated, then I will appoint thee a place [whither he may flee], the reference being to the cities of refuge. However, he who presumptuously kills and flees, even if he seeks refuge at the altar as Yoav did, shall be put to death. Our sages said even a priest who wants to perform the service at the altar shall be put to death.

And he that smiteth his father. Since Scripture had previously mentioned, He that smiteth a man, so that he dieth, shall surely be put to death (v. 12), Scripture had to explain that there is an instance where one is put to death for smiting someone even when the one who is struck does not die. This is the case when one hits one’s father. The word u-makkeh (and he that smiteth) is to be read as if written twice. It was out of regard for the parents’ honor that Scripture found it necessary to state that even when one does not strike one’s parents but curses them, he is to be put to death.

And he that stealeth a man. Saadiah Gaon asks: Why was this verse inserted between He that smiteth his father (v. 15) and And he that curseth his father (v. 17)? He answers that Scripture speaks only of the commonplace. Those stolen were young children. They were brought up in a strange country and did not recognize their parents. It is thus possible for them to strike and curse their parents. The punishment for this will fall upon the kidnapper.
Or if he be found in his hand. In the market before he sells him, then he shall be put to death.
And he that curseth. We find a curse that invokes the name of Hashem, as in and cursed them in the name of Hashem (Melachim II 2:24). We also find curses that do not invoke the name of Hashem.

And if men contend. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that be-egrof (with his fist) is similar to egrofin (strong) in “strong men.” The reference is to something strong and hard. Rabbi Merinus says that the alef of egrof is superfluous. It is like the alef of ezro’i (my shoulder) (Iyov 31:22). It comes from the same root as ge-rafam (swept them away) (Jud. 5:21). The reference is to something that one drags in one’s hand. The same is true in Arabic.
If he rise again. We will rely on our sages of blessed memory who said that al mishanto (upon his staff) means that he supports himself and does not lean on others as sick people do.
Then shall he that smote him be quit. They shall release him from prison.

[Loss of his time.] Shivto (loss of his time) comes from the same root as shevitah (rest), for his work stopped. This interpretation is correct. Shivto follows the paradigm of shivro (his corn money) (Bereshit 44:2), for the tav is a root letter. It is possible that shivto comes from the same root as shivtah (tarried) in save that she tarried a little in the house (Rut 2:7). Shivtah comes from the same root as the word yashav (sat). Shivto refers to the time that the one who was struck sat at home resting, without work. What proves that this interpretation is correct is that it is the reverse of and walk abroad.

And shall cause him to be thoroughly healed. This is a sign that permission has been granted to physicians to heal blows and wounds that are visible on the surface. However, it is in Hashem’s hand to heal any illness which strikes inside of the body. It is thus written, For He maketh sore, and bindeth up (Iyov 5:18). Furthermore, Scripture tells us concerning King Asa, yet in his disease he sought not to Hashem, but to the physicians (Divrei Hayamim II 16:12). Now Scripture distinguished between them. It does not state, verafo yirpe (and he shall surely heal), which is in the kal. It rather reads, ve-rappo yerappe (and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed). The latter is in the pi’el. I will explain this very well later on in this portion. The rabbis received a tradition concerning other payments in addition to the two mentioned in our verse. They similarly received a tradition to include spices which are not stated in the Torah among the incense spices.

And if a man smite his bondman. There is no doubt that according to Yisraeli jurisprudence the same ordinances that apply to a free man apply to a person sold into bondage. Hence it is impossible for the bondman to be a Hebrew servant. Furthermore, Scripture states at the end, for he is his money. Now the bondman and bondwoman are the ones concerning whom Scripture writes, of them shall ye buy bondmen and bondmaids (Vayikra 25:44). The bet of ba-shevet (with a rod) is vocalized with a pattach. The reference is to the rod which the master was in the habit of using to beat his servants. Now all those who dispute the words of our sages are forced to agree with them with regard to the phrase nakom yinnakem (he shall surely be avenged), for vengeance takes many forms. Now logic will not help them in this case. The fathers have received the tradition that nakem yenakem (he shall surely be avenged) is similar to a sword that shall avenge (nokemet) the vengeance of the covenant (nekam berit) (Vayikra 26:25).

Notwithstanding. Observe that the word yukkam (be punished), which is a hofal, has the same meaning as yinnakem (be punished), which is a nifal. The heretics say that the meaning of nakom yinnakem (he shall surely be avenged) is that great vengeance shall be exacted, namely, that the master shall be beaten. However, if the bondman lives for a day, less vengeance shall be exacted. If he lives for two days no vengeance shall be taken. They argue that we do not find the term vengeance used with reference to the death penalty inflicted by a law court. They also say, that there is no positive proof that a sword that shall avenge (Vayikra 26:25) refers to being put to death. Furthermore, what need is there to say “two days” after saying “a day”? However, their real difficulty lies in accepting the idea that the master would be executed because of the death of a bondman. I will now answer them. Why didn’t Scripture specify what greater or lesser vengeance is to be exacted? Let us now pursue what is written in Scripture. Scripture states, nekom nikmat bene yisrael (avenge the children of Yisrael) (Bamidbar 31:2). It then goes on to tell us that all the Midyanim were killed. Note that Shimshon said, ki im nikkamti ba-khem (surely I will be avenged of you) (Jud. 15:7). It then states, And he smote them hip [and thigh with a great slaughter] (Jud. 15:8). Shimshon said, ve-innakemah nekam achat (that I may be this once avenged) (Jud. 16:28) and they died in the house. Scripture states, And a two-edged sword in their hand (Tehillim 149:6). It then goes on to say, To execute vengeance (nikamah) upon the nations (Tehillim 149:7). The Bible states, For he doth avenge (yikkom) the blood of his servants (Devarim 32:43). Now blood indicates slaughter. This is the way the term is always used. The reason Scripture here refers to execution by vengeance is that a master seeks excuses to fall upon his bondman because he is in his power, as he cannot smite a fellow Yisraeli. Now let us turn to Scripture’s statement a day or two. Observe that the latter is like At the mouth of two witnesses [or three witnesses] (Devarim 17:6). They said that they do not know its meaning. Let them put our verse along with it. Our sages of blessed memory said that the meaning of a day or two is that the hours shall add up to the twenty-four of a day. Now when we examined the verse we found that Scripture says, “with the rod,” the reference being to the disciplining rod, as in Thou beatest him with the rod (Mishlei 23:14). It is thus clear that the master wanted to punish the bondman. Scripture did not mention what the laws are regarding a master who kills his bondman, because a master normally takes pity on the bondman, whom he owns, and refrains from killing him even as he takes pity upon his cattle. Now Hashem commanded that a master shall not act sadistically when he punishes his bondman. When he sees the bondman dying under his rod the master shall let him be. If he does not leave the bondman alone then he will be put to death on the bondman’s account, for Hashem’s mercy is upon all of His creatures. Indeed, concerning David we read, Thou hast shed blood abundantly (Divrei Hayamim I 22:8). The reference was to non-Israelite blood.
And if men strive together. The reference is to Hebrew men who strive together and hit each other. Scripture similarly reads, Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow? (Shemot 2:13)

And hurt. Both are included. Sometimes its meaning is one or the other. Thus the meaning of they shall be burnt with fire, both he and they (Vayikra 20:14) is, either this one or that one. If both are Bnei Yisrael one law applies to them. The woman spoken of in this verse is a Yisraeli woman.
Yet no harm follow. To the woman.
He shall be surely fined. Because of the children who were aborted and died.

According as the woman’s husband shall lay upon him. If the one who hurt the woman wants to do according to the will of the father of the children. Otherwise he shall pay in accordance to the ruling of the law court. Bi-fililim (as the judges determine) is similar to the word u-fillelo (shall judge him).

But if any harm follow. To the woman. We find a difference of opinion. Some say that the one who caused the women’s death is put to death because he intended to kill a fellow Yisraeli. They offer as proof the fact that Scripture states, he shall surely be fined (v. 22) with regard to the children, but it states with regard to the woman, then thou shalt give life for life. Now if the reference is to a fine, then in what way is the woman’s death worse than that of the children? On the other hand, if we say that one is to be punished with death for killing the children, why did Scripture alter its style and read, life for life? The opposing opinion maintains that one who intends to kill one individual and kills another is not put to death, and the reason the Torah altered its language and stated life for life is that the fine for killing a person is much greater than that for killing an embryo. They offer as proof the fact that the Torah afterwards reads, eye for eye, tooth for tooth (v. 24). The latter is not to be taken literally. On the contrary, it refers to ransom. This portion was written because of the clause eye for eye, tooth for tooth. Scripture afterwards codifies the law dealing with the eye and tooth of a bondman.

Eye. Rabbi Saadiah says that we cannot interpret this verse according to its plain meaning. For if a man struck his neighbor’s eye and the eye lost a third of its sight, how is it possible to punish the culprit with an equivalent blow, that is, with a blow which is neither greater nor lesser? There is a possibility that the culprit will lose his entire eyesight. Burns, wounds, and stripes present even greater difficulties, for if they were inflicted on a dangerous area it is possible for the culprit to die. The mind cannot accept this. Ben Zuta said to Saadiah Gaon: Does not Scripture elsewhere state, as he hath maimed a man, so shall it be rendered unto him (Vayikra 24:20)? Rabbi Saadiah answered him: We have a bet taking the place of the word al (on). Its meaning is, so shall a fine be placed upon him. However, Ben Zuta responded, as he hath done, so shall it be done to him (Vayikra 24:19). The Gaon retorted: Observe, Shimshon said, As they did unto me, so have I done unto them (Jud. 15:11). Now Shimshon did not take their wives and hand them over to others. He only repaid them for their dastardly acts. Ben Zuta responded: If the culprit is a poor man what shall his punishment be? The Gaon answered: If a blind person shall blind one who can see, what shall be done to him, for it is possible for a poor person to become wealthy and pay. However, it is eternally impossible for the blind to pay. The general rule is that we cannot fully explain any commandment written in the Torah unless we rely on the words of our sages of blessed memory. Just as we received the Torah from the sages, so did we receive the Oral Law. There is no difference between them. Now the interpretation of eye for eye is, it is fitting for the culprit to give his eye in place of his victim’s eye if he does not pay ransom for it.

[Tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.] Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says: In some cases the payment for taking out a tooth is very small. This is the case when a youth is struck, because if his tooth is uprooted another will take its place. Scripture mentions the hand because one does work with it. Scripture mentions the foot because the loss of a foot is worse than the loss of a hand, as a person cannot walk on one foot. However, I believe that Scripture mentions these organs because they are the ones that are usually harmed. When a man strikes his neighbor he strikes him in the eye which faces him, or the mouth which faces him and thus breaks his teeth, or in the hand that his neighbor fights with or protects his face with, or his foot when he runs away from him.
Burn. Keviyyah (bum) is to be taken at face value; that is, it refers to a burn caused by fire.

Some say that petza (wound) refers to a bleeding wound and chabburah (stripe) to a blow that does not draw blood. However, the Gaon says that petza refers to breaking a bone and chabburah to a bleeding wound.

And if a man smite. Hashem commanded that a bondman should go free because of his eye or tooth to prevent masters from cruelly striking their servants with terrible blows. Thus if the master destroys his bondman’s eye or even his tooth, then the bondman will pass from his control free of charge and the master will forfeit his property.
And if he smite out his bondman’s tooth. Scripture, as I have noted, speaks about the most usual. According to tradition a bondman similarly goes free if any of his major organs are destroyed.

And if an ox gore a man. This portion is mentioned because of if the ox gore a bondman or a bondwoman (v. 32). The man and the woman referred to in our verse are Bnei Yisrael. Our verse reads, or a woman. Scripture does not mention a woman in He that smiteth a man, so that he dieth (v. 12) because it is the manner of Scripture to mention the more important, namely, the male. Nevertheless, the same law applies to a female. Scripture now mentions a woman so that the owner of the ox does not protest and argue that the woman did not follow the normal practice. For there are places where it is not the custom for women to go out of the city to a field where oxen are found. It is because of this that Scripture afterwards states, Whether it have gored a son, or gored a daughter (v. 31). The law concerning one that smiteth a man applies equally whether the victim is an adult or a minor. Scripture mentions son or a daughter so that the owner of the ox does not protest against the parents and say that the parents should have watched their children.

The ox shall be surely stoned. The meaning of and its flesh shall not be eaten is that its flesh shall not be eaten as the flesh of an animal that dies of itself, which the stranger in the gate or the foreigner may eat. Our sages said that every time Scripture states, it shall not he eaten, it means that it is prohibited to derive any pleasure from it.
But the owner of the ox shall be quit. Of punishment.

But if the ox was wont to gore. There is no doubt that there is no ransom for those who are to be executed by a court of law. The transmitters of tradition therefore said that shall also be put to death refers to death at the hands of heaven. Now I believe that here [the term shall be put to death] is similar to eye for eye. Its meaning is, the owner shall be put to death if he does not give a redemption for his life. All of this because Scripture reads, yumat (shall be put to death); not yamut (he will die).

If there be laid on him a ransom. This does not contradict Moreover ye shall take no ransom for the life of a murderer (Bamidbar 35:31), for Scripture speaks there of a real murderer. However, the person spoken of in our verse did not commit murder. He is only punished because he did not restrain the ox by tying it up. Or, if he tied the ox up, he did not do so properly so that the ox was able to free itself. Or, the ox did not find the door closed and it went out and caused damage.
Laid upon him. By the decree of the judges.

Whether it have gored a son, or have gored a daughter. Both of whom are Bnei Yisrael, for Scripture afterwards reads, If the ox gore a bondman (v. 32). God decreed that the owner of the ox be punished because it is hard for God to see an animal kill a person who is created in the image of God. Because of this, the ox is also stoned.

And if a man shall open a pit. Which was dug. Scripture mentions this because Hashem does not want an animal to die in vain, that is, if its death does not serve human needs. Furthermore, he injures the owner of the beast.
The owner of the pit. The one who opened it or the one who dug it. This is the law even though the pit is on public property. He made it for his use; therefore he is called the owner of the pit.
He shall give money. He shall pay what the fallen animal was worth when alive after deducting the value of the carcass.

And if one man’s ox hurt another’s. Ben Zuta says that re’ehu (another’s) is an adjective describing the ox. However, Ben Zuta did not notice that the word shor (ox) is in the construct with ish (man’s). This is also the case with the word shor (ox) and re’ehu (another’s). However, an ox has no neighbor except for Ben Zuta. The owner of a tame ox pays half of the damage.

Or if it be known. On the other hand, if the ox was a gorer he shall pay the entire damage. Scripture mentions the laws dealing with the ox up to If a man steal an ox (v. 37). All of this because of the bondman who is sold because of his theft. This is the way our Torah portion opened, namely, If thou buy a Hebrew servant (v. 2).

If a man steal. Rabbi Yehoshua says that Hashem was stricter with an ox than with a sheep because the thief cannot hide an ox as he can a sheep. One cannot steal it unless one is experienced in the art of theft. However, Saadiah Gaon says that the theft of an ox is more severely punished because the owner of the ox suffers more than that of a sheep because the ox is used for plowing.
If a thief be found breaking in. At night, as the thief would not break in during the day. If the sun he risen upon him in the verse which follows proves this.

[There shall be no bloodguiltiness for him.] That is, the one who kills the thief is not guilty of bloodshed. One has to be amazed at those who interpret damim (bloodguiltiness) as life. If this is so, what is the meaning of because thou art a man of blood (damim) (Shmuel II 16:8) and his blood (damav) shall be upon him (Vayikra 20:9).

If the sun be risen upon him…he shall make restitution. This refers to he shall pay five oxen for an ox, etc. (Shemot 21:37), which is written above. It is like unto a foreign people (Shemot 21:8) and And also unto thy bondwoman thou shalt do likewise (Devarim 15:17), which refers to thou shalt furnish him liberally (Devarim 15:14), which is written above it.
He shall be sold for his theft. Because of his theft.

If the theft be found in his hand. This verse refers to all beasts. Our sages received a tradition that Scripture decrees that the law concerning the payment of “four and five” applies only to oxen and sheep.

If a man cause a field or a vineyard to be eaten. This too is connected to what is written above wherein the damage cause by an ox is mentioned. Scripture reads, ki yaver (if…cause…to be eaten). The word yaver (cause to be eaten) comes from the same root as be’irenu (our cattle) in we and our cattle (Bamidbar 22:4). It is a pi’el.
[And it feed in another man’s field.] Bi-sedeh acker means in another man’s field. Ye that have eaten up the vineyard (Is. 3:4) is similar.
If fire break out. This too is connected to what is written above, for it speaks of damage caused to a field.

[He that kindled.] The word ha-mavir (he that kindled) does not have the same meaning as the word yaver (cause to be eaten) in if a man cause…to be eaten (v. 4) even though they both come from the same conjugation. For the word fire indicates what ha-mavir means. It is considered beautiful Hebrew style to employ the same word with two meanings, as in With the jawbone of an ass (ha-chamor), heaps upon heaps (chamor chamorotayim) (Jud. 15:16), and in that rode on thirty ass colts (ayarim), and they had thirty cities (u-sheloshim ayarim lahem) (Jud. 10:4). Now in the latter verse the second ayarim means cities, as which are called Chavot Yair (Ibid.) proves.
If a man delivers. This is also connected to what is written above. Scripture speaks of theft so as to complete the ordinances concerning theft.

Whether he have not put his hand unto his neighbor’s goods. This indicates that then the master of the house shall come near unto God refers to an oath sworn before judges. Hence, For every matter of trespass (v. 8) follows. This means that the one who swore sinned. Rabbi Yehoshua says that pesha (trespass) means that it went out of the owner’s possession, as in “Then did Edom revolt from under the hand of Yehudah.” (Melachim II 8:22). For every matter of trespass (v. 8) includes everything that follows and everything that passes out of the owner’s possession, whether stolen or lost, with the finder denying and not admitting that he found it.
Whereof one saith. The witness saith, This is it.
This is it…he whom Elokim shall condemn. If Elokim shall condemn the keeper, because he himself stole it, or one who found an object and denied finding it, and thus became a thief because of it.
If a man deliver. Our verse speaks of a paid bailee.
Unto his neighbor’s goods. According to the pace of the cattle (Bereshit 33:14.) is similar. The owner takes nothing from the keeper except for the oath.
If it be torn in pieces. He was paid for this.
Let him bring it for witness. Let him bring a piece of the carcass as proof. This is in line with As a shepherd rescueth out of the mouth of the lion, Two legs, or a piece of an ear (Amos 3:12).
And if a man borrow aught. According to the plain meaning of the text, the owner thereof not being with it means that the owner can claim that the borrower overworked his animal.

If the owner thereof be with it. If the owner himself saw how the animal was hurt or died. The same law applies to a hired animal accompanied on the way by its lessee and lessor. Scripture concludes its dealing with theft of property and proceeds to discuss theft of confidence namely, seduction, for we often find men seducing young women of immature mind.
That is not betrothed. For a betrothed woman is considered to be married even though she has not slept with her husband.

[He shall surely pay a dowry for her.] Mahor yimharennah (he shall surely pay a dowry for her) is similar to the word mohar used in the sense of attachment, as in acher maharu (that attach themselves unto another) (Tehillim 16:4). The root mem, heh, resh having the meaning of quickly (meherah) is only found in the pi’el in all of Scripture.
He shall pay money. For seducing her.

A sorceress. Scripture mentions the law of the sorceress after the law dealing with a seduced virgin because those who lust desire to satisfy their cravings through magic. Scripture speaks of a sorceress because women practice sorcery more than men.

Whosoever lieth with a beast. Scripture first mentions the laws dealing with the seduction of an immature young woman. It also mentions intercourse with an animal that, unlike a woman, cannot cry for help. It then mentions the law concerning a woman who can cry for help.

He that sacrificeth unto the gods. According to the plain meaning of the text the verse does not speak of a Yisraeli, for Scripture already warned against this in the second statement. It is only mentioned because of the stranger who is mentioned in the next verse. It is because of the stranger that Scripture reads, Whosoever lieth with a beast (v. 18), for this is the manner of the foreign nations. Now a stranger may live in the Land of Yisrael on the following conditions: that he does not lie with a beast and that he does not sacrifice unto idols. Scripture reads, la-elohim (unto the gods) because the reference is to the gods that the stranger was previously accustomed to worship. The term la-elohim (the gods) also takes in the angels.
Unto Hashem only. Only unto the glorious name which is a common noun not used for any other being.

And a stranger. When a stranger commits himself not to worship idols you shall not wrong him in your country because you are more powerful than he is. Remember that you were strangers like him. When Scripture makes mention of the stranger who is powerless, it similarly takes note of the orphan and widow who are powerless Bnei Yisrael. After saying lo te’annun (ye shall not afflict) (v. 21) which is in the plural, Scripture says im te’anneh (if thou afflict) (v. 22) because whoever sees a person afflicting the orphan and the widow and does not aid them, is also considered an afflicter.

If thou afflict them. Note the punishment. If a person afflicts an orphan or a widow and no one comes to their aid, all are punished. The next verse therefore reads, My wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you, that is, all of you. Scripture says, “for if he cry at all unto me” in regard to the orphan. The same applies to a widow. However, it is possible that the orphan is very young and cannot articulate his pain like the widow.

If thou lend money. If Hashem gave you enough wealth so that you are able to lend to the poor. This section is mentioned here because the poor are like the stranger, the orphan, and the widow. Hashem calls the poor My people because the pious do not seek to acquire wealth in this world, as can be seen from Eliyahu’s behavior. Elisha, who did not want to accept Naaman’s gift (Melachim II 5:16), also proves this point. So does Shmuel from Ramah.
[With thee.] Its meaning is, in the place where you dwell.
Thou shalt not be to him as a creditor. In that he favors you because of your kindness. Scripture reads, tesimun (shall ye lay) because the lender, the scribe, and the witnesses all violate the law.

If thou at all take thy neighbor’s garment to pledge. After saying salmat re’ekha (thy neighbor’s garment), which is the feminine, and similarly, after saying, ki hi kesuto levaddah (for that is his only covering) (v. 26). Scripture says, teshivennu (thou shalt restore it). Scripture reads teshivennu because it refers to the pledge. Saadiah Gaon asks, what reason is there to take the pledge during the day and to return it at night? He answers, because the lender fears that the borrower might secure an additional loan from someone else and give him the pledge as security for the loan.
For that is his only covering. Its meaning is, you should pity him.

[For I am gracious.] According to the Gaon the term chanun (gracious) is similar in meaning to channuni channuni (Have pity upon me, have pity on me) (Iyov 19:21). Its meaning is, I will give him money and take away your money. I believe that this is not the meaning of chaninah (graciousness). What did David seek in saying, Be gracious unto me, O Elokim. according to Thy mercy (Tehillim 51:3)? Chanun rather has the same meaning as the word rachum (merciful) although there is a difference between them, as I will note in the Torah portion Ki Tissa.

Now the phrase that I will hear which follows and it shall come to pass, when He crieth unto Me is similar to for if they cry at all unto Me, I will surely hear their cry — My wrath shall wax hot (v. 22,23). How shall you know that I will surely hear their cry? You will know it from My wrath which follows.
Thou shalt not revile Elokim. The reference is to the judges, namely, the priests, the sons of Levi, who have the Torah with them. NOR CURSE

A ruler of thy people. In secret or in public. The Geonim differentiated between revile and curse. The ruler spoken of in our verse is the king noted in Deuteronomy. When we examined all the verses that come one after the other until And in all things that I have said unto you take ye heed (Shemot 23:13), we discovered that most of them deal with the poor. They appear to be connected to the section If thou lend money…to the poor (v. 24). Yefet says the reason Scripture mentions Thou shalt not revile Elokim is that if the lender should violate the law and not return the pledge, the poor man, while in pain during the night, might revile the judge who ruled that the lender should take the pledge.

The fulness of thy harvest, and of the outflow of thy presses. Mele’atekha (the fulness of thy harvest) is another name for wine and dimakha (the outflow) another name for oil. However, Saadiah Gaon says that mele’atekha refers to both the fullness of the seed and the fullness of the winepress. He says that dimakha alludes to oil, because when an olive is pressed the oil drips like a tear (dema). Now this verse is explained elsewhere, namely, The first-fruits of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the first of the fleece of thy sheep (Devarim 18:4). Scripture therefore couples The first-born of thy sons shalt thou give unto Me with it. For the first-born are the first of one’s strength. Ben Zuta says that mele’atekha (the fulness of thy harvest) refers to pregnancy and dimakha (the outflow of the press) is another term for sperm, which is a drop. He also says that Thou shalt not delay means that one should not delay taking a wife. Hence, The first-born of thy sons shalt thou give unto Me follows it. However, this is sheer insanity. Why did Scripture mention mele’atekha before dimakha? According to Ben Zuta, dimakha refers to the ejaculation of semen into a woman, which is then followed by pregnancy. Furthermore, pregnancy is not in the hand of man. It depends only upon Hashem. Yefet says that this verse is mentioned so that the poor person does not delay to give that which he is obligated to give. SHALT THOU DO WITH THINE OXEN, AND WITH THY SHEEP.] Likewise thou shalt give the first-born to the priest.

And ye shall be holy men unto me. Since Scripture mentions thine oxen and thy sheep, which are permitted to be eaten, it warns one not to eat meat which is torn, for it is possible that a poor person might eat torn meat because of his poverty.
[In the field.] Scripture speaks of what is most common. The same law applies if the animal was torn in the midst of a city. That chanceth him by night (Devarim 23:11) is similar.

[To the dogs.] The lamed prefaced to kelev (dogs) was vocalized with a pattach because the reference is to the dog who guards the oxen and the flock. Torn meat is not fit for anyone, only for a dog Rabbi Moshe Ha-Kohen says that torn meat is unhealthier than meat from an animal that dies of natural causes. There is something poison-like in torn meat that is harmful to the health of a human being. Hence Scripture does not permit one to give torn meat unto the stranger that is within thy gates (Devarim 14:21) or to sell it unto a foreigner (Ibid.) as it does to meat from an animal that dies of natural causes (Ibid.).
Thou shalt not utter a false report. One should not invent fantasies in order to spread lies.
[Put not thy hand with the wicked.] Its meaning is, do not join a wicked person in testifying falsely to harm the innocent. A poor person might do this because of his poverty.

Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil. If you see many people testifying concerning something that you know nothing of, do not say to yourself all of these people cannot be lying. Saadiah Gaon says that there are two commandments in this verse. One is a negative commandment, the other a positive commandment. The Gaon says that we are obligated to follow the majority, for Saadiah thought that the word le-hattot (to pervert) has the same meaning as li-netot (to turn). However, this is not the case. Le-hattot is a pi’el. It is similar to the word matteh (perverteth) in Cursed be he that perverteth the justice due to the stranger, fatherless, and widow (Devarim 27:19). This form is also found without the word justice following it. See u-matteh ger (and pervert the stranger) (Malachi 3:5). Our rabbis of blessed memory derived the law that the halakha follows the majority opinion from this verse. They transmitted the truth to us, for after Scripture states, Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil, we learn that we are commanded to follow a multitude that wants to do good.
Neither shalt thou bear witness. This commandment falls upon all of Yisrael. How much more so is a judge, before whom a dispute comes, obligated to help his neighbor.

Neither shalt thou favor a poor man. This too is connected [to If thou lend money to any of My people even to the poor], as you might think that you are doing good in helping the poor. Scripture elsewhere states, nor favor the person of the mighty (Vayikra 19:15).

Thine enemy’s ox. Oyivkha (thine enemy’s) is spelled with a chirik beneath the yod. Oyivkha is a verb, for the word ve-ayavti (then I will be an enemy) (v. 22) is a transitive verb. Its meaning is, even though you know that he is your enemy. The same is true of the word sona’akha (him that hateth thee) (v. 5). Scripture uses the term oyivkha because it is proper usage. This is also the case with sona’akha. It is possible that this section was written because if the ox and the ass belong to a poor person, then the reward for returning them is very great. One observes Hashem’s law and one also acts kindly with the poor.

Thou shalt forbear. Ve-chadalta (thou shalt forbear) is similar to chadal (forbear) (Divrei Hayamim II 25:16), the meaning of which is, forbear from doing this thing. Ve-shamarta (and thou shalt observe) (Devarim 17:10) is similar. The meaning of ve-chadalta ma’azov lo (thou shalt forbear to pass by him) is, forbear from leaving the matter to him alone. On the contrary, assist him in opening the knots and leave the burden as it is, and it will fall down on both sides of the donkey. The beast will then rise. Some say that its meaning is similar to va-ya’azevu (and they restored) in and they restored Yerushalayim (Nechemyah 3:8), its meaning being, thou shalt surely load the burden. However, this is far-fetched.

Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor. This is directed to judges. Thou shalt eat it before Hashem thy Elokim (Devarim 15:20) similarly refers to the one who is fit to eat it. Scripture, as it were, separates the kohen from Bnei Yisrael and addresses him. The person who says that the reference is to the first-born of the flock speaks nonsense.
Keep thee far from a false matter. This is directed to judges. They are not to judge falsely. Justice, justice shalt thou follow (Devarim 16:20) is similar.

And the innocent and righteous slay thou not. Those who are innocent and righteous in this case. If you know, that the defendant is wicked in some other matter do not say, because he committed some other horrible act, let me kill him and remove him from society. I will exact punishment from him and he will not escape My hand.
And thou shalt take no gift. This verse is also mentioned because the wealthy give bribes to the judges to divert justice from the poor.
And perverteth the words of the righteous. Saadiah Gaon says that the word tzaddikim (righteous) modifies divre (words of). However, this is not possible, for divre is in the construct.
[Righteous.] Righteous refers to righteous in the matter before the judges, not righteous with regard to the observance of the commandments.
And six years. This too is mentioned because of that the poor of thy people may eat (v. 11).
But the seventh year thou shalt let it rest. This is the year that Hashem’s release is proclaimed. One is then prohibited from exacting a debt from his needy neighbor.
And lie fallow. U-netashta (and lie fallow) means it shall not be sown. And we would forego (ve-nittosh) the seventh year (Nechemyah 10:32) is similar.
Six days. Scripture also mentions that the son of thy handmaid, and the stranger, who is in your gate, who is poor, and [who] hires himself out to you, may be refreshed.

And in all things that I have said unto you take ye heed. Scripture now mentions idolatry. And in all things that I have said unto you refers to Elokim’s commandments and ordinances. Observe them, not the ordinances of other gods. Scripture says, and make no mention of the name of other gods ; that is, do not mention their names in any oath or cause their adherents to swear by their names. The precise meaning of neither let it be heard out of thy mouth is: you shall not cause others to swear by their names; that is, do not tell an idolater, “Swear to me by your god.”

[Three times.] The meaning of regalim is times. You shall serve only Me. You shall serve Me three times a year by coming before Me like a servant who comes before his master to bring him a gift. Scripture therefore afterwards reads, el pene ha-adon Adonai (v. 17), the meaning of which is, before Hashem Hashem (v. 17). And none shall appear before Me empty (v. 15) is similar. Scripture mentions this because pagans go to worship their vanities on specific days. Scripture therefore reads, thou shalt keep a feast unto Me, the meaning of which is, only unto Me.
[Thou shalt keep a feast.] The word tachog (thou shalt keep a feast) means thou shalt sacrifice. It is similar to the word chag (sacrifice) in tie the sacrifice with ropes (Tehillim 118:27).
Times. The word regalim comes from the same root as regel (foot), for most of the people come on foot.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread. Scripture starts with the festival of unleavened bread because it falls in the first month of the year. Now Scripture states, seven days thou shalt eat unleavened bread. This is similar to Thou shalt keep the feast of tabernacles seven days (Devarim 16:13). It is thus an obligation. However, Six days thou shalt do thy work (v. 12) differs. For Scripture immediately states that one has to rest on the seventh day (Ibid.). Seven days thou shalt eat unleavened bread differs from it. Furthermore, why doesn’t Scripture read, seven days you shall not eat leavened bread?
In the month abib. I have already explained this.

[And none shall appear before me empty.] Many think that ve-lo yera’u fanai rekam (and none shall appear before Me empty) is like u-fanai lo yera’u (but My face shall not be seen) (Shemot 33:23). However, this is incorrect, for those who come to the house of Hashem are there seen. Venireh et pene Adonai (That he may appear before Hashem) (Shmuel I 1:22) is proof of this. The phrase et pene Adonai in yera’eh khol zekhurekha et pene Adonai (shall all thy males appear before Hashem thy Hashem) (Devarim 16:16) means before Hashem.

And the feast of harvest. The harvest of the first of the wheat. Now the barley crop which is what Aviv refers to is always there when the festival of unleavened bread arrives. There are seven weeks from the arrival of the first barley to the arrival of the first wheat. Compare, Seven weeks shalt thou number unto thee (Devarim 16:9).
And the feast of ingathering, at the end of the year. And a new year commences. Sowing begins in the month of Marcheshvan.

Three times. These three times, concerning which I said, None shall appear before Me empty (v. 15), was said only with regard to males who are of the age when they are obligated to observe the commandments. Those who are ill and cannot come are exempt.
The blood of my sacrifice. The reference is to the sacrifice of the paschal offering, which is eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.

The fat of my feast. The reference is to the unblemished lamb which one is obligated to offer. It is similarly written, in offering the portions that were to be burnt and the fat till the morning (Divrei Hayamim II 35:14).

The choicest first-fruits of thy land. This is what And if thou bring a meal-offering of first-fruits unto the Lord (Vayikra 2:14) refers to. As I will explain in its place, the verse is directed to the individual. Scripture mentions this law after Thou shalt not offer the blood of My sacrifice with leavened bread (v. 18), for the first fruits begin then.

[Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother’s milk.] The fools say that the word gedi (a kid) comes from the same root as meged (precious fruit). However, this is impossible, for the mem of meged is a root letter. The word megadim (precious fruit) in with precious fruit (Cant. 4:13) is definite proof of this. We do not find such a thing in the Hebrew language. Furthermore, how are we to explain lo tivashel (thou shalt not seethe)? A person cannot ripen the precious fruit. Indeed, Scripture states, And for the precious things (u-mi-meged) of the fruits of the sun (Devarim 33:14). Additionally, what reason is there to say in…milk? Where do we find such an expression? Additionally, what is the meaning of its mother’s? Where else is the tree called the mother of the precious fruit? The fools came to this conclusion because they found this commandment coupled with The choicest first-fruits of thy land. Elsewhere we find this commandment coupled with Ye shall not eat of any thing that dieth of itself (Devarim 14:21). The latter is its proper place. However, it was only mentioned together with the first-fruits because the kids increase and grow then. There is another commentator who says that the meaning of Thou shalt not seethe is, thou shalt not prolong; that is, a kid shall not be with its mother more than seven days. Now if this is the case, why does Scripture mention this law again? Furthermore, their proof is in the phrase bashel katzir (the harvest is ripe) (Yoel 4:13). However, the term bashel means to seethe, for the sun seethes like fire. It is the same case with hivshilu (ripe) in and the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes (Bereshit 40:10). Rabbi Shlomo says that gedi (a kid) means young and tender. He says it applies to young oxen and young lambs. He claims that the phrase gedi izzim (a kid of the goats) (Bereshit 38:17) proves this, since there is no reason to connect them. However, this is not so. The term gedi applies only to a goat. Thus in Arabic the term gedi means a goat. It is never used for any other kind. However, there is a difference between a gedi and a gedi izzim. A gedi is larger than a gedi izzim. A gedi izzim still needs to be with other goats. The same applies to the terms sa’ir (a he-goat) and se’ir izzim. Our sages have received the tradition that a Yisraeli is not permitted to eat meat and milk. I will now explain. Note that it is the Torah’s custom to speak of that which is most prevalent. For example, the Torah refers to the ostrich as a bat ha-ya’anah (Vayikra 11:16). Now why does the Torah do something here which it does not do in any other place? For in no other place does the Torah refer to an entire species by the term “daughter of” (bat). Note that the flesh of the ya’anah is as dry as wood. It is not customary for people to eat it, as it contains no moisture. The only flesh of this species that is eaten is that of the “daughter” (bat), whose flesh has a little moisture in it because it is a young female. However, young ostrich males have no moisture in them. Similarly, people do not eat meat and milk, for it is not pleasant to do so. Meat takes long to cook, but milk boils quickly. It is not the custom even today in the land of the Yishmeelim for a person to eat a lamb cooked in milk because the lamb is very moist and so is milk. It is thus harmful. Hence it is not eaten. On the other hand, the flesh of the kid contains no moisture. When a goat is small it is hot. Therefore they [inhabitants of Yishmeeli lands] cook the kid with milk. Do not be surprised that the people of the surrounding areas are not in the habit of eating a kid of the goats. All the physicians admit that there is no comparable meat, and they even permit the sick to eat it. They similarly eat it in Spain, Africa, the Land of Yisrael, Paras, and Bavel. It was similarly the custom of the ancients to eat it. We thus read: two good kids of the goats (Bereshit 27:9); that we may make ready a kid for thee (Jud. 13:15). We also find that the kohen eats the kid of the goats that is brought as a sin offering (Vayikra 6:19; 23:19,20). It is because it is not the custom for a person to eat raw meat that the Torah prohibited a person from cooking a kid in its mother’s milk. Some say that bishul (seething) only applies to meat roasted over a fire. However, is it not written, u-vasel mevushal bamayim (sodden…with water) (Shemot 12:9)? We similarly find that the Book of Divrei Hayamim states bi-shelu ba-sirot (sod they in pots) (Divrei Hayamim II 35:13). There is no need for us to search for the reason it is prohibited. The reason is hidden from the eyes of the intelligent. It is possible that it is prohibited to seethe a kid in its mother’s milk because to do so is very cruel. The idea behind this law is like the idea behind And whether it be cow or ewe, ye shall not kill it and its young both in one day (Vayikra 22:28), and thou shalt not take the dam with the young (Devarim 22:6). It is the practice of most people that do not have a flock to buy milk in the market. In such a case the milk usually consists of a mixture coming from many goats. It is possible for the buyer of a kid not to know where the mother is. Now if the one who has bought a kid later buys milk, it is possible that some of this milk contains milk from the mother of the kid which he previously purchased. He will then violate the law. We must be strict when in doubt regarding a Biblical law. The Yishmeelim also admit that if one cooks a kid in its mother’s milk the resulting dish tastes better because the mother and the kid are similar in nature. Scripture speaks of what is most usual. The ancients of blessed memory were strict in order to remove all doubt. They thus prohibited meat and milk. Hashem who gave them wisdom will fully reward them. I will further explain in each of their respective places why Scripture noted this law a second and a third time.

Behold, I send an angel before thee. Hashem told Moshe that he should also tell Yisrael that if they accept all the laws and ordinances, starting from Ye yourselves have seen (Shemot 20:19), then Hashem would bring them into the land.

[An angel.] Many err concerning the angel. Some say that the angel refers to the Book of the Torah, for Scripture says, for My name is in him (v. 21). Others say that the reference is to the ark of the covenant. They interpret and hearken unto his voice (v. 21) as: and hearken to what is written in it. They also say that for he will not pardon your transgression (Ibid.) means: for Elokim will not pardon your transgressions. Now all of this is nonsense, as this theme is found throughout Scripture. We thus read: He will send His angel before thee (Bereshit 24:7); the angel who hath redeemed me from all evil (Bereshit 48:16). Moshe similarly said, and sent an angel, and brought us forth out of Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 20:16). We likewise read, And the angel of His presence saved them (Is. 63:9); And the angel of Hashem went forth (Is. 37:36); and said to the angel that destroyed the people (Shmuel II 24:16); My Elokim hath sent His angel (Daniel 6:23); and the appearance of the fourth is like that of an angel (Daniel 3:25). There are many similar instances. We read in the book of Daniel, The prince of Paras…the prince of Yavan (Daniel 10:20); except Michael your prince (Daniel 10:21). Michael is the angel referred to as the great prince, for he is exalted above many others. Scripture also states regarding Michael, one of the first princes, came to help me (Daniel 10:13). The meaning of first is, first in rank. It is like and sat first in the kingdom (Esther 1:14). The angel referred to is Michael.
To keep thee by the way. So that nothing evil happens to you.
Which I have prepared. For you. Our verse follows the idea When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance (Devarim 32:8), which I will discuss later.

Take heed of him. Every angel follows Hashem’s command. The angel does not add or subtract from what Hashem has commanded him. The same applies to Satan, who tormented Iyov. He was an angel. It was the same case with the angel who went out to hinder Bilam. Now, whoever hearkens to the voice of the angel is hearkening to the voice of Hashem the glorious.

[Be not rebellious against him.] The word tammer (rebellious) is difficult. Its meaning appears to be similar to va-yamru (rebelled) in but they rebelled against Me (Yechezkel 20:8). However, in this case our word should have read tamreh. The Spanish scholars were therefore forced to say that tammer comes from a double root. It is like vayassev (led about) in But the Lord led the people about (Shemot 13:18), for the entire form comes from a double root. Venasevah (wound about) in were broader as they wound about (Yechezkel 41:7) is a nifal. It is like ve-navela (confound) in and there confound (Bereshit 11:7), which comes from the same root as balal (mixed). It is also similar to ve-navekah (empty) in And the spirit of Mitzrayim shall be made empty (Is. 19:3), which comes from the same root as bokek (empty) (Is. 24:1). Do not be surprised that we have two roots with one meaning. For we find this to be the case with the words sorer (bear rule) and sarita (striven) in that every man shall bear rule (sorer) in his own house (Esther 1:22) and in for thou hast striven (sarita) with Elokim (Bereshit 32:29). The same is true of tammer (rebellious) in be not rebellious against him and memer (rebellious) in And rebellious to her that bore him (Mishlei 17:25). Memer follows the paradigm of mekhes (tribute) (Bamidbar 31:28), which comes from the same root as takhossu (ye shall make your count) in ye shall make your count for the lamb (Shemot 12:4). It comes from a double root.

[For my name is in him.] Note that for My name is in him is connected to Take heed of him, and hearken unto his voice (v. 21). It is like And also unto thy bondwoman thou shalt do likewise (Devarim 15:17). I have already explained that Hashem’s glorious name is a proper name, as it refers only to Hashem. It is also found as an adjective. For Hashem is all, and all comes from Him.

[In him.] Hashem is said to be in him in the same sense that the center of a circle is equally distant to all points on the circumference of the circle. It is only in this sense that Scripture tells us that Hashem’s glory is in the midst of the camp, and that Hashem’s glory journeys in the camps. It is thus written, that Thou Hashem art in the midst of this people (Bamidbar 14:14). Scripture likewise reads, And formed the spirit of man within him (Zecharyah 12:1). Do not be astonished that Scripture first reads, But if thou shalt indeed hearken unto his voice (Ex. v. 22) and then goes on to say, and do all that I speak (Ibid.). I will give you an example by which you can understand the above. All the scientists who study astronomy have proven beyond a shadow of a doubt that the moon is a body which receives its light from the sun, for the moon has no light. It is for this reason that the sun grows dark when the moon joins it during the day. The sun and the moon are both embedded in spheres that are similar to the spheres of the constellations. The darkness results only from the fact that the moon, which like the sun is circular, passes beneath the sun. Now the side of the moon which faces the sun is totally illuminated. However, the side which is above it is dark. It is not illuminated. Observe that the moon thereby blocks the light of the sun. The moon is also left without light even in the middle of a lunar month if the shadow of the earth comes between it and the sun. Look! We know that the light of the moon at night illuminates the air. Now if Reuven calls the light of the moon moonlight, he speaks the truth. If Shimon refers to the light of the moon as sunlight, he too speaks the truth.

[An adversary.] The wise men of Spain found the word evah (enmity) spelled with a silent yod (Bereshit 3:15). However, our verse reads, ve-ayavti et oyevekha (I will be an enemy unto thine enemies). They also found Scripture reading tzed chayyah (in hunting any beast) (Vayikra 17:13) and tzayyadim (hunters) (Yirmiyahu 16:16). They also found the word din (the cause) in They plead not the cause of the poor (Yirmiyahu 5:28) and dayyan (judge) in Hashem therefore be judge (Shmuel I 24:16). They therefore said that a verb has no less than three letters. Hence evah comes from a root whose middle letter is silent.

For. God commanded Yisrael to remove all idols immediately upon coming to the Land of Yisrael. He mentioned six nations and did not bother to mention the smallest among them. It is concerning the latter that God said, and I will [immediately] cut him off. As to the others, By little and little I will drive them out (v. 29). It is also possible that and I will cut him off means: and I will cut off each one of them. It is like Its branches run over the wall (Bereshit 49:22).

Thou shalt not bow down to their gods. This is what I referred to earlier when I said that the Book of the Covenant opens and closes with a warning against idol worship. For Ye yourselves have seen (Shemot 20:19), which opens the Book of the Covenant, is a warning against idolatry, as is for they will be a snare unto thee (v. 33), which closes the book. However, there is a difference between the two. At the beginning of the book Elokim commanded [Yisrael] not to make a god of silver alongside Hashem. At the end of the book He commanded Yisrael to uproot from the land of Kenaan all the idols that its inhabitants had made. For whoever worships idols violates, as it were, all the negative commandments of the Torah. Furthermore, all of the positive commandments which he observes are of no avail to him in this world or in the next world.

And ye shall serve Hashem…he will bless thy bread and thy water. Its meaning is, you shall serve only Hashem who took you out of the house of bondage and brought you to the land of nations which served other gods who were not able to save them from your hands. Serving Elokim is defined as doing all that Hashem has commanded, namely, to love Hashem, to cleave unto Him, to swear by His name, to pray to Him, to sacrifice the daily and the additional offerings unto Him and to honor Him by giving tithes. One who does the above has his reward with him. The latter consists of the following four things which he will receive in this world. One, And He (Elokim) will bless thy bread and thy water. Two, I (Elokim) will take sickness away from the midst of thee. Three, None shall miscarry, nor be barren, in thy land (v. 26). Four, The number of thy days I (Elokim) will fulfill (Ibid.). Now all of these rewards pertain to the body. In addition, Elokim will do the reverse of these blessings to your enemies; namely, I will send My terror before thee (v. 27); And I will send the hornet before thee (v. 28).

Avraham the author writes: There are some great scholars who are very learned in the two laws but have not studied the sciences. I therefore cannot begin to explain the abovementioned blessings without first mentioning a bit of the sciences. Man’s body comes from the lowest world. However, man’s soul (neshamah), which is tied to the body, comes from on high. There are two powers that are intermediate between the body and the soul. These two powers are referred to in the main in Hebrew as ru’ach (spirit) and nefesh (life force, appetite, desire), for the soul (neshamah) is the rational part of man and its place is in the brain of man. From it comes the power of all emotions and the desire to move. The ru’ach (spirit) is situated in the heart. Life depends on the ru’ach. The ru’ach desires to dominate; that is, it seeks to overcome all opposition. It is the source of anger. Shlomo similarly said, Be not hasty in thy spirit (ruchakha) to be angry (Kohelet 7:9), and A fool spendeth all his spirit (rucho) (Mishlei 29:11). The seat of the nefesh (life force, appetite, desire) is in the liver. It is the nefesh that desires to eat. It is thus written, because thy soul (nafshekha) desires (Devarim 12:20). The nefesh is the source of sexual desire. Now some people are created in such a way that these three souls are strong. In others they are weak. In other instances one soul is strong, another weak, or neither weak nor strong. Now, people fall into twenty-seven categories. Hashem gave the Torah to strengthen, to intensify, and to increase the power of man’s supernal soul. When this happens the body does not rule over it. However, if the Torah is not observed, then the body overpowers the neshamah. I will explain with the following parable. We know from the teachings of the sciences that any person whose constitution is overcome by red bile will be angry, for this is the nature of fire and red bile is like fire. Now when the neshamah is unintelligent it pursues the wants of the body because it cannot overcome its desires. Additionally, let us consider a person who is not by nature hot.
