If another person comes along and curses him to the point where he becomes angry, he begets heat in his body which was not there before he became angry. Hashem the exalted, in his kindness, chose Yisrael and taught them His Torah. If Yisrael observes the Torah they become wise. Their wisdom guides them in a straight path to all things that will not harm them. The general rule is: the body must be subservient to the dictates of the soul (neshamah) rather than the soul being subservient to the dictates of the body. When the soul (neshamah) is strong, then the heavenly power known as nature, which preserves the body, grows in might. Now our verse tells us that Hashem’s blessing shall be upon all our food and drink. For there is a curse that adversely effects the power of nature, as in Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied (Michah 6:14). Observe that all illnesses come from the food that enters the body. Now a person who observes the Torah will not fear them. This is the meaning of and He will bless thy bread. There are other diseases that come from outside the body due to a change in the air caused by a shift in the arrangement of the planets. It is concerning this that our verse states, and I will take sickness away from the midst of thee. Look, a person who observes the Torah has no need for a physician along with Hashem the Revered. Scripture thus writes, yet in his disease he sought not to Hashem, but to the physicians (Divrei Hayamim II 16:12). I have thus spoken on the science of medicine. I will now speak on the science dealing with the heavenly bodies. Note that what befalls human beings depends on the alignment of the planets and what their arrangement indicates at the time of a person’s birth. The aforementioned is extremely difficult to understand. If a woman is born under an arrangement that decrees she will not be able to carry her children to term, then it will be the nature of her womb to abort the children in it. The same is true if the woman is born under an arrangement that decrees that she be barren and not have children. Now if a person who is born under an arrangement of the planets that determines that he will have a physical makeup that is unable to beget children cleaves to Hashem, then if he truly cleaves to Hashem, the revered Hashem will strengthen the power of this man’s kidneys and see to it that his sperm functions properly so that he will be able to have children. Hashem therefore told Avraham, I am Hashem Almighty; walk before Me, and be thou whole-hearted (Bereshit 17:1). This is what the rabbis meant by “Cease thy planet gazing.” Hashem told Avraham, “If you make a treaty to serve Me, I will greatly multiply you, as I will overcome what nature has decreed for you.” This is not a victory over the arrangements of the stars, for they were not created to do good or ill to the lowest world. On the contrary, they always go and do the service of Hashem, as that is what they need to do. The inhabitants of the lowest world receive a thing and its opposite from them in accordance with their desire. Thus if we observe the Torah we will not receive evil from the heavenly bodies. I will yet speak on this in the Torah portion Ki Tissa. The third blessing is a blessing to the effect that all of Yisrael have children and that none of their children die in the lifetime of their parents.
[Barren.] The reference is both to one’s wife and to his cattle.

[The number of thy days I will fulfill.] This, the fourth blessing, is a blessing for long life. We know that there is a fixed and established time to every person’s life in accordance with the heat and moisture which are the natural components of the human body. One’s life is not fixed in accordance with the foreign fire and foreign moisture which are unnatural components of the body. The person who cleaves to Hashem strengthens his body’s heat and moisture through the power of his soul. Such a person will live longer than his allotted life span. We thus read, The fear of Hashem prolongeth days (Mishlei 10:27). It is also stated, In the midst of his days he shall leave them (Yirmiyahu 17:11). We further read, but Hashem shall smite him; or his day shall come to die (Shmuel I 26:10). Now a person who dies in war or in a plague does not die on the day set aside for his death in accordance with the nature of the heat and moisture in his body. He dies because of outside events. Now if a person cleaves to Hashem, Hashem will save him from all of these things. We find that the Torah states, lest he die in battle (Devarim 20:5). We also read, why shouldest thou die before thy time (Kohelet 7:17). This does not contradict the science of astrology. For a star’s decree is dependent upon many things, as I will explain in commenting on so that we are distinguished, I and Thy people (Shemot 33:16). Scripture therefore states, behold, I will add unto thy days (Is. 38:5). Why should I continue to go on and on?

I will send my terror. The reference is to a fear in the soul. The body immediately weakens. This is what and I will make all thine enemies’ necks towards thee refers to. Its meaning is: your enemies will turn their necks to you; that is, they will flee from you when you look at them.

And I will send the hornet. The reference is to a plague in the body which saps its strength. The word tzirah (hornet) comes from the same root as tzara’at (leprosy). Scripture mentions three of the seven Kenaani nations. However, the same applies to all of the other Kenaani nations. It is also possible that this plague ravaged these three nations more than it did the others.

I will not. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that this will serve as a sign. When Yisrael will see that they have become fruitful and multiplied, then the seven nations will be uprooted. However, there is no need for this interpretation, for Scripture mentions the reason that God will not drive out the Kenaani in one year, namely, lest the land become desolate. The borders of the Land of Yisrael will be too large for those who left Mitzrayim to be able to settle all of it. Pen (lest) in lest the land is like pen (lest) in lest the fulness of the seed….be forfeited (Devarim 22:9).
By little and little. Until you increase and are able to inhabit the entire land. Scripture now goes on to describe the length and breadth of the land.
And I will set thy border. This is what May he have dominion also from sea to sea, And from the River unto the ends of the earth (Tehillim 72:8) refers to. The River refers to the Perat.
Thou shalt make no covenant with them. Do not make a covenant with them in any case.
[Nor with their gods.] Its meaning is, you shall destroy their gods.
They shall not dwell in thy land. When you increase, you shall destroy and annihilate all the seven nations. The Book of the Covenant ends here.

And unto Moshe he said. All that God mentioned from above until now consisted of the conditions that Moshe was to place before Yisrael. God then told Moshe, after you make the covenant with Yisrael you, Aharon, Aharon’s sons, and seventy of the elders of Yisrael, namely, the holy first-born, shall come up unto Me.

And Moshe alone shall come near. Do not be amazed that Hashem first said, Come up unto Hashem (v. 1) and then, And Moshe alone shall come near unto Hashem, rather than, and you will come near unto Hashem, for this is Hebrew style. We thus read, Then Hashem caused to rain upon Sedom and upon Amorah brimstone and fire from Hashem out of heaven (Bereshit 19:24), the meaning of which is, from Him. However, Shmuel said, And Hashem sent Yeruba'al, and Bedan, and Yiftach, and Shmuel (Shmuel I 12:11). Shmuel did not say, and me. There are many such instances.

And Moshe came. Scripture does not mention that Moshe came down from the mountain because there was no need to do so. The meaning of And Moshe came and told the people all the words of the Lord is, and Moshe came in the midst of the camp of Yisrael and told the people all the positive and negative commandments that are codified between ye your-selves have seen (Shemot 20:19) and for they will be a snare unto thee (Shemot 23:33).
And all the ordinances. Which he placed before them. They are mentioned in this portion.
And all the people answered. As if they were one person.
And Moshe wrote. After Moshe related all the words of Hashem, the commandments, and the ordinances, he wrote them down. This is what the Book of the Covenant consists of.

And builded an altar under the Mount. At the place where Yisrael stood at the time that the Torah was given. The word va-yiven (and builded) is to be read as if written twice. Our verse is to be read as if written: and he builded twelve pillars.
And he sent the young men of the children of Yisrael. The reference is to the young men who were the sons of the chosen elders who were to go up on the mountain with Moshe.
Who offered burnt-offerings. This is what and shalt sacrifice thereon (Shemot 20:21) refers to.
Scripture mentions that oxen were offered as peaceofferings because many people partook of the peaceofferings.
And Moshe took half of the blood. Of the burnt and peaceofferings.
[Basins.] The word agganot (basins) refers to round vessels. Compare, aggan ha-sahar (round goblets) (Cant. 7:3). It is ajan in Arabic.

And half of the blood. Of the burnt and peaceofferings he dashed against the altar for God. Observe, the word agganot is to be read as if written twice. Moshe placed half of the blood in basins, and he also placed the other half of the blood in basins.

And he took. When Moshe read the Book of the Covenant to the elders and they accepted it upon themselves, he then took the remaining half of blood and sprinkled it upon the people, that is, the elders, for they stood for all of Yisrael. We similarly find the same regarding the bullock offered for an error made by the congregation. We read there, And the elders of the congregation, who were representing all of Yisrael, shall lay their hands upon the head of the bullock (Vayikra 4:15).
[And sprinkled it upon the people.] This sprinkling is like and sprinkled it upon Aharon, and upon his garments (Vayikra 8:30).
[Behold the blood of the covenant.] Moshe called it the blood of the covenant.
Then went up Moshe. Scripture does not mention the mountain because there was no need to do so.
And they saw the Hashem of Yisrael. In a prophetic vision. It is similar to I saw Hashem sitting on His throne (Melachim I 22:19; Divrei Hayamim II 18:18).

[A paved work of sapphire stone.] Saadiah Gaon says that the sappir (sapphire) is white. He offers the phrase livnat ha-sappir as proof. However, this is not the case. The sappir comes in no color but red. The fact that it is the style of Scripture to repeat itself in different words proves this. Now it is written, Her princes were purer than snow, They were whiter than milk (Eichah 4:7). We thus see that Scripture repeats itself in different words. The verse continues, They were more ruddy in body than rubies, Their polishing was as of sapphire (sappir) (Ibid.). The term sappir thus has the same connotation as rubies. Furthermore, if livnat ha-sappir means like the whiteness of sapphire what reason is there for Scripture to say, like a work? It should have read, like the appearance of. Actually, the word livnat is etymologically related to the word levanah (brick). It is like the word cheshkat (darkness of) in Darkness of waters (Tehillim 18:12), which is etymologically related to the word chashekhah (darkness) (Bereshit 15:12). Now the paved work of sapphire stone (livnat ha-sappir) was similar to the vision of the sapphire stone which had the form of a throne seen by Yechezkel in his prophetic vision (Yechezkel 1:26; 10:1).

And the like of the very heaven for clearness. Its meaning is, beneath the paved work of sapphire stone there was the likeness of the very heaven. The latter refers to the ice-like firmament that was stretched over the heads of the beasts Yechezkel saw in his vision (Yechezkel 1:22). Now our verse reads, and they saw the Elokim of Yisrael. However, in Yechezkel Scripture reads, This is the living creature that I saw under the Elokim of Yisrael (Yechezkel 10:20). Scripture was being brief. The creature was under the firmament, and the firmament was under the throne of glory. All of this was under Hashem the revered.
And upon the nobles. The word atzile (nobles of) is similar to the word u-me’atzilehah (from its nobles). The term elders is not used because the term nobles include Nadav and Avihu.
[He laid not his hand.] Its meaning is: that they saw Hashem and did not die, as I will explain in my comments on the verse for man shall not see Me and live (Shemot 33:20).
[And did eat and drink.] They came down from the mountain happy.
And did eat. The peaceofferings which their young people sacrificed.

And drink. In happiness. Rabbi Yehudah Ha-Levi says that the meaning of and did eat is, they had to eat even though they enjoyed the splendor of God’s presence. Scripture mentions this because Moshe lived for forty days and forty nights without eating and drinking, as is noted in the next section.

And Hashem said unto Moshe: come up to me into the Mount. And be there until I give you [the tables of stone, and the law, etc.]. A Spanish sage said that the first tablets which were the work of Elokim, which means were finished by Elokim, were created the same size as the ark. The second tablets also were The work of Elokim, who is the One who created everything. However, Moshe finished the second tablets. A finished product is called a work. We thus read, va-yemaher la’asototo (and he hastened to dress it) (Bereshit 18:7). The sage said this because Scripture reads, tables of stone and does not employ the term stones as it does in reference to the second tablets. Now I pointed out to the above sage that Scripture states, When I was gone up into the mount to receive the tables of stone (avanim) (Devarim 9:9). Furthermore, Scripture there employs the phrase luchot avanim (tables of stone) three times. The meaning of luchot even (tables of stone) therefore is tables made of stone and not of wood. The Gaon says that which I have written is connected to tablets of stone and not to the law and the commandment, for Elokim only wrote the Ten Statements. He explains that the meaning of the law is the written law and that of the commandment is the oral law, as all the commandments were given to Moshe on Sinai during the days that Moshe was on the mountain. It is similarly written, But as for thee, stand thou here by Me (Devarim 5:28). However, I believe that the law refers to the first and fifth statements of the Decalogue, and and the commandment refers to the other eight statements.

And Moshe rose up. We may logically conclude that Yehoshua left the camp of Yisrael with Moshe and stayed beneath the mountain until Moshe came down. Observe, Yehoshua knew nothing about the making of the golden calf. There is no reason to ask, what did Yehoshua eat? Yehoshua gathered the manna which was around the camp and ate it daily.
And unto the elders. The known elders, namely, the elders who saw Hashem the revered.

And, behold Aharon. Aharon was also a first-born. It is possible that Chur was a first-born too and he was one of the seventy. Both of them were to judge in place of Moshe until Moshe came back. I have already explained that Yitro only came in the second year.
And Moshe went up…and the cloud covered. The cloud had already covered the mountain on the sixth day of the month.

And the glory of Hashem abode. This means that the glory of Elokim had already abode, for Scripture clearly states, And Hashem came down upon mount Sinai. (Shemot 19:20). Furthermore, Scripture states, but Moshe drew near unto the thick darkness where Elokim was (Shemot 20:18).
And the cloud covered it. The cloud covered Moshe and no one was able to see him.

And the seventh day he called unto Moshe. There is no reason for the Gaon’s question, “Why didn’t Moshe go up to the top of the mountain when he went up at first?” Moshe was not able to go up without permission.
And the appearance. Now the mountain was entirely covered by a cloud. Hashem’s glory was on top of the mountain. Hashem the revered was seen there in the form of burning fire.
And Moshe entered…and went up into the Mount. Its meaning is, and Moshe went up to the top of the mount where God’s glory was.

And Moshe was in the Mount. He did not come down. Scripture writes concerning these forty days, I did neither eat bread nor drink water (Devarim 9:9). This is a great wonder. There never was such a miracle before.
God who gave a perfect Torah to his children; The Lord who brings to light all hidden things; Will explain to us the words of wisdom inscribed In the Torah portion That They Take For Me An Offering.

And the Lord spoke unto Moshe. When Moshe went up to the top of the mountain God spoke to him regarding the tabernacle. God told Moshe that Yisrael should construct a sanctuary dedicated to God the revered. The Lord would dwell in this tabernacle and speak therein with Moshe. Moshe would no longer come up on the mountain.

[That they take for me.] The words ve-yikchu li (that they take for Me) is similar to the form surah elai (turn in to me) (Jud. 4:18). Surah elai means turn from your place and come to me. Ve-yikchu li has a similar connotation. It means let him take from what he owns and give it to me. The same is true of Fetch me (kechi li), I pray thee, a little water (Melachim I 17:10).

And this is the offering. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that we do not find silver mentioned in connection with the tabernacle except for the silver of those who were counted. This being the case, how could Scripture state that the silver was an offering? The Gaon answers that other silver was donated for use in the construction of a silver table, since it is highly unlikely that there was no table for preparing things, for cutting, for washing, or for the trumpets and basins. However, I believe that there is no need for the Gaon’s interpretation. Scripture did not bother to exclude one of the sixteen materials, as fifteen were donated. It is the same with These are the sons of Yaakov, that were born to him in Paddanaram (Bereshit 35:26). However, Binyamin was born in the land of Kenaan. He was not born elsewhere. Furthermore, Scripture states, Thy fathers went down into Mitzrayim with threescore and ten persons (Devarim 10:22). However, the sons of Yosef did not go down to Mitzrayim, for they were born in Mitzrayim. Scripture begins with a precious gift, namely, gold. It concludes with a precious gift, onyx stones, and stones to be set, which only the princes possessed. However, this was not the case with gold, as most of the people had gold. Now, no iron was used in the construction of the tabernacle. Scripture tells us regarding the first temple, and there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building (Melachim I 6:7).

And blue. Yefet says that tekhelet (blue) is a blacklike color. Black is the final color, as all colors turn black, and no human hands can change black. However, we will rely on the sages of the Talmud who said that tekhelet is green wool.

And purple. Argaman (purple) is a red-like color. It is referred to as argevan in the Book of Divrei Hayamim (Divrei Hayamim II 2:6) and as arju’an in Arabic. This color is only found in wool or silk.

And scarlet. However, Scripture elsewhere reads, sheni ha-tola’at (and the scarlet) (Vayikra 14:6). We find the same with mi-tzur ha-challamish (out of the rock of flint) (Devarim 8:15) and chelmish tzur (out of the flinty rock) (Devarim 32:13). Saadiah Gaon rendered tola’at shani as krimez (red). Although tola’at shani is also red, it is not the same color that argaman is. Many people identify tola’at shani with silk because of the word tola’at.

And fine linen. Shesh refers to linen, which is a type of flax that is found only in Mitzrayim. It comes only in white and is not dyed. We thus read, Of fine linen (shesh) and richly woven work from Mitzrayim (Yechezkel 27:7). The Gaon translated shesh as osher in Arabic. This material is in existence until this very day.
And goats’ hair. Izzim is to be rendered as goats’ hair.
And rams’ skins. Skins from large rams. Such skins are prepared in the land of Al Gudmas and are referred to as gudmasi.

And sealskins. Techashim (seals) refers to a type of animal that was known then, as it is written, va-ena’alekh tachash (and shod thee with sealskin) (Yechezkel 27:7). It is thus clear that it was already known.

And acacia-wood. Some of our ancient sages said that the patriarch Yaakov planted acacia trees in Mitzrayim, and Yisrael, upon the command of Moshe, brought them out. And every man, with whom was found acacia-wood…brought it (Shemot 35:24) is proof of this. They possessed acacia as they possessed the blue and the purple. However, one wonders, why does Scripture say, with whom was found, which means it was used for personal needs. Now, if we so interpret it, then we must ask, why did Bnei Yisrael take acacia wood out of Mitzrayim? What need did they have for acacia wood? Furthermore, it is clear that the Mitzrim thought that Bnei Yisrael were going to offer sacrifices and then return to Mitzrayim. That is why the Mitzrim lent Bnei Yisrael [gold and silver jewels plus raiment]. How could Bnei Yisrael take out many boards, each one of which was ten cubits? The boards were also accompanied by bars. In Mitzrayim they passed by the seat of the king. What was their answer to those who asked them why they were carrying acacia wood when they were going on a three-day journey to offer sacrifices? Now we do not know whether our ancestors had a tradition that Bnei Yisrael took the acacia wood out of Mitzrayim. If they did, then we will accept their tradition. However, if their statement is based on reasoning, then we must seek another explanation. We suggest that there was a forest of acacia trees next to Mount Sinai. When Yisrael came to Sinai, Moshe told them that they would be spending a long time there. I have already explained that there was no cloud over them at this time. Each one of them then made a booth. The princes made court-like structures, each one in accordance with his status. They cut the entire forest down, for they were a large nation. They made booths. Moshe did not speak to them regarding the tabernacle until after the Day of Atonement. This is the meaning of with whom was found (Shemot 35:24).

Oil for the light. Oil needed for the light in accordance with the requirements of the law. The wise men of this generation say that ve-liktoret ha-sammim (and for the sweet incense) has to be inverted in order to be understood. Its meaning is, and the perfumes for the incense. Now if this is the case, then why didn’t Scripture say, for the anointing oil spices (ve-le-shemen ha-mishchah besamim)? Furthermore, Scripture reads, and the spice, and the oil, for the light (ve’et ha-shamen le-ma’or), and for the anointing oil, and for the sweet incense (ve-liktoret hasammim) (Shemot 35:28). I believe that the word spices (besamim) takes in the spices needed for anointing oil and the spices that were mixed with the incense perfumes. This is also the true tradition.
Onyx stones. This includes all the stones of the ephod and the one of the breastplate.
To be set. I will explain later the meaning of me-lu’im (to be set).
And let them make me a Sanctuary. The tabemacle is called a mikdash (a sanctuary) because it is the tabernacle of Hashem the holy.

I show thee. You will see it with your eye. Unlike the visions of Yechezkel, which were in prophetic dreams. Scripture adds the emphatic heh and reads ha-mishkan (the tabernacle) after it mentions the term sanctuary.

[Even so shall ye make it.] A vav is placed in front of the word ken (even so) in the phrase ve-khen ta’asu (even so shall ye make it) regarding the vessels, for Scripture earlier states, ve-asu li mikdash (And let them make Me a sanctuary) (v. 8).
And they shall make. Scripture begins by saying, And they shall make an ark because it had at first said, And let them make Me a sanctuary (v. 8).

[Two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof.] We do not know if these measurements refer to the outside or to the inside of the ark. Now if the reference is to the outside of the ark, then the width of the two sides of the ark, each of which was covered by gold on the inside and the outside, added up to half a cubit, making the size of the tablets a cubit in width and a cubit in length. Now if we say that the height of the ark was also half a cubit thick, then each tablet was extremely heavy. Perhaps Hashem gave strength to the hands of Moshe, which were “heavy” to begin with, so that he was able to bring down a tablet of stone in one hand. Now Scripture states, tables that were written on both their sides (Shemot 32:15). Perhaps it was so, for a tablet is a cube having six sides. We similarly find it written that there were three arks. Its weight raises questions. Furthermore, the width of the ark cover was a handbreadth Additionally, we read in Scripture that the gold which was donated came to less than one thousand and four hundred parts of the gold which king David left. Observe, the cherubim were made of olive wood. The incense altar was also not completely made of gold. If we look at it logically, then it appears that the ark was covered with gold for appearance sake and that very little gold actually went into the covering. Were not the boards, the bars, the table, and the incense altar all covered with gold? Nothing except for the menorah was made entirely of gold. Now once they made an ark out of gold, what need was there for wood? The fact that Shlomo covered the porch and the house with gold demonstrates how the covering was actually done.
A crown of gold. The word zer (crown) comes from the same root as the word zareta (you crowned) in, You crowned my going about and my lying down (Tehillim 139:3).

The four feet thereof. I searched all of Scripture and did not find the word pa’am (foot) used in the sense of corner. It is always employed in the sense of a foot. We thus read: Even the feet of the poor, and the steps (pa’ame) of the needy (Is. 26:6); And shall make His footsteps (pe’amav) a way (Tehillim 85:14); How beautiful are thy steps (fe’amayikh) (Cant. 7:2). There are many other instances. I was therefore forced to explain that the ark had feet, for it would be disrespectful for the ark to sit on the ground. Furthermore, what reason is there for Scripture to place a connective vav before the word u-shete (and two) when dealing with the two rings of gold (v. 12)? If the reference was to the rings already mentioned, then Scripture should have read, shete taba’ot (two rings), as that is the proper syntax if the Torah wants to indicate that it is dealing with the four gold rings previously noted. One of the wise men of our generation understood this. He says that the staves were placed in the ark in the rings that were on its feet. He further says that they would remove the staves from the lower rings and place them in the upper rings when it was necessary to carry the ark. It is similarly written, and shall set the staves thereof (Bamidbar 4:6). However, I believe that the staves were never removed once they were placed in the upper rings, for Scripture states, they shall not be taken from it (v. 15). As to And shall set the staves thereof (Bamidbar 4:6), it means that the priests shall place the staves upon the shoulders of Bnei Kehat. When the ark was placed in the Holy of Holies it was necessary to place it near the wall so that the cherubim would cover the ark and its staves. The end of each one of the staves therefore extended. This is what Scripture refers to when it states, And the staves were so long (Melachim I 8:8). The four lower rings thus served, as is the case with chests, for beauty and elegance.
In the rings of the ark. In the rings that are on the sides of the ark.

And thou shalt put. The tablets and the testimony are one and the same. They were, as it were, a marriage contract. They were the tablets of testimony. And he took and put the testimony into the ark (Shemot 40:20) is perfect proof of this. Furthermore, Moshe did not write the scroll of the Torah. The scroll of the Torah was placed by the priests next to the outer side of the ark of the covenant. It is additionally written, There was nothing in the ark save the two tables of stone (Melachim I 8:9). There is a difference of opinion concerning this. One may raise the following question. Scripture reports that Hashem told Moshe (v. 16), And thou shalt put into the ark the tables which I shall give thee. The Torah then tells us, And He gave unto Moshe, when He had made an end of speaking with him…the two tables of the testimony (Shemot 31:18). Now Moshe broke these tablets. Moshe thus did not fulfill the command of Hashem. It is possible to give the following answer. Perhaps this is the reason why our sages said that the broken tablets were placed in the ark. Scripture does not contradict their words, for both the first and the second tablets were tablets of the covenant. It is also possible to answer that Scripture (v. 16) speaks only about the second tablets. The statement which I shall give thee does not contradict this. For Scripture also says concerning the second tablets, And Hashem gave them unto me (Devarim 10:4). Furthermore, note that we do not find that Hashem told Moshe that he should make an ark and place the first set of tablets there. For Hashem knew that Moshe would break them. It was only concerning the tablets that Moshe hewed that Hashem said, and make thee an ark of wood (Devarim 10:1). Now our sages said that and make thee an ark of wood does not refer to the ark made by Betzalel. This is correct. However, if we follow the plain meaning of the text, then it does not appear to me to be far-fetched to interpret the text as referring to the ark which Betzalel constructed. Scripture similarly reads, And they shall make an ark of acacia-wood (v. 10). There is no reason to ask, where were these tablets placed before the tabernacle was constructed? For there is no need to mention this. What forced me to offer this explanation was the fact that Moshe says, and [I] put the tables in the ark which I had made (Devarim 10:5). Now if we assume that Moshe relates the account as it happened, even though we do not know the reason why he should mention this, what shall we do with what follows, namely, as Hashem commanded me (Devarim 10:5). This is proof that Scripture speaks of the tablets which Moshe placed in the ark of the covenant. [Moshe tells us that] these tablets are there until this very day (Ibid.). This is the meaning of and there they are unto this very day (Melachim I 8:8). This is also a sign and a witness that there was no Torah scroll in the ark, for Moshe first put the tablets in the ark. He then placed the ark cover with the cherubim over the ark. Now Hashem’s glory dwelled upon the cherubim. Scripture explicitly reads, Thou art enthroned upon the cherubim (Tehillim 80:2). This being the case, how could Moshe place a Torah scroll inside the ark in the fortieth year without first removing the ark cover with the cherubim from on top of the ark? There is no need for all of this.

And thou shalt make an ark-cover. The word kapporet means a cover. Yefet says that the word le-khapper (to make atonement) in to make atonement for him (Vayikra 1:4) is similar. Its meaning is similar to whose sin is covered (Tehillim 32:1). However, I believe that the word le-khapper (to make atonement for him) (Vayikra 1:4) is similar in meaning to the form kofer (ransom). Now this is clearly stated, for Scripture states, then shall they give every man a ransom (kofer) for his soul unto the Lord (Shemot 30:12). Scripture then goes on to say, le-khapper al nafshotekhem (to make atonement for your souls) (Shemot 30:15). Scripture does not mention the thickness of the ark cover.

And thou shalt make two cherubim. Our sages said that the cherubim looked like two youths. They said that the kaf in keruvim is a preposition and the word keruvim (cherubim) means the same as the Aramaic word ke-ravia (like youths). Now if they had a tradition that the cherubim were youth-like images, then what they said was true. They interpreted the word in a manner that would recall the tradition. They did the same with the word chanukkah. The kaf in the word keruv (cherub) is a root letter, as the word hakeruvim (the cherubim) in And the cherubim shall (v. 20) proves. The heh of ha-keruvim indicates the definite article. It is not an interrogative heh like the heh in ha-kemakkat (or is he slain) in Or is he slain according to the slaughter of them that were slain by Him (Is. 27:7). Now when I searched for the meaning of the word keruvim (cherubim) I found that it refers to various forms. Compare, Thou wast the far-covering cherub (keruv) (Yechezkel 28:14). Yechezkel said that each one of the beasts which he beheld had four faces (Yechezkel 1:6). One of these faces was the face of an ox (Yechezkel 1:10). However, elsewhere he describes this very creature as having the face of a cherub in place of the face of an ox (Yechezkel 10:14). Its meaning is that the creature had the image that Yechezkel had mentioned earlier. At the end Yechezkel says, This is the living creature that I saw under the God of Yisrael by the river Kvar; and I knew that they were cherubim (Yechezkel 10:20). Yechezkel thus called the four creatures cherubim. The kaf in the word keruvim thus is a root letter.

Of beaten work. Mikshah (of beaten work) means equal. The word mikshah (the same size) in And instead of hair trimmed to the same size (ma’aseh mikshah) baldness (Is. 3:24)is similar. Ma’aseh (trimmed) has the same meaning as asah (trimmed) in nor trimmed his beard (Shmuel II 19:25). Its meaning is that each cherub was equally distant from the edge of the ark cover.

Keruv. Observe! The cherubs were positioned on the long side of the ark. The staves were therefore placed to the width of the ark. There is someone who disagrees and says that side refers only to the long side. He offers proof from and for the second side of the tabernacle (Shemot 26:20). However, and five bars for the boards of the side of the tabernacle (Shemot 26:27), which is right next to the verse that he quotes, destroys his proof. The cherubim which were upon the two edges of the ark were made out of the ark cover itself

And the cherubim shall. Yefet says that the meaning of toward the ark-cover shall the faces of the cherubim be means that the cherubim shall face the center of the ark cover. However, I believe that the faces of the cherubim did not stand erect, but rather inclined a bit towards the ark cover.
And in the ark. This is in keeping with Hebrew syntax. Moshe had already put the testimonies into the ark. He was told: afterwards place the ark cover [over the ark].

And there I will meet with thee. I do not understand in what way this verse contradicts And Hashem called unto Moshe, and spoke unto him out of the tent of meeting, saying (Vayikra 1:1). For the phrase tent of meeting takes in the tabernacle and everything in it. There is no need for a clarifying verse.

[Of all things which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Yisrael.] The word et in and (ve-et) of all things which I will give thee in commandment has a vav placed before it for the following reason. The word ve-dibbarti (and I will speak) is to be read as if written twice. Our verse is to be read as if written: and I will speak with thee from above the ark cover, from between the two cherubim. Scripture does not mention what will be spoken. Its meaning is, I will speak with you in order to inform you of My secret and to answer your questions. And I will speak to you of all the things which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Yisrael. We have reason to ask, why did Hashem mention the ark first when Scripture reads, the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the furniture thereof (v. 9). The answer is that it is linguistic style to explain the last item with which one has closed. Compare, And I gave unto Yitzchak Yaakov and Esav; and I gave unto Esav mount Seir (Yehoshua 24:4). Hashem therefore began with an explanation of the tabernacle’s furniture. Hashem started with the most important piece of furniture and then went on to the explain the table and the menorah. After this, Hashem said, Moreover thou shalt make the tabernacle (Shemot 26:1). Now when Moshe gathered the congregation he spoke to them about the tabernacle and the tent first. Then he told them about the ark. There was no need for anyone to teach Moshe. There is reason to wonder why Hashem didn’t mention the altar of incense. The answer by way of parable is: Hashem’s glory did not depart [from the tabernacle]. The ark was therefore in the form of a throne. Observe, a menorah and a prepared table [were placed in the sanctuary]. Hashem did not mention the altar of incense until He first mentioned the altar of the burnt offering, because Hashem wanted to issue the command, You shall offer no…burnt-offering, nor meal-offering; and ye shall pour no drink-offering thereon (Shemot 30:9). Moshe mentioned the incense altar to the children of Yisrael following the menorah. The incense altar was similarly constructed after the menorah.
And thou shalt make. There is no doubt that the dimensions mentioned in our verse refer to the thickness of the table plus the height of its legs.
And thou shalt make. The border was on top as is the case with tables.
And thou shalt make a golden crown. Scripture now explains that the crown which was mentioned earlier should be around the borders.
And thou shalt make…four rings…and put the rings in the four corners. East, west, north, and south.
Close by the border. Scripture mentions the place where the rings were to be placed.

That the table may be borne with them. Venissa (may be borne) is a nifal. Ve-nissa is similar to ve-nikkah (be quit) in then shall he that smote him be quit (Shemot 21:19). For nissa and nikkah have a dagesh in them to make up for the dropped first root letter.
And thou shalt make. What the rabbis said is known.

[Wherewith to pour out.] The phrase wherewith to pour out refers to the jars thereof (kesotav). It does not relate to and the bowls thereof, which immediately precedes it. The following is similar: Moshe and Aharon among His priests, And Shmuel among them (Tehillim 99:6). Scripture then goes on to say, He spoke unto them in the pillar of cloud (Tehillim 99:7). The latter refers to Moshe and Aharon, not to Shmuel. The fact that Scripture says with regard to the making of the vessels, the jars thereof (ha-kesot) wherewith to pour out (Shemot 37:16) proves that wherewith to pour out refers to the jars thereof. So does and the jars (kesot) wherewith to pour out (Bamidbar 4:7). The word nasakh (pour) has many meanings. We thus read, They shall not pour out wine-offerings (nesekh) to Hashem (Hoshea 9:4); The image perchance, which the craftsman hath melted (nasakh) (Is. 40:19); and Truly it is I that have established (nasakhti) My king (Tehillim 2:6). Rabbi Natan, the author of the Arukh, says that kesavot (jars) are rods, as that is how they are referred to in Arabic. However, the one who told this to him did not know the Arabic language and spoke it laughably. Rods in Arabic are referred to as katzab, which is spelled with a tzadi and a bet. There is an error in the Book of Divrei Hayamim. Chronicles mentions basins in place of dishes, bowls in place of pans. It mentions jars as Scripture does here. In place of the bowls it mentions forks. They were all made of gold for use at the table. It is possible that David commanded that other utensils be placed upon the tables which Shlomo would make. However, the table placed in the tabernacle differed.

And thou shalt set up upon the table showbread. According to the plain meaning of the text, the bread was called showbread because of the explanation which follows it. That which the sages said is also true, as the ka’arot (dishes) were molds.

And thou shalt make a candlestick. I have seen copies of Scripture which the wise men of Tiberias have examined. Behold, I found the word te’aseh (be made) spelled with a yod. Fifteen of their wise men swore that they checked every word, vowel, full and deficient spelling, three times. I did not find this to be the case with the books of Scripture in Spain, France, and on the other side of the sea. Our sages said that the additional yod in te’aseh alludes to the ten candlesticks which Shlomo would make. Let me generalize. If there is a yod in te’aseh, then te’aseh is irregular. The Midrash tells us that the menorah made itself. The meaning of this midrash is that all who saw the menorah marveled and asked, “How could a human being make it?” Look! Scripture states, and he made candlesticks and so he made the candlestick (Bamidbar 8:4). Behold, Scripture writes, On a griddle it shall be made (te’aseh) with oil; when it is soaked, thou shalt bring it in (Vayikra 6:14). Observe, the word miksheh (of beaten work) here has the same meaning as the word miksheh which is written in connection with the cherubim.
Even its base and its shaft. This is the body of the menorah.
And there shall be six branches. Kanim (branches) refers to a round, long, and hollow object.

Three cups. The Gaon says that meshukkadim (almond blossoms) means in the shape of almonds. However, the word meshukkadim really is related to the word li-shekod (attached) in Attached daily at my gates (Mishlei 8:34).
Pure gold. Refined gold without any impurities.
And see. The making of the menorah required wisdom. One had to have intellectual perception to know how to make all these utensils out of one talent of gold.

[Which is being shown.] The word moreh (being shown) is irregular. It is not employed in the same way that the word mushlakh (be thrown) (Shmuel II 20:21) is, for the verb ra’ah (saw) does not come in the pa’ul. Only the term nireh (seen) is employed. This is so because one who sees is not acting on anything. He merely perceives an image. Those who are versed in the sciences will understand this. I wish to lay down a fundamental principle to you before I speak on the tabernacle, which also was made out of curtains [decorated] with cherubim.

Avraham the author says: All that exists, exists in one of the following two ways. One, it exists as a body that has length, width, and depth. The aforementioned results in six sides. From the length of an object comes front and back, from its width right and left, and from its height up and down. There are also incorporeal beings, namely, God’s holy angels and man’s soul. These two types of beings were created by God alone. It is not in the power of any created being to create a corporeal being. It is certainly beyond the power of any being to create an incorporeal being, for incorporeal beings are more important than corporeal beings. It is also beyond the power of any created being to totally annihilate another being There is something which comes very close to existence and is tied to existence but does not exist independently. This thing is called form. Form also comes in two ways. One type of form is permanent and does not pass away, namely, the form of the holy angels and the wisdom which is in the soul. Form is also found in corporeal elements. The heat of fire and the wetness of water are examples. The accidents are the second way in which form manifests itself. The accidents are not permanent. They come and go. They change. They turn and disappear. Man is able to produce accidents. It is impossible for the glorious God to have a permanent or unchanging image or picture because God created the essence of all things. Now, all forms are either permanent or accidents. Let me give you one example. The moon is eclipsed when the earth’s shadow enters between the moon and the sun at the head or tail of the dragon. I will give you another example. We know that the power of the soul is all over the body. However, there are places in the human body such as the eyes or the nose that are more sensitive than others because of the nerves that go out from the brain. The bones and liver are devoid of sensation. Now the heart is more receptive to the power of the soul than are all other organs of the body. Many organs therefore serve it. Similarly with the glorious God. We know that God’s glory fills the world. However, there are places where God’s power is more manifest than in other places. This is so for the following two reasons. Divine manifestation varies in accordance with the natural makeup of the recipient and in accordance with the upper power that is above the receiver. Therefore, the place of the holy temple [Mount Moriyah] was chosen. If God will give you wisdom, then you will understand the secret of the ark, the ark covering, and the cherubim which spread their wings. You will also understand the secret of the objects which were placed outside of the curtain, namely, the menorah, the incense altar, and the table. You will also comprehend the secret of the objects placed outside of the opening of the tabernacle, namely, the altar of the burnt offering and its utensils and the basin and its base. These objects served to honor God. I gave you these hints because there are many people in our generations who think they are wise. Perhaps they will mock my words. He who knows the secret of his soul and the makeup of his body is able to understand the workings of the upper world. This is so because man is a microcosm. Man was the last thing created by God when he created the earth. Let this serve as a sign: He began with the largest and finished with the youngest (Bereshit 44:12). Saadiah Gaon notes that there are eighteen objects in the tabernacle which serves as the intermediary world. The same number of objects is found in the upper word and also in the microcosm. Here is a general rule. Each cherub was made to receive power from above. It was also made so that the intelligent will learn. There is no need to go on.
Moreover thou shalt make the Tabernacle. As you were first told, namely, the pattern of the tabernacle (Shemot 25:9).

The work of the skillful workman. Our sages said that ma’aseh choshev (the work of the skillful workman) refers to two faces, and [ma’aseh] rokem (the work of the weaver) (v. 36) to one image. What they said is correct. However, according to the plain meaning of the text, ma’aseh choshev is neither needle-work nor weaving. It refers rather to a process employed today in making silk garments. The image that arises in the heart comes from insight and thought. The artist draws it upon a tablet. He then places two threads upon the image which he thought up in order to draw it from a distance.

The length. The uninformed say that the curtains were twenty-eight cubits in length because of the twenty-eight stages of the moon. However, actually there were ten curtains over the tabernacle to correspond with Who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain (Tehillim 104:2). The place of the Holy of Holies therefore was a cube in measure.

Coupled. Choverot (coupled) is an adjective. On the other hand, it might be a verb meaning that this curtain coupled the other curtain. Efraim is joined (chavur) to idols (Hoshea 4:17), wherein chavur is a pu’al, is proof of the aforementioned.

Loops. Some say that the word u-ve-lullim (and by winding stairs) in and they went up by winding stairs into the middle row (Melachim I 6:8) is similar to the word lule’ot (loops), for the bet in u-ve-lullim is a preposition.
That is outmost. The word ha-kitzonah (that is outmost) is an adjective like the word ha-elyonah (that is uppermost).
Fifty. Scripture now mentions the number of loops.

[Opposite.] The word makbilot (opposite) means this one was opposite the other. There are those who say that the word koval (before) in and smote him before the people (Melachim II 15:10) and kavolo (opposite it) in and shall strike that which is opposite it (Yechezkel 26:9) are similar.
[One.] The word ishah (one) means the very thing. The same is true with the word ish (man). Scripture therefore reads, ve-ha-ish gavri’el (the man Gabriel) (Daniel 9:21).
And thou shalt make fifty clasps of gold. The word kores (stoopeth) in Bel boweth down, Nevo stoopeth (Is. 46:1) is similar.

[That the Tabernacle may be one whole.] Look, the term tabernacle refers to the ten curtains. The tabernacle is called one, and it encompass all ten [curtains] for all physical entities are made of various elements. Similarly Hashem the revered, who is One. Hashem includes everything and is called One. The same is true with the microcosm and the macrocosm.
And thou shalt make curtains of goats’ hair for a tent. Le-ohel (for a tent) means to serve as a tent.
[Them.] The word otam (them) is there for purposes of additional explanation, as it refers to the curtains of goats’ hair.

The length of each curtain. The word achat (each) is irregular. The word should have read achedet, for the dalet is not a letter that serves as a prefix or a suffix. However, the dalet was dropped because it is very hard to sound a dalet and a tav, both of which are dentals, back to back. It was dropped for the same reason that the tav in mesharat (ministered) in ministered unto the king (Melachim II 1:15) was dropped.
Five. The word chamesh (five) is vocalized with a sheva and a pattach. It is an abridged form, like the word shelosh (three) in shelosh se’im (three measures) (Bereshit 18:6).

[And shalt double over the sixth curtain in the forefront of the tent.] Observe, when the sixth curtain was doubled, half of a curtain was left at the end. Hence Scripture states, the half curtain that remaineth over (v. 12). There is no need to mention that the length of the curtains was placed over the width of the tabernacle. Now the width of the tabernacle was ten cubits, and the height of its two sides was nine cubits. Scripture therefore states, And the cubit on the one side (v. 13) to cover the tabernacle.

And thou shalt make fifty loops. The number of loops on the curtains of the tent was the same as the number of loops of the tabernacle. The same applies to the clasps. However, the loops and the clasps of the tent were not opposite the loops and the clasps of the tabernacle. On the contrary, they were two cubits behind them towards the west.
And thou shalt make. The clasps of the curtains which made up the tabernacle were made of gold because they were used for the most important curtains.
The tent served as a cover over the tabernacle. Its clasps were therefore made of brass. The brass clasps were not visible because there were two covers over the tent.

And as for the overhanging part…the half curtain. The term half is sometimes used in the sense of close to a half, as in and the half-tribe of Menashe (Yehoshua 22:9). When we come to the description of the boards you will understand that which requires explanation.
And the cubit…which remaineth over. The word ba-odef (which remaineth over) is like the word oved (perishing). It is an adjective, as the cantillical note is placed on the last syllable.
And thou shalt make a covering. Over the covering because of the rain.
And thou shalt make the boards for the Tabernacle. The term tabernacle only applies to the curtains and the boards. As God informed Moshe of the tabernacle, so did He inform him of the boards.

[Standing up.] The word omedim means standing up as it grew on the tree, for the length of the wood is its height. The same applies to a person when he stands. The opposite is the case when he lies down. On the other hand, the word omedim might mean standing straight up.

Ten cubits. We do not know whether the cubits of the tabernacle were measured from the armpits like Yechezkel’s cubits. Logically, the cubits of the first temple were of such cubits, as we find that the Book Of Chronicles speaks of the earlier measure.
Two tenons. The word yadot (tenons) comes from the same root as yad (hands).
Joined. The word meshullavot (joined) has no cognate except for the word ha-shelabbim (the stays) (Melachim I 7:29).

And thou shalt make. Observe! Scripture does not record the thickness of the boards. The ancients said that each board was a cubit thick. If this is the case then the southern wall, which was thirty cubits, [was a cubit thick]. This was also the case with the northern wall. Thus a space measuring eight cubits in width was left for the western wall. However, eight boards had to be placed there. It is possible that the ancients were compelled to say that the boards were a cubit thick. They were compelled to say that the boards were a cubit thick because of the middle bar which was inserted into the boards. According to Rabbi Shlomo the bar could only lay there by a miracle. According to the plain meaning of the text there were three middle bars. Scripture similarly writes, from end to end (v. 28). It does not state from end to the ends. Now if the sages received a tradition that the boards were a cubit in thickness, then we will accept their tradition. However, if they arrived at this measurement by reasoning, then we can explain it differently. The two bars, namely, the upper two bars, and likewise the two lower bars, reached half of the wall. The middle bar that was placed in the midst (be-tokh) of the boards (v. 28) passed through from end to end. To work it in the midst (be-tokh) of the blue, and in the midst of the purple (Shemot 39:3) is similar, as is and put the bells in the midst (be-tokh) of the pomegranates (Shemot 39:25). The middle bars would not have been covered with gold if they were not placed on the surface of the boards. If we admit that we do not know the thickness of each board, then we can explain the structure of the western wall. Now, they first set up the western wall. For two boards were set aside to serve as corners of the tabernacle, as the meaning of mekutzot is corners. The same was true of half of the corners of the courtyard, for the courtyard was in the form of a parallelogram. We thus have two corners. Now these two corner boards were not the same size as the other boards mentioned in Scripture. Scripture therefore separates these boards and says, thus shall it be for them both (v. 24), that is, only for them and not for any of the other boards. The tabernacle was erected by utilizing these two boards. The remaining six boards were placed in the middle. The width of the tabernacle was thus ten cubits. We do not know if the corner boards were square or round, for we have only one remaining cubit. According to Rabbi Shlomo’s explanation, these boards did not stand in a straight line because half a cubit was inside the tabernacle. We are dealing with boards, not with garments. They then set up the boards on the northern and southern sides. Now an amount equivalent to the thickness of the boards protruded from the tabernacle. The pillar of the opening of the tabernacle was therefore opposite it. The half a curtain of goatskin fixed it.

And thou shalt rear up the Tabernacle. Moshe should tell this to the wise-hearted. Or, Scripture states, And thou shalt rear up the tabernacle because Moshe reared it up first. However, there were others with him, for many people were required to rear up the tabernacle.

And thou shalt make a veil. We find that Shlomo acted similarly with regard to the opening of the Holy of Holies. The wall was possibly made out of wood. Scripture notes that the entire house measured sixty cubits, and Rashi, of blessed memory, explains the Holy measured forty cubits and the Holy of Holies twenty cubits. The sockets were made of silver out of respect for the ark. The Holy of Holies in the temple was double that of the one in the tabernacle in length, width, and height. Do not be astonished that Scripture writes that the temple was thirty cubits in height and the Holy of Holies took up a third of the temple. For there were upper stories directly above the ark cover that is over the Holy of Holies. The Book of Divrei Hayamim tells us, And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold (Divrei Hayamim II 3:9).

And the veil shall divide unto you. The word ve-hivdilah (shall divide) is irregular in that it is ultimately accented. The same is true of the word ve-hikkita (and thou shalt smite) in and thou shalt smite the rock (Shemot 17:6).

And thou shalt make a screen…the work of the weaver. Ma’aseh rokem (the work of the weaver) is inferior to ma’aseh chosev (the work of the skillful workman). The pillars were covered with gold and the hooks were likewise covered with gold of respect for God. The sockets of the pillars were made out of brass because the screen was in between.
And thou shalt make. Any shape whose length is the same size as its width is called a square. The latter is a true square, as quadrilaterals come in five shapes.

[And the height thereof shall be three cubits.] Look, if contrary to the opinion of our sages, we say that there was no need for a ramp because the altar was three cubits high, what then will the opponents of the sages do with the altar which Shlomo made? That altar was ten cubits high whereas the height of a person is only four cubits.
[Four-square.] Scripture describes the altar as being ravu’a (four-square) because the length of the altar was the same as its width.
Corners. The word pinnot means corners.

[To take away its ashes.] The meaning of ledasheno is, to take away its ashes. The meaning of yedasheneh (accept the fat) in And accept the fat of thy burnt-sacrifice; Selah (Tehillim 20:4) is, he shall make ashes out of it. Its meaning is that the sacrifice will be burnt on the altar and accepted. Observe the word tedashen (make fat) in maketh the bones fat (Mishlei 15:30). They all belong to the same conjugational form, namely, the pi’el. The meaning of tedashen is to fatten, as in As for Asher, his bread shall be fat (Bereshit 49:20).
And its shovels. The word ve-ya’av (and its shovels) is similar to the word ve-ya’ah (shall sweep away) in And the hail shall sweep away (Is. 28:17).

[All the vessels thereof.] The lamed in le-khol (all) in le-khol kelav (all the vessels thereof) is superfluous. It is like the lamed in le-min (from) in from the day that the foundation of Hashem’s temple was laid (Chaggai 2:18).
A grating. The word mikhbar (a grating) is similar in meaning to the word kevarah (sieve) (Amos 9:9).
Brass. The word brass (nechoshet) is connected [to the word grating]. The text should be interpreted as if it read, a grating of brass, constructed like a net.
[Ledge.] The word karkov (ledge) does not appear in any other place.

[Hollow with planks.] Nevuv luchot (hollow with planks) is to be explained in accordance with the Aramaic translation. The phrase ve-ish nevuv yillavev (But an empty man will get understanding) (Iyov 11:12) is similar, for ish nevuv means an empty person, that is, a person lacking intelligence. The verse is similar to the aphorism, a head without a brain. The laver is not mentioned because it was not made from the gifts which were donated by all of Yisrael. It was made only from the gifts of the women. Hence the basin was mentioned with the chapter dealing with the spices, for the spices were also not donated by all of Yisrael. The spices were given only by the princes.

And thou shalt make. We find that Scripture says, kedemah mizrachah (on the east side eastward) (v. 13). We know that there are three “heads” to the east. The first is opposite the point of the head of Capricorn, which is the furthermost southern position of the sun. The second is opposite the celestial equator, which is the head of Aries and Libra. The third is opposite the head of Cancer, which is the sun’s furthermost northern position. The same applies to the phrase negbah temanah (south…southward) in the south.
Southward. The word temanah (southward) comes from the same root as yamin (south). Compare, The north and the south (yamin), Thou hast created them (Tehillim 89:13).

[And their fillets.] The meaning of chashukehem (their fillets) is their attachments, the hooks being attached to the pillars. Va-tidbak nafsho (and his soul did cleave) (Bereshit 34:3) means the same as chashekah nafsho (his soul longeth) (Bereshit 34:8).

And for the breadth…fifty cubits. The width of the courtyard was thus half of its length. The commentaries tell us that the tabernacle was placed fifty cubits westward. Now its width was fifty cubits. This is what and the breadth fifty every where (v. 18) means. However, I believe that the meaning of the breadth fifty every where is that the courtyard was a right-angled parallelogram, and its width was fifty cubits on all sides. There is no necessity to explain the breadth fifty every where as referring to the side of the courtyard, as Scripture does not repeat the dimensions length by width as it normally does.

All. The meaning of All the instruments of the tabernacle is, all the instruments that were for the use of the tabernacle. The pins of the tent and the pins of the court were of brass. So were the hammers.

If your heart desires to know the truth Look at the body, And consider the most glorious thing in it. I will secretly reveal the mystery of the Urim and Tumim In the Torah portion entitled, And Thou Shalt Command.

And thou shalt command. I will first note the reason for the position of this Torah portion. After God finished enumerating all the holy utensils, the veil, the tabernacle, the tent, the cover, the altar of the burnt offering, the courtyard, and the screen, He commenced to deal with those who ministered in the tabernacle. He explained the service which they alone were to perform. No stranger was permitted to perform the service alongside them. God opened with the command that they cause a lamp to burn using pure olive oil. They were not to employ any other oil. It is only fitting that those who ministered in the tabernacle were to be distinguished and set apart, both in family and in dress. Scripture lists the garments one after the other. Scripture then mentions that those who served in the tabernacle were obligated to learn the service during the seven days of consecration. Moshe was to teach and train them. After this, the priests would serve in the tabernacle. They would offer the daily burnt offering on the altar of the burnt offering. They were not to offer it upon the golden altar. The priests were to offer only incense upon the golden altar and to make atonement upon its horns once a year.

And thou shalt command means that there is an eternal command upon the congregation to continually provide olive oil to kindle a perpetual light. Do not be troubled by the oil which the princes brought. It was anointing oil. The congregation, on the other hand, was obligated to bring oil for the light. There is a practice in countries where olives grow to choose pure olives, that is, olives that do not have any rot on them or olives that have not been partially eaten. These olives are then used to make oil for the king’s food. This is the reason that Scripture mentions pure before beaten.
For the light. For the light needed during the night.
To cause a lamp to burn. To kindle the lamps. Scripture states, that they should burnaccording to the ordinance (Divrei Hayamim II 4:20) concerning Shlomo’s candelabra.

[Continually.] The meaning of tamid (continually) is nightly. There is a more difficult usage of the term tamid, namely, and it shall be always (tamid) upon his forehead (Shemot 28:38). The meaning of the latter is that the holy plate shall always be upon the miter whenever the miter is placed upon the head of the high priest.

Which is before the testimony. The testimony is short for the ark of testimony. Yefet says that ya’arokh (shall set) is similar in meaning to ke-erkekha (as thou valuest it) in as thou the priest valuest it (Vayikra 27:12). It means that the priest shall estimate the amount of oil that will be sufficient for the lamps to give light from evening till morning. The same applies to the phrase nerot ha-ma’arakha (even the lamps to be set in order) (Shemot 39:37). Ya’arokh may also be properly interpreted as meaning shall set, for the lamps were set in a semicircle. I will yet speak on this.

And bring thou. Scripture says, And bring thou near unto thee [Aharon thy brother, and his sons…that they may minister unto me] because at first Moshe was the high priest. I have already hinted at why Aharon was chosen to be sanctified to the Lord so that the priests would make atonement for Yisrael. Aharon was chosen because of the importance of Nachshon’s family. We cannot find fault with Moshe, our master, as Moshe was a fugitive. Who would have given him a Hebrew woman? Furthermore, the burden of all of Yisrael was upon Moshe. Moshe had to teach Yisrael the commandments. He also had to judge all difficult cases.

[That they may minister unto me.] The vav in lekhahano (that they minister) in that they may minister unto me is superfluous. It is like the vav in chayeto (beast) in every beast of the field (Tehillim 104:11) and beno (son of) in the son of Beor (Bamidbar 24:3). Our verse lists the sons of Aharon. It is possible that Aharon had other sons besides these. There is no doubt that Aharon’s family increased greatly in the wilderness. Hence they were given the many cities enumerated in the Book of Yehoshua.

And thou shalt make holy garments. They are called holy garments because they were worn during the sanctuary service. On the other hand, it is possible that they were called holy garments in accordance with that they sanctify not the people with their garments (Yechezkel 44:19). The garments of Aharon referred to in our verse are the ones which Scripture later enumerates.
For splendour and for beauty. They shall glorify themselves with these garments, for no other Yisraeli shall wear similar garments.
And thou shalt. The vav in milletiv (I have filled) refers to lev (hearted).

And these are the garments. Scripture first mentions the breastplate, which was worn over the ephod, which was worn over the robe. It then mentions the tunic and the girdle which went around it after the mitre was placed on Aharon’s head. This is what happened when Aharon washed and put on linen breeches. However, there was no reason to mention the breeches here nor in the description of the actual investiture of Aharon, for it is the manner of all men to wear breeches. Now Moshe put the tunic upon Aharon. He then placed the mitre upon Aharon’s head, and He placed “the plate of the holy crown” upon the mitre. Our verse, which enumerates the priestly garments, does not mention “the plate of the holy crown” because “the plate of the holy crown” was not a garment. However, our sages mentioned the holy plate among the priestly garments because most of the objects worn by the high priest were garments. Hence the sages speak of the eight garments worn by the high priest. The Urim and Tumim were not garments. Neither were the stones, nor the cards. After this Moshe encircled Aharon with the girdle. Moshe then placed the robe upon Aharon. He then placed the ephod upon the robe and put the ephod upon him, and he girded him with the skilfully woven band of the ephod and bound it unto him therewith (Vayikra 8:7). The skillfully woven band was part of the ephod. The ephod was so called because of the skillfully woven band. Moshe dressed Aharon according to the order described in our verse. Do not be bothered by the fact that Scripture later states, regarding the actual investiture of Aharon, And he set the mitre upon his head (Vayikra 8:9). Its meaning is, he had already placed the mitre with the golden plate on Aharon’s head when he dressed him in the tunic. The meaning of and clothed him with garments (Zecharyah 3:5) is similar; i.e., they had already clothed him. For Scripture previously states, So they set a fair mitre upon his head (Ibid.).
And they shall take the gold. The wise-hearted who made the priestly garments were trustworthy.

And they shall make the ephod. Scripture starts with the ephod because it was larger than the breastplate. The Torah tells us that the breastplate be not loosed from the skilfully woven band of the ephod (v. 28). There are some very difficult questions relating to the ephod and the breastplate. Moshe only made one ephod. However, Scripture states, that he came down with an ephod in his hand (Shmuel I 23:6). The latter does not refer to the ephod made by Moshe, for Scripture does not read “the ephod,” the meaning of which is, the well-known ephod, as it does when it states, “Bring hither the ephod” (Shmuel I 23:9). Furthermore, why does Scripture state, he came down, but it does not say he brought down? It thus appears that the ephod was accidentally among his possessions. Additionally, Scripture there states, fourscore persons that did wear a linen (bad) ephod (Shmuel I 22:18). Many commentaries explain this verse as meaning that the persons were fit to wear the ephod. However, they did not bother to learn the truth. A bad (linen) ephod is an ephod made from a type of flax. However, the ephod made by Moshe was not made of bad (linen). It was made of gold, blue wool, purple wool, and scarlet, with shesh (linen) intertwined with all of the aforementioned. They only inquired of the breastplate of judgment which had the Urim and Tumim upon it. Scripture similarly writes, by the judgment of the Urim before Hashem (Bamidbar 27:21). Bring hither the ephod (Shmuel I 23:9) does not present a counterargument because the breastplate was connected to it. The Urim went along with the breastplate. We similarly read, till there stood up a priest with Urim and Tumim (Nechemyah 7:65). Scripture likewise states, Thy Tumim and Thy Urim (Devarim 33:8). Now, Scripture tells us that Hashem answered David through Evyatar’s ephod. However, we also read that when Shaul went to war he inquired of the Urim (Shmuel I 28:6). These were the very Urim that were placed in the breastplate of judgment which was with the ephod and the ark. However, David inquired of Evyatar’s ephod in Tziklag. Evyatar’s ephod was thus not Moshe’s ephod. The following problem is even more difficult. It is clear that the Urim do not refer to the stones of the breastplate, as Scripture openly states, And thou shalt set in it settings of stones (v. 17). The setting of the stones was the work of a stonecutter and not the work of Moshe. Hashem then told Moshe, And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Tumim (v. 30). Scripture, in describing the making of the breastplate, tells us, And they set in it four rows of stones (Shemot 39:10). Scripture then describes the four rows of stones. Scripture tells us that Moshe placed the breastplate upon Aharon and in the breastplate he put the Urim and the Tumim (Vayikra 8:8). Now according to the plain meaning of the text the stones were not the objects that enlightened or fulfilled, because inquiries were made of the Urim and Tumim. We do not know what they were. The explanation that the names of the tribes and the patriarchs were inscribed on the breastplate is of no help, for the breastplate of judgment was so called only because of the Urim that were on it. There is an additional question: we cannot identify the Urim with the Tumim, for Scripture states, with Urim and Tumim (Nechemyah 7:65). Furthermore, the words with Urim and Tumim are in the plural. They thus consisted of many objects. Rabbi Shlomo says that the Urim and Tumim consisted of an inscription of Hashem’s explicit name. However, he would not have said this had he seen the responsa of Rabbi Hai Gaon. There is a very deep secret behind the ephod and the breastplate. I will allude only to a part of this secret. Perhaps he who knows the mind of the Most High will understand it. The following are the keys to the secret of the ephod. The two wreathen chains on the two rings [represent the head of Aries and Libra]. The band of the ephod represents the celestial equator. Hence six names were inscribed on the stone which was on the other shoulder. Now these things can only be grasped by the mind. Hence six names were inscribed on one stone in accordance with the number, names, and order of birth of the tribes of the children of Yisrael. Six names were similarly inscribed on the second stone. On the other hand, the names on the breastplate were not divided in the same manner as they are grasped by the mind. They were divided in a way that could be perceived by the eye. Scripture states, And they shall bind the breastplate by the rings thereof unto the rings of the ephod with a thread of blue (v. 28) to prevent the breastplate from moving to the side. The breastplate was folded, for the Urim and Tumim were kept there until such time as they were needed. They were then placed outside of the breastplate. Note, the stones of the ephod were like each other. They were of one color. This was not the case with the stones of the breastplate, for the sapphire stones served as a memorial, while the judgment of the children of Yisrael was upon the stones of the breastplate. The word Urim is related to the word ur (fire) in I am warm, I have seen the fire (Is. 44:16). The Tumim are so called because they are whole. The Urim were of gold and silver. This was not the case with the Tumim. The [importance of the] number [twelve] has been established by irrefutable proof from the upper and lower worlds. The intelligent will understand what I say. Now the priests had many ephodim. They all had bands. However, they lacked the breastplate and the Urim. A priest who was an expert in using the Urim and Tumim was able to respond to an inquirer because the ephod at hand resembled [the ephod made by Moshe]. However, the priest did not always get an answer. Now if I wanted to even begin to reveal this secret it would take up more space than the entire commentary which I have composed on this book. For only an individual who has studied works on geometry and the secret of the way the sky works can understand the secret of the ephod. There is no need to expand on the form of the ephod, the breastplate, and the rings.

Onyx stones. The avne shoham (onyx stones) were white. They are called burla in Aramaic and balor in Arabic. We have no way to positively identify the stones that were set in the breastplate. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon translated them as he saw fit, as he had no tradition to rely upon. We read the Gaon’s translation and noticed that he rendered sappir (sapphire) as white. However, this is not the case. Sappir is red. The fact that the first stone mentioned by the Torah was a carnelian does not refute this, for there are five visible colors: white, lightning, red, green, and black. Now since red is the middle color it comes in various shades. Saadiah Gaon renders nofekh (carbuncle) as black on the basis of and she painted (ba-pukh) her eyes (Melachim II 9:30). However, the nun in nofekh is undoubtedly a root letter, for nofekh follows the paradigm of odem (carnelian). A great Sephardic scholar said that yahalom (emerald) is a diamond. This stone has the ability to break up all other stones and to bore through bdellium. Yahalom is related to the word holem (smiteth) in smiteth the anvil (Is. 41:7). The yod of yahalom is not a root letter. It is like the yod of yitzhar (oil). Also achlamah (amethyst) is to be identified with the dream stone. This is a stone that always induces dreams in the person who wears it. One should not be surprised at this, as every stone has a specific power placed in it by nature. Thus there is a stone that attracts iron. There is likewise a stone that stops bleeding. Another stone is repelled by vinegar. There is also a stone whose pieces always form a triangle when broken.

Chains. The middle root letter has been doubled in sharsherot (chains). However, the word has the same meaning when the middle root letter is not doubled. Compare, sharshot gavlut (plaited chains) (v. 22). It is very difficult to explain the meaning of gavlut (plaited) in Hebrew. The same applies to many of the words employed by Scripture that refer to the making of the breastplate as well as to the word choshen (breastplate) itself.
And they shall bind. Ve-yirkesu is related to the word me-rukhse (from the plottings) in from the plottings of man (Tehillim 31:21). It means twisted.
And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment. Judgment refers to the laws of Hashem and his decrees concerning the future. It is these things that people inquire of the Urim and Tumim.

And thou shalt make. Rabbi Saadiah Gaon translates the word me’il (robe) by the Arabic memtar, which is a cloak-like garment except that its opening was in the midst of the robe. Our sages said that the pomegranates (v. 33) were placed all around the robe. A bell was placed between every two pomegranates. However, others say that the bells were not visible. They were placed inside the pomegranates, where they rang.

And thou shalt make a plate. The Gaon renders tzitz (plate) atzabah. It was placed on the mitre. It was not shaped like a crown, as the plate was placed only on the forehead. According to the plain meaning of the text, the migba’ot (head-tires) (Vayikra 8:13) were not shaped like the mitre (mitznefet). The head-tires are similar to the high hats which men in this and surrounding countries place upon their heads as a head covering. [37.] THE MITRE. The mitre is made from long thin material which is twisted only around the head. The turbans worn by women in these areas are somewhat similar. In Spain, Africa, Mitzrayim, Bavel, and Baghdad and in the land of the Yishmeelim, only men of respect, not the women, wear turbans on their heads. The important officials place a golden plate on the turban over the forehead. I have already noted that the ornaments in the Land of Yisrael and the customs practiced there differ from those in these areas. Rabbi Shlomo found it necessary to harmonize Scripture by explaining that three blue threads were attached to the plate. However, according to the plain meaning of the text only one blue thread was necessary to keep the plate, which was on the face of the mitre on the forehead, in place.

And thou shalt put it on a thread of blue. The meaning of al petil techelt (on a thread of blue) is, with a thread of blue, as the thread was tied to the plate on two sides. There is no doubt that the front of the mitre was placed over the forehead. It was not placed over the head. Scripture elsewhere states, And they tied unto it a thread of blue, to fasten it upon the mitre (Shemot 39:31), that is, upon the forehead. Do not be surprised that Scripture uses the term al. We find the same in the following, And they came, both men with (al) women (Shemot 35:22);And the priest shall wave them with (al) the bread of the first-fruits for a wave-offering before Hashem (Vayikra 23:20); with (al) the two lambs (Ibid.); the fat with (al) the breast (Vayikra 7:30). There are many similar instances in Scripture. Now you will never find [the mitre and the head-tires interchanging]. For the mitre was set aside only for Aharon, and the head-tires for his children. Some say that the word migba’ot (head-tires) is related to the word givot (hills) (Bereshit 49:26). The mitre surrounded and wrapped the head.
